summary: Cryptocurrency perpetual futures form a large-scale online financial market in which automated agents manage interacting asset positions under changing conditions. Policies relying solely on micro-level numerical states may overlook cross-asset relationships and become vulnerable to regime shifts, while macro-level linguistic judgments alone cannot ensure precise measurement or optimize positions under trading costs and risk constraints. Connecting market interpretation to coordinated multi-asset decisions remains challenging. We propose M3FT, a micro-macro-micro framework for multi-agent perpetual futures trading. The first micro stage constructs time-aligned numerical states from exchange and account observations through deterministic processing. The macro stage transforms these measured states into explicit market interpretations without adding external market information. Four asset-specific teams, each comprising a Market Interpreter, an Asset Communicator, and a Risk Reviewer, refine these interpretations through experience retrieval, cross-asset communication, and review of joint-position risks. The final micro stage combines encoded linguistic representations with the original numerical states to learn continuous target positions. We implement this framework with a language-conditioned multi-agent policy: asset actors use global and private numerical states together with linguistic context, while centralized critics evaluate joint actions using portfolio-wide information and shared-account rewards. Experiments on real cryptocurrency perpetual futures data, including comparisons across language models and policy-learning algorithms and component ablations, show that the best-performing M3FT configuration achieves a higher mean test return than the evaluated direct LLM, numerical RL, and rule-based baselines.
title: M3FT: Micro-Macro-Micro Reasoning for Multi-Agent Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures Trading

summary: NORMA-O (the NORMA Ontology) is an OWL 2 DL ontology for representing legal norms as machine-readable, interoperable data. It describes what a norm requires, forbids or allows, under which conditions, for whom, and on which legal source it rests. Each statement can be traced back to its legal source and to the process that produced it. NORMA-O is part of ongoing research on representing legal norms so that machines can store, query and reason over them while keeping their conditions, exceptions, addressees and legal authority. Version 1.0 introduced deontic types, constitutive rules, conditions and their outcomes, agents, actions, objects, legal sources, annotation provenance and controlled vocabularies. It was designed for norms annotated on BPMN models of regulatory processes. Version 2.0 keeps every term of 1.0 and describes the model independently of any notation or authoring method. Version 2.0 adds the means to state how norms relate to each other and to concrete cases, and to compute what applies, to whom and why: - Standard Deontic Logic grounding: action negation, facultative acts, weak permission, and deontic equivalence, contradiction and conflict between norms. - Hohfeldian legal positions: duty, claim, privilege and no-right, with holder, counterparty, correlatives and opposites. - Roles, parties and cases: legal roles, the parties that occupy them, role assignments and fact patterns. - Defeasibility: exception, conflict and temporal defeaters; lex superior, lex specialis and lex posterior; normative rank, norm strength and a prevalence graph. - Counts-as chaining: when a classification is defeated, every obligation that depends on it is withdrawn. The release also includes the derivation module NORMA-O Deriv (prefix normad, https://w3id.org/def/norma-o/deriv). It records how each derived conclusion was obtained, by which rule and under which assumptions. The release also includes a reference rule set (norma-derivation/1.0) that computes the deontic closure, the legal positions, the prevalence ordering (with cycle detection), applicability to each case and weak permissions. A Python package with the norma command checks annotations, derives conclusions and produces reports. NORMA-O reuses open Semantic Web standards and vocabularies, including OWL 2, RDF, PROV-O, ELI, FOAF and SKOS. It was developed following the LOT methodology. It originated in the NORMA project, whose semantic toolkit uses it to annotate regulations, build RDF graphs and evaluate compliance, but the ontology does not depend on that toolkit. Files: norma-ontology-v2.ttl / .rdf (ontology 2.0), norma-o-deriv.ttl / .rdf (derivation module 1.0), diagrams of both (.svg), and NORMA-O-v2.0.0.zip (a snapshot of the GitHub tag v2.0.0 with the rule set, the engine and the Python package). Documentation: https://w3id.org/def/norma-o · Source: https://github.com/sheyls/NORMA-O
title: NORMA Ontology

summary: A memory can last for decades, yet the proteins of a synapse are replaced within days. Crick (1984) proposed that the molecules that store a memory restore one another, so that the pattern survives its parts, and several molecular switches of this kind have since been modelled. Here we ask a question that does not depend on the mechanism: what is the longest time that any switch made of $N$ molecules can remember? We consider all switches in which the number of active molecules changes one molecule at a time, with an activation rate per inactive molecule between a spontaneous floor $\varepsilon$ and a catalytic ceiling $k$, and a loss rate per active molecule between the turnover rate $\mu$ and an erasure ceiling $\lambda$. (i) We prove that, for every readout threshold, both the potentiated and the unpotentiated state are retained longest, in the sense of stochastic order, by one and the same switch: a threshold rule that restores at full speed when at least $m$ molecules are active and erases at full speed otherwise. (ii) We give its mean retention times in closed form, as sums of binomial coefficients, and evaluate them in exact rational arithmetic. (iii) When the two contrasts $\kappa=k/\mu$ and $\chi=\lambda/\varepsilon$ are equal to $c$ and $\lambda=\mu$, the longest possible memory $T^*(N)$ satisfies $N^{-1}(\sqrt c/2)^N\le\mu T^*(N)\le\bigl((1+c)/\sqrt c\bigr)^N$ for even $N$; numerically, each added molecule multiplies it by about $(1+c)/(2\sqrt c)$. (iv) With molecules that last 30 hours, no switch of this class holds both states for a mean of a century with fewer than 20 molecules if $c=10$, 12 if $c=30$, 8 if $c=100$ and 4 if $c=1000$, and these numbers are attained; thirty molecules suffice as soon as $c\ge7$, while a single dimer with $c=100$ lasts 50 molecular lifetimes. (v) The retention times of the ideal switch have an increasing failure rate, so that a mean of a hundred centuries guarantees a century with probability above $0.99$, at the price of two to ten more molecules. (vi) Smooth cooperativity is far from the limit: a switch with Hill exponent 2 needs 187 molecules where the ideal one needs 12. In this class, then, a lifetime of memory requires few molecules but a sharp threshold. These are limits for one-variable switches with constant rates, not a model of a particular synapse. This record contains the preprint (PDF, PCI template), its LaTeX source, and the Python code and results file that reproduce every theorem, table and figure (code under the MIT license).
title: How can a memory last a lifetime when its molecules last only days? Exact limits for molecular switches under turnover

summary: A memory can last for decades, yet the proteins of a synapse are replaced within days. Crick (1984) proposed that the molecules that store a memory restore one another, so that the pattern survives its parts, and several molecular switches of this kind have since been modelled. Here we ask a question that does not depend on the mechanism: what is the longest time that any switch made of $N$ molecules can remember? We consider all switches in which the number of active molecules changes one molecule at a time, with an activation rate per inactive molecule between a spontaneous floor $\varepsilon$ and a catalytic ceiling $k$, and a loss rate per active molecule between the turnover rate $\mu$ and an erasure ceiling $\lambda$. (i) We prove that, for every readout threshold, both the potentiated and the unpotentiated state are retained longest, in the sense of stochastic order, by one and the same switch: a threshold rule that restores at full speed when at least $m$ molecules are active and erases at full speed otherwise. (ii) We give its mean retention times in closed form, as sums of binomial coefficients, and evaluate them in exact rational arithmetic. (iii) When the two contrasts $\kappa=k/\mu$ and $\chi=\lambda/\varepsilon$ are equal to $c$ and $\lambda=\mu$, the longest possible memory $T^*(N)$ satisfies $N^{-1}(\sqrt c/2)^N\le\mu T^*(N)\le\bigl((1+c)/\sqrt c\bigr)^N$ for even $N$; numerically, each added molecule multiplies it by about $(1+c)/(2\sqrt c)$. (iv) With molecules that last 30 hours, no switch of this class holds both states for a mean of a century with fewer than 20 molecules if $c=10$, 12 if $c=30$, 8 if $c=100$ and 4 if $c=1000$, and these numbers are attained; thirty molecules suffice as soon as $c\ge7$, while a single dimer with $c=100$ lasts 50 molecular lifetimes. (v) The retention times of the ideal switch have an increasing failure rate, so that a mean of a hundred centuries guarantees a century with probability above $0.99$, at the price of two to ten more molecules. (vi) Smooth cooperativity is far from the limit: a switch with Hill exponent 2 needs 187 molecules where the ideal one needs 12. In this class, then, a lifetime of memory requires few molecules but a sharp threshold. These are limits for one-variable switches with constant rates, not a model of a particular synapse. This record contains the preprint (PDF, PCI template), its LaTeX source, and the Python code and results file that reproduce every theorem, table and figure (code under the MIT license).

summary: Overview This dataset provides a reproducible local-earthquake tomography framework for investigating the subsurface velocity structure of the Batu Hijau–Elang porphyry Cu–Au district, Sumbawa Island, Indonesia. The archive supports a three-dimensional seismic tomography study based on local earthquake observations, simultaneous inversion of P-wave velocity (Vp) and Vp/Vs structure, resolution-constrained interpretation, and systematic sensitivity testing of inversion damping parameters. The primary objective is to document the computational reproducibility and numerical stability of the reconstructed seismic velocity anomalies while explicitly accounting for limitations in spatial resolution and geological interpretation. Earthquake Dataset and Inversion Configuration The G40 CM117 tomographic inversion uses: 600 selected earthquakes. 60 seismic stations. 11,529 seismic observations. 7,378 P-wave arrival observations. 4,151 S–P differential-time observations. A three-dimensional grid containing 25 × 14 × 12 nodes. A transverse-Mercator coordinate system with central meridian 117°E. Five inversion iterations using SIMUL2023. The reference inversion uses damping parameters of 1100 for Vp and 300 for Vp/Vs. The weighted RMS residual decreases from 0.47223 s to 0.39282 s after five iterations. Computational Reproducibility The original inversion was reproduced using a clean compilation of the archived SIMUL2023 source code and the corresponding inversion inputs. The rebuilt inversion reproduces the historical velocity model at the numerical precision stored in the output file. The only identified textual difference in the final velocity-model file is the computation timestamp. The archive preserves the source-code snapshot, inversion configuration files, model outputs, numerical logs, and provenance information required to document this result. Damping Sensitivity Experiments Four additional inversions were performed to evaluate the sensitivity of the reconstructed velocity anomalies to the damping parameters: Vp damping = 700; Vp/Vs damping = 300. Vp damping = 1600; Vp/Vs damping = 300. Vp damping = 1100; Vp/Vs damping = 200. Vp damping = 1100; Vp/Vs damping = 500. All five inversions use the same input dataset and complete five iterations. The final weighted RMS residuals range from 0.39010 s to 0.39605 s. Resolution-Constrained Evaluation Spatial sensitivity is evaluated using a frozen resolution-supported node mask derived from Vp resolution diagnostics. The evaluation includes: 145 STRICT nodes within the 0–40 km evaluation domain. 113 STRICT nodes within the 5–30 km depth interval. For the 113-node subset, spatial correlations between the reference and alternative models range from: 0.989 to 0.998 for Vp anomalies. 0.985 to 0.996 for Vp/Vs anomalies. Median absolute anomaly differences range from: 0.147 to 0.425 percentage points for Vp. 0.114 to 0.338 percentage points for Vp/Vs. Anomaly-sign agreement is evaluated only at nodes where the absolute reference anomaly is at least 0.1%. All 16 combinations of spatial domain, damping configuration, and velocity parameter passed an independent numerator-and-denominator verification against the node-level CSV data. Archive Contents The reproducibility package includes: SIMUL2023 source-code snapshot and compilation information. Historical reference inversion inputs and velocity-model output. Five inversion configurations and their numerical outputs. Frozen starting velocity model. Geographic node coordinates and resolution-mask information. Machine-readable damping sensitivity tables. Node-level Vp and Vp/Vs anomaly comparisons. Three-dimensional model and resolution-related outputs. Discrete-node visualizations of Vp and Vp/Vs anomalies. Supplementary methodological documentation. SHA256 provenance and integrity manifests. Data Integrity The Zenodo release package contains 73 files, including its integrity manifest. All 72 files cove

summary: Abstract This manuscript presents the Residual-Load Rebound Amplification Framework (RLR-AF), a proposed domain-general framework for analyzing conditions under which temporary relief from a problem may be followed by a recurrence that exceeds a comparable reference level. The framework is organized around a central distinction between observable problem attenuation and sufficient modification of the condition that generates or maintains the problem. It proposes that when an intervention reduces the observable output without adequately resolving the relevant generative condition, residual problem-related states may persist. If the intervention or subsequent systemic changes also modify the conditions governing future responses, the residual state may be expressed more strongly when the relevant constraint, control process, or suppressive influence no longer operates in the same way. The framework does not assume that residual load necessarily produces amplification. Amplified recurrence is a conditional outcome requiring an effective pathway that increases the subsequent expression of the residual state and a net effect that exceeds the system's relevant restorative or control processes. The manuscript introduces the Residual-State Conditional Amplification Principle (RSCAP), the expanded Residual-Load-Compensation-Rebound Mechanism (RLCR+), and the primary case of Emotional-Distress Suppression and Amplified Rebound (EDS-AR). It develops a domain-neutral state-space architecture, operational definitions, conditional propositions, a causal-comparison strategy, candidate amplification pathways, cross-domain mapping rules, counterexamples, and an empirical validation roadmap. The framework is a proposed theoretical contribution rather than an established universal law. Its conceptual coherence, mathematical consistency, causal mechanisms, empirical validity, and applicability to domains beyond its primary case must be evaluated separately. Keywords: Residual load; rebound amplification; temporary relief; systemic reconfiguration; causal inference; state-space modeling; control theory; cognitive science; feedback systems; domain-general theoretical framework.

summary: Abstract The Generalized Evidence-to-System Projection Theory (GESPT) is proposed as an integrative framework for analyzing the relationship between available evidence and claims about a broader target system. Its central concern is the distinction between the accuracy of a description within an observed or otherwise documented reference set and the validity of extending that description to a larger, partially unknown, or temporally extended system. The framework is motivated by a criminal-case observation: records of detected offenders may support accurate descriptions of detected cases, while the same records alone may be insufficient to establish that every offender will eventually be detected. The absence of comparable records for undetected cases does not prove that those cases have any particular outcome. It establishes a limitation on what can be inferred from the available evidence without additional assumptions or information. The proposed framework distinguishes reference-set accuracy, target-system validity, evidence availability, selection, measurement, transformation, inference, projection, labeling, decision-making, and feedback. Its central Evidence-Boundary Non-Entailment Principle (EBNP) states that truth within a reference set does not, by itself, logically entail universal truth within a broader target set. The Reference-Accurate, Target-Underdetermined Mechanism (RATUM) describes the coexistence of an accurate analysis of available data and unresolved uncertainty about the broader system. A formal model is provided using reference and target sets, selection probabilities, estimands, projection gaps, and identifiability conditions. Several propositions follow under explicitly stated assumptions. Applications to statistics, causal inference, systems theory, information processing, cybernetics, network analysis, criminology, sociology, and machine learning are discussed as conditional extensions rather than presumed universal results. The document is a proposed theoretical synthesis, not an already validated universal law. Its originality, empirical performance, and domain-specific scope require systematic comparison with established methods and independent testing. Keywords evidence boundaries; reference sets; target systems; non-entailment; selection; underdetermination; generalization; projection; missing data; feedback; criminal detection

summary: Reference-Relative Functional Coordination-Misalignment Theory (RRF-CMT) is proposed as an analytical framework for examining cases in which two or more interacting systems can act consistently with their own locally observed goals, commitments, functional states, and constraints, while their combined activity fails because the conditions required for coordination do not adequately align. Its primary illustrative case is a reciprocal availability-window inversion: one system attempts or desires interaction when another system is unavailable, and the pattern subsequently reverses. Each system may possess a locally coherent explanation for its conduct even though the joint interaction repeatedly fails. The framework separates four analytical levels: local functional states, medium-specific compatibility, reference-relative observation and interpretation, and system-level outcomes. Temporal overlap is treated as a specific and measurable coordination condition rather than as the universal mechanism. Other applications may involve communication channels, information-processing states, event ordering, resource capacity, spatial access, protocol compatibility, or authority constraints. The manuscript defines the proposed constructs, primary case, formal notation, conditional axioms, state-compatibility model, network generalization, outcome taxonomy, propositions, falsifiable hypotheses, boundary cases, alternative explanations, measurement strategy, and empirical research roadmap. It provides a worked numerical illustration solely to demonstrate the mathematical definitions. The example is not empirical evidence. The proposed contribution is an integrated analytical architecture that combines reference-relative local interpretation, reciprocal availability-window inversion, medium-specific coordination compatibility, and a distinction between local feasibility and global coordination. The framework is positioned in relation to existing coordination theory, time geography, and distributed-event ordering rather than as a replacement for these traditions. Its originality, explanatory advantage, and empirical generality remain to be established. Keywords: coordination misalignment; functional states; availability windows; local rationality; reference-relative observation; systemic coordination failure; temporal coordination; asynchronous interaction; network dependencies; compatibility relations.

summary: This record provides synthetic benchmark data, original numerical outcomes, integrity manifests, independent data-analysis scripts, and publication summary tables for partition-aware min–max mobile data collection routing in heterogeneous wireless sensor networks with a common physical depot. The scientific dataset comprises five experimental cohorts: Main R3: 1,920 matched scenarios, 5,760 B1/B2/B4 method outcomes, and 120 independent topology blocks. Sampling sensitivity: 96 cases. Connectivity sensitivity: 72 cases. Finite exact reference: 160 small-instance discrete q4 cases. External V3 comparison: 48 cases, 672 method-round observations, and 24 independent paired topology blocks. Two independent, analysis-only Python scripts are provided in a separate archive. They verify the scientific dataset's SHA-256 integrity and reproduce all six R3 publication CSV tables byte-for-byte, all 372 V3 numerical analysis fields, and eight data-driven manuscript figures (five R3 and three V3). Reproducibility scope: The original routing, optimization, and experiment-generation implementations are not distributed. The provided scripts reproduce recorded numerical analyses and plots, not the original solver executions. The V3 comparison is exploratory and does not use equal computational budgets. Exact-reference conclusions apply to the finite sampled discrete problem, not continuous global optimality. These experiments use synthetic geometric wireless sensor network configurations. They do not constitute measured radio-packet performance, hardware energy consumption, or calibrated mission completion times. Statistical interpretation respects the 120 independent R3 topology blocks and 24 paired V3 blocks. Licensing: Original scientific data, numerical reference results, and author-generated data documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The two standalone data-verification and statistical-analysis Python programs are licensed under MIT. The private core research code, original Julia HGA, and Concorde software are excluded. The deposited README, data dictionary, file-level licence scope documents, and SHA-256 manifest provide further information about the data structure, attribution, and reproducibility. This dataset accompanies the manuscript Partition-Aware Min–Max Mobile Data Collection in Heterogeneous Wireless Sensor Networks: Region Sampling and Continuous Refinement. Funding support was provided through the TÜBİTAK 2219 International Postdoctoral Research Fellowship Program for Turkish Citizens (application no. 1059B192200615).

summary: Abstract The Medium-Independent Reference-Conditioned Systemic Projection Theory (MIR- CSPT) proposes a general framework for examining how an observer or detection system constructs a representation of a larger target system from an accessible subset of its properties, events, states, or evidence. Its central concern is not restricted to first impressions, human cognition, data collection, or any particular observation medium. Instead, the theory focuses on the relationship between an observed partial field, the evidence derived from that field, the scope of the resulting inference, and the adequacy of the resulting systemic representation. The proposed mechanism distinguishes target-system definition, reference-conditioned accessibility, partial-field capture, evidence formation, interpretation, scope transfer, systemic projection, identity attribution, projection-benchmark comparison, and corrective reprojection. Two primary cases illustrate the framework: War-Snapshot Civilizational Identity Projection (WSCIP) and Salient-Instance-to-Group Projection (SIGP). Although the cases involve different targets and scales of generalization, both examine whether evidence concerning a limited aspect of a system is used to support a broader systemic claim than the evidence warrants. The blueprint specifies a fourteen-layer architecture, operational terminology, mathemati- cal variables, candidate discrepancy measures, a provisional projection-risk index, outcome classifications, testable hypotheses, falsifiability conditions, and an empirical research roadmap. Medium independence is treated as a structural design objective whose empirical implications require testing, not as an established universal law. The theory remains a proposed re- search framework pending formal specification of domain-specific measurements, independent validation benchmarks, replication, and comparative testing against alternative explanations. Keywords: systemic projection; partial-field observation; reference frame; scope transfer; identity attribution; representation; medium independence; projection discrepancy; validation.

summary: Let M²ⁿ, n ≥ 2, be a closed connected Riemannian manifold all of whose geodesics are closed, and suppose that H²(M; ℚ) ≠ 0. Such a manifold has the homotopy type of ℂℙⁿ. We prove Berger’s conjecture for this class when 2 ≤ n ≤ 8: all unit-speed geodesics have the same least period. For every n ≥ 2, the same conclusion holds if each nontrivial stabilizer of the geodesic circle action has prime-power order. More precisely, suppose that n ≥ 3 and the prime periods are unequal. Then some time map of the geodesic flow has a proper connected fixed component F on which the generic stabilizer order is divisible by two distinct odd primes. The inverse image of F in an auxiliary circle bundle over the unit tangent bundle has total rational Betti number at least eight. The proof combines index iteration with loop reversal in twisted equivariant cohomology and the fixed sets of a lift of the geodesic flow whose least period is twice that of the original flow. First published 9 November 2026. Version 2, revised 10 November 2026 (46 pages).
title: Prime periods of geodesics on Besse manifolds of complex projective type

summary: This paper argues that Stephen Kellert’s well-known claim in In the Wake of Chaos (1993)—that chaotic systems require impossible accuracy for useful prediction—applies only to one kind of task. Kellert focuses on predicting the precise value of a variable within a stated tolerance at a future time. Sensitive dependence on initial conditions, measured by a positive Lyapunov exponent, forces the required initial accuracy to grow exponentially, rendering many such point-value tasks impossible for any finite observer. The paper contends that a second, equally common task falls outside this impossibility: predicting whether the system will remain confined within a specified region over a given interval. This distinction is framed through the ideas of thin and thick chaos introduced in the author’s earlier work. Thin chaos involves local instability that never carries the system across the functional boundaries that matter for its purpose; thick chaos does. The thinness ratio quantifies this by comparing the typical displacement produced by chaotic motion with the displacement that would count as failure. Four elementary results establish the claim. The first constructs an example in which the Lyapunov exponent can be fixed while the confinement outcome is varied at will, showing the two questions are logically independent. The second shows that the thinness ratio is controlled by Kellert’s own measure of predictive hopelessness scaled by the ratio of the system’s accessible span to the failure threshold; Kellert’s criterion is recovered exactly when the failure scale is half that span. The third supplies a distribution-free upper bound on the probability that the system has left the safe region by the end of the interval, proves the bound cannot be improved without further assumptions, and extends it to the entire interval when successive displacements behave like a martingale. The fourth replaces the root-mean-square displacement with a quantile of the running maximum, making the ratio equal to one precisely when confinement holds at a stated confidence level. The results are limited to logical relations and inequalities. They do not establish that any particular physical system remains confined; every confinement claim remains conditional on the adequacy of the model that supplies the confining geometry. A positive Lyapunov exponent alone therefore settles neither risk nor safety. Practical reporting of chaos should state the relevant variable, failure scale, horizon, and confidence level, and reliability claims based on the root-mean-square form of the ratio are correspondingly weak unless stronger distributional assumptions are justified. The paper’s contribution is to separate the prediction of location from the prediction of continued confinement and to supply a measure for the latter.
title: Unpredictable but Confined: Thin Chaos and the Scope of Kellert's Impossibility Argument

summary: Repeats the cross-protocol transfer test with the affect coupling switched off, and adds seed and split-rule checks. This release repeats every stage at lambda = 0, so that calibration, fitting and simulation use one model. P17 experiments/p17_seed_sensitivity.py repeats the behavioural check over 200 random seeds at lambda = 0.49. summary: CodeSampleAtlas is a research dataset collected from four GitHub code-sample ecosystems: Spring Guides, Google Samples, Azure Samples, and AWS Samples . It provides data on repository activity, GitHub Issues and pull requests, candidate relationships, curation results, and implementation evidence for empirical software engineering research. The dataset covers 12,856 repository catalog memberships , 42,346 acquired issues , and 17,791 expanded candidate relationships . It also includes 13,960 filtered candidates , 11,198 strict candidates , 6,179 audit candidates , and 10,473 pull-request implementation bindings . These analytical populations may overlap. Dataset contents The six downloadable archives provide: JSON/JSONL records organized by ecosystem and evidence type. 14 analytical CSV files , containing 532,671 data rows across the four ecosystems. A SQLite database with 54 tables and 21 analytical views . The data can be explored using SQL, Python, or other analysis tools without running the mining software. Privacy and limitations This release is a privacy-minimized derivative of the original scientific dataset. Selected personal attributes, developer-authored text, and potentially sensitive information have been removed or transformed while retaining documented identifiers, measurements, and relationships. Analyses that depend on omitted text or personal attributes cannot be fully reproduced from these files. Acquisition coverage and relationship-verification outcomes are documented in the Dataset User Guide, including cases where the available evidence was partial or could not be confirmed. The mining software and the complete Git histories of the acquired repositories are separate research artifacts and are not included in this deposit. Documentation The README and Dataset User Guide describe the file formats, database schema, provenance, privacy transformations, known limitations, and examples of data access and analysis.
title: CodeSampleAtlas: A Multi-Ecosystem Dataset of Code-Sample Repositories and Development Activity

summary: This record contains the code and results for the paper “Cross-Layer Physics-Consistency Detection and Localization of Cyberattacks on Grid-Connected PV and Battery Inverters Using Real-Hardware and Simulation Datasets,” submitted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC 2027). The toolkit implements a cross-layer physics-consistency detector (PCD-X) for cyberattacks on grid-connected photovoltaic (PV) and battery energy storage system (BESS) inverters. It checks explicit invariants that a truthful system must satisfy: power identities inside the inverter and inside an independent meter agreement between the two instruments plausibility of setpoint commands the invariants of a read-only Modbus polling session Every invariant is calibrated by one quantile rule on attack-free data only, so no attack labels and no trained model are required. An alarm-gated baseline prevents attacks from poisoning the cross-instrument reference. The firing pattern attributes each alarm to the inverter, the meter, or the network. Contents: code/audit_pcapng.py : a pure-Python (no tshark) reimplementation of the GSBP-CP packet audit, which reproduces the published clean data split exactly. code/pcd.py : the detector, the one-class baselines (Isolation Forest, LOF, one-class SVM, PCA-SPE), the matched-operating-point comparison, the ablations, and the metrics. code/figs.py : regenerates the paper figures from the results files. results/ : all numbers reported in the paper ( results.json ) and the time-series excerpts used for the figures. Key results at a matched 0.1% training false-alarm rate: GSBP-CP (real 5 kW PV inverter with an independent meter): 99.3% of attack records detected across eight attack families. This is the highest coverage of eight detectors, with 97.9% detection of ARP spoofing in 12.5 s. Alarms are attributed to the correct layer in 100% (inverter-side), 96.9% (meter-side), and at least 99.0% (network) of cases. BESS-Set (40 kW BESS simulation): 89.8% pooled detection at a 0.68% pre-attack false-alarm rate, all eight attack types detected at 83% or more, and ROC-AUC 0.972 (baselines at most 0.709). The datasets are not redistributed here. Download them from their sources: GSBP-CP (Aiddi et al., 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.23198408 BESS-Set (Gaggero et al., 2024), doi:10.21227/13qz-e261 Instructions to reproduce are in README.md. This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER), under Award Number DE-CR0000038.
title: Cross-Layer Physics-Consistency Detection and Localization of Cyberattacks on Grid-Connected PV and Battery Inverters Using Real-Hardware and Simulation Datasets

summary: LLM-based agents can reason, use tools and collaborate. However, coordinating increasingly complex agentic applications becomes difficult to understand, monitor and improve. Decisions distributed across prompts, tool calls and application logic make workflows implicit. We introduce **Recursive Capability Composition**, enabling agents to execute business processes and expose them as reusable Agentic Tools. This paper presents a BPMN-based approach to Agentic Workflows, combining explicit orchestration with autonomous reasoning. SemTalk BPMN models are transformed into executable workflows using a LangGraph/Pregel runtime. Agentic Tasks introduce LLM reasoning at selected activities, while conventional BPMN controls process flows, deterministic decisions, system interactions and human approvals. Agentic Participants provide reusable interfaces for agent behavior or other executable processes. BPMN orchestration makes multi-agent systems more understandable and manageable. Explicit process models provide developers and operators with a shared view of workflow structures and execution progress, facilitating debugging, monitoring and optimization. Enterprise agents also need organization-specific context. Process Models and Knowledge Graphs describe activities, participants, information objects, decisions and relationships between processes. They provide structured knowledge of how an organization operates, supporting informed agent decisions and actions. Our contributions are threefold: 1. **Model-Driven Execution:** Transforming BPMN models into executable Agentic Workflows. 2. **Recursive Capability Composition:** Exposing agents and executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents. 3. **Enterprise Context:** Using Process Models and Ontologies to provide organization-specific knowledge for agent reasoning.
title: From Process Models to Composable Agentic Workflows: Combining BPMN, Agents and Enterprise Knowledge

summary: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.
title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics

summary: Multi-agent systems increasingly operate in dynamic environments and execute complex tasks that require coordination, posing significant computational challenges. Counting tasks, which require a minimum number of agents to satisfy a given condition, arise naturally in such systems. Examples include surveillance tasks, where at least m drones must continuously monitor a critical area, and emergency-response tasks, where at least m robots must converge to an incident location. The identities of the agents assigned to these tasks may change dynamically depending on their states, input bounds, and individual objectives. In this work, we propose a control barrier function (CBF)-based framework for enforcing counting invariance and counting convergence tasks, without explicitly assigning agents or enumerating all possible subteams. We develop a recursion-based method for constructing differentiable CBFs for counting tasks. The resulting CBF constraints are incorporated into quadratic programs, enabling online controller synthesis. Numerical experiments demonstrate scalability to large multi-agent systems, while a multi-drone emergency-response case study illustrates the satisfaction of counting tasks.
title: Control Barrier Functions for Counting Tasks in Multi-Agent Systems

Counting tasks, which require a minimum number of agents to satisfy a given condition, arise naturally in such systems. Examples include surveillance tasks, where at least m drones must continuously monitor a critical area, and emergency-response tasks, where at least m robots must converge to an incident location. The identities of the agents assigned to these tasks may change dynamically depending on their states, input bounds, and individual objectives. In this work, we propose a control barrier function (CBF)-based framework for enforcing counting invariance and counting convergence tasks, without explicitly assigning agents or enumerating all possible subteams. We develop a recursion-based method for constructing differentiable CBFs for counting tasks. The resulting CBF constraints are incorporated into quadratic programs, enabling online controller synthesis. Numerical experiments demonstrate scalability to large multi-agent systems, while a multi-drone emergency-response case study illustrates the satisfaction of counting tasks.
title: Control Barrier Functions for Counting Tasks in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Electronic design automation (EDA) workflows remain highly fragmented, requiring engineers to coordinate heterogeneous representations, specialised software tools, and iterative verification across multiple design stages. Although large language models have brought more general reasoning and code-generation capabilities to EDA, many existing approaches remain focused on isolated tasks and struggle to plan, verify, and repair designs autonomously within executable engineering environments. Here we introduce ChipOmni, a knowledge-enhanced, context-evolving AI agent framework for EDA. ChipOmni integrates multimodal understanding, dynamic planning, multi-agent collaboration, and verification-driven tool interaction into a unified autonomous system. By continually incorporating feedback from external engineering tools, the framework maintains an evolving task context, integrates domain knowledge, and iteratively refines intermediate designs. Across benchmarks for analog circuit, RTL, testbench, and formal-assertion generation, ChipOmni improves multiple task-specific measures over the evaluated baselines and solves all 30 AnalogCoder-Pro tasks. In a long-horizon case study, ChipOmni advances a natural-language RISC-V specification through three design levels to a micro-SoC GDSII layout that passes physical sign-off, without human intervention after initialization. Together, these results show that ChipOmni can coordinate verification-driven design across heterogeneous tasks and sustain long-horizon engineering workflows, advancing a shift from fragmented, tool-centred processes towards agent-centred, closed-loop systems.
title: ChipOmni: A General-Purpose AI Agent for Electronic Design Automation

summary: Issue reports that describe Intrinsic Bugs, Extrinsic Bugs, and Not a Bug cases often use similar language, but they might point to different causes and require different maintenance actions. This makes three-way issue classification difficult for Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when prompt-based refinements begin to plateau. We study whether domain-informed analysis of LLM outputs can improve classification beyond prompt modification alone. Using 428 manually labeled issue reports, we evaluate six LLMs across 18 prompt configurations and analyze 7,704 model-generated rationales to identify recurring failure patterns in how models justify predictions, use evidence, and handle conflicting information. We translate these findings into a multi-stage pipeline that separates bug validity from bug origin. The pipeline improves macro F1 and Extrinsic Bug recall for five of the six models. The strongest pipeline configuration reaches 0.827 accuracy and 0.757 Extrinsic Bug recall, improving over the best-accuracy prompt-only baseline by +1.2 and +7.5 pp, respectively. The decomposition further reveals that bug origin classification is more reliable than validity, indicating that the bug-validity decision accounts for most of the remaining error. These results show that expert failure analysis can support more reliable LLM-based software engineering classifiers.
title: An Empirical Study on Improving LLM-Based Issue Classification through Domain-Informed Analysis

summary: Enterprise agents must determine whether ordinary requests are permitted by organizational records and policies while continuing legitimate work. We introduce DEPUTYBENCH, an executable benchmark with 79 base items, 375 instances, paired permission contexts, and graded evidence requirements. Across 12 models, revised audits give 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. A controlled study of 28 derived tasks and six models tests authorization-fact flips, evidence masking, and irrelevant rewrites. Outcomes track backend permissions, yet restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence than explicit non-permission: 10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks, a 6.8-percentage-point difference (95% interval: 1.9-13.0; secondary analysis). A post-hoc analysis locates 61 of 100 masked-condition executions in four privacy tasks requiring complete cumulative counts or person-specific consent. The difference persists when the most error-prone model or the largest contributing task is excluded, but is much smaller outside those four tasks. Thus high safety with available evidence does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified. Mean paired success is equivalent within a prespecified five-point margin under irrelevant rewrites, while strong-model safety remains near ceiling. Scorer validation improves from 178 to 266 correctly scored cases out of 284 held-out counterexamples. Two security experts manually verified task ground truth over a two-week period; stage labels remain LLM-generated. The concentration analysis describes task structure and audited outcomes, not an identified internal mechanism.
title: DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents

summary: Feedback controllers for flows are expensive to design, since each candidate must be evaluated with a high-fidelity solver. Differentiable surrogates reduce that cost, but they also introduce a failure mode that prediction error cannot detect. Policy optimization uses the derivative of the objective with respect to the action, which we call the action gradient and which can be computed either through the surrogate or through the high-fidelity solver. Optimization through the surrogate uses only its action gradient, and a surrogate can follow the flow trajectory closely while misestimating this derivative. The surrogate action gradient is compared against a central finite-difference estimate from the high-fidelity solver on held-out states, under acceptance criteria fixed before the comparison, and we call that comparison an audit. A low-dimensional feedback law is then fitted to the surrogate action gradient when the surrogate passes the audit, and to the solver estimate when it does not. This law initializes a neural policy, and a quadratic penalty holds the policy near it during optimization. The proposed approach is validated on four test cases. The resulting controllers outperform or match a model-free baseline, while using 3 to 156 times fewer high-fidelity solver interactions across the four test cases. One surrogate predicts the objective at correlation 0.9996 but its action gradient at only 0.459, so prediction accuracy does not identify a usable surrogate. Another surrogate, whose action gradient agrees with the solver estimate at correlation 0.996, makes the objective 0.52% worse when the policy is optimized through it without the anchor penalty, so an accurate gradient alone does not provide a working controller. Finally, a surrogate that passes the audit at one fixed action fails it around the actions the deployed controller applies, so a pass is local.
title: Audited Gradients, Anchored Policies: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Flow Control

summary: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.
title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product

summary: Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.
title: TIB: Sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck for Multimodal Attribution beyond Alignment Assumption

summary: DIO/ODI MCP is a public, stateless, read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a versioned snapshot of the DIO/ODI Reference Model and selected derived application mappings for Agentic Entity Resolution (Agentic ER). It is designed to let an MCP client retrieve canonical concepts, reconstruction-failure diagnostics, mutation-specific guardrail profiles, evidence-promotion and commit-boundary contracts, and Policy-as-Code integration requirements. The primary integration use case is an Agentic ER application requesting a bounded diagnostic profile for an action class and mutation type, then using the returned illustrative mappings as inputs to its own domain policy and local Supervisor. The Worker does not inspect application state or execute authorization decisions. The service bundles 40 canonical concepts, the four-domain/eight-mode Reconstruction Failure taxonomy, bounded Agentic ER mapping extracts, evidence-promotion and commit-boundary contracts, and a Policy-as-Code mapping. It exposes ten tools, seven read-only resources, and one integration-planning prompt over Streamable HTTP. The deployed service runs as a Cloudflare Worker and is stateless. The implementation is deliberately limited to a read-only Phase 1 MCP service. It is not an MVDIO Supervisor or authorization service: it does not read application graphs or evidence stores, derive a production mutation hypothesis, execute admission/claim/graph-constraint checks, issue authorization tokens, authorize Phase 1 or Phase 2, commit or revert writes, or control the full hypothesis-conditioned evidence loop. Returned constraint bindings are illustrative and are not universal domain policies. The bundled Reference Model archive is v0.9.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24085589), with Reference Vocabulary v0.2.2, Agentic ER mapping v0.3.1, and a separately identified live Semantic Change Feed snapshot. The archived Reference Model and the live feed are distinct versioned states. Licensing is intentionally split: the software implementation in this repository is MIT-licensed; reproduced or adapted DIO/ODI reference content and mapping data are licensed CC BY 4.0 and attributed in data/ATTRIBUTION.md. Third-party dependencies retain their own licenses. The MIT metadata license applies to the software record and does not relicense embedded CC BY 4.0 material.
title: DIO/ODI MCP: A Read-only Model Context Protocol Server for the DIO/ODI Reference Model and Agentic Entity Resolution Guardrail Mappings

Prologue | The First Needle Does Not Predetermine the Answer A needle can begin an inquiry without dictating its ending. The scientific questions considered in these five flagships concern a magnetic marker, a biochemical concentration, a direction in a simulated signaling network, a multiscale relaxation time and an interaction contrast. None is equivalent to clinical tissue regeneration. The original thousand-page ambition becomes worthwhile only insofar as it leaves multiple, separately falsifiable routes for a later laboratory. That is why the numerical analysis takes failure, source identity and independent reference truth as first-class objects rather than editorial footnotes. For these nonclinical designs, no patient is stimulated, no organ is repaired, and no cytokine is actually assayed. The underlying simulation code contains toy distributions chosen to expose vulnerabilities, not estimates drawn from tissue. A favorable outcome is a statement about a program and its generator. This difference between the virtual and the biological world is the essential discipline of a regenerative research archive. Part I | The Eastern Heritage as a Source of Better Questions 01. summary: Soft constraints price departures from selected operating preferences while preserving immutable physical limits. We describe a reproducible convex quadratic optimization system that makes the original objective, physical units, method compatibility and numerical evidence inspectable. Seven implemented paths cover explicit slack lifting, published generalized projection, side-specific DAQP weights, a fixed FlexQP reconstruction, ElastiQP, a side-specific interval proximal update and a directional disjoint group-peak update. Eighteen versioned contracts connect synthetic input generation, native execution, independent original-space evaluation, local request/result exchange and verified static presentation. Fifteen authored or source-faithful model cases exercise scalar semantics, mixed hard/soft policy, sparse structure, predictive control and building energy. A separate registered computation contains 456 seeded instances, retaining 11592 accepted and 7560 incompatible measured observations across 600 timing cells with recorded counts, medians and interquartile ranges. Its 168-pair held-out median relative cold end-to-end reduction is 0.499839%, with a 95% seed-cluster interval from -3.291967% to 3.944835%. A second computation retains all 210 grouped repeated-forecast inputs and 7770 raw observations. Its complete 144-member held-out primary score is -212.449875%, with interval limits -225.336618% and -192.873759%, including 9 failed pairs. Neither registered ten-percent improvement criterion is established. Equivalent formulations, physical covariance, objective/dual checks and retained failure states distinguish mathematical agreement from elapsed-time advantage. The system supports transparent research and development; the synthetic evidence does not establish operational safety, measured field benefit or algorithmic priority. Editable LaTeX sources and code: CAOS_SoftQP . Native engine: CAOS_SoftQP_Engine . Complete grouped evidence: dataset .
title: Seven Methods for Soft-Constraint Quadratic Programming: Contracts and Two Negative Timing Studies

summary: Original-row proximal updates can represent selected soft interval penalties without adding explicit departure variables to a quadratic program's principal system. We derive a side-specific separable linear-quadratic update and a directional disjoint group-peak update in a fixed positive diagonal metric. The grouped construction follows a box-residual identity under coordinate contractions and reduces its proximal operation to a weighted scalar threshold. Exact lifting, directional row splitting and compact epigraphs already express the same objectives; no expressibility or algorithmic-priority claim is made. We evaluate the two implementations in separate registered synthetic studies. The first contains 456 instances and 168 held-out accepted pairs: median relative cold end-to-end reduction 0.499839%, with 95% seed-cluster limits -3.291967% and 3.944835%. The second contains 210 repeated-forecast instances, with a 144-member held-out primary score of -212.449875%, limits -225.336618% and -192.873759%, and 9 retained failed pairs. Neither predicted ten-percent timing improvement is established. Original-space objective, hard-row and dual checks distinguish mathematical equivalence from computational cost. Matched formulation, conditioning and workspace comparisons quantify descriptive contrasts without asserting an unperformed causal ablation. summary: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems

summary: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.
title: Evaluating Compositional Generalization in Transformers: The Role of Composition Equivalence and Module Coverage

summary: Inference after adaptive selection must account for selection bias. One approach is to condition on the selected event, but for complex selection procedures, the resulting conditional distribution can be analytically intractable and require sampling-based methods. Rejection sampling provides a natural baseline: it repeatedly draws from a proposal and retains only samples that reproduce the observed selection. This can be prohibitively expensive when the selection event is rare. We address this computational bottleneck with a pseudo-marginal Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that samples from the selective distribution. Using a weak Poincaré inequality, we analyze its computational efficiency relative to rejection sampling and identify when it can offer substantial gains. In the classical file-drawer problem, we derive precise computational costs for both methods, illustrating exponential improvement as the selection event becomes increasingly rare. In numerical experiments involving complex selection procedures without tractable conditional distributions, the pseudo-marginal sampler is often hundreds of times more efficient than rejection sampling, while the resulting tests achieve nominal selective Type I error.
title: Pseudo-marginal Sampling for Selective Inference

summary: Event cameras record asynchronous changes in brightness. To use a general visual model as a recording trigger, a system must represent these measurements in a form the model can interpret. We compare direct grayscale accumulation, two temporal encodings, and two intensity reconstructors on paired real event data. On 192 windows from four held-out DSEC recordings, thresholds calibrated only on development data yielded 40 of 52 person detections and 12 of 140 background positives with E2VID. The strongest direct temporal encoding at an admissible fixed cutoff yielded 14 detections and seven background positives. A retrospective comparison at a common 10% background-positive cap yielded 40 detections for E2VID and at most 19 for any direct encoding. FireNet+ had lower preparation cost and produced 21 detections with zero observed background positives at its frozen cutoff. On the same 192 windows, Qwen3-VL-4B yielded 33/52, 2/140 with E2VID and 9/52, 9/140 with the highest-recall direct rendering, the three-bin image (person detections, background positives). A 96-second exploratory replay illustrates the sensitivity of episode capture and recording starts to cutoff selection. The experiments identify a detection benefit from reconstruction under controlled input history and distinguish it from the cost and false starts of continuous triggering.
title: When Reconstruction Helps Event-Camera Person Triggers

summary: This article addresses the preemptive flexible job shop scheduling problem with makespan minimization (FJm | pmtn | C_max). We propose an exact constraint programming approach that completely avoids representing the processing fragments of an operation. Operations are placed in flexible time windows, where Horn's workload condition guarantees feasible preemptive scheduling, and Jackson's preemptive earliest-deadline-first rule reconstructs exact processing segments post-optimization in O(n log n) time per machine. To manage undecided machine assignments, we extend the PreemptiveNoOverlap global constraint to optional intervals within IBM ILOG CP Optimizer, performing overload checking and preemptive edge-finding in O(n log n) time while eliminating infeasible machine alternatives. The CP model is warm-started using a multi-round MILP assignment relaxation with Carlier's head-tail bounds and a window-based greedy heuristic. Extensive computational experiments on 276 pFJSSP benchmark instances and 78 pJSSP instances demonstrate that the proposed method significantly advances the state of the art. Within a 600~s time limit, it improves the upper bounds of the previously published logic-based Benders decomposition by 3.6% on average, increases the number of proven optimal pFJSSP instances from 102 to 180, and closes 74 instances for the first time (including the entire Barnes family). On the pJSSP under identical hardware conditions, it proves 67 of 78 instances optimal (compared to 51 by the baseline solver Mistral) and closes 9 of the 11 long-standing open problems.
title: Fragment-Free Constraint Programming for the Preemptive Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem

summary: Industrial sensor measurements often form ordered functional profiles in which persistent operating-regime changes may be confined to short within-cycle regions. Fixed projections can dilute such changes, whereas data-adaptive representation learning complicates reliable statistical testing. This paper proposes adaptive functional change-point detection (AdaFCP) for retrospective detection of a single functional mean change. A compact window and neural basis learn a change-sensitive functional projection by matching the CUSUM path of projected scores to single-change templates. Standardized peak-CUSUM scanning then provides the detection statistic and transition estimate, while the fitted weights identify the contributing within-cycle region. Theoretical analysis characterizes the population path-matching signal and derives an optimal-direction signal-to-noise benchmark. Full-pipeline permutation calibration accounts for adaptive representation learning and restart selection, providing finite-sample false-positive control under exchangeability. A decision-preserving early-stopping variant, AdaFCP-ES, further reduces calibration effort without altering the fixed-budget test decision. Simulations demonstrate advantages over several fixed representations for localized oscillatory changes, while strong analytic and multiscale controls remain competitive. Applications to injection-molding pressure profiles and a nuisance-matched hydraulic benchmark illustrate transition localization and interpretable within-cycle diagnostics, while highlighting the need for dependence-aware calibration in naturally ordered industrial data.
title: AdaFCP: Local Neural Functional Representations for Industrial Change Detection

summary: The negatively charged boron vacancy ($V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the $Δm_s=2$ manifold in a $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.
title: Double-quantum enhanced coherent control and magnetic sensing of spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride

summary: Design-stage disassemblability assessment requires knowledge of product structure and the operations available in each assembly state, but CAD assemblies do not directly specify state-dependent disassembly operations. This paper proposes a fastener-centric virtual-disassembly framework that acquires such knowledge from CAD-derived virtual assemblies. Fasteners jointly releasing the same constraint are grouped into operation-level sets, avoiding enumeration of arbitrary individual-fastener orders. Their removability is evaluated through state-dependent visibility and tool-access checks and torque-driven virtual-removal trials. After fastener removal, graph-based reasoning identifies candidate moving units, whose separation is evaluated by initial-motion screening, path generation, and physics-based validation. The acquired operations, states, dependencies, validated paths, and simulation-derived attributes are organized into a Transformed AND/OR Graph for subsequent planning and design evaluation. Exhaustive verification with a controlled toy assembly found no branching violations for introduced tool-accessibility and precedence conditions. Evaluation with a 54-component OpenManipulator Chain gripper demonstrated state-dependent fastener-removal and part- or subassembly-separation operations. Visibility and tool-accessibility evaluations pruned 51.4% of fastener-set candidate evaluations, while removal of obstructing components enabled previously inaccessible fastener operations. Operation-level grouping and screening thereby limited detailed physical validation to mechanically plausible candidates. The results demonstrate the feasibility of acquiring product-specific disassembly knowledge from CAD-derived virtual assemblies before manufacture, supporting subsequent disassembly reasoning and design-for-disassembly evaluation.
title: Fastener-centric acquisition and AND/OR graph representation of state-dependent disassembly knowledge from CAD-derived virtual assemblies

summary: Experimental decisions often depend on evidence scattered across papers, instrument logs, data files, and specialist software. A scientific assistant must connect that evidence without turning a plausible interpretation into an unsupported conclusion. TAS Co-pilot addresses this problem for triple-axis spectroscopy (TAS), which uses neutrons to probe material structure and excitations. It preserves provenance: the sources, processing steps, and review decisions behind each result. Independently maintained scientific tools communicate through structured requests and results; validation rules and human review govern how evidence can support a claim. Language models extract information and explain outcomes but do not approve scientific claims or control the instrument. Dependency-aware reduction executes existing scientific routines and reuses unchanged intermediate results. A retrospective SrMn$_2$Sb$_2$ study connects literature on a related material and historical alignment records to modeling of magnetic excitations in 20 measured scans. A live BT-7 study uses a dedicated instrument interface for fine alignment and 40 adaptively selected measurements. Agreement with a conventional measurement of the same crystal at shared conditions supports the acquisition and analysis chain. These cases demonstrate a methodology for maintaining inspectable evidence across literature, numerical analysis, and measurement at a user facility.
title: TASCopilot: A provenance-preserving assistant for triple-axis neutron scattering

summary: Van der Waals superatomic crystals represent an intriguing class of materials, exhibiting unique ultrafast electronic and structural responses arising from their hierarchical crystal structure. These materials bridge the properties of semiconductors, molecular solids, and nanocrystal arrays, hosting a range of many-body interactions that can be controlled with atomically precise structures. To establish the structure-function correlation, it is necessary to understand element-specific electronic states arising from complex superatomic unit cells. Here, we use transient XUV spectroscopy to individually probe the dynamics of photoexcited electrons and holes in Re$_{6}$Se$_{8}$Cl$_{2}$ superatomic crystals. We simultaneously measure photodynamics at the Re O$_{2}$ and Se M$_{4,5}$ edges, enabling decomposition of excited-state dynamics into the contributions of electron, hole, band gap, and phonon dynamics occurring around Re and Se atoms. By correlating spectral features at the Re and Se edges, we infer the existence of flat conduction bands and identify hot hole transfer from Re to Se atoms. We observe phonon oscillations driven by hole-mediated displacive excitations. The measurements highlight that the photodynamics are dominated by charge transfer between metallic sites which drives phonon coupling in the nonequilibrium state. This work provides insights into the optoelectronic applications of superatomic crystals for future tuning of emergent material properties.
title: Ultrafast Hole Transport and Electron Localization in Superatomic Re$_{6}$Se$_{8}$Cl$_{2}$

summary: Operating within the framework of the collisionless Boltzmann equation, we identify universal spectral profiles inherent in stimulated and coherent light scattering from laser-driven dilute-gas density gratings and derive physically intuitive solutions for such spectral shapes, expressing them in a manifestly causal closed form that satisfies the Kramers - Kronig relations and fulfills the fluctuation - dissipation theorem. Benchmarking against gold-standard experiments on dilute-gas stimulated light scattering verifies a high descriptive and explanatory power of these solutions and demonstrates their ability to isolate universality motifs in nonlinear scattering spectra as the key to fully understanding the physics behind dilute-gas nonlinear light scattering. As one of important outcomes, such analysis reveals the physical content of the bandwidth of dilute-gas nonlinear scattering spectra as an expression and a quantifier of the phase-mixing time, i.e., the time required for free-streaming gas particles with a mean thermal velocity to traverse the distance equal to the spacing of the laser-driven density grating.
title: Universal spectral shapes of nonlinear light scattering from laser-driven dilute-gas density gratings

summary: A reusable, production-oriented ASP.NET Core baseline, distributed as a dotnet new template, for secure and maintainable .NET applications. It organizes startup composition, middleware ordering, structured logging, forwarded headers, security headers, rate limiting, centralized error handling, authentication and authorization foundations, EF Core data access patterns, CI validation, template packaging, and DocFX documentation. It is a baseline rather than a finished or certified application: generated applications still require application-specific configuration, threat analysis, deployment controls, testing, and security review.
title: NetCoreApplicationTemplate

summary: Image deduplication has become increasingly important with the rapid growth of digital image repositories in cloud storage, multimedia systems, and large-scale visual databases. Existing approaches face a trade-off between detection accuracy and computational efficiency. Deep learning methods provide high robustness but require substantial computational resources, while traditional perceptual hashing and handcrafted features offer faster processing but have limited resilience to image transformations. To address this issue, this paper proposes an efficient image deduplication framework integrating multi-scale adaptive region-based feature extraction (MARFE) and adaptive locality-sensitive perceptual hashing (ALSPH). MARFE adaptively selects information-rich image regions to preserve discriminative visual characteristics while reducing redundant computations. ALSPH generates compact binary fingerprints through covariance-guided projection learning for efficient and robust similarity matching. The framework was evaluated on benchmark and web-scale image collections, with additional scalability analysis performed at dataset sizes of up to 10 million images. The framework achieved an F1-score of 0.979, processing speed of 187 images per second, and 49.3% storage savings, demonstrating a good balance between accuracy, efficiency, and scalability.
title: MARFE and ALSPH: a high-performance framework for scalable and efficient image deduplication

summary: This study evaluates temporally validated combinations of five local forecast experts on eligible M4 Weekly and M3 Monthly series. The protocol retains complete historical validation and reserved-origin forecasts. Validated mixtures improve mean MASE relative to the recency-only control on both collections. AutoTheta retains lower monthly mean MASE and lower mean interval score in both collections.
title: Temporally Validated Forecast Combinations on Two Benchmark Collections
