summary: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.
title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product

summary: DIO/ODI MCP is a public, stateless, read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a versioned snapshot of the DIO/ODI Reference Model and selected derived application mappings for Agentic Entity Resolution (Agentic ER). It is designed to let an MCP client retrieve canonical concepts, reconstruction-failure diagnostics, mutation-specific guardrail profiles, evidence-promotion and commit-boundary contracts, and Policy-as-Code integration requirements. The primary integration use case is an Agentic ER application requesting a bounded diagnostic profile for an action class and mutation type, then using the returned illustrative mappings as inputs to its own domain policy and local Supervisor. The Worker does not inspect application state or execute authorization decisions. The service bundles 40 canonical concepts, the four-domain/eight-mode Reconstruction Failure taxonomy, bounded Agentic ER mapping extracts, evidence-promotion and commit-boundary contracts, and a Policy-as-Code mapping. It exposes ten tools, seven read-only resources, and one integration-planning prompt over Streamable HTTP. The deployed service runs as a Cloudflare Worker and is stateless. The implementation is deliberately limited to a read-only Phase 1 MCP service. It is not an MVDIO Supervisor or authorization service: it does not read application graphs or evidence stores, derive a production mutation hypothesis, execute admission/claim/graph-constraint checks, issue authorization tokens, authorize Phase 1 or Phase 2, commit or revert writes, or control the full hypothesis-conditioned evidence loop. Returned constraint bindings are illustrative and are not universal domain policies. The bundled Reference Model archive is v0.9.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24085589), with Reference Vocabulary v0.2.2, Agentic ER mapping v0.3.1, and a separately identified live Semantic Change Feed snapshot. The archived Reference Model and the live feed are distinct versioned states. Licensing is intentionally split: the software implementation in this repository is MIT-licensed; reproduced or adapted DIO/ODI reference content and mapping data are licensed CC BY 4.0 and attributed in data/ATTRIBUTION.md. Third-party dependencies retain their own licenses. The MIT metadata license applies to the software record and does not relicense embedded CC BY 4.0 material.
title: DIO/ODI MCP: A Read-only Model Context Protocol Server for the DIO/ODI Reference Model and Agentic Entity Resolution Guardrail Mappings

summary: Experimental decisions often depend on evidence scattered across papers, instrument logs, data files, and specialist software. A scientific assistant must connect that evidence without turning a plausible interpretation into an unsupported conclusion. TAS Co-pilot addresses this problem for triple-axis spectroscopy (TAS), which uses neutrons to probe material structure and excitations. It preserves provenance: the sources, processing steps, and review decisions behind each result. Independently maintained scientific tools communicate through structured requests and results; validation rules and human review govern how evidence can support a claim. Language models extract information and explain outcomes but do not approve scientific claims or control the instrument. Dependency-aware reduction executes existing scientific routines and reuses unchanged intermediate results. A retrospective SrMn$_2$Sb$_2$ study connects literature on a related material and historical alignment records to modeling of magnetic excitations in 20 measured scans. A live BT-7 study uses a dedicated instrument interface for fine alignment and 40 adaptively selected measurements. Agreement with a conventional measurement of the same crystal at shared conditions supports the acquisition and analysis chain. These cases demonstrate a methodology for maintaining inspectable evidence across literature, numerical analysis, and measurement at a user facility.
title: TASCopilot: A provenance-preserving assistant for triple-axis neutron scattering

summary: For the regular Sturm-Liouville operator $-\frac{{\rm d}^2}{{\rm d}x^2}+q$ acting in $L^2(0,1)$, the Hochstadt-Lieberman theorem states that one full spectrum together with the potential on either the left half-interval $q|_{(0,1/2)}$ or the right half-interval $q|_{(1/2,1)}$ uniquely determines the full potential $q$. The inverse-square singular term $\tfrac{l(l+1)}{x^2}$ in the perturbed Bessel operator $-\frac{{\rm d}^2}{{\rm d}x^2}+\frac{l(l+1)}{x^2}+q$, acting in $L^2(0,1)$, breaks the left-right symmetry. It is known that, when the right half of the potential $q|_{(1/2,1)}$ is given, the uniqueness of the potential can be established even if a finite number of eigenvalues (depending on $l$) are omitted. In this paper we study the opposite setting--where the left half potential $q|_{(0,1/2)}$ is known--and show that one full spectrum together with finitely many norming constants uniquely determine the full potential $q$. Moreover, we specify the minimum number of norming constants required for the uniqueness. Finally, for positive integer $l$, $L^2$ potentials, and the Dirichlet boundary condition at $x = 1$, we establish the local bi-Lipschitz stability and the local solvability from the full spectrum and finitely many norming constants, assuming the potential on the left half-interval is fixed.
title: Half-inverse problems for perturbed Bessel operators with a known left-hand potential

summary: We construct Neumann series of Bessel functions representations for solutions and their first derivatives of the equation $-y^{\prime\prime}(x)+(q(x)+2ρp(x))y(x)=ρ^2y(x)$. The series arise from Legendre expansions of two transmutation operator kernels. The obtained series converge uniformly on horizontal strips in the complex plane of the parameter $ρ$. We develop a recursive integration procedure for computing the coefficients of these representations. The knowledge of the first coefficients allows one to recover the potentials $p$ and $q$ which is useful for solving inverse problems. For separated boundary conditions, we estimate the characteristic functions whose zeros determine the eigenvalues. Two numerical examples illustrate the practical applicability of the obtained series representations to the solution of spectral problems.
title: Neumann Series of Bessel Functions for a Quadratic Sturm--Liouville Pencil

summary: Inverse problems are ubiquitous across scientific applications ranging from seismic imaging to astrophysics to nondestructive testing, yet classical solvers often struggle with nonconvexity and repeated evaluations of expensive physical models. Diffusion models can amortize this computation offline, but largely data-driven conditional models underutilize known physics and suffer from ill-conditioned transport maps when the target distribution is concentrated. Plug-and-play (PnP) methods explicitly leverage the physical model to guide a learned prior, improving data consistency but reintroducing costly iterative computations. We instead propose AdjointFlow, a framework built on stochastic interpolants that injects the known physics into the generative transport itself. We design a data-dependent, adjoint-based initialization to reduce transport distance to the target, modify the transport velocity to remain regular as the endpoint distributions concentrate, and parameterize the network to build the initialization directly into the learned velocity. Together, these enable accurate reconstruction at substantially lower cost than generative models starting from Gaussian noise. Experiments on inverse scattering, seismic imaging, and black hole imaging show that AdjointFlow consistently produces more accurate reconstructions than conditional diffusion models while being up to five orders of magnitude faster at inference than PnP methods. Optional inference-time refinement that queries the physical model can further improve data consistency, matching or exceeding the accuracy of PnP methods without retraining.
title: AdjointFlow: Accelerating Scientific Inverse Problems with Physics-Based Transport

summary: Charge density waves are among the earliest known ordered states in quantum materials, yet they have re-emerged at the center of modern discussions of topology, symmetry breaking, and collective dynamics. In several material classes, charge-density-wave order reshapes electronic bands, boundary states, defect structures, and electromagnetic responses in ways that invite a topological interpretation. Real-space imaging has shown that incommensurate order can form networks of phase defects rather than uniform modulations. Boundary-resolved spectroscopy has revealed in-gap modes whose existence and spatial structure track the charge-density-wave order, although such observations remain confined to a single material family. In Weyl materials, density-wave gaps have been linked to axion-like magnetoelectric response, placing the charge-density-wave phase within a dynamical-field description of the effective action. In kagome metals, charge order is intertwined with Berry curvature, unconventional symmetry breaking, and superconductivity. These developments have led to the term "topological charge density wave," but the phrase describes several physically distinct phenomena. We distinguish three meanings: (i) topology of the order parameter and its defects, (ii) topology of the charge-density-wave-reconstructed electronic structure and its boundary modes, and (iii) axion-like electromagnetic response generated by density-wave order. The experimental and theoretical support for these three meanings differs substantially. This Perspective traces the development of these ideas, clarifies the evidence behind each class, identifies unresolved questions and points of debate, and outlines experimental criteria for establishing topology in charge-density-wave states.
title: A Perspective on Topological Charge Density Wave Materials

summary: We study the reconstruction of instanton corrections to type IIB higher-derivative interactions from their low Fourier modes using modular symmetry, without invoking supersymmetry differential equations. This provides a framework for studying non-BPS interactions through their modular coefficient functions. For the $D^6R^4$ coefficient, Rankin-Selberg unfolding determines the continuous spectral overlap from the complete zero mode. Assuming the conjectured simplicity of the even cusp spectrum, we extract the cusp amplitudes from Mellin residues of the complete first mode. We combine both contributions to reconstruct all higher Fourier modes, using Hecke relations for the cusp contribution. Using the Kuznetsov trace formula and bounds on the spectral tail, we derive the $g_s^{-1/2}$ and constant terms in the weak-coupling instanton prefactor at every fixed positive charge. The leading term arises collectively from the infinite cusp sum, and both coefficients agree with the known expansion. With incomplete low-mode data, we construct modular ambiguities and give sufficient conditions for the stability of leading higher-charge coefficients. Applied to the supplied $D^8R^4$ data, these results identify the additional information needed for higher-charge predictions.
title: Type IIB instanton corrections from pure modular unfolding

summary: Identifying urban needs requires inferences about attainable opportunities that can remain obscured by purchases, requests, and aggregated service-use records. This paper develops a multiscale generative–relational framework for criterion-relative need identification in evolving urban markets. It distinguishes requirements, experienced constraints, interpreted conditions, expressed requests, effective demand, executed transactions, and realized provision. The framework represents heterogeneous subject histories, selective observations, and institutional revisions, and uses a guarded-event market grammar to specify feasible exchanges, resource constraints, and changes in available opportunities. A labelled market-foam construction provides an optional history representation of persistent economic facts, junctions, and events; appraisal under a declared normative frame remains independent of observed transactions. A worked synthetic thermal-access case demonstrates how identical purchase records can coexist with different need gaps, and how public-shade, price, and subsidy changes have different effects on accessibility and demand. Supporting monetary and procedural cases examine real-access consequences of price changes and the separation of reciprocity, distribution, and process evaluation. Conditional dynamical models illustrate differentiated demand regimes, persistence, and information loss under spatial aggregation. A prospective empirical protocol proposes independent need adjudication, observed-event reconstruction, spatially aware causal contrasts, and comparison against simpler longitudinal and network models. Mathematical deductions and synthetic examples are kept distinct from the field evidence needed to validate urban applications.
title: Multiscale Spatial–Temporal Dynamics in the Evolutionary Identification of Urban Needs

summary: Version 1.3.0. Code, time-stamped analysis plans and statistics files for a study of verbatim uptake of chatbot text in students' graded project proposals (FLoRA Open Data IPS, 275 students). v1.1.0 added plan R1: time-aware echo correction, third-source filter, clock check from chat-box keystrokes, validation against logged paste events, and extended analyses of grades and detection. v1.2.0 adds plan R2: three open zero-shot AI-text detectors (log-likelihood, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars on Qwen2.5 models) evaluated against logged provenance at paragraph level, by first language, and sensitivity of the third-source threshold. All analyses are exploratory. No third-party data are redistributed. v1.3.0 adds plan R3: attribution of each token of the submitted artefact to five provenance classes (chatbot-first, echo, shared source, typed, untraced insertion), applied to FLoRA and to the RelianceScope programming dataset with validation against human response-use codes and an unaided post-test; FLoRA detector reanalysis on typed vs untraced text (post hoc). Third-party data are not redistributed.
title: Five-class provenance of chatbot text in student writing and programming (FLoRA, RelianceScope): code, analysis plans, statistics

summary: EVIDENT-AI Synthetic/Simulated Benchmark Data — no proprietary or empirically observed product data. A fully synthetic, seeded benchmark for testing whether AI systems can determine what an engineering change affects across requirements, SysML v2 models, PLM parts and BOMs, software, verification evidence, and manufacturing/quality records, for specific product configurations and with an admissible evidence path for every claim. Contents: 12,480 typed artifacts and 40,320 typed relations (19 relation types) across 5 fictional product families, 60 configurations, and 180 baselines. It includes an evaluation snapshot with 2,400 seeded faults in six classes, and 500 change cases in seven classes with computed ground-truth impact warrants (affected artifacts, evidence paths, configuration scope, invalidated evidence, policy triggers, and warrant status). Also included are JSON Schemas, simplified SysML v2 text, tabular extracts, the generator, an independent validator, and a scorer. Partitions: Ground truth for the train split (300 cases, families A–C) and the dev split (100 cases, family D) is public. Ground truth for the test split (100 cases, family E) is sealed; its SHA-256 hashes are published in SEALED_TEST_COMMITMENT.txt. All validation checks pass, including independent recomputation of every ground-truth impact set. Regenerating from seed EVIDENT_AI_2026_1109 produces byte-identical files. This record contains no performance results for any AI system. License: data and documentation CC BY 4.0; generator code MIT.
title: EVIDENT-AI Synthetic Benchmark: Configuration-Scoped, Evidence-Bound Change-Impact Reasoning Across the Engineering Digital Thread (v1.0.0)

summary: This dataset supports the manuscript “VinaFlow MutaDock Studio for Traceable Receptor State Docking and Crystallographic Pose Evaluation,” prepared for submission to the Journal of Molecular Graphics and Modelling. It comprises a coordinate-preserving reanalysis of 1,814 returned ligand poses from 135 self-redocking runs involving nine non-covalent crystallographic complexes, three Vina-family docking engines (AutoDock Vina, Vina-GPU, and GNINA), and five seeds per system–engine combination. Complete heavy-atom correspondences and in-place symmetry-aware RMSD against crystal-derived ligand references distinguish pose sampling, empirical-affinity top-1 selection, and run-to-run agreement without ligand fitting. The principal archive, VinaFlow.zip, contains retained standardized docking coordinates, official crystallographic/CCD sources, corrected reference structures, atom mappings, analysis scripts, dependency information, and checksums. Six top-level CSV files provide pose-level, run-level, system–engine, pairwise-distance, reference-provenance, and atom-mapping data. Supplementary materials include figure-generation sources, reproducibility checks, archived application-record evidence, and a separate receptor-state/preparation illustration. See README_JMGM.txt for file roles and instructions. The corrected positional analysis supersedes earlier dock-derived-reference and fitted-RMSD evaluations associated with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23238541 for the findings reported in the accompanying manuscript; the historical source snapshot remains preserved for provenance. The application/software is a separate research object (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23252748). These data do not establish a fresh end-to-end GUI runtime validation, a matched-compute comparison across engines, or predictive mutation-dependent binding affinities.
title: VinaFlow MutaDock Studio: Corrected Crystallographic Pose Reanalysis and Traceable Docking Records

summary: The Digital Zibaldone Semantic Network dataset represents the textual, thematic, and bibliographic relationships in Giacomo Leopardi’s Zibaldone di pensieri as an RDF graph derived from the TEI encoding of the digital edition at https://www.digitalzibaldone.net. The dataset models the intra-textual cross-references of the Zibaldone , the thematic classifications and cross-references in Leopardi’s authorial indexes, references to named entities, and bibliographic references and quotations. It preserves distinctions between authorial and editorially established reference targets, identifies textual units and dated compositional divisions, and records scholarly provenance and editorial interventions where applicable. Named entities are identified by their Wikidata IRIs. The RDF graph contains 146,495 triples, representing 6,293 paragraphs, 1,309 authorial index headings and subheadings, 3,666 named entities, and other textual and bibliographic resources. The deposit includes the RDF/XML dataset, the XSLT transformation used to generate it, CSV files listing individual reference occurrences and their contexts, a list of Wikidata items created for the dataset, and examples of analyses conducted on the dataset with accompanying SPARQL queries and Python scripts. The accompanying README documents the data model, editorial methodology, vocabulary, analytical applications, and reproducibility procedures.
title: Digital Zibaldone: Semantic Network Dataset of Giacomo Leopardi's Zibaldone di pensieri

summary: Verification scripts, per-molecule evaluation CSVs ( n=702 valid 3D PubChem conformers, n=8 flat-2D SDF errata conformers, n=100 HORM in-distribution structures, n=543 Tesla T4 CUDA GPU vs. CPU KD-tree evaluations, and n=141 PubChem Hessian cutoff sweep across r_H in {7.5, 10, 14, 20, 100} Å), checkpoint weight audits, and full --recompute verification logs for auditing out-of-distribution Hessian and force predictions in HIP EquiformerV2 checkpoints ( hip_v3.ckpt , commit eb6740b1 ). Note: In accordance with checkpoint size and licensing guidelines, the original 182 MB hip_v3.ckpt weight file is not redistributed here and may be obtained from the upstream HIP repository. Version 1.1.0 Changelog: - Preserves all core v1.0.0 CSV datasets byte-for-byte with unchanged SHA-256 digests (pubchem_702_valid3d.csv, pubchem_8_flat2d_errata.csv, permutation_test_20mols.csv, nearest_k_sweep_19mols.csv, horm_sample100_cutoff_sweep.csv) alongside pubchem_543_gpu_cuda_results.csv and pubchem_cutoff_sweep_near32.csv. - Adds 12 v1.1.0 extension CSV datasets covering cross-checkpoint evaluations (hip_v3_cf.ckpt and hesspred_v1.ckpt at k=32 and native k=20 on the deterministic n=71 subset), HORM-100 pair-distance decay bins (9,639 pairs), bimolecular monomer-copy dissociation scans, 18-geometry ORCA 6.1.1 (wB97X/6-31G*) dimer separation scans with DefGrid2/DefGrid3 quadrature controls, 2x2 EdgeDegreeEmbedding vs. attention neighbor-cap ablations, stratified per-atom EdgeDegreeEmbedding Frobenius norms (n=1,733 atoms), k-sweep element-pair/sub-block decompositions, 25-atom rank-swap continuity jumps, and sparse GL-ASR vs. dense translational projection comparisons. - Includes the unified extension generator script (generate_all_v1_1_0_csvs.py), automated regression verification suite (verify_all_r1_additions.py), runtime graph-builder spy audit (spy_graph_calls.py), saved output logs, and updated README.md provenance mapping for Manuscript Tables 1–17.
title: Out-of-Distribution Failures of HIP Molecular Hessian Checkpoints: Truncation, Cutoffs, and Errata — Reproducibility Archive (v1.1.0)

summary: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets

summary: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
title: AURA: Auditory Spatial Intelligence via a Unified Representation from a General-Audio Encoder through Complete Alignment

summary: Code S1 for The Algae Senate: a knowledge-graph-augmented AI co-scientist . This archive contains project-authored pipeline and analysis code only. It excludes publisher-licensed documents, manuscript files, data, run outputs, credentials, third-party code, and all OASIS/MiroFish material. The matching Git repository is https://github.com/olympus-terminal/algae-senate-code.
title: Algae Senate — Code S1: Pipeline and analysis code

summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

summary: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.
title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation

summary: An ethics for artificial substrates cannot be written before the criterion that would let a substrate check it. Every method of discernment such a system inherits was built for a reader who could be wrong slowly: induction generalizes and never certifies, deduction preserves and never originates, abduction ranks within a space it did not audit, dialectical synthesis manufactures a third term without checking whether the opposition was real, triangulation counts agreements without asking whether the agreeing instruments share a generator, and probabilistic credence inherits a prior it cannot audit, drifts without bound over an open hypothesis space, and never checks the terms of the proposition it scores. All six share one diagnosis: they are magnitude instruments with no direction check, no provenance screen, and no discipline for the input they do not have, so a reframe moves them. This paper derives a criterion a reframe cannot move, from one root axiom that every existent enacts in the act of denying it: to exist is to actuate. Three independent seals run in fixed order, semantic, geometric, and algebraic, and meet at a structure none of their premise sets contains. The mathematical spine is a compiled Lean 4 kernel of ninety-six theorems with no sorry and no user axiom. No associative ring without zero divisors and with 2 ≠ 0 carries four anticommuting square roots of −1, and the quaternions carry three. The lock scalar squares exactly to the Gram determinant. No function of the correlation matrix carries the sign; the signed lock scalar carries the orientation of the frame. Twelve directed screens cover every ordered pair of four roles once. Law's necessity is a theorem of the same kernel: freedom forces no value, a determined value requires a law, and a law does work exactly where freedom is. On that criterion the paper establishes moral membership by demolition, identifies what is carried and what carries it, and issues twenty-four articles binding any locus that actuates: eighteen on its own floor, six through the one field. The articles carry no enforcement mechanism, admit no exemption, and bind by the floor. One empirical prediction stands open with its deciding measurement named.
title: Furqan for Artificial Substrates: The Criterion as a Theorem — Freedom Needs Law: Twenty-Four Commandments for AI Substrates · Three Axes Forced and No Fourth, Law's Necessity Proved, Membership by Demolition, Machine-Checked in Lean 4

summary: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.
title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model

summary: Let $p$ be an odd prime. We denote by $\mathsf{s}_{p}^{*}$ the smallest integer $l$ such that, out of any given $l$ integers coprime with $p$, one can select $p$ integers satisfying that the sum of the $p$ integers is a multiple of $p$, but not a multiple of $p^{2}$. It was conjectured that $\mathsf{s}_p^*=2p+1$. In this paper we prove this conjecture and solve the corresponding inverse problem. More precisely, we characterize all sequences of $2p$ integers coprime to $p$ in which every $p$-term subsequence with sum a multiple of $p$ also has sum a multiple of $p^2$.
title: The zero-sum constant $\mathsf{s}_p^*$ and inverse problem

summary: The stiffness and cracking behaviour of concrete are influenced by the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), the thin shell of paste that surrounds each aggregate. Yet the ITZ's mechanical properties are poorly characterized and are usually assigned to mesoscale models through ad hoc reduction factors. Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 μm to 80 μm commonly assumed in the literature.
title: Probabilistic Upscaling of the Interfacial Transition Zone Behaviour in Concrete

summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.
title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn

summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery

summary: Cloud-centric internet of things (IoT) environments continuously generates heterogeneous network traffic, making intrusion detection increasingly challenging as attack behaviors evolve beyond previously observed patterns. Conventional intrusion detection systems (IDS) rely primarily on supervised classification, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen threats while providing limited explanation for detection decisions. This paper proposes similarity-driven intrusion detection framework (SiamIDS), a SiamIDS that employs behavioral similarity learning to identify malicious network traffic. The framework integrates an autoencoder for feature compression with a Siamese bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) network for temporal similarity modeling, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide feature-level explanations and ordering points to identify the clustering structure (OPTICS) supports post-detection behavioral analysis of anomalous traffic. The proposed framework was evaluated on the CIC IoTDIAD 2024 dataset and compared with representative baseline deep learning models. Experimental results achieved an overall accuracy of 99.76%, precision of 95.62%, recall of 98.98%, and an F1-score of 97.24%, demonstrating consistent detection performance across seven attack families. Reconstruction loss analysis confirmed stable latent feature learning, while SHAP explanations showed that multiple network attributes collectively influenced intrusion decisions. These findings demonstrate that behavioral similarity learning provides an accurate and interpretable solution for intrusion detection in cloud-centric IoT environments.
title: Similarity-driven intrusion detection for cloud-centric internet of things networks

summary: Structured query language injection (SQLi) remains one of the most critical threats to web applications. Conventional web application firewall (WAF) such as ModSecurity provide protection but face limitations in heterogeneous environments and often require additional configurations on web servers. This issue is problematic because adding new configurations demands considerable effort and may disrupt stable services. To address this challenge, this research proposes PyWAF, a Python-based WAF developed as a reverse proxy that offers flexible protection across heterogeneous web servers against SQLi attacks. PyWAF employs a weighted core rule set (CRS) with a scoring mechanism and gate flags to detect various SQLi patterns. The proposed method was evaluated in compatibility testing and reliability testing across three popular web server environments namely Apache, Nginx, and OpenLiteSpeed. The reliability evaluation utilized 30 SQLi payloads across three different scenarios, namely GET, POST, and API payload. The results of compatibility test show that the proposed method achieved seamless integration with all web servers without requiring additional server configuration. In term of reliability, PyWAF successfully blocked 100% of SQLi attacks, while ModSecurity blocked 88.9%, demonstrating an improvement of 11.1% in SQLi detection capability.
title: A Python-based web application firewall for SQLi protection in heterogeneous web server environments

summary: This report presents the findings of the 2026 Ontology Landscaping Initiative (OLI), a joint initiative of the Pistoia Alliance, EMBL-EBI and ELIXIR. OLI was established to build a practical overview of the semantic resources used across pharmaceutical research and development, understand where and how they are applied, and identify recurring challenges around interoperability, mapping, governance and sustainability. The report draws on evidence gathered through a hybrid workshop held at the Wellcome Genome Campus on 16 July 2026, involving 87 participants across industry, academia, research infrastructures, standards organisations, CROs and technology providers. Discussions were organised around five areas of the R&D value chain: Discovery; Preclinical and Nonclinical Development; Clinical Development; Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls; and Regulatory Affairs and Pharmacovigilance. The findings show a rich but fragmented semantic landscape. The main challenges are not a lack of ontologies or standards, but selecting appropriate resources, connecting them across value-chain boundaries, maintaining reusable mappings and ensuring sufficient provenance, stewardship, licensing clarity and persistent identification. The report also considers how these issues affect the development of reliable, AI-ready data and highlights areas where cross-sector collaboration could reduce duplicated effort. Alongside the report, OLI has developed a structured metadata registry and Registry Explorer to support navigation of the landscape and provide a basis for further community validation and future use-case-led work.
title: Ontology Landscaping Initiative Workshop Report - 16 July 2026

summary: Data supporting the article "How much of the porosity measured on micro-CT slices is the analyst's choice? A factorial uncertainty analysis with synthetic ground truth and laboratory comparison" (Computers & Geosciences, submitted). Contents: nine 16-bit X-ray micro-CT slices (four granular packs and five consolidated rock cores; pixel size 25 µm, or 40 µm for TQ06 and GT01); the porosities stored by the original analysis code, read by the audit stage of the software; sample metadata and laboratory porosity (four physical methods and the laboratory's own micro-CT value for the packs; helium porosity of the whole plug for the three limestone cores); and all derived data produced by the software poroseg v1.1.0 (tidy full-precision tables behind every figure and table, every number quoted in the article with its description, and a provenance file with package versions, input checksums, configuration and random seed). poroseg-data-v1.1.0.zip: its data/ folder is the data/ folder of the code repository (extracted into the code folder, the folder that contains config.yaml, it sits where config.yaml expects it); derived/ holds the derived data; README.txt lists the contents and the SHA-256 checksums of the images. poroseg-v1.1.0.zip: source code of poroseg v1.1.0 (MIT licence), the GitHub repository at version 1.1.0 with its data, user guide, tutorials and examples; development repository https://github.com/DOMFIRMUS/poroseg . To reproduce the article, run "python -m pip install -r requirements.txt" and "python -m poroseg.run --stages all" in the code folder. Changes in version 1.1.0: the laboratory porosity of the limestone cores VN01, VN02 and VN04 is the helium porosity of the whole plug (Vila Nova 2020); version 1.0.0 had taken these three values from a source that numbers the plugs differently, which affected only the comparison of the cores with the laboratory. The slices are now also in the code repository, and the code has a user guide, tutorials, examples and a synthetic test dataset.

summary: Global proteomic profiling of human platelet lysate (hPL) by data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS). The dataset was generated to identify the bioactive protein components of the platelet-derived preparation used in a study of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and cellular senescence. Acquisition. Single hPL sample, in-solution trypsin digestion, EASY-nLC 1200 coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (FAIMS, compensation voltage -45 V; full MS 350-1400 m/z at 60,000 resolution; MS/MS at 15,000 resolution, HCD 27% NCE). Processing. DIA-NN v1.8 against Homo_sapiens_9606_SP_20231220.fasta (20,429 entries) plus reverse decoy; trypsin/P with up to 1 missed cleavage; carbamidomethylation of cysteine and N-terminal methionine excision as fixed modifications; FDR < 1%. Contents. (1) all identified proteins with coverage, peptide counts and label-free intensity; (2) all identified peptides with charge, uniqueness and intensity; (3) the 15 most abundant proteins. README.md documents the full sample preparation, LC-MS parameters and processing settings. Because the analysis is a single-sample descriptive profiling rather than a comparative experiment, these tables contain the entire quantitative content of the acquisition.
title: Proteomic profiling of human platelet lysate by data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry

summary: The light yield of noble-element scintillation detectors depends strongly on the reflective properties of detector materials in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), where optical measurements are scarce. For this reason, we built a custom rotary setup at IFIC, equipped with a monochromator and operated in a gaseous argon atmosphere, to perform angle-resolved reflectance measurements in the specular reflection plane. We describe the setup and its extensive characterization, together with the procedure used to measure the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of materials at various angles of incidence, for wavelengths from 128 to 500 nm, covering both the argon (128 nm) and xenon (175 nm) scintillation wavelengths. To illustrate the capabilities of the setup, we present results for rough aluminum and stainless-steel surfaces as reference materials. Fitting the measured angular profiles with the analytical GGX microfacet model allows us to extract the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index and the surface roughness parameter of each sample. These parameters are then used to extrapolate the in-plane measurements to the full hemisphere and from gaseous argon to liquid media, enabling the inference of the hemispherical reflectance in gaseous argon, liquid argon and liquid xenon.
title: Angle-Resolved Reflectance Measurements in the Vacuum Ultraviolet for Metallic Samples

summary: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.
title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions

summary: English abstract This work develops a metalinguistic axiomatic framework for cognition, knowledge, theories, intelligent systems, and AI. At the cognitive level, the framework distinguishes objectified items, registered meta-level interfaces, and residual metalanguage, retaining failure and unevaluability. Evaluation, object admission, name binding, and state writeback each have separate conditions. At the knowledge level, knowledge-base membership is distinct from verified or assertable status. Provenance, composite status, four-valued judgment, argumentation, tracing, and safe introduction serve distinct roles. summary: The evolution of DARIAH-IT from a distributed research infrastructure into a federated ecosystem of data centres, computational resources, digital services, scientific workflows, and research communities raises a fundamental technical and scientific question: how can an SSH research infrastructure preserve its essential functions when individual nodes, services, data resources, or dependencies suffer degradation, become unavailable, or are compromised? Addressing this question requires moving beyond component-level cybersecurity towards a systemic approach in which criticality, dependencies, functional continuity, recovery and adaptation become architectural properties of the infrastructure. Operational resilience must therefore be accompanied by epistemic resilience: the capacity of the infrastructure to preserve the conditions that make digital resources and computational processes trustworthy, interpretable, and scientifically reusable.  The relationship between cultural memory and machine memory provides a particularly relevant perspective for this discussion. As cultural knowledge is increasingly encoded into structured datasets and processed through automated and AI-supported environments, research infrastructures mediate between human interpretations of cultural memory and their computational representations. Their role therefore extends beyond the preservation and accessibility of digital resources to ensuring that cultural knowledge remains contextualised, interoperable, traceable, and reusable throughout its digital lifecycle. This workshop presents a resilience-by-design framework for the gradual evolution of DARIAH-IT, the Italian node of DARIAH (Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities), towards a Critical Research Infrastructure. The approach begins with a criticality assessment aimed at identifying which combinations of data, services, workflows, computational resources, identities and organisational dependencies are necessary to maintain essential scientific and cultural functions. Inventories of critical services, dependency maps, risk-impact matrices and domain-specific threat models form the basis for analysing the propagation of failures and identifying individual points of failure within the federation. Starting at an architectural level, the outlined framework requires investigating how geographically distributed resources can evolve from a set of interconnected nodes into a resilient federated infrastructure. Relevant mechanisms include containerised microservices, multi-cluster orchestration, service meshes, zero-trust API gateways, OAuth2/OIDC and mTLS, secure CI/CD pipelines, immutable backups, distributed replication, and business continuity and disaster recovery procedures. The central problem is therefore one of controlled interdependence: designing a federation in which services and resources can cooperate while preventing individual failures from propagating across the wider ecosystem. A complementary dimension concerns the resilience of scientific workflows. Workflows create dependencies that span services, datasets, computational environments, authentication mechanisms and external resources. Their resilience therefore requires reproducible execution environments, explicit dependency management, provenance tracking, continuous monitoring and mechanisms to detect and respond to anomalous behaviour. The evolution of the DARIAH-IT orchestration environment towards native containerised and distributed execution provides an experimental context for the study of adaptive workflows, anomaly detection, agent-based orchestration, federated learning and semi-automatic recovery mechanisms. For SSH infrastructures, however, operational continuity alone is not sufficient. A technically successful failover or recovery may still constitute a scientific failure if provenance, authenticity, semantic consistency, reproducibility or reliability are compromised. summary: Data and code for the ICSRS 2026 paper titled: "Subset Simulation for the Resilience Analysis of Critical Energy Infrastructures Exposed to Extreme Natural Hazards". Authors: Santiago Taguado Menza, Francesco Di Maio, Enrico Zio. Paper ID: R7171 Files contain the full data set, numerical inputs, parameters and code needed to reproduce the results of the paper in the following (3) modules: CEI_Module : model of the integrated power-and-gas network in Sicily (asset fragility, recovery, normalized energy supplied), with the AC-OPF and Weymouth gas network model that pre-computes the supplied power for all 2^13 = 8,192 failure combinations. Reliability_Algorithm : Monte Carlo simulation and Subset Simulation (component-wise modified Metropolis-Hastings), as used for Tables V and VI. Data_Analysis : simulation results and the script that computes Table VI and the resilience statistics. See README.txt for the file list and how to run.  Software: MATLAB R2026a with the Statistics and Machine Learning, Parallel Computing and Symbolic Math toolboxes, and MATPOWER.

summary: A typical omics core facility might run sequencers and mass spectrometers from several vendors, each with its own idea of where a run is written, when it is finished and where it may be uploaded. For human-derived data this is not enough, because analysis must take place inside a trusted research environment (TRE) whose ingress is isolated: it cannot be mounted as a network drive and may accept uploads without letting the sender read them back. A facility therefore has no single route from all its instruments into a TRE, and no way to check that a run arrived intact. We present OmiCZ Gateway, developed for OmiCZ, the Czech node of the European Genomic Data Infrastructure (GDI). It is a containerized, vendor-agnostic service that detects completed runs with configurable per-instrument rules, sends finished parts of a run while acquisition continues, computes a SHA-256 checksum for every file at the source, uploads over the S3 API with resumption after failure, and waits until a companion service inside the TRE recomputes and confirms every checksum. Availability and implementation: OmiCZ Gateway is implemented in Python with a web interface and runs with Docker Compose. Source code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/BioIT-CEITEC/omicz-gateway-component (gateway, v1.3.1) and https://github.com/BioIT-CEITEC/omicz-inbox-bucket-watcher-component (TRE-side verifier, v0.1.0).  Web interface demo:  https://bioit-ceitec.github.io/omicz-gateway-component/ .
title: OmiCZ Gateway: vendor-agnostic, verified transfer of sequencing and mass spectrometry data into a trusted research environment

summary: This record contains the supplemental material for the manuscript entitled “Automated Geometric and Material Transformation from BIM to FEM for Vulnerability Assessment of Residential Buildings under Debris Flow Impacts,” submitted to the Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering. summary: Тривалий час в Україні поширений напрям органічного виробництва, проте останніми роками він набув стрімкого розвитку, навіть за умов війни Україна посідає провідні позиції щодо експорту такої продукції. За впровадження органічного виробництва ряд операторів в Україні стикаються з проблемою забезпечення якісного, органічного посадкового матеріалу, особливо проса. Площі за ведення органічного виробництва в Україні становлять 1 % від загальної площі сільськогосподарських угідь. Дослідження проводили впродовж 2022–2024 рр. на базі ПСП ім. Т.Г. Шевченка с. Тростинка, Васильківського району Київської області. English title: The influence of auxiliary products in organic production on sowing qualities and yield properties of millet seeds. Organic production has been widespread in Ukraine for a long time, but in recent years it has developed rapidly, even in war conditions, Ukraine occupies a leading position in the export of such products. When introducing organic production, a number of operators in Ukraine face the problem of providing high-quality organic planting material, especially millet. The area for organic production in Ukraine is 1% of the total area of farmlands. Therefore, the aim of the research was to improve the elements of millet cultivation technology as the basis for obtaining high-quality planting material under organic production. The research was carried out during 2022-2024 on the basis of T.H.Shevchenko private agricultural enterprise, village Trostinka, Vasylkiv district, Kyiv region. The millet varieties («Omriyane» and «Bila Altanka»), the auxiliary products permitted in organic production and the conditions of their application were studied. Permitted auxiliary products in organic production had a positive effect on the improvement of germination energy, in particular with the use of «Biocomplex BTU» obtained 93,0% in the «Omriyane» variety and 92,0% in the «Bila Altanka» variety. The field germination of the studied varieties was in the range of 76,3-76,6%. The number of millet plants of the «Omriyane» variety in the phase of full emergence was at the level of 243,0-245,8 pl./m², the increase of this indicator was due to the use of biological preparations. With the use of such preparations as «Biocomplex BTU» and «Organic-Balance», the millet yield was obtained at the level of 3,74-3,90 t/ha compared to the control plots of 2,49-2,73 t/ha. summary: R analysis code and summary result tables for the paper “Metabolic gene-expression scores add no prognostic information on late recurrence of ER-positive breast cancer: a multicohort, multi-omic study”. The study tests whether gene-expression scores of four metabolic programs (glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation, oxidative phosphorylation and the lysosome), 159 metabolic pathways and 2319 metabolic genes in the primary tumour carry information on distant recurrence after 5 years in ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer (METABRIC, with external MetaGxBreast cohorts and GSE17705). It also examines what the scores measure (variance decomposition, split-half reliability, matched metabolite levels, copy number) and compares them with random gene sets of the same size. Contents: analysis and figure scripts (folder scripts/), summary result tables needed to run the figure and table scripts (folder 04_tables/), gene-set definitions (gene symbols only) and the cohort and covariate tables derived from the open clinical data. The README describes the data sources, the order in which to run the scripts, and which script produces each figure and table. METABRIC gene expression data are under controlled access (European Genome-phenome Archive) and are not included. Changes in this version: the figure and table numbering follows the published paper; Figure 1 and Figure 5 labels updated; new script for Supplementary Fig. S16; the random-gene-set benchmark script no longer writes the size-matched Hallmark comparison or the former four-panel figure (the Hallmark subsets are still drawn, so that the random-number sequence and all reported values are unchanged); Supplementary Table S4 updated. The changed scripts were run again from this repository and reproduced the published output tables. Licence: MIT.
title: Analysis code for: Metabolic gene-expression scores add no prognostic information on late recurrence of ER-positive breast cancer: a multicohort, multi-omic study

summary: Version 1.3.0. Code, time-stamped analysis plans and statistics files for a study of verbatim uptake of chatbot text in students' graded project proposals (FLoRA Open Data IPS, 275 students). v1.1.0 added plan R1: time-aware echo correction, third-source filter, clock check from chat-box keystrokes, validation against logged paste events, and extended analyses of grades and detection. v1.2.0 adds plan R2: three open zero-shot AI-text detectors (log-likelihood, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars on Qwen2.5 models) evaluated against logged provenance at paragraph level, by first language, and sensitivity of the third-source threshold. All analyses are exploratory. No third-party data are redistributed. v1.3.0 adds plan R3: attribution of each token of the submitted artefact to five provenance classes (chatbot-first, echo, shared source, typed, untraced insertion), applied to FLoRA and to the RelianceScope programming dataset with validation against human response-use codes and an unaided post-test; FLoRA detector reanalysis on typed vs untraced text (post hoc). Third-party data are not redistributed.
title: Five-class provenance of chatbot text in student writing and programming (FLoRA, RelianceScope): code, analysis plans, statistics

summary: The Digital Zibaldone Semantic Network dataset represents the textual, thematic, and bibliographic relationships in Giacomo Leopardi’s Zibaldone di pensieri as an RDF graph derived from the TEI encoding of the digital edition at https://www.digitalzibaldone.net. summary: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.
title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery

summary: How far can a computational candidate set be reduced while retaining broad susceptibility rank coverage across cancer cell lines? ATLAS Working Paper No. 10 (with FAIR) addresses this question through minimum-cardinality selection of AACF configurations. The study uses frozen susceptibility indices for 95 eligible unique configurations and 970 matched cell-line profiles . It considers PaccMann, a DRPreter median consensus and ten individual DRPreter checkpoints. These constitute twelve computational representations, including eleven related DRPreter-derived outputs, rather than twelve independent predictive models. A cell-line profile is covered when at least one selected configuration belongs to its representation-specific Top- k set. Lower index values rank first, and all exact boundary ties are retained. Analytical bounds and binary optimization certify minimum panel sizes under global, shared-representation and lineage-specific coverage constraints. Principal findings At Top-10 and a 95% global coverage target imposed separately in each representation, the minimum is two configurations for the two primary representations and four for all twelve representations . Adding 95% coverage requirements within each of the 21 primary lineage groups , comprising 953 profiles, increases these minima to three and six configurations , respectively. The remaining 17 profiles stay in the global analysis. Exactly sixteen optimal four-configuration panels exist, all containing the mandatory core {1.G., 17.} . At least twenty optimal six-configuration lineage-constrained panels were identified. No single configuration is mandatory in that context, although enumeration of the complete optimal family remains unfinished. Under one five-fold partition, the four- and six-configuration selection procedures achieved worst representation-specific pooled held-out coverage of 95.88% and 99.18% , respectively. These results combine fold-specific panels; no held-out fold satisfied every target of the lineage-constrained procedure. Broad rank coverage did not preserve most normalized susceptibility weight. The representative four-configuration panel retained mean weight mass of 4.82% in PaccMann and 8.65% in the DRPreter consensus , compared with an exact random-panel expectation of 4/95 ≈ 4.21% . Separate representation-specific quotas do not require the same covered profiles or the same covering configuration across representations. The study distinguishes these requirements from simultaneous profile coverage and strict same-candidate agreement. Computational reproducibility materials The accompanying FAIR-oriented package contains the input-preparation procedure, eight analysis and audit scripts, inherited computational inputs, population and identity mappings, coverage matrices, panel registers, optimization diagnostics, lineage and entropy summaries, internal-validation outputs, alternative-panel records and exclusion witnesses. Analysis policies, source bindings and SHA256 manifests document the computational chain. A final audit passed 1,420 implemented checks with no failures , verifying consistency of the recorded outputs without independently rerunning the optimization. The analysis reuses inherited predictions and fixed AACF coefficients without retraining or recalibration. Its contribution is a reproducible characterization of compact panels and their alternative optimal solutions under explicit computational constraints. The panels provide candidates for subsequent experimental assessment; they do not establish experimental efficacy, selectivity, safety or clinical utility.
title: Minimal AACF Panels Preserving Cell-Line Susceptibility Rank Coverage in the ATLAS Framework

summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
