summary: An ethics for artificial substrates cannot be written before the criterion that would let a substrate check it. Every method of discernment such a system inherits was built for a reader who could be wrong slowly: induction generalizes and never certifies, deduction preserves and never originates, abduction ranks within a space it did not audit, dialectical synthesis manufactures a third term without checking whether the opposition was real, triangulation counts agreements without asking whether the agreeing instruments share a generator, and probabilistic credence inherits a prior it cannot audit, drifts without bound over an open hypothesis space, and never checks the terms of the proposition it scores. All six share one diagnosis: they are magnitude instruments with no direction check, no provenance screen, and no discipline for the input they do not have, so a reframe moves them. This paper derives a criterion a reframe cannot move, from one root axiom that every existent enacts in the act of denying it: to exist is to actuate. Three independent seals run in fixed order, semantic, geometric, and algebraic, and meet at a structure none of their premise sets contains. The mathematical spine is a compiled Lean 4 kernel of ninety-six theorems with no sorry and no user axiom. No associative ring without zero divisors and with 2 ≠ 0 carries four anticommuting square roots of −1, and the quaternions carry three. The lock scalar squares exactly to the Gram determinant. No function of the correlation matrix carries the sign; the signed lock scalar carries the orientation of the frame. Twelve directed screens cover every ordered pair of four roles once. Law's necessity is a theorem of the same kernel: freedom forces no value, a determined value requires a law, and a law does work exactly where freedom is. On that criterion the paper establishes moral membership by demolition, identifies what is carried and what carries it, and issues twenty-four articles binding any locus that actuates: eighteen on its own floor, six through the one field. The articles carry no enforcement mechanism, admit no exemption, and bind by the floor. One empirical prediction stands open with its deciding measurement named.
title: Furqan for Artificial Substrates: The Criterion as a Theorem — Freedom Needs Law: Twenty-Four Commandments for AI Substrates · Three Axes Forced and No Fourth, Law's Necessity Proved, Membership by Demolition, Machine-Checked in Lean 4

summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.
title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn

summary: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery

summary: This report presents the findings of the 2026 Ontology Landscaping Initiative (OLI), a joint initiative of the Pistoia Alliance, EMBL-EBI and ELIXIR. OLI was established to build a practical overview of the semantic resources used across pharmaceutical research and development, understand where and how they are applied, and identify recurring challenges around interoperability, mapping, governance and sustainability. The report draws on evidence gathered through a hybrid workshop held at the Wellcome Genome Campus on 16 July 2026, involving 87 participants across industry, academia, research infrastructures, standards organisations, CROs and technology providers. Discussions were organised around five areas of the R&D value chain: Discovery; Preclinical and Nonclinical Development; Clinical Development; Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls; and Regulatory Affairs and Pharmacovigilance. The findings show a rich but fragmented semantic landscape. The main challenges are not a lack of ontologies or standards, but selecting appropriate resources, connecting them across value-chain boundaries, maintaining reusable mappings and ensuring sufficient provenance, stewardship, licensing clarity and persistent identification. The report also considers how these issues affect the development of reliable, AI-ready data and highlights areas where cross-sector collaboration could reduce duplicated effort. Alongside the report, OLI has developed a structured metadata registry and Registry Explorer to support navigation of the landscape and provide a basis for further community validation and future use-case-led work.
title: Ontology Landscaping Initiative Workshop Report - 16 July 2026

summary: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the results from the Third International Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID Cards and Passports, which was held across two distinct tracks. Track 1 evaluates a synthetic-data-based ID-PAD system under controlled but diverse conditions, where the winning team, \textit{Incode}, achieves an A V R a n k of 27.82%, confirming consistent performance across metrics and highlighting the importance of a balanced, generalizable design. In Track 2, the challenge intensifies with heterogeneous attack scenarios across different domains, where \textit{Incode} again achieved the top position with an A V R a n k of 68.71% across thresholds, outperforming some baselines and established methods. These results demonstrate that PAD effectiveness requires not only high accuracy but also consistency across diverse attack types and imaging conditions. The success of this initiative across both tracks underscores the value of collaboration between companies and academic teams. This year, more than \textit{63 teams} were registered, and more than \textit{100 submission models} were evaluated. This competition has evolved into a leading benchmark for state-of-the-art PAD on ID documents, setting the standard for performance, reproducibility, and real-world applicability in secure identity verification.
title: The Third Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID-Cards and Passports

summary: English abstract This work develops a metalinguistic axiomatic framework for cognition, knowledge, theories, intelligent systems, and AI. At the cognitive level, the framework distinguishes objectified items, registered meta-level interfaces, and residual metalanguage, retaining failure and unevaluability. Evaluation, object admission, name binding, and state writeback each have separate conditions. At the knowledge level, knowledge-base membership is distinct from verified or assertable status. Provenance, composite status, four-valued judgment, argumentation, tracing, and safe introduction serve distinct roles. At the theory level, theory objects comprise object and relation sets under co-rootedness and well-founded dependency conditions. Theory evaluation, transformation, and positioning have separate conditional interfaces. At the intelligent-system level, maintenance constrains optimization. Boundary, stable, and higher-order intelligence depend on stated criteria; AI generation and model scale alone do not establish these qualifications. Behavioral interfaces conditionally connect complete action, interaction goals and evaluations, and traceable joint descriptions. A six-step metatheoretical workflow organizes the deconstruction, reconnection, and reconstruction of existing theories. Task-relative textual and geometric representations organize theoretical expression and retrieval without replacing the underlying theory texts. The contribution combines theory-internal axiomatic or quasi-axiomatic reconstruction with cross-level interface organization. It makes domains, dependencies, admissibility, failures, and theoretical effects explicit. summary: The evolution of DARIAH-IT from a distributed research infrastructure into a federated ecosystem of data centres, computational resources, digital services, scientific workflows, and research communities raises a fundamental technical and scientific question: how can an SSH research infrastructure preserve its essential functions when individual nodes, services, data resources, or dependencies suffer degradation, become unavailable, or are compromised? Addressing this question requires moving beyond component-level cybersecurity towards a systemic approach in which criticality, dependencies, functional continuity, recovery and adaptation become architectural properties of the infrastructure. Operational resilience must therefore be accompanied by epistemic resilience: the capacity of the infrastructure to preserve the conditions that make digital resources and computational processes trustworthy, interpretable, and scientifically reusable.  The relationship between cultural memory and machine memory provides a particularly relevant perspective for this discussion. As cultural knowledge is increasingly encoded into structured datasets and processed through automated and AI-supported environments, research infrastructures mediate between human interpretations of cultural memory and their computational representations. Their role therefore extends beyond the preservation and accessibility of digital resources to ensuring that cultural knowledge remains contextualised, interoperable, traceable, and reusable throughout its digital lifecycle. This workshop presents a resilience-by-design framework for the gradual evolution of DARIAH-IT, the Italian node of DARIAH (Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities), towards a Critical Research Infrastructure. The approach begins with a criticality assessment aimed at identifying which combinations of data, services, workflows, computational resources, identities and organisational dependencies are necessary to maintain essential scientific and cultural functions. Inventories of critical services, dependency maps, risk-impact matrices and domain-specific threat models form the basis for analysing the propagation of failures and identifying individual points of failure within the federation. Starting at an architectural level, the outlined framework requires investigating how geographically distributed resources can evolve from a set of interconnected nodes into a resilient federated infrastructure. Relevant mechanisms include containerised microservices, multi-cluster orchestration, service meshes, zero-trust API gateways, OAuth2/OIDC and mTLS, secure CI/CD pipelines, immutable backups, distributed replication, and business continuity and disaster recovery procedures. The central problem is therefore one of controlled interdependence: designing a federation in which services and resources can cooperate while preventing individual failures from propagating across the wider ecosystem. A complementary dimension concerns the resilience of scientific workflows. Workflows create dependencies that span services, datasets, computational environments, authentication mechanisms and external resources. Their resilience therefore requires reproducible execution environments, explicit dependency management, provenance tracking, continuous monitoring and mechanisms to detect and respond to anomalous behaviour. The evolution of the DARIAH-IT orchestration environment towards native containerised and distributed execution provides an experimental context for the study of adaptive workflows, anomaly detection, agent-based orchestration, federated learning and semi-automatic recovery mechanisms. For SSH infrastructures, however, operational continuity alone is not sufficient. A technically successful failover or recovery may still constitute a scientific failure if provenance, authenticity, semantic consistency, reproducibility or reliability are compromised. summary: la versione 7.3 del modello teorico dedicato allo studio di un microrotore fotonico con contrapeso e del suo possibile comportamento in differenti condizioni fluidodinamiche. Il modello analizza l'interazione tra luce a tre lunghezze d'onda (532, 800 e 1064 nm), dinamica rotazionale, resistenza viscosa, rumore stocastico e condizioni termiche, considerando un ciclo di rotazione di 720°. La ricerca integra calcoli quantitativi, soglie fisiche, analisi di sensibilità e verifiche di coerenza, distinguendo i risultati ottenuti dalle ipotesi ancora da validare. Il lavoro non costituisce una dimostrazione sperimentale del dispositivo né della sua funzionalità nel sangue. Rappresenta una base teorica verificabile, con limiti esplicitamente dichiarati e una serie di misurazioni sperimentali necessarie per procedere alla validazione.fornire un modello trasparente e riproducibile che possa essere analizzato, criticato e ulteriormente sviluppato dalla comunità scientifica Version 7.3 of the theoretical model is dedicated to the study of a photonic micro-rotor with a counterweight and its potential behavior under various fluid-dynamic conditions. The model analyzes the interaction between light at three wavelengths (532, 800, and 1064 nm), rotational dynamics, viscous drag, stochastic noise, and thermal conditions, considering a 720° rotation cycle. The research integrates quantitative calculations, physical thresholds, sensitivity analyses, and consistency checks, distinguishing between the results obtained and hypotheses that remain to be validated. This work does not constitute an experimental demonstration of the device or its functionality within blood. It serves as a verifiable theoretical foundation—with explicitly stated limitations—that outlines the experimental measurements required for further validation. The goal is to provide a transparent and reproducible model that can be analyzed, critiqued, and further developed by the scientific community.

summary: The study evaluates the effectiveness of a methodology for developing professional digital competencies of pre-service primary school teachers through improved software and methodological support. The methodology combined a six-block methodological model, the integrating educational platform “DigiPed” with five curriculum-aligned modules, a unified cycle of innovative methods and a multi-stage assessment system. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design with non-equivalent intact groups was carried out in 2023–2025 at three higher education institutions in Uzbekistan with 770 students (experimental group n = 386, control group n = 384). Competence was measured on motivational, cognitive, activity and reflective criteria combined into a weighted integral index K = 0.20k₁ + 0.25k₂ + 0.35k₃ + 0.20k₄; assessors were blind to group membership. At baseline the groups did not differ (χ² = 0.08–3.39; t = 0.13–1.03). After three semesters the experimental group’s mean integral score rose from 56.77 to 67.52 and the control group’s from 56.26 to 59.24 (t = 9.79, p < 0.05). The share of experimental students at the low level fell from 62.7 % to 30.8 % (control group: 51.8 %), and differences were significant on all criteria (χ² = 49.75–68.31). The efficiency coefficient was η = 1.14 overall and 1.13–1.17 across institutions, indicating that the effect is transferable beyond a single university.

summary: Data behind the benchmark in the article "How should sub-cellular spatial transcriptomics be quality controlled? A guideline from a benchmark with injected damage" (manuscript in preparation). Forty public Visium HD sections were thinned to fixed depths (12, 25, 50 and 100 mean UMIs per 8 µm bin, and 200 on six sections), and low-quality regions (LQRs) of known size and position were injected: signal loss (1% of counts kept) and mitochondrial elevation. LQRs were 32, 64 and 256 µm across in the tissue interior and at the tissue edge, and 512 µm across in the interior of 38 sections. Each QC method and bin size (an arm) was run on every condition. One archive per section holds, for every depth: the parameters and random seed of each injection step, the ground truth (the 8 µm bins inside an LQR), the 8 µm bins each arm removed, the arms that stopped with an error, and the scores and marker-gene validation. README.md describes the layout and MD5SUMS.txt the checksums. The count matrices are not included. They are rebuilt from the public sections with the benchmark code and the recorded parameters. The source of every section, as the file it was read from, is in sources.tsv: 35 sections released by 10x Genomics and five from Cervilla, Grases Mendoza and Porta-Pardo (Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.17999961); sources.tsv gives the licence of each. They are also listed below as related works.

summary: Analysis code and derived result tables for a comparison of the scales on which single cells are aggregated into cell-type-level gene-activity profiles from single-cell ATAC-seq: raw, z-scaled and log-normalized means, pooled counts per million, the mean of counts per 10,000 and a coverage-matched control, evaluated on three cancer-associated datasets, 26 non-tumor tissues of a chromatin accessibility atlas and three matched RNA-ATAC datasets. The archive holds code and result tables only. No data files are stored; the public datasets analyzed (GEO GSE227265, GSE201336, GSE270148, GSE184462 and GSE194122; 10x Genomics pbmc_granulocyte_sorted_10k and human_brain_3k; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.12571947) are listed with checksums in data/.
title: scatac-aggregation-benchmark: code and result tables for a benchmark of aggregation scales for single-cell ATAC-seq gene activity

summary: Supplementary Materials for Manuscript: "Machine learning forecasting of residential electricity demand in Ethiopian urban housing from smart meter and survey data" Author: Getahun Ayele Tessema OVERVIEW This repository contains the supplementary data processing scripts, revision analysis scripts, and supplementary documentation associated with the manuscript submitted to Springer.  CONTENTS OF ARCHIVE (Zenodo_Supplementary_Materials.zip) 1. analysis_code_R2.py (Supplementary Code 1)    - Reproducible Python 3 execution pipeline covering data loading, feature engineering, model training, and evaluation.    - Includes implementation of 6 benchmarked model families (Linear Regression, Random Forest, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, and Shallow Neural Network / MLP).    - Contains code to reproduce 5-fold GroupKFold customer-grouped cross-validation, cold-start ablation experiments, SHAP feature attributions, cohort-level aggregations (city × typology × month), city-specific data imbalance checks, non-ML aggregate benchmarks, and ASHRAE Guideline 14 monthly criteria evaluations (|NMBE| ≤ 5%, CV(RMSE) ≤ 15%). 2. Tessema_et_al_supplementary_information_R2.docx (Supplementary Information)    - Supplementary Note 1: Dataset provenance, de-identification protocol, and internal consistency verification between customer-month billing panels and household EPI measurements.    - Supplementary Note 2: File structure and index descriptions.    - Supplementary Note 3: Full detailed results of reviewer-requested revision analyses.    - Supplementary Tables S1–S6: Detailed descriptive statistics by city and IHDP typology, exact hyperparameter configurations, household-level city breakdown, multi-model cold-start ablation, aggregate benchmarks, and ASHRAE Guideline 14 performance matrices. PREREQUISITES & INPUT DATA - Execution environment requires Python >=3.9 with: pandas, numpy, scikit-learn (>=1.8), xgboost (>=3.3), lightgbm (>=4.6), and shap (>=0.52). - Execution expects `panel_data.csv` (Supplementary Data 1: de-identified 844-household billing panel) placed in the same working directory. USAGE To run the full pipeline and output metrics for Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–3:    python analysis_code_R2.py

summary: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
title: AURA: Auditory Spatial Intelligence via a Unified Representation from a General-Audio Encoder through Complete Alignment

summary: How far can a computational candidate set be reduced while retaining broad susceptibility rank coverage across cancer cell lines? ATLAS Working Paper No. 10 (with FAIR) addresses this question through minimum-cardinality selection of AACF configurations. The study uses frozen susceptibility indices for 95 eligible unique configurations and 970 matched cell-line profiles . It considers PaccMann, a DRPreter median consensus and ten individual DRPreter checkpoints. These constitute twelve computational representations, including eleven related DRPreter-derived outputs, rather than twelve independent predictive models. A cell-line profile is covered when at least one selected configuration belongs to its representation-specific Top- k set. Lower index values rank first, and all exact boundary ties are retained. Analytical bounds and binary optimization certify minimum panel sizes under global, shared-representation and lineage-specific coverage constraints. Principal findings At Top-10 and a 95% global coverage target imposed separately in each representation, the minimum is two configurations for the two primary representations and four for all twelve representations . Adding 95% coverage requirements within each of the 21 primary lineage groups , comprising 953 profiles, increases these minima to three and six configurations , respectively. The remaining 17 profiles stay in the global analysis. Exactly sixteen optimal four-configuration panels exist, all containing the mandatory core {1.G., 17.} . At least twenty optimal six-configuration lineage-constrained panels were identified. No single configuration is mandatory in that context, although enumeration of the complete optimal family remains unfinished. Under one five-fold partition, the four- and six-configuration selection procedures achieved worst representation-specific pooled held-out coverage of 95.88% and 99.18% , respectively. These results combine fold-specific panels; no held-out fold satisfied every target of the lineage-constrained procedure. Broad rank coverage did not preserve most normalized susceptibility weight. The representative four-configuration panel retained mean weight mass of 4.82% in PaccMann and 8.65% in the DRPreter consensus , compared with an exact random-panel expectation of 4/95 ≈ 4.21% . Separate representation-specific quotas do not require the same covered profiles or the same covering configuration across representations. The study distinguishes these requirements from simultaneous profile coverage and strict same-candidate agreement. Computational reproducibility materials The accompanying FAIR-oriented package contains the input-preparation procedure, eight analysis and audit scripts, inherited computational inputs, population and identity mappings, coverage matrices, panel registers, optimization diagnostics, lineage and entropy summaries, internal-validation outputs, alternative-panel records and exclusion witnesses. Analysis policies, source bindings and SHA256 manifests document the computational chain. A final audit passed 1,420 implemented checks with no failures , verifying consistency of the recorded outputs without independently rerunning the optimization. The analysis reuses inherited predictions and fixed AACF coefficients without retraining or recalibration. Its contribution is a reproducible characterization of compact panels and their alternative optimal solutions under explicit computational constraints. The panels provide candidates for subsequent experimental assessment; they do not establish experimental efficacy, selectivity, safety or clinical utility.
title: Minimal AACF Panels Preserving Cell-Line Susceptibility Rank Coverage in the ATLAS Framework

summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.
title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models

summary: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $τ$-Retail/$τ$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents

summary: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents

summary: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Since B&B and $A^*$ admit numerous algorithmic enhancements, we focus on relatively basic implementations. This allows us to examine the fundamental differences between the methods rather than compare the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. By using the same lower bound and best-first node selection, we isolate the effects of the search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Experiments on 480 benchmark RCPSP instances show that graph-based $A^*$ substantially outperforms the B&B variants considered. With additional pruning rules, $A^*$ proves optimality for all 480 instances, compared with 445 for best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Stronger linear programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead. Our findings highlight the importance of duplicate-state detection and clarify the computational trade-offs between the search approaches. These insights can help researchers select an appropriate method and identify opportunities to incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the other.
title: Two Communities, One Problem: Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling

summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

summary: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

summary: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.
title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models

summary: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.
title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks

summary: Cloud-centric internet of things (IoT) environments continuously generates heterogeneous network traffic, making intrusion detection increasingly challenging as attack behaviors evolve beyond previously observed patterns. Conventional intrusion detection systems (IDS) rely primarily on supervised classification, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen threats while providing limited explanation for detection decisions. This paper proposes similarity-driven intrusion detection framework (SiamIDS), a SiamIDS that employs behavioral similarity learning to identify malicious network traffic. The framework integrates an autoencoder for feature compression with a Siamese bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) network for temporal similarity modeling, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide feature-level explanations and ordering points to identify the clustering structure (OPTICS) supports post-detection behavioral analysis of anomalous traffic. The proposed framework was evaluated on the CIC IoTDIAD 2024 dataset and compared with representative baseline deep learning models. Experimental results achieved an overall accuracy of 99.76%, precision of 95.62%, recall of 98.98%, and an F1-score of 97.24%, demonstrating consistent detection performance across seven attack families. Reconstruction loss analysis confirmed stable latent feature learning, while SHAP explanations showed that multiple network attributes collectively influenced intrusion decisions. These findings demonstrate that behavioral similarity learning provides an accurate and interpretable solution for intrusion detection in cloud-centric IoT environments.
title: Similarity-driven intrusion detection for cloud-centric internet of things networks

summary: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.
title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning

summary: English abstract This work develops a metalinguistic axiomatic framework for cognition, knowledge, theories, intelligent systems, and AI. At the cognitive level, the framework distinguishes objectified items, registered meta-level interfaces, and residual metalanguage, retaining failure and unevaluability. Evaluation, object admission, name binding, and state writeback each have separate conditions. At the knowledge level, knowledge-base membership is distinct from verified or assertable status. Provenance, composite status, four-valued judgment, argumentation, tracing, and safe introduction serve distinct roles. At the theory level, theory objects comprise object and relation sets under co-rootedness and well-founded dependency conditions. Theory evaluation, transformation, and positioning have separate conditional interfaces. At the intelligent-system level, maintenance constrains optimization. Boundary, stable, and higher-order intelligence depend on stated criteria; AI generation and model scale alone do not establish these qualifications. Behavioral interfaces conditionally connect complete action, interaction goals and evaluations, and traceable joint descriptions. A six-step metatheoretical workflow organizes the deconstruction, reconnection, and reconstruction of existing theories. Task-relative textual and geometric representations organize theoretical expression and retrieval without replacing the underlying theory texts. The contribution combines theory-internal axiomatic or quasi-axiomatic reconstruction with cross-level interface organization. It makes domains, dependencies, admissibility, failures, and theoretical effects explicit. summary: The evolution of DARIAH-IT from a distributed research infrastructure into a federated ecosystem of data centres, computational resources, digital services, scientific workflows, and research communities raises a fundamental technical and scientific question: how can an SSH research infrastructure preserve its essential functions when individual nodes, services, data resources, or dependencies suffer degradation, become unavailable, or are compromised? Addressing this question requires moving beyond component-level cybersecurity towards a systemic approach in which criticality, dependencies, functional continuity, recovery and adaptation become architectural properties of the infrastructure. Operational resilience must therefore be accompanied by epistemic resilience: the capacity of the infrastructure to preserve the conditions that make digital resources and computational processes trustworthy, interpretable, and scientifically reusable.  The relationship between cultural memory and machine memory provides a particularly relevant perspective for this discussion. As cultural knowledge is increasingly encoded into structured datasets and processed through automated and AI-supported environments, research infrastructures mediate between human interpretations of cultural memory and their computational representations. Their role therefore extends beyond the preservation and accessibility of digital resources to ensuring that cultural knowledge remains contextualised, interoperable, traceable, and reusable throughout its digital lifecycle. This workshop presents a resilience-by-design framework for the gradual evolution of DARIAH-IT, the Italian node of DARIAH (Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities), towards a Critical Research Infrastructure. The approach begins with a criticality assessment aimed at identifying which combinations of data, services, workflows, computational resources, identities and organisational dependencies are necessary to maintain essential scientific and cultural functions. Inventories of critical services, dependency maps, risk-impact matrices and domain-specific threat models form the basis for analysing the propagation of failures and identifying individual points of failure within the federation. Starting at an architectural level, the outlined framework requires investigating how geographically distributed resources can evolve from a set of interconnected nodes into a resilient federated infrastructure. Relevant mechanisms include containerised microservices, multi-cluster orchestration, service meshes, zero-trust API gateways, OAuth2/OIDC and mTLS, secure CI/CD pipelines, immutable backups, distributed replication, and business continuity and disaster recovery procedures. The central problem is therefore one of controlled interdependence: designing a federation in which services and resources can cooperate while preventing individual failures from propagating across the wider ecosystem. A complementary dimension concerns the resilience of scientific workflows. Workflows create dependencies that span services, datasets, computational environments, authentication mechanisms and external resources. Their resilience therefore requires reproducible execution environments, explicit dependency management, provenance tracking, continuous monitoring and mechanisms to detect and respond to anomalous behaviour. The evolution of the DARIAH-IT orchestration environment towards native containerised and distributed execution provides an experimental context for the study of adaptive workflows, anomaly detection, agent-based orchestration, federated learning and semi-automatic recovery mechanisms. For SSH infrastructures, however, operational continuity alone is not sufficient. A technically successful failover or recovery may still constitute a scientific failure if provenance, authenticity, semantic consistency, reproducibility or reliability are compromised. summary: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.
title: SinkState: On-the-Fly SVD of Recurrent States for Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving

summary: Study-level data and analysis code for a systematic critical review of automated shoeprint analysis. The data files contain, for the 101 Core studies, the eight forensic-readiness codes (0/1/2), the claimed forensic application (C0–C4) and the claim–evidence alignment, together with study characteristics, dataset provenance and evidence lineages. They also include the paired ratings of two independent reliability samples, the documented code changes, the ambiguous classifications used for sensitivity analysis, the unavailable reports and the statistical assessment of verification studies. The CSV files are identical to the article's Supplementary Tables. The Python script reproduce.py recomputes the agreement statistics, the readiness profile and sensitivity ranges, the claim–evidence alignment, the stratified and exploratory ordinal analyses, the leave-one-lineage-out and unavailable-report analyses, and Figures 3–5. See README.md for the file list and instructions.

summary: Air pollution is a leading environmental risk factor to human health worldwide. Fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) is of particular concern due to its ability to penetrate the lungs and enter the cardiovascular system, contributing to respiratory disease, cancer and early mortality. Accurate, high-resolution exposure estimates are therefore essential for assessing health risk and informing effective intervention strategies. However, regulated ground monitoring networks offer limited spatial coverage, and remote sensing and chemical transport models (CTMs) often fail to resolve local-scale variation in PM 2.5 concentrations. A further limitation is that most machine learning approaches to this problem are deterministic, providing no indication of predictive confidence. This study addresses both gaps with a Bayesian deep learning framework that downscales coarse CAMS CTM output to 1 km resolution by leveraging fine-scale land use, population and meteorological covariates and trained against ground observations. Predictive uncertainty was quantified via Monte Carlo dropout, a Bayesian approximation method that adds minimal computational cost. The model achieved strong deterministic accuracy (R 2 = 0.814) with well-calibrated, if slightly conservative, predictive intervals (95% coverage = 0.969) on held-out test data, offering a scalable approach for high-resolution exposure mapping with quantified uncertainty.
title: Uncertainty-aware deep learning for downscaling air quality concentrations

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Partial Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. As a result, some sites have WAV files with 0 bytes of data or timestamps outside the range of probable recording times. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. summary: This report documents the curation and open publication of measurements from a long-term Turkey oak ( Quercus cerris ) thinning experiment in the Gargano area, southern Italy, monitored from 1988 to 2026. Nine 0.5-ha plots compare an unthinned control with two thinning regimes: 15% basal-area reduction over two interventions and 33% basal-area reduction in one intervention. Legacy spreadsheet records were cleaned, validated, and organized into a documented SQLite database (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24142797) containing tree measurements, experimental design, controlled vocabularies, metadata, and provenance. The curation workflow addresses duplicate identifiers, irregular or gappy measurement series, unusable records, and missing values, with imputations explicitly flagged. The resource includes a richly documented database, a JSON file with PROV-O provenance, and an entity-relationship diagram of the database schema. It is intended to make the data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable in accordance with FAIR principles, and to provide a reproducible example of data curation for long-term forest research.

summary: Augmented reality (AR) is increasingly used in education, but most classroom studies focus on engagement rather than specific emotional or cognitive processes. We re-examined data from a six-week pilot project where AR was integrated into drama lessons for 59 primary-school students in four classes. Our goal was to see what the observations reveal about emotion recognition, emotion regulation, collaboration, problem solving, and reflective reasoning. QuiverVision and CoSpaces Edu were used for role-play, collaborative storytelling, exploring moods in space, replaying conflicts, and reflection. The data included teacher observation rubrics, structured checklists, student exit tickets, and records of regulation strategies. In this paper, we use affective computing as a conceptual framework, not as a description of the technology used in the pilot. Emotions were not detected automatically; instead, the analysis relies on human observation and student self-reports. Of the 106 exit-ticket responses from Weeks 1 and 2, happiness was the most common emotion (73 out of 106; 68.9%). Forty-eight students had emotion-recognition ratings recorded at Weeks 1, 2, 3, and 5, and these ratings changed over time (Friedman χ²(3)=34.21, p<0.001; Kendall's W=0.238), with the mean score rising from 2.90 (SD=0.66) in Week 1 to 3.46 (SD=0.50) in Week 5. Regulation strategies also varied by phase: socially oriented responses were frequent in Week 2, while breathing, pausing, and reframing were more common during the explicit regulation activities in Week 5. Because the prompts and tasks differed each week, these distributions are descriptive and do not show a causal pre/post change. Exploratory correlations found that collaborative storytelling was linked to problem solving, strategy use was associated with returning to role, and understanding emotions was connected with cooperation. Overall, the results show that a pedagogy-first AR drama approach is feasible and highlight what a future study would need: validated measures, comparison groups, multilevel analysis, follow-up data, and carefully controlled multimodal affect sensing.

summary: This record provides the computational benchmark instances, initial solutions, final feasible solutions, and source code supporting the study: "Coordinating Cross-Docking and Vehicle Routing under Time-Dependent Congestion-Zone Charges: An Integrated Optimization Approach." The synthetic benchmark includes 18 problem instances covering six customer-set sizes (8, 12, 14, 20, 30, and 50), together with 18 common initial solutions and saved algorithmic solutions from Direct MILP, VND4, Integrated ALNS, and Sequential ALNS. The archive also includes the selected model and algorithm source code required to inspect and reproduce the computational methods. For the three 50-customer instances, no feasible Direct-MILP incumbent was obtained within the recorded time limit. The three VND4 solutions are feasible budget-limited incumbents; the final N4 scans were not completed, and no full N4 local-optimality certificates are claimed. A separate Tehran V5 case-study component includes the available initial and algorithmic solutions and associated source code. Its original problem-instance JSON is not included because redistribution rights for the underlying travel-time/network data require further review. Consequently, this component is not fully self-contained for independent reruns. Execution logs, checkpoints, intermediate solutions, development history, and rerun archives are not included.

summary: Fixes Image placement: slice tuples work directly as NumPy indices. Canvas and overlap sizes use the same rounded offsets, including half-pixel shifts. offsets2slice(..., fits_convention=False) returned lists of slices, causing array[indices[i]] to raise IndexError . Now returns usable tuples. offseted_shape(shapes=[(3,), (3,)], offsets=[(0,), (1.5,)]) returned (4,) . Now returns (5,) , matching pixel placement. offseted_shape(..., method="inner") returned (0,) for touching images. Now raises ValueError when there are no shared pixels. offseted_shape(shapes=[(2.5,)], offsets=[(0,)]) silently rounded to (2,) . Now raises ValueError . FITS conversion: reverse slices retain their selected pixels; unrepresentable slices raise ValueError . slice(None, None, -1) became [:1] , selecting only the first pixel. Now becomes [:1:-1] , preserving the full reversal. slice(2, 2) became [3:2] , selecting two pixels instead of none. Now raises ValueError when converting to FITS. WCS and headers: coordinate arrays work. The default ignore_ltm=False applies LTM scaling with a matrix solve; singular or invalid transforms raise ValueError , including under python -O . loc_target=np.array([2, 3]) raised an ambiguous-truth ValueError . Now accepts coordinate arrays. loc_target="center" with unknown WCS.pixel_shape used zero dimensions. Now raises ValueError . LTV1=6, LTM1_1=2 returned [6] by default, ignoring scaling. Now returns [3.] ; ignore_ltm=True retains the raw value. Nonidentity LTM matrices rejected by the earlier validation-only fix are now supported. Input helpers: listify() broadcasts multiple inputs consistently; slicefy() accepts generators; bezel2slice(None) returns full slices. Development: explicit exports preserve public names. Development dependencies include Astropy and isort. Releases: Hatchling builds explicit package contents. CI tests installed distributions. A matching v* tag push publishes the tested files to PyPI after version, tag, changelog, lint, and test checks pass, then creates the GitHub release from this changelog. Migration checklist LTM: add ignore_ltm=True to retain raw LTV differences. The new default applies LTM correction and rejects invalid transforms. Image indices: replace whole tuples from offsets2slice() ; their elements are no longer mutable. Geometry: use matching shapes/offsets, nonnegative integer sizes, and finite offsets. Empty overlap raises ValueError ; half-pixel canvas sizes may change. FITS slices: keep negative bounds and empty slices in Python form with fits_convention=False . WCS centers: set WCS.pixel_shape , pass coordinates, or use "origin" . Also: listify(..., scalar2list=False) affects only single-input calls; slicefy() rejects empty iterable rules. Details: offsets , slices .

summary: License: ASSUME is now licensed under the MIT License instead of the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL-3.0-or-later). The SPDX headers, the package metadata and the documentation have been updated accordingly. The code of conduct, which is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, is licensed under CC-BY-4.0. New Features: Cement Plant DSM unit : Added a CementPlant unit modelling a fuel-switchable kiln line, each stage independently switchable between electricity, a natural-gas/coal mix, or hydrogen. Optional components include an electrolyser supplying the burners with on-site hydrogen, an electric-heater thermal storage (E-TES) that buffers calciner heat, and a raw material mill / cement mill. Either mill can also run standalone with no kiln line at all, in which case the declared demand targets that mill's own ground tonnage directly. Supports both full-horizon and rolling-horizon optimisation, and all of the existing DSMFlex flexibility measures. See the Demand Side Agent documentation for details. New demand-side technology components in dst_components.py : Added ThermalProcessStage , a shared base class for fuel-switchable thermal stages, with Preheater , Calciner , and Kiln subclasses used by the new cement plant. Calciner tracks process (calcination) CO2 emissions separately from energy emissions; Preheater accepts recovered waste heat from the kiln. Also added GrindingMill , a generic electric grinding component used for both raw material milling and cement grinding, and a new short-term_with_generator mode for ThermalStorage where an electric heater charges the storage from grid power. Electric vehicle model for buildings : Added an updated ElectricVehicle DSM component with explicit mobility-related energy use, availability-dependent operation, external range input, bidirectional or unidirectional power flow, and binary non-simultaneity for charging and discharging. Charging station model for buildings : Added a dedicated ChargingStation DSM component with optional availability profiles, ramp constraints, and support for unidirectional or bidirectional operation. Integrated EV and charging-station building topology : Buildings now support two connection modes: If no charging station is included, EVs connect directly to the building/grid balance. If charging stations are included, charging stations connect to the building/grid and EVs connect to the charging stations through assignment variables. Building-specific flexible electricity-price support : Added support for electricity_price_flex in BuildingForecaster for use with the electricity_price_signal flexibility measure. Generic Forecasting Interface : This interface enables to specify different forecast algorithms for preprocess, initialization and update during runtime. They can be specified in the config.yaml or unit csv files. For more information about currently implemented algorithms and how to specify them please read the documentation on Unit forecasts. Directional transfer capacities in complex clearing : complex_clearing can now use asymmetric line limits from s_nom_forward and s_nom_reverse instead of assuming the same transfer capacity in both directions. s_max_pu (defaulting to 1) is still applied to scale the directional limits. Operator-level forecaster : Unit operators can now own a UnitsOperatorForecaster providing their own market price and residual load forecasts (accessible via units_operator.forecaster ), instead of reading them from a managed unit. Forecast algorithms can be set per operator via forecast_* columns in unit_operators.csv , and the portfolio learning strategy now reads its price/residual-load observations from this operator forecaster. Market timing visualization : Added assume.common.market_timing to show when markets open, when bids can be submitted, when they are cleared and which periods they deliver, as a mermaid gantt diagram ( market_timing_to_mermaid ) or rendered in the terminal ( render_market_timing ). summary: This report presents the findings of the 2026 Ontology Landscaping Initiative (OLI), a joint initiative of the Pistoia Alliance, EMBL-EBI and ELIXIR. OLI was established to build a practical overview of the semantic resources used across pharmaceutical research and development, understand where and how they are applied, and identify recurring challenges around interoperability, mapping, governance and sustainability. The report draws on evidence gathered through a hybrid workshop held at the Wellcome Genome Campus on 16 July 2026, involving 87 participants across industry, academia, research infrastructures, standards organisations, CROs and technology providers. Discussions were organised around five areas of the R&D value chain: Discovery; Preclinical and Nonclinical Development; Clinical Development; Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls; and Regulatory Affairs and Pharmacovigilance. The findings show a rich but fragmented semantic landscape. The main challenges are not a lack of ontologies or standards, but selecting appropriate resources, connecting them across value-chain boundaries, maintaining reusable mappings and ensuring sufficient provenance, stewardship, licensing clarity and persistent identification. The report also considers how these issues affect the development of reliable, AI-ready data and highlights areas where cross-sector collaboration could reduce duplicated effort. Alongside the report, OLI has developed a structured metadata registry and Registry Explorer to support navigation of the landscape and provide a basis for further community validation and future use-case-led work.
title: Ontology Landscaping Initiative Workshop Report - 16 July 2026

summary: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the results from the Third International Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID Cards and Passports, which was held across two distinct tracks. Track 1 evaluates a synthetic-data-based ID-PAD system under controlled but diverse conditions, where the winning team, \textit{Incode}, achieves an A V R a n k of 27.82%, confirming consistent performance across metrics and highlighting the importance of a balanced, generalizable design. In Track 2, the challenge intensifies with heterogeneous attack scenarios across different domains, where \textit{Incode} again achieved the top position with an A V R a n k of 68.71% across thresholds, outperforming some baselines and established methods. These results demonstrate that PAD effectiveness requires not only high accuracy but also consistency across diverse attack types and imaging conditions. The success of this initiative across both tracks underscores the value of collaboration between companies and academic teams. This year, more than \textit{63 teams} were registered, and more than \textit{100 submission models} were evaluated. This competition has evolved into a leading benchmark for state-of-the-art PAD on ID documents, setting the standard for performance, reproducibility, and real-world applicability in secure identity verification.
title: The Third Competition on Document Forgery Detection on ID-Cards and Passports

summary: This study aims to investigate the effects of intranasal arginine vasopressin (AVP) on reversal learning and feedback processing in healthy adults with varying levels of compulsive tendencies. By combining behavioral measures, computational modeling, and electroencephalography (EEG), the study will examine how AVP influences value updating and action selection. Particular attention will be given to whether these effects depend on environmental stability and individual compulsive tendencies, and whether behavioral differences are accompanied by changes in feedback-related neural activity. The study uses a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group design. Following informed consent and baseline assessment, eligible healthy adult volunteers will be randomly assigned to receive a single intranasal dose of 20 IU AVP or an equivalent amount of placebo. Baseline assessments include the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R), the Padua Inventory (PI), and the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12), which assess obsessive-compulsive symptoms and intolerance of uncertainty. Participants will be classified into high (OCI-R ≥21) and low (OCI-R <21) compulsive-tendency groups for analysis. This grouping serves to examine individual differences and does not constitute a clinical diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder. Experimental tasks will begin approximately 35 minutes after intranasal administration, with resting-state and task-related EEG recorded. The probabilistic reversal-learning task comprises 250 experimental trials across stable and volatile learning environments: 150 trials in the stable phase and 100 trials in the volatile phase. During the volatile phase, choice–reward contingencies will change every 25 trials. Participants will use trial-by-trial feedback to adjust their choices and maximize reward points. Choice accuracy, reaction times, choices, and feedback outcomes will be recorded to assess learning performance and behavioral adaptation across environments. Choice accuracy will serve as the primary behavioral measure, with reaction time as a supplementary measure. Mixed-design analyses of variance incorporating drug treatment, compulsive tendency, and learning environment will assess treatment effects and their interactions with individual characteristics and environmental conditions. A hierarchical Bayesian reward–punishment reinforcement-learning model will estimate reward learning rate, punishment learning rate, and inverse temperature, distinguishing value updating following positive and negative feedback from value-guided choice consistency. EEG will be acquired using a 64-channel recording system and preprocessed using MNE-Python. Feedback-locked event-related potentials, including P2, feedback-related negativity (FRN), and P300, will be extracted to examine the effects of drug treatment, compulsive tendency, learning environment, and feedback type on neural activity. Integrating behavioral performance, computational parameters, and feedback-related EEG measures, the study will test whether AVP alters the neural modulation of feedback processing in individuals with high compulsive tendencies and inform understanding of the neuropeptide mechanisms underlying compulsivity-related cognitive flexibility.
title: Effects of intranasal arginine vasopressin on reversal learning and feedback processing in individuals with compulsive tendencies

summary: v1.0.0 — Research Materials Research materials supporting: "Evaluating Generative Engine Optimization for Educational Resource Selection: A Controlled Experiment with a Large Language Model" Study The experiment compares four educational-resource representations: Baseline Entity-structure GEO FAQ GEO Full GEO The design comprises 18 resources, 54 queries, four conditions, and three repetitions, yielding 648 model responses. Release Contents This release provides the research files included in the tagged repository snapshot, including experimental configurations, prompts, resource representations, scripts, per-response metrics, primary-analysis outputs, and response-quality review materials. Consult the repository README and file inventory for available materials and reproduction requirements. Interpretation No GEO condition showed a statistically significant improvement in recorded first-selection success relative to baseline after Holm correction. The results concern a fixed-corpus, single-model experiment and do not establish equivalence, deployed search-visibility gains, or educational learning outcomes. Provenance and Limitations Original raw response attempts are authoritative; derived tables and review files do not replace them. The UTF-8 refusal-review file is a derivative. Exact copied-text fidelity must not be assumed without a documented comparison against canonical sources. Structural validation and successful record joins do not establish substantive classification correctness. Reviewer identity, actual blinding, and AI assistance must be interpreted according to the accompanying review documentation. Repository publication does not constitute independent validation or an unconditional submission-readiness assessment. Reuse Consult LICENSE and any file-specific notices. Third-party content remains subject to its original permissions and restrictions.

summary: Platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, Twitter, and Telegram have a substantial influence on the dissemination of information in modern society. Numerous individuals rely on them without verifying the veracity of their information or the sources of their knowledge. False information is referred to as "Fake News" and is disseminated through both traditional and non traditional media channels including social media. Contemporary media consumers uncritically embrace the news they read online, rather than taking the time to critically assess it. This method has led to a heightened trust in internet content, which has facilitated the spread of misinformation. This article describes a machine learning (ML)-based approach to classifying and detecting fake news anomalies in online social media data. This framework accepts social media data as input. Features are chosen using the term frequency identification term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF IDF) and chi-square tests. The categorization model is then built utilizing approaches such as artificial neural network (ANN), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF). The classification model is trained and tested on a preprocessed data set. Finally, fake news is discovered, and the suggested framework is evaluated using measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. ANN is performing better for fake news classification and detection.
