summary: Global proteomic profiling of human platelet lysate (hPL) by data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS). The dataset was generated to identify the bioactive protein components of the platelet-derived preparation used in a study of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and cellular senescence. Acquisition. Single hPL sample, in-solution trypsin digestion, EASY-nLC 1200 coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (FAIMS, compensation voltage -45 V; full MS 350-1400 m/z at 60,000 resolution; MS/MS at 15,000 resolution, HCD 27% NCE). Processing. DIA-NN v1.8 against Homo_sapiens_9606_SP_20231220.fasta (20,429 entries) plus reverse decoy; trypsin/P with up to 1 missed cleavage; carbamidomethylation of cysteine and N-terminal methionine excision as fixed modifications; FDR < 1%. Contents. (1) all identified proteins with coverage, peptide counts and label-free intensity; (2) all identified peptides with charge, uniqueness and intensity; (3) the 15 most abundant proteins. README.md documents the full sample preparation, LC-MS parameters and processing settings. Because the analysis is a single-sample descriptive profiling rather than a comparative experiment, these tables contain the entire quantitative content of the acquisition.
title: Proteomic profiling of human platelet lysate by data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry

summary: The light yield of noble-element scintillation detectors depends strongly on the reflective properties of detector materials in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), where optical measurements are scarce. For this reason, we built a custom rotary setup at IFIC, equipped with a monochromator and operated in a gaseous argon atmosphere, to perform angle-resolved reflectance measurements in the specular reflection plane. We describe the setup and its extensive characterization, together with the procedure used to measure the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of materials at various angles of incidence, for wavelengths from 128 to 500 nm, covering both the argon (128 nm) and xenon (175 nm) scintillation wavelengths. To illustrate the capabilities of the setup, we present results for rough aluminum and stainless-steel surfaces as reference materials. Fitting the measured angular profiles with the analytical GGX microfacet model allows us to extract the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index and the surface roughness parameter of each sample. These parameters are then used to extrapolate the in-plane measurements to the full hemisphere and from gaseous argon to liquid media, enabling the inference of the hemispherical reflectance in gaseous argon, liquid argon and liquid xenon.
title: Angle-Resolved Reflectance Measurements in the Vacuum Ultraviolet for Metallic Samples

summary: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.
title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions

summary: English abstract This work develops a metalinguistic axiomatic framework for cognition, knowledge, theories, intelligent systems, and AI. At the cognitive level, the framework distinguishes objectified items, registered meta-level interfaces, and residual metalanguage, retaining failure and unevaluability. Evaluation, object admission, name binding, and state writeback each have separate conditions. At the knowledge level, knowledge-base membership is distinct from verified or assertable status. Provenance, composite status, four-valued judgment, argumentation, tracing, and safe introduction serve distinct roles. At the theory level, theory objects comprise object and relation sets under co-rootedness and well-founded dependency conditions. Theory evaluation, transformation, and positioning have separate conditional interfaces. At the intelligent-system level, maintenance constrains optimization. Boundary, stable, and higher-order intelligence depend on stated criteria; AI generation and model scale alone do not establish these qualifications. Behavioral interfaces conditionally connect complete action, interaction goals and evaluations, and traceable joint descriptions. A six-step metatheoretical workflow organizes the deconstruction, reconnection, and reconstruction of existing theories. Task-relative textual and geometric representations organize theoretical expression and retrieval without replacing the underlying theory texts. The contribution combines theory-internal axiomatic or quasi-axiomatic reconstruction with cross-level interface organization. It makes domains, dependencies, admissibility, failures, and theoretical effects explicit. Empirical scales, engineering realizations, and system effectiveness require independent implementation and testing. 中文摘要 认知、知识、理论、智能系统与人工智能研究常使用相互分离的概念语言。产生结果与引入对象、保存信息与接受知识、改善输出与维持系统等不同任务,也因此容易混淆。本文建立一套元语言公理化框架,通过对象层与元层接口连接这些研究层次。框架区分已对象化项目、已登记元语言接口,以及当前对象语言不能吸收的元语言余项,并保留失败与不可评价。 在认知与知识方面,框架分别规定求值、对象引入、名称绑定与状态写回的资格。知识库成员不等于已验证或可断言知识。来源、复合知识标签、主显示、四值判断、论证、回溯和安全引入各有职责;它们不构成所有候选必经的流水线。 在理论层,理论由对象集及其中的关系对象集构成,对象集须满足共根与依赖良基条件。原始对象与基本原理由内部前驱读取,理论品质、变换和结构位置则通过各自的条件接口处理。 在系统层,维持约束优化,边界、稳定和高阶智能按明示判据区分。AI的生成与规模本身不证明这些资格成立。行为附录通过条件接口接入完整行为结构、互动目标与评估,以及可追溯的联合描述。行为分类不等同于趋人化或主体资格。 前四章的部分接口被组织为六步流程,并由四组异质方法示例说明。收束命题仅在各步资格与输入输出条件成立时连接环节;示例本身不独立证明这些条件。第8章规定任务相关的文本与几何表示,并区分假设与待定承接位。索引调用受答案覆盖、局部正确性和完整成本约束。 本文结合选定概念的理论内重建与跨层接口组织,明确各项内容的对象域或元层角色、资格、依赖、失败值与理论效力。工程实现、经验量尺和系统效果仍需独立实现与检验。 Full texts and supplementary material This record provides the full text in English and Chinese, together with separate English and bilingual Chinese-English theory-framework diagrams to support reading and cross-referencing of the main text. summary: The evolution of DARIAH-IT from a distributed research infrastructure into a federated ecosystem of data centres, computational resources, digital services, scientific workflows, and research communities raises a fundamental technical and scientific question: how can an SSH research infrastructure preserve its essential functions when individual nodes, services, data resources, or dependencies suffer degradation, become unavailable, or are compromised? Addressing this question requires moving beyond component-level cybersecurity towards a systemic approach in which criticality, dependencies, functional continuity, recovery and adaptation become architectural properties of the infrastructure. Operational resilience must therefore be accompanied by epistemic resilience: the capacity of the infrastructure to preserve the conditions that make digital resources and computational processes trustworthy, interpretable, and scientifically reusable.  The relationship between cultural memory and machine memory provides a particularly relevant perspective for this discussion. As cultural knowledge is increasingly encoded into structured datasets and processed through automated and AI-supported environments, research infrastructures mediate between human interpretations of cultural memory and their computational representations. Their role therefore extends beyond the preservation and accessibility of digital resources to ensuring that cultural knowledge remains contextualised, interoperable, traceable, and reusable throughout its digital lifecycle. This workshop presents a resilience-by-design framework for the gradual evolution of DARIAH-IT, the Italian node of DARIAH (Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities), towards a Critical Research Infrastructure. The approach begins with a criticality assessment aimed at identifying which combinations of data, services, workflows, computational resources, identities and organisational dependencies are necessary to maintain essential scientific and cultural functions. Inventories of critical services, dependency maps, risk-impact matrices and domain-specific threat models form the basis for analysing the propagation of failures and identifying individual points of failure within the federation. Starting at an architectural level, the outlined framework requires investigating how geographically distributed resources can evolve from a set of interconnected nodes into a resilient federated infrastructure. Relevant mechanisms include containerised microservices, multi-cluster orchestration, service meshes, zero-trust API gateways, OAuth2/OIDC and mTLS, secure CI/CD pipelines, immutable backups, distributed replication, and business continuity and disaster recovery procedures. The central problem is therefore one of controlled interdependence: designing a federation in which services and resources can cooperate while preventing individual failures from propagating across the wider ecosystem. A complementary dimension concerns the resilience of scientific workflows. Workflows create dependencies that span services, datasets, computational environments, authentication mechanisms and external resources. Their resilience therefore requires reproducible execution environments, explicit dependency management, provenance tracking, continuous monitoring and mechanisms to detect and respond to anomalous behaviour. The evolution of the DARIAH-IT orchestration environment towards native containerised and distributed execution provides an experimental context for the study of adaptive workflows, anomaly detection, agent-based orchestration, federated learning and semi-automatic recovery mechanisms. For SSH infrastructures, however, operational continuity alone is not sufficient. A technically successful failover or recovery may still constitute a scientific failure if provenance, authenticity, semantic consistency, reproducibility or reliability are compromised. title: From a Federated Research Infrastructure to a Critical Research Infrastructure: A "Resilience by Design" Approach for DARIAH-IT

summary: Data and code for the ICSRS 2026 paper titled: "Subset Simulation for the Resilience Analysis of Critical Energy Infrastructures Exposed to Extreme Natural Hazards". Authors: Santiago Taguado Menza, Francesco Di Maio, Enrico Zio. Paper ID: R7171 Files contain the full data set, numerical inputs, parameters and code needed to reproduce the results of the paper in the following (3) modules: CEI_Module : model of the integrated power-and-gas network in Sicily (asset fragility, recovery, normalized energy supplied), with the AC-OPF and Weymouth gas network model that pre-computes the supplied power for all 2^13 = 8,192 failure combinations. Reliability_Algorithm : Monte Carlo simulation and Subset Simulation (component-wise modified Metropolis-Hastings), as used for Tables V and VI. Data_Analysis : simulation results and the script that computes Table VI and the resilience statistics. See README.txt for the file list and how to run.  Software: MATLAB R2026a with the Statistics and Machine Learning, Parallel Computing and Symbolic Math toolboxes, and MATPOWER.
title: Data and Code: Subset Simulation for the Resilience Analysis of Critical Energy Infrastructures Exposed to Extreme Natural Hazards

summary: Тривалий час в Україні поширений напрям органічного виробництва, проте останніми роками він набув стрімкого розвитку, навіть за умов війни Україна посідає провідні позиції щодо експорту такої продукції. За впровадження органічного виробництва ряд операторів в Україні стикаються з проблемою забезпечення якісного, органічного посадкового матеріалу, особливо проса. Площі за ведення органічного виробництва в Україні становлять 1 % від загальної площі сільськогосподарських угідь. Тому метою досліджень було вдосконалення елементів технології вирощування проса, як основи для отримання якісного посадкового матеріалу за органічного виробництва. Дослідження проводили впродовж 2022–2024 рр. на базі ПСП ім. Т.Г. Шевченка с. Тростинка, Васильківського району Київської області. Вивчали сорти проса Омріяне і Біла Альтанка та дозволені в органічному виробництві допоміжні продукти й умови їх внесення. Дозволені допоміжні продукти в органічному виробництві позитивно впливали на покращення енергії проростання, зокрема за застосування Біокомплексу-БТУ отримали 93,0 % у сорту Омріяне та 92,0 % – у сорту Біла Альтанка. Польова схожість досліджуваних сортів становила в межах 76,3–76,6 %. Кількість рослин проса у сорту Омріяне у фазу повних сходів була на рівні 243,0–245,8 шт./м², підвищення цього показника обумовлено застосуванням біопрепаратів. У разі застосування таких препаратів як Біокомплекс-БТУ та Органік-Баланс отримали врожайність проса на рівні 3,74–3,90 т/га порівняно з контрольними ділянками 2,49–2,73 т/га. English title: The influence of auxiliary products in organic production on sowing qualities and yield properties of millet seeds. Organic production has been widespread in Ukraine for a long time, but in recent years it has developed rapidly, even in war conditions, Ukraine occupies a leading position in the export of such products. When introducing organic production, a number of operators in Ukraine face the problem of providing high-quality organic planting material, especially millet. The area for organic production in Ukraine is 1% of the total area of farmlands. Therefore, the aim of the research was to improve the elements of millet cultivation technology as the basis for obtaining high-quality planting material under organic production. The research was carried out during 2022-2024 on the basis of T.H.Shevchenko private agricultural enterprise, village Trostinka, Vasylkiv district, Kyiv region. The millet varieties («Omriyane» and «Bila Altanka»), the auxiliary products permitted in organic production and the conditions of their application were studied. Permitted auxiliary products in organic production had a positive effect on the improvement of germination energy, in particular with the use of «Biocomplex BTU» obtained 93,0% in the «Omriyane» variety and 92,0% in the «Bila Altanka» variety. The field germination of the studied varieties was in the range of 76,3-76,6%. The number of millet plants of the «Omriyane» variety in the phase of full emergence was at the level of 243,0-245,8 pl./m², the increase of this indicator was due to the use of biological preparations. With the use of such preparations as «Biocomplex BTU» and «Organic-Balance», the millet yield was obtained at the level of 3,74-3,90 t/ha compared to the control plots of 2,49-2,73 t/ha. С. 43–50. https://doi.org/10.33245/2310-9270-2024-191-2-43-50
title: Вплив допоміжних продуктів в органічному виробництві на посівні якості та врожайні властивості насіння проса

summary: R analysis code and summary result tables for the paper “Metabolic gene-expression scores add no prognostic information on late recurrence of ER-positive breast cancer: a multicohort, multi-omic study”. The study tests whether gene-expression scores of four metabolic programs (glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation, oxidative phosphorylation and the lysosome), 159 metabolic pathways and 2319 metabolic genes in the primary tumour carry information on distant recurrence after 5 years in ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer (METABRIC, with external MetaGxBreast cohorts and GSE17705). It also examines what the scores measure (variance decomposition, split-half reliability, matched metabolite levels, copy number) and compares them with random gene sets of the same size. Contents: analysis and figure scripts (folder scripts/), summary result tables needed to run the figure and table scripts (folder 04_tables/), gene-set definitions (gene symbols only) and the cohort and covariate tables derived from the open clinical data. The README describes the data sources, the order in which to run the scripts, and which script produces each figure and table. METABRIC gene expression data are under controlled access (European Genome-phenome Archive) and are not included. Changes in this version: the figure and table numbering follows the published paper; Figure 1 and Figure 5 labels updated; new script for Supplementary Fig. S16; the random-gene-set benchmark script no longer writes the size-matched Hallmark comparison or the former four-panel figure (the Hallmark subsets are still drawn, so that the random-number sequence and all reported values are unchanged); Supplementary Table S4 updated. The changed scripts were run again from this repository and reproduced the published output tables. Licence: MIT.
title: Analysis code for: Metabolic gene-expression scores add no prognostic information on late recurrence of ER-positive breast cancer: a multicohort, multi-omic study

summary: The study evaluates the effectiveness of a methodology for developing professional digital competencies of pre-service primary school teachers through improved software and methodological support. The methodology combined a six-block methodological model, the integrating educational platform “DigiPed” with five curriculum-aligned modules, a unified cycle of innovative methods and a multi-stage assessment system. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design with non-equivalent intact groups was carried out in 2023–2025 at three higher education institutions in Uzbekistan with 770 students (experimental group n = 386, control group n = 384). Competence was measured on motivational, cognitive, activity and reflective criteria combined into a weighted integral index K = 0.20k₁ + 0.25k₂ + 0.35k₃ + 0.20k₄; assessors were blind to group membership. At baseline the groups did not differ (χ² = 0.08–3.39; t = 0.13–1.03). After three semesters the experimental group’s mean integral score rose from 56.77 to 67.52 and the control group’s from 56.26 to 59.24 (t = 9.79, p < 0.05). The share of experimental students at the low level fell from 62.7 % to 30.8 % (control group: 51.8 %), and differences were significant on all criteria (χ² = 49.75–68.31). The efficiency coefficient was η = 1.14 overall and 1.13–1.17 across institutions, indicating that the effect is transferable beyond a single university.

summary: This release contains measurement-while-drilling (MWD) azimuthal resistivity and geosignal data from ten horizontal wellbores in the Ekofisk field, Norwegian North Sea (block 2/4). The data are phase and attenuation resistivity at three frequencies (2 MHz, 500 kHz and 125 kHz) and several transmitter–receiver spacings, with geosignals and 32-bin azimuthal images. Each run also includes composite logs and the well path from DISKOS, Norway's national subsurface data repository, all on one measured-depth index. Motivation Deep azimuthal resistivity is widely used to map boundaries and steer wells. However, few public datasets contain the multi-frequency, multi-spacing and azimuthal measurements that inversion needs. We release these data to: Build and test new inversion algorithms  on field measurements rather than synthetic data alone. Provide a shared benchmark , so different inversion workflows can be run on the same wells and their results compared and reproduced. Each run includes the image channels, conventional logs and well trajectory, so a full inversion can be set up from one file. This notebook describes what is delivered, then opens a DLIS file, inspects its channels, plots conventional logs against measured depth, and provides an interactive viewer for the azimuthal image channels. What is included Each of the eleven delivered DLIS files represents one wellbore run. The two 2/4-Z-25 runs remain separate files; they have not been spliced together. Files contain: New MWD measurements:  averaged resistivity ( AR* ), azimuthal resistivity ( ZR* ), and geosignal ( ZG* ) channels, including azimuthal image channels with 32 bins per depth sample. 2/4-VB-5 H T5 and 2/4-VC-2 Y3H have no  ZG  data. DISKOS composite logs:  where available, gamma ray ( GR ), deep and medium resistivity ( RDEP ,  RMED ), density ( DEN ,  DENC ), neutron ( NEU ), photoelectric factor ( PEF ), caliper ( CALI ), bit size ( BS ), rate of penetration ( ROP ), and acoustic ( AC / ACS ) measurements. DISKOS well path:  measured-depth-aligned  TVD ,  TVDSS ,  INC ,  AZI ,  UTMX , and  UTMY values. summary: Data behind the benchmark in the article "How should sub-cellular spatial transcriptomics be quality controlled? A guideline from a benchmark with injected damage" (manuscript in preparation). Forty public Visium HD sections were thinned to fixed depths (12, 25, 50 and 100 mean UMIs per 8 µm bin, and 200 on six sections), and low-quality regions (LQRs) of known size and position were injected: signal loss (1% of counts kept) and mitochondrial elevation. LQRs were 32, 64 and 256 µm across in the tissue interior and at the tissue edge, and 512 µm across in the interior of 38 sections. Each QC method and bin size (an arm) was run on every condition. One archive per section holds, for every depth: the parameters and random seed of each injection step, the ground truth (the 8 µm bins inside an LQR), the 8 µm bins each arm removed, the arms that stopped with an error, and the scores and marker-gene validation. README.md describes the layout and MD5SUMS.txt the checksums. The count matrices are not included. They are rebuilt from the public sections with the benchmark code and the recorded parameters. The source of every section, as the file it was read from, is in sources.tsv: 35 sections released by 10x Genomics and five from Cervilla, Grases Mendoza and Porta-Pardo (Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.17999961); sources.tsv gives the licence of each. They are also listed below as related works.
title: Benchmark data for: How should sub-cellular spatial transcriptomics be quality controlled? A guideline from a benchmark with injected damage

The data files contain, for the 101 Core studies, the eight forensic-readiness codes (0/1/2), the claimed forensic application (C0–C4) and the claim–evidence alignment, together with study characteristics, dataset provenance and evidence lineages. summary: This report documents the curation and open publication of measurements from a long-term Turkey oak ( Quercus cerris ) thinning experiment in the Gargano area, southern Italy, monitored from 1988 to 2026. Nine 0.5-ha plots compare an unthinned control with two thinning regimes: 15% basal-area reduction over two interventions and 33% basal-area reduction in one intervention. Legacy spreadsheet records were cleaned, validated, and organized into a documented SQLite database (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24142797) containing tree measurements, experimental design, controlled vocabularies, metadata, and provenance. The curation workflow addresses duplicate identifiers, irregular or gappy measurement series, unusable records, and missing values, with imputations explicitly flagged. The resource includes a richly documented database, a JSON file with PROV-O provenance, and an entity-relationship diagram of the database schema. It is intended to make the data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable in accordance with FAIR principles, and to provide a reproducible example of data curation for long-term forest research.
title: Data curation example - Almost 50 years of forest monitoring

summary: This repository provides the data, spatial analysis polygons, statistical outputs and reproducible Python workflows associated with the manuscript “Satellite-based aftercare screening for data-scarce landfills: 27 years of vegetation trajectories and baseline sensitivity in Vietnam”. The study examines six Vietnamese landfill sites represented by eight analysis polygons over 1999–2025. The archive includes date-level Landsat Collection 2 observations and Sentinel-2 cross-check exports; approximate site and sector polygons; controlled interrupted time-series analysis; recovery and repeated-parity metrics; Kieu Ky within-site contrasts and baseline-length sensitivity; Typhoon Yagi relative vegetation departures; and supplementary results tables B1–B9. The supplied scripts reproduce statistical tables and article figures from the archived exports without requiring Google Earth Engine access. Google Earth Engine scripts and a Colab notebook are included for re-extraction, subject to user credentials and project setup. These observations support first-stage landfill aftercare screening and prioritisation of field inspections; the analysis polygons are interpreted study areas rather than surveyed waste footprints. summary: Augmented reality (AR) is increasingly used in education, but most classroom studies focus on engagement rather than specific emotional or cognitive processes. We re-examined data from a six-week pilot project where AR was integrated into drama lessons for 59 primary-school students in four classes. Our goal was to see what the observations reveal about emotion recognition, emotion regulation, collaboration, problem solving, and reflective reasoning. QuiverVision and CoSpaces Edu were used for role-play, collaborative storytelling, exploring moods in space, replaying conflicts, and reflection. The data included teacher observation rubrics, structured checklists, student exit tickets, and records of regulation strategies. In this paper, we use affective computing as a conceptual framework, not as a description of the technology used in the pilot. Emotions were not detected automatically; instead, the analysis relies on human observation and student self-reports. Of the 106 exit-ticket responses from Weeks 1 and 2, happiness was the most common emotion (73 out of 106; 68.9%). Forty-eight students had emotion-recognition ratings recorded at Weeks 1, 2, 3, and 5, and these ratings changed over time (Friedman χ²(3)=34.21, p<0.001; Kendall's W=0.238), with the mean score rising from 2.90 (SD=0.66) in Week 1 to 3.46 (SD=0.50) in Week 5. Regulation strategies also varied by phase: socially oriented responses were frequent in Week 2, while breathing, pausing, and reframing were more common during the explicit regulation activities in Week 5. Because the prompts and tasks differed each week, these distributions are descriptive and do not show a causal pre/post change. Exploratory correlations found that collaborative storytelling was linked to problem solving, strategy use was associated with returning to role, and understanding emotions was connected with cooperation. Overall, the results show that a pedagogy-first AR drama approach is feasible and highlight what a future study would need: validated measures, comparison groups, multilevel analysis, follow-up data, and carefully controlled multimodal affect sensing.
title: GENEDIS 2026 – Paper 79 – Augmented Reality-Enhanced Drama Through an Affective Computing Lens: A Six-Week Pilot Study of Emotional Intelligence, Emotion Regulation, and Reflective Reasoning in Children

summary: This record provides the computational benchmark instances, initial solutions, final feasible solutions, and source code supporting the study: "Coordinating Cross-Docking and Vehicle Routing under Time-Dependent Congestion-Zone Charges: An Integrated Optimization Approach." The synthetic benchmark includes 18 problem instances covering six customer-set sizes (8, 12, 14, 20, 30, and 50), together with 18 common initial solutions and saved algorithmic solutions from Direct MILP, VND4, Integrated ALNS, and Sequential ALNS. The archive also includes the selected model and algorithm source code required to inspect and reproduce the computational methods. For the three 50-customer instances, no feasible Direct-MILP incumbent was obtained within the recorded time limit. The three VND4 solutions are feasible budget-limited incumbents; the final N4 scans were not completed, and no full N4 local-optimality certificates are claimed. A separate Tehran V5 case-study component includes the available initial and algorithmic solutions and associated source code. Its original problem-instance JSON is not included because redistribution rights for the underlying travel-time/network data require further review. Consequently, this component is not fully self-contained for independent reruns. Execution logs, checkpoints, intermediate solutions, development history, and rerun archives are not included.
title: Computational Dataset and Source Code for Coordinating Cross-Docking and Vehicle Routing under Time-Dependent Congestion-Zone Charges

summary: Fixes Image placement: slice tuples work directly as NumPy indices. Canvas and overlap sizes use the same rounded offsets, including half-pixel shifts. offsets2slice(..., fits_convention=False) returned lists of slices, causing array[indices[i]] to raise IndexError . Now returns usable tuples. offseted_shape(shapes=[(3,), (3,)], offsets=[(0,), (1.5,)]) returned (4,) . Now returns (5,) , matching pixel placement. offseted_shape(..., method="inner") returned (0,) for touching images. Now raises ValueError when there are no shared pixels. offseted_shape(shapes=[(2.5,)], offsets=[(0,)]) silently rounded to (2,) . Now raises ValueError . FITS conversion: reverse slices retain their selected pixels; unrepresentable slices raise ValueError . slice(None, None, -1) became [:1] , selecting only the first pixel. Now becomes [:1:-1] , preserving the full reversal. slice(2, 2) became [3:2] , selecting two pixels instead of none. Now raises ValueError when converting to FITS. WCS and headers: coordinate arrays work. The default ignore_ltm=False applies LTM scaling with a matrix solve; singular or invalid transforms raise ValueError , including under python -O . loc_target=np.array([2, 3]) raised an ambiguous-truth ValueError . Now accepts coordinate arrays. loc_target="center" with unknown WCS.pixel_shape used zero dimensions. Now raises ValueError . LTV1=6, LTM1_1=2 returned [6] by default, ignoring scaling. Now returns [3.] ; ignore_ltm=True retains the raw value. Nonidentity LTM matrices rejected by the earlier validation-only fix are now supported. Input helpers: listify() broadcasts multiple inputs consistently; slicefy() accepts generators; bezel2slice(None) returns full slices. Development: explicit exports preserve public names. Development dependencies include Astropy and isort. Releases: Hatchling builds explicit package contents. CI tests installed distributions. A matching v* tag push publishes the tested files to PyPI after version, tag, changelog, lint, and test checks pass, then creates the GitHub release from this changelog. Migration checklist LTM: add ignore_ltm=True to retain raw LTV differences. The new default applies LTM correction and rejects invalid transforms. Image indices: replace whole tuples from offsets2slice() ; their elements are no longer mutable. Geometry: use matching shapes/offsets, nonnegative integer sizes, and finite offsets. Empty overlap raises ValueError ; half-pixel canvas sizes may change. FITS slices: keep negative bounds and empty slices in Python form with fits_convention=False . WCS centers: set WCS.pixel_shape , pass coordinates, or use "origin" . Also: listify(..., scalar2list=False) affects only single-input calls; slicefy() rejects empty iterable rules. Details: offsets , slices .
title: ysBach/astro-ndslice: v0.4

New Features: Cement Plant DSM unit : Added a CementPlant unit modelling a fuel-switchable kiln line, each stage independently switchable between electricity, a natural-gas/coal mix, or hydrogen. Optional components include an electrolyser supplying the burners with on-site hydrogen, an electric-heater thermal storage (E-TES) that buffers calciner heat, and a raw material mill / cement mill. Either mill can also run standalone with no kiln line at all, in which case the declared demand targets that mill's own ground tonnage directly. Supports both full-horizon and rolling-horizon optimisation, and all of the existing DSMFlex flexibility measures. See the Demand Side Agent documentation for details. New demand-side technology components in dst_components.py : Added ThermalProcessStage , a shared base class for fuel-switchable thermal stages, with Preheater , Calciner , and Kiln subclasses used by the new cement plant. Calciner tracks process (calcination) CO2 emissions separately from energy emissions; Preheater accepts recovered waste heat from the kiln. Also added GrindingMill , a generic electric grinding component used for both raw material milling and cement grinding, and a new short-term_with_generator mode for ThermalStorage where an electric heater charges the storage from grid power. Electric vehicle model for buildings : Added an updated ElectricVehicle DSM component with explicit mobility-related energy use, availability-dependent operation, external range input, bidirectional or unidirectional power flow, and binary non-simultaneity for charging and discharging. Charging station model for buildings : Added a dedicated ChargingStation DSM component with optional availability profiles, ramp constraints, and support for unidirectional or bidirectional operation. Integrated EV and charging-station building topology : Buildings now support two connection modes: If no charging station is included, EVs connect directly to the building/grid balance. If charging stations are included, charging stations connect to the building/grid and EVs connect to the charging stations through assignment variables. Building-specific flexible electricity-price support : Added support for electricity_price_flex in BuildingForecaster for use with the electricity_price_signal flexibility measure. Generic Forecasting Interface : This interface enables to specify different forecast algorithms for preprocess, initialization and update during runtime. They can be specified in the config.yaml or unit csv files. For more information about currently implemented algorithms and how to specify them please read the documentation on Unit forecasts. Directional transfer capacities in complex clearing : complex_clearing can now use asymmetric line limits from s_nom_forward and s_nom_reverse instead of assuming the same transfer capacity in both directions. s_max_pu (defaulting to 1) is still applied to scale the directional limits. Operator-level forecaster : Unit operators can now own a UnitsOperatorForecaster providing their own market price and residual load forecasts (accessible via units_operator.forecaster ), instead of reading them from a managed unit. Forecast algorithms can be set per operator via forecast_* columns in unit_operators.csv , and the portfolio learning strategy now reads its price/residual-load observations from this operator forecaster. Market timing visualization : Added assume.common.market_timing to show when markets open, when bids can be submitted, when they are cleared and which periods they deliver, as a mermaid gantt diagram ( market_timing_to_mermaid ) or rendered in the terminal ( render_market_timing ). summary: This record contains the Python code and the reference outputs for the manuscript *What bonus–malus claims identify about accidents that are never claimed* by Wei Zhu (University of Groningen). The code simulates a bonus–malus portfolio in which policyholders report only losses above Lemaire-type retentions, and computes the cross-cell envelope lower bound on unclaimed accidents, its plug-in and fixed-comparison-cell estimates with a one-sided confidence bound, sensitivity factors for departures from common severity, the power of the tail restriction, and the bias and error of audit designs selected on claim history. It also produces the empirical analysis of the French motor liability data freMTPL2: claim frequencies by recorded bonus–malus coefficient, the contrast built on the protection of a first claim and its placebo, and a check on the fremotor1 data. README.md maps every table and result of the paper to the script that produces it, and run_all.py reruns all scripts and compares the regenerated tables with the reference ones. The data (freMTPL2 from OpenML and CASdatasets, fremotor1 from CASdatasets) are public and are not included; data/README.md lists the files and their SHA-256 checksums. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, statsmodels, patsy and pyreadr.
title: Code for: What bonus-malus claims identify about accidents that are never claimed

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24146492 . Peer review report: Caetano et al., investigate the diversity of mammalian box C/D small nucleolar RNAs (SNORDs) by combining Fibrillarin- and Snu13-associated RNA sequencing with extensive analysis of publicly available datasets. They identify 21,732 candidate loci, including a large population of unusually short single-stranded RNAs (20-50 nt), termed tiSNORDs. This work is important because it challenges the current annotation of the mammalian snoRNAs and raises fundamental questions about snoRNP biogenesis and the emergence of regulatory RNAs. Particularly convincing are the enrichment of characteristic box C/D sequence signatures, the association of selected candidates with Fibrillarin, and the demonstration that a 36-nt tiSNORD can guide RNA methylation. The observations concerning terminal stem structures, RNA stability and host-gene expression provide further support for the biological relevance of at least a subset of these RNAs. Therefore, the study is interesting and potentially significant. Addressing several methodological and interpretative concerns , particularly regarding library-preparation biases, statistical validation of candidate identification, and the distinction between mature RNAs and RNA fragments would strengthen claims and introduce reproducibility. Major points: 1. RNA library preparation and size-selection bias. Approximately ~70 % of tiSNORDs are 20-50 nt long, yet the size-selection used with the TruSeq small RNA library preparation kit is not specified. Size-dependent recovery and sequence-dependent ligation biases could substantially influence this distribution. The authors acknowledge such biases for SNORD50 and substantial technical variability between datasets. Clarification of the selected insert range and, ideally, independent analysis of RNAs across a broader size range would strengthen this central conclusion. One would be to use splint-ligation library preparation to get 'unbiased' small RNA library for sequencing (e.g. Maguire et al., 2020; PMID: 32496547). 2. Statistical validation of sequence signatures. The identification of tiSNORDs relies heavily on canonical C/D-box motifs, their terminal positions and uridine enrichment (Figures 1C to 1G). However, no explicit null model accounts for the search criteria, meaning that some positional enrichment is expected by construction. Small RNA-seq ligation biases may also influence nucleotide frequencies (Kim et al., 2019; PMID: 30605524). Permutation analyses using length- and composition-matched intronic sequences processed through the same pipeline would help ensure statistical significance and estimate false-positive rates. Potential spike ins would be of use as well. 3. Distinguishing mature tiSNORDs from RNA fragments. Although the authors demonstrate stable endogenous expression of tiSNORD candidate and successful processing of selected ectopically expressed candidates, these findings cannot necessarily be extrapolated to thousands of low-abundance sequences. Examining coverage across candidate loci, overlapping fragments, flanking regions and potential longer precursors would help distinguish independently matured tiSNORDs from RNA processing or degradation/fragmentation products. 4. Confidence in the proposed repertoire. 12% of candidates exceed one count per million, and substantial discrepancies are observed between independent datasets (Supplementary Figure 3). The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations further in the text, but the claim that more than 20,000 loci substantially expand the snoRNA repertoire is a potential since it does not have biochemical validation and mentioning that they are "putative" in the abstract would help the reader to understand the scope of this article. Stratification by abundance, reproducibility and independent experimental evidence wou
title: PREreview of "A novel class of tiny box C/D-like RNAs reveals hidden complexity in the mouse box C/D RNA repertoire"

summary: Text from Wikipedia in 17 languages (Catalan, Mandarin, German, English, Basque, Finnish, French, Hungarian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, Serbian, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese and Cantonese), 19,436,200 rows, each with the syllables a counting pipeline found in it: 391,330,566 syllables in all. It is the text of the second of two corpora used by the study "Context-window sensitivity of cross-linguistic information rate", a replication and extension of Coupé, Oh, Dediu & Pellegrino (2019), Science Advances 5(9): eaaw2594, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aaw2594. Each language appears under the counting convention listed first for it in the study's pre-registered list of conventions. The rows are those the analysis read: every held-out article, and the training articles up to the largest training budget the language reached. Files: README.md is the datasheet (format, counts, source and sampling, the syllabification tools and conventions for each language, how the analysis reads the rows, known limits, attribution, use of AI). syllabified-wikipedia-v1.tar holds the release folder: one gzipped, tab-separated file per language (article, line, split, status, the syllables as a JSON array of words, and the text), the article URLs, each training budget's cut, a summary, the scripts that wrote it, the licence files and SHA-256 checksums of every file. LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff are also given separately. The study's decision record, with each convention's sources, is public at https://github.com/BrettRey/info-rate-context-prereg and registered at https://osf.io/m4cjp. The text is from Wikipedia (Hugging Face wikimedia/wikipedia, snapshot 20231101), by its contributors, and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0.

It is the text of the second of two corpora used by the study "Context-window sensitivity of cross-linguistic information rate", a replication and extension of Coupé, Oh, Dediu & Pellegrino (2019), Science Advances 5(9): eaaw2594, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aaw2594. Each language appears under the counting convention listed first for it in the study's pre-registered list of conventions. The rows are those the analysis read: every held-out article, and the training articles up to the largest training budget the language reached. Files: README.md is the datasheet (format, counts, source and sampling, the syllabification tools and conventions for each language, how the analysis reads the rows, known limits, attribution, use of AI). syllabified-wikipedia-v1.tar holds the release folder: one gzipped, tab-separated file per language (article, line, split, status, the syllables as a JSON array of words, and the text), the article URLs, each training budget's cut, a summary, the scripts that wrote it, the licence files and SHA-256 checksums of every file. LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff are also given separately. The study's decision record, with each convention's sources, is public at https://github.com/BrettRey/info-rate-context-prereg and registered at https://osf.io/m4cjp. The text is from Wikipedia (Hugging Face wikimedia/wikipedia, snapshot 20231101), by its contributors, and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0.
title: Syllabified Wikipedia text in 17 languages, as counted for a study of cross-linguistic information rate

summary: Code, configuration, results and annotation protocol for the manuscript "Measurable Wording of Course Learning Outcomes: An Auditable Design-Time Screen in One Computer Science Program". The package contains a rule-based screener for measurable wording of course learning outcomes (CLOs), a multi-label assessment-instrument recommender evaluated on 20 seeded course-disjoint resamples, baselines (PLO only, sentence embeddings, classifier chain, zero-shot LLM), calibration and routing analyses, a verb-level alignment analysis, and scripts that score the screener against expert labels. The CLO texts are institutional course-report records and are not included. They are available from the corresponding author on request, subject to the institution's permission.
title: Replication package: Measurable Wording of Course Learning Outcomes: An Auditable Design-Time Screen in One Computer Science Program

summary: Data and code to reproduce all tables and figures in "Priced In, Not Zoned Out: Social Capital, Land-Use Regulation, and US Housing Prices." The package tests whether bridging social capital lowers housing prices through trust, or civic and bonding social capital raises them by restricting supply. It contains: - County data (1,747 counties): FHFA residential land prices per acre (Davis, Larson, Oliner and Shui 2021), Social Capital Atlas measures (Chetty et al. 2022), Census building permits 2012-2024, and Wharton WRLURI 2018 metropolitan means. - Metropolitan data (530 CBSAs): WRLURI 2018 and population-weighted social capital. - State panel, 1975-2019: OECD regional house price indices (FHFA), BEA per-capita income and population (SAINC4), CPI-U; 51-unit and 50-state (DC excluded) versions. - Stata 19.5 do-files: CD, CIPS, Westerlund bootstrap cointegration, PMG/MG, CS-ARDL, CS-DL, CCE-MG, Driscoll-Kraay, Mundlak CRE, MMQR, and county/metro fixed-effects models. - Python scripts: 50-state estimates, MMQR with state-cluster bootstrap, density interactions, and robustness checks. - Codebook, README with sources and terms of use, and Figures 1-2. WRLURI survey microdata are not redistributed; only metropolitan-area means derived from them are included.
title: Replication package: Priced In, Not Zoned Out: Social Capital, Land-Use Regulation, and US Housing Prices

summary: R code to reproduce all estimates in the article "Gateway or add-on? Prepaid cards and banking depth in Chilean households". The script uses the 2024 Chilean Household Finance Survey (Encuesta Financiera de Hogares, EFH 2024) of the Central Bank of Chile. It estimates survey-weighted probit models of prepaid card use (EFH item u_tprepago) as a function of banking depth (unbanked, demand account only, current account), non-bank credit, and respondent and household characteristics. Models are estimated separately in each of the 30 implicates, variances are computed with the 1,000 EFH bootstrap replicate weights, and estimates are combined with Rubin's rules. The script reports average marginal effects, contrast models for prepaid vouchers and any prepaid use, interaction analyses (current account x income stratum, age x gender), regressions for a digital financial inclusion index, and Oster (2019) bounds. Results are exported to an Excel workbook. The EFH microdata are not included. They are available from the Central Bank of Chile upon registration. See README.md for data access, software requirements, run instructions and the mapping between output sheets and the article's tables.
title: Replication code for: Gateway or add-on? Prepaid cards and banking depth in Chilean households

summary: Abstract Generative visual AI is increasingly used in early-stage design to produce sketches, concept renderings and alternative visual directions. However, visually convincing outputs do not necessarily constitute traceable or justified design decisions. In human–AI co-creation, generated images may remain weakly connected to design intent, evaluation criteria, evidence and design rationale, making the creative process difficult to review, reuse, and, where applicable, assess consistently. This paper proposes a process-level methodological framework for human–AI co-creation with generative visual AI systems. The framework is conceived as a lightweight traceability schema linking design problem, design intent, evaluation criteria, generative input, AI output, selected and rejected features, specifications, evidence, design decisions and iteration records. Its purpose is not to explain the internal behaviour of the generative model, but to document the human interpretation and decision-making process around generated visual artefacts. The proposal is illustrated through a postgraduate conceptual product design case in which generative visual AI was introduced after a systemic intent-structuring phase. The case provides evidence of feasibility for reconstructing the relationship between prior intent, generated outputs, and design decisions, but it is not presented as a controlled validation. The paper contributes to creative AI and human–AI interaction by reframing generated outputs as intermediate artefacts that require explicit links to intent, evidence and accountable design decisions.
title: From Generative Output to Traceable Design Decisions: A Process-Level Framework for Human–AI Co-Creation in Conceptual Design

summary: The triangular Lagrange point of the restricted three-body problem and the radial motion of a charged particle in a Penning trap are both equilibria held at a maximum of an effective potential by a gyroscopic force. Each possesses one mode of negative energy, and each loses linear stability when its two frequencies collide—one at Routh’s mass ratio, the other at the trapping limit. Both systems belong to a single family of planar gyroscopic Hamiltonians. On every level of the conserved angular-momentum invariant, the degree-four normal form of any member at such a collision coincides with the reduced Hamiltonian of an axisymmetric Penning trap whose detuning is shifted by a term proportional to the invariant and whose quartic coefficient is fixed by a single normal-form invariant. On the level containing orbits that start at rest, this reduction yields closed-form laws for the largest excursion, the escape threshold, and the escape time. These laws depend only on the sign of the quartic coefficient and on scaled variables. At the triangular point the coefficient is positive, placing the collision in the soft class: orbits remain confined after stability is lost, with an excursion that grows like the square root of the distance past the critical value. Direct integration confirms the soft law to a fraction of a percent at the smallest detunings tested. Two traps whose quartic coefficient matches that of the triangular point reproduce the same law. Traps with the opposite sign escape at the predicted threshold and in the predicted times. A randomized ensemble of members confirms the classification by the sign of the coefficient. Two further results hold for every member of the family. Before the collision the linear transient gain is exactly the inverse square root of the frequency splitting. With isotropic velocity damping the first-order growth rates depend only on the undamped frequencies, and at the collision they scale with the square root of the damping rate. The first of these explains earlier reports of apparent escape just below Routh’s value as ordinary linear transients that reach a fixed radius. The second recovers the classical magnetron-instability formula as a special case. The results are local, planar, and classical. What transfers between the asteroid and the trap is the normal-form dynamics on each level of the invariant, the transient gain, and the damped linear rates. What does not transfer without further work is the behaviour beyond the normal-form neighbourhood, where the gravitational terms of every order cause the triangular point to deviate from any purely quartic trap.
title: An Asteroid in a Penning Trap

summary: v2026-11-10b release — scoring-shortcut full fix (correctness patch, no new data). Fixes four shortcuts in the v4 scoring pipeline discovered during audit of scripts/score_v4.py + scripts/enrich_v7_scores.py . Same v7 union peak set (2,085,175 peaks), same 10 cohorts (67 patients), same 430 pseudobulks as v2026-11-10. enhancer_candidate_matrix.parquet , peak_provenance.parquet , and union_peak_reference.bed are byte-identical. Only the scores and derived reports changed. Shortcuts fixed: (1) spec_pct_myeloid was ranking log1p(cpm_myeloid) — strength on a different scale — not specificity; now the percentile rank over distal peaks of log2(min(cpm_microglia, cpm_TAM) / max cpm among 8 non-myeloid primary CTs) , the honest pan-myeloid AAV-designer ratio. (2) spec_pct_{malignant_AC,MES,NPC,OPC} was hardcoded 0 for all four subtypes (they weren't in PRIMARY_CTS), which capped subtype primary_score at 0.5 — pure strength ranking. Now each subtype's spec is the rank of log2(cpm_sub / max cpm among {other 3 subtypes, malignant pooled, 9 non-malignant primaries}) . (3) The column named strength_frags_per_cell_wn_<ct> was computed as raw_count_mean / 1000 × width_scale with a hardcoded 1000 cell-count divisor. Now it's the true per-cell density: mean over patients of (raw_count / n_cells_patient × 500 / peak_width) . Per-pseudobulk cell counts were gathered for all 10 cohorts: 5 from existing TSVs, 4 from per-cohort h5ads via patient_id × pool_label , dejong non-myeloid from the 103 GB integrated atlas h5ad via a fine→coarse pool rule, raviram from integrated per-sample h5ads. The unified pseudobulk_cellcounts.tsv (671 rows, 97.4% of matrix pseudobulks) is included for provenance. (4) All percentile ranks now computed over distal peaks (|dist_to_tss| ≥ 2 kb) only, not all peaks including promoters. Visible impact: subtype primary_score rose from median ~0.498 (strength-only, capped) to ~0.998 (honest spec + strength). Myeloid median log2FC rose from 0.232 to 1.308 (shortcut ranked strength twice; honest ranks true selectivity). Strength rankings no longer biased toward peaks whose signal comes disproportionately from large pseudobulks. HTML viewer: same template as v2026-11-10 (expansion rows with UCSC Genome Browser links, 14-CT bar pairs on shared atlas-wide CPM scale, per-patient CPM grid, per-cohort detection chips, distance-band + patient-detection filters). Tab labels updated: Excitatory neurons , Inhibitory neurons , and first-letter capitalization on remaining CTs. Residual approximations documented in CHANGELOG: dejong fine→coarse pool rule is a label-pattern-based inference, not the canonical pipeline rule; 11 *__unassigned pseudobulks use per-cohort median n_cells as fallback (unassigned is not a scored CT so this only affects CPM pool denominators). summary: Version 5: Documentation corrections only; code, data, and results are unchanged from v4. Version 4  adds the analyses of the second revision: time-ordered and cross-project evaluation, structured label noise, a drop-one process-feature ablation, a Random Forest hyperparameter check, and label-provenance analyses (results/r2_experiments/), with the per-row revision metadata and commit dates they need. All Java runners now read the datasets from a configurable data directory (JML_DATA_DIR). Everything in v3 is otherwise unchanged; the audit labels are the same as in v3. Version 3. Supersedes version 2 (distributed as package v1.1) and version 1 (package v1.0). Prepared for the revised submission to Science of Computer Programming. Figures from earlier versions should not be cited. Manual validation re-run with a two-rater protocol. Estimated commit-level SZZ label precision is now  49.5% (197/398) with inter-rater agreement Cohen's κ = 0.799 , replacing the 29.2% reported in versions 1 and 2, which came from a single-rater audit with no documented agreement statistic. Per-project precision: Kafka 57.1%, Gson 48.5%, Commons-IO 42.9%. Both raters' blind passes, the disagreement-resolution record for the 10 conflicting cases, and a per-instance false-positive taxonomy of all 201 false positives are included. The labelling question changed, so labels are not directly comparable across versions. The is_valid_fix column has been renamed is_true_bic . The earlier audit recorded whether a candidate was itself a valid fix; the current audit records whether the candidate introduced the defect that its traced fix later repaired. These are different questions, and the resulting labels cannot be compared row by row with earlier versions. A central claim has been withdrawn. Earlier versions of the paper argued that feature-engineering quality has a stronger influence on predictive performance than label purity. A label-noise sensitivity experiment, included here, does not support that claim: adding 20 percentage points of label noise erases more MCC than the entire static-to-hybrid feature-engineering gain, in every project. The claim has been removed from the manuscript and replaced with the measured finding that process features hold a consistent advantage over static features at the observed noise level, while performance remains sensitive to further label degradation. Ablation and significance results re-derived from logged runs. All values now come from 270 independently seeded 10-fold cross-validation runs (30 seeds × 3 projects × 3 feature sets), with per-seed raw results, runner scripts and exact seeds included. The reported Hybrid-over-Static improvement on Commons-IO is 55%, not the 128% stated previously; Static-only MCC on Commons-IO is +0.166, not negative. Statistical testing is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired by seed with Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni correction over nine comparisons per metric. MCC replaces F1 as the primary metric, and class prevalence, trivial baselines and confusion matrices are now reported. Prevalence differs by a factor of ~2.7 across the three projects (55.4% / 44.9% / 20.9%), so F1 is not comparable across them; all trivial baselines have MCC = 0. The reported pipeline does not use SMOTE. A direct comparison, included here, shows no benefit in any project and a measurable cost on Commons-IO. SMOTE remains available as a configuration option in the framework. Runtime and energy figures are measured, not extrapolated: 30.6 minutes wall-clock across all three projects for the reported configuration, with per-phase timings and logs. New in this version: the label-noise sensitivity sweep; an AGE-feature ablation; confusion matrices and specificity per project and feature set; a Process-versus-Static significance test; a read-only exporter for the SZZ fix-to-BIC mapping, which the original pipeline did not persist; and a replication configuration annotated with the exact s

summary: Se estudia la variante del algoritmo de Collatz que aplica 3m+1 a los impares congruentes con 1 módulo 4 y 3m−1 a los congruentes con 3 módulo 4, introducida por el autor en 2019. La regla equivale a elegir, entre 3m−1 y 3m+1, el término divisible por 4, de modo que cada paso impar va seguido al menos de dos divisiones por 2. Se demuestra que la distancia al punto fijo 1 se contrae al menos en el factor 3/4 en cada transición entre impares. De ello se siguen la convergencia a 1 de toda órbita, una cota explícita para el número de términos impares y una cota logarítmica para la longitud total de la trayectoria. Se establecen dos acoplamientos exactos. El primero relaciona, en un solo paso, la variante con la aplicación de Collatz acelerada y sitúa su diferencia en una única valuación 2-ádica. El segundo la relaciona con la permutación considerada por Collatz en 1932: sobre cada impar, la inversa de la permutación realiza en un paso el resultado de tres pasos elementales de la variante, y los retornos impares de ambos sistemas difieren en una potencia de 3 determinada por la valuación 2-ádica del paso. Se demuestra que el retorno impar de la permutación es biyectivo y que la variante se obtiene suprimiendo los factores de 3 de su resultado, y se precisa que esta factorización no es una conjugación. Se señalan además obstáculos a la conjugación de la variante con la aplicación de Collatz y con el retorno de la permutación. El resultado central es de naturaleza simbólica. El lenguaje de paridades de la variante es exactamente el conjunto de palabras binarias que evitan el factor 11, con entropía topológica igual al logaritmo de la razón áurea, y la densidad de las clases residuales que realizan cada palabra viene dada por una medida de Markov explícita y no uniforme. Ello contrasta con el teorema de paridades de Terras y Lagarias para la aplicación de Collatz, donde todas las palabras se realizan con la misma densidad. Se plantea como problema abierto la geometría de las clases residuales asociadas a cada palabra, con datos de enumeración exhaustiva. El escrito discute con precisión qué no se sigue de estos resultados acerca de la conjetura de Collatz, y propone controles positivos y negativos para evaluar argumentos generales. Los enunciados efectivos se han comprobado computacionalmente, y el suplemento contiene el programa en Python que reproduce esas comprobaciones con aritmética entera, junto con sus resultados. Versión 2. Se añaden un índice, las referencias a los escritos del autor sobre la permutación de Collatz de 1932 y sobre los filtros bilaterales de los mínimos de sus órbitas, y un suplemento computacional formado por el programa de verificación, un resumen de sus resultados y la tabla de las pruebas sobre las clases residuales. La sección de verificación numérica se reescribe para describir ese suplemento.
title: Una variación en el algoritmo de la conjetura de Collatz.

summary: The KV cache is the bottleneck of long-context LLM inference.  Every modern serving system —  vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake  — is, at its core, a memory manager for the cache that grows one token at a time as the model decodes.  PagedAttention, RadixAttention , and the various  prefix caching  schemes each solve a piece of the problem, but none of them is  lock-free , none of them is  position-keyed , and none of them uses  structural sharing  to handle both beam-search branching and multi-tenant prefix sharing at the same time. This book introduces the  persistent rope  — a single data structure that does all of these things, derived from two pieces of prior art that were never combined before: the  persistent vector  (which gives the rope its branching semantics) and the  Bw-tree  (which gives the rope its lock-free properties). The book is a design document and API reference for the rope, written for engineers who build serving systems, GPU kernels, and lock-free data structures.  It is  not  a benchmark paper,  not  a tutorial, and  not  a complete serving system. The Python reference implementation is  correct but not lock-free ; the  lock-free Rust port is scaffolded in the repository  and described in detail in Chapter 22. The book covers the design (Ch 1–9), the Python reference (Ch 10–11), the verification (Ch 12–14), the public API (Ch 15–19), and the honest framing of what works, what doesn't, and what's left for future work (Ch 20–23). The appendices include a full  glossary, references, and index . Read it in order if you want to understand the design end-to-end; jump to Chapters 10–19 if you want to use the Python reference; read Chapter 22 if you're planning the Rust port.

summary: This deliverable presents practical and adaptable protocols for scaling citizen science initiatives, developed through a user-centred design (UCD) process informed by co-design and validation workshops, interviews with citizen science experts, researchers, and practitioners, and a literature review. Rather than proposing a single, one-size-fits-all model, the protocols are organised around five CROPS scaling strategies: institutional scaling (driving policy and governance change), expansion and replication scaling (extending reach and participation), transformative change scaling (influencing values, attitudes, and behaviours), downscaling (reducing scope while maintaining impact), and combined scaling (pursuing multiple pathways simultaneously). These strategies reflect a multidimensional understanding of scaling that extends beyond geographic or numerical growth. To support projects in deciding whether and how to scale, the deliverable also highlights the CROPS Scalability Framework, a diagnostic tool built around nine constructs relating to the intrinsic characteristics of a project, the scaling process itself, and the target context. This is complemented by a six-step Strategic Scaling Decision process that helps projects determine whether scaling is not only feasible but strategically appropriate. In this deliverable, the protocols are first presented through concise, visually structured informative briefs, providing accessible overviews of guidance for each scaling strategy. These are followed by more detailed guidance, including summary tables of protocols, pillars, and objectives, illustrative examples, and practical dos and don'ts. Additional resources, tools, and guidelines support implementation. The protocols are designed to be adopted in full or in part, depending on a project's context, resources, and objectives, and are intended to remain useful not only for scaling but also for the design of new citizen science initiatives from the outset. Ethical considerations, including privacy, inclusivity, fairness, and transparency, are treated as a cross-cutting requirement throughout. The primary audience for the protocols is the citizen science practitioner community, represented through personas developed as part of the UCD process, alongside researchers, policymakers, EU and international organisation representatives, and other stakeholders engaged in scaling citizen science, particularly in relation to the Horizon Europe EU Missions. The CROPS protocols are intended as an evolving, non-prescriptive resource rather than a definitive model for scaling. Their value lies in providing a structured basis for reflection, planning, and decision-making, while recognising that successful scaling also depends on a broader enabling ecosystem of institutional readiness, sustainable funding, and supportive technical and policy infrastructure. The methodology underpinning protocol development, including persona creation and the wider UCD process, is described in detail in Section 7 and the accompanying annexes.

Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics to examine the pressure–temperature behavior of model membranes composed of dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) or its cis-unsaturated analogue Δ9-cis-PC. Within the studied range (288–308 K, 1–2000 bar), DMPC undergoes a liquid–gel transition, while Δ9-cis-PC remains fluid due to unsaturation. The CHARMM36 force field reproduces experimental boundaries with high fidelity: simulated DMPC transitions fall within 5–10 K and 100–300 bar of experimental values, and Δ9-cis-PC exhibits no transition. Hysteresis is modest but most pronounced when starting from low-temperature gels; we propose a split-phase simulation protocol that alleviates the hysteresis problem. We identify the area per lipid, bilayer thickness, and acyl-chain gauche fractions as sensitive phase markers; among these, the gauche fraction provides the most robust signature. Simulations indicate that an interdigitated gel is the equilibrium structure under finite-size conditions, and we propose a novel metric to quantify the extent of this phenomenon. However, at low temperature and high pressure, interdigitation decreases, consistent with the experimental lamellar gel phase. This long-lived interdigitation critically impacts standard order parameters, specifically, area per lipid and membrane thickness. Finally, we discuss in detail how finite-size effects influence phase transition and interdigitation. Overall, these results underscore the accuracy of modern force fields and highlight how simulations are essential to mechanistically complement experimental studies of pressure-sensitive membranes. summary: LOADX (workLOad Assessment in Dual-task eXecution) is a multimodal dataset developed to support research on physical and mental workload estimation during single- and dual-task activities. The dataset contains synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data collected from 20 participants performing a structured experimental protocol designed to elicit different combinations of physical and cognitive demand. The protocol includes 16 experimental conditions: three physical tasks, three cognitive tasks, nine dual-task combinations, and one resting baseline. The physical tasks consist of repeated shoulder flexion–extension, marching in place, and squats. The cognitive tasks include a Stroop test, a 2-back working-memory task, and backward counting by seven. Each active condition lasted 90 seconds and was followed by a resting interval. Physiological data were acquired using wearable sensors and include raw electrocardiographic signals, raw respiratory waveforms, heart rate, inter-beat interval, respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and triaxial acceleration. Full-body kinematic data were collected using a contactless vision-based monitoring system based on MediaPipe Pose, providing the three-dimensional coordinates of 33 anatomical landmarks. All acquisition streams share a common temporal reference, enabling the alignment of physiological signals, body movements, task execution, and workload annotations. After each experimental condition, participants rated their perceived physical and mental demand using selected dimensions of the NASA Task Load Index. The dataset therefore includes task-level Physical Demand and Mental Demand scores, which can be used as subjective workload annotations for supervised learning, correlation analysis, clustering, and validation of multimodal workload-estimation methods. The dataset is organized into one folder for each participant, identified through an anonymized numerical code such as S01, S02, and so forth. Each participant folder contains: Sxx.csv: synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data; Sxx_ecg.csv: raw ECG waveform; Sxx_breath.csv: raw respiratory waveform; Sxx_nasa.xlsx: task-level NASA-TLX Physical Demand and Mental Demand ratings. LOADX can support research on multimodal workload assessment, physiological and movement-signal processing, sensor fusion, feature extraction, task recognition, modality-ablation analysis, subject-independent validation, and the development of adaptive human–machine interaction systems. The inclusion of physical-only, cognitive-only, and dual-task conditions enables the investigation of how physical and mental demands interact and how they are reflected in complementary sensing modalities. LOADX should be considered a structured multimodal research dataset rather than a population-level normative dataset. Inter-individual variability was intentionally retained to support the investigation of personalized and subject-independent workload-estimation approaches.

summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. summary: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. summary: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. summary: Attention to notable people rises sharply when they die and then fades, but how far it fades, and for whom, has rarely been measured at scale. summary: A memory can last for decades, yet the proteins of a synapse are replaced within days. Crick (1984) proposed that the molecules that store a memory restore one another, so that the pattern survives its parts, and several molecular switches of this kind have since been modelled. Here we ask a question that does not depend on the mechanism: what is the longest time that any switch made of $N$ molecules can remember? We consider all switches in which the number of active molecules changes one molecule at a time, with an activation rate per inactive molecule between a spontaneous floor $\varepsilon$ and a catalytic ceiling $k$, and a loss rate per active molecule between the turnover rate $\mu$ and an erasure ceiling $\lambda$. (i) We prove that, for every readout threshold, both the potentiated and the unpotentiated state are retained longest, in the sense of stochastic order, by one and the same switch: a threshold rule that restores at full speed when at least $m$ molecules are active and erases at full speed otherwise. (ii) We give its mean retention times in closed form, as sums of binomial coefficients, and evaluate them in exact rational arithmetic. (iii) When the two contrasts $\kappa=k/\mu$ and $\chi=\lambda/\varepsilon$ are equal to $c$ and $\lambda=\mu$, the longest possible memory $T^*(N)$ satisfies $N^{-1}(\sqrt c/2)^N\le\mu T^*(N)\le\bigl((1+c)/\sqrt c\bigr)^N$ for even $N$; numerically, each added molecule multiplies it by about $(1+c)/(2\sqrt c)$. (iv) With molecules that last 30 hours, no switch of this class holds both states for a mean of a century with fewer than 20 molecules if $c=10$, 12 if $c=30$, 8 if $c=100$ and 4 if $c=1000$, and these numbers are attained; thirty molecules suffice as soon as $c\ge7$, while a single dimer with $c=100$ lasts 50 molecular lifetimes. (v) The retention times of the ideal switch have an increasing failure rate, so that a mean of a hundred centuries guarantees a century with probability above $0.99$, at the price of two to ten more molecules. (vi) Smooth cooperativity is far from the limit: a switch with Hill exponent 2 needs 187 molecules where the ideal one needs 12. In this class, then, a lifetime of memory requires few molecules but a sharp threshold. These are limits for one-variable switches with constant rates, not a model of a particular synapse. This record contains the preprint (PDF, PCI template), its LaTeX source, and the Python code and results file that reproduce every theorem, table and figure (code under the MIT license).
