summary: Run records, analysis of record and code of the component study reported in the appendix "Design, Provenance and Component Study of KAYROS" of the PhD thesis of Florian Rascoussier, "Improving Anytime Resolution of Large-Scale VRPTW and its Time-Dependent Extension" (ED SPIN, IMT Atlantique and INSA Lyon). Every table, figure and number of the component-study section of that appendix is computed from the files of this dataset. KAYROS is an exact and anytime solver for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with time windows (TDVRPTW) under the Duration objective. Its exact mode is a branch-price-and-cut derived from the open-source solver of Lera-Romero, Miranda-Bront and Soulignac (Networks, 2020), and its heuristic mode is an iterated local search. The study asks 3 questions: whether the exact mode of KAYROS still performs as the solver it comes from once embedded, repaired and extended, what the open LP backend HiGHS costs compared with CPLEX, and what the heuristic and exact modes bring to each other. Design. The panel is the complete set of 56 Dabia et al. (2013) TDVRPTW instances with 100 customers, as distributed by MAMUT-routing. The 5 arms are the repaired baseline (the solver of Lera-Romero et al. at its public commit cabc56a plus 3 patches, with CPLEX 12.10), the exact mode of KAYROS 1.7.0 alone with CPLEX, the same with HiGHS 1.14.0, the heuristic mode of KAYROS alone, and the full solver (15 s of heuristic search, then the warm-started exact mode with CPLEX). Each arm runs 5 trials on each instance, 1,400 runs in total, each with 7,200 s from process launch, one pinned core and an address space limited to 16 GiB, with 10 concurrent runs per node on the grvingt cluster of the Grid'5000 testbed. The heuristic and full arms use 5 paired seeds. KAYROS runs used commit 25d8f0088337b9667956f07fe365c749def9894f of https://github.com/0nyr/kayros , released as version 1.7.0. The sources of the repaired baseline are also public, as the tag component-study-as-run of https://github.com/0nyr/lera-tdvrptw-bpc-repaired . Contents. cells/ holds one directory per run with the run summary (cell.json), the timestamped stream of incumbents, lower bounds and closures (events.jsonl), the native solver result (native.json, absent for the 185 runs ended by the memory limit or killed after the budget), the solver standard error (stderr.log) and the claim record (claim.json). plan.json is the plan of the 1,400 runs, runners/ the runner and job logs, scripts/ the frozen runner scripts. analysis/ holds the analysis of record (final-summary.json, which re-checks every route set with the reference checker mamut-routing-lib 0.11.0), the main and per-instance tables, and a comparison of the proofs with the stored optimality certificates. code/ holds the experiment harness, the analysis scripts, the frozen best-known-solution snapshot used as reference, the script that produces the tables and figures of the appendix, and the 3 patches of the baseline. The bundled README.md decodes the layout, the record fields, the acceptance rule of a proof and the integrity hashes. Main results. Accepted proofs: 165 of 280 runs for the repaired baseline, 172 for the exact mode of KAYROS with CPLEX, 135 with HiGHS (5 proofs rejected because a priced column fails the checker), 171 for the full solver, and none for the heuristic arm, which cannot prove optimality. Restricted mean time to proof: 3,295.0 s, 3,181.3 s, 4,256.3 s and 3,197.5 s. Mean anytime score: 0.37914, 0.35880, 0.49777, 0.00238 for the heuristic arm and 0.00644 for the full solver. 177 runs end at the memory limit, on 13 instances that no arm proves. Limits. The baseline is the repaired solver, not the published one. The pricing changes of KAYROS 1.7.0 were selected on this same panel. The panel is one family at one size, run on one machine type. The proofs are computational closures of single runs, checked for consistency, and not independent certificates. The records keep their original Grid
title: Component Study of KAYROS on the Dabia2013 TDVRPTW Instances with 100 Customers: Run Records and Analysis

Every table, figure and number of the component-study section of that appendix is computed from the files of this dataset. KAYROS is an exact and anytime solver for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with time windows (TDVRPTW) under the Duration objective. Its exact mode is a branch-price-and-cut derived from the open-source solver of Lera-Romero, Miranda-Bront and Soulignac (Networks, 2020), and its heuristic mode is an iterated local search. The study asks 3 questions: whether the exact mode of KAYROS still performs as the solver it comes from once embedded, repaired and extended, what the open LP backend HiGHS costs compared with CPLEX, and what the heuristic and exact modes bring to each other. Design. The panel is the complete set of 56 Dabia et al. (2013) TDVRPTW instances with 100 customers, as distributed by MAMUT-routing. The 5 arms are the repaired baseline (the solver of Lera-Romero et al. at its public commit cabc56a plus 3 patches, with CPLEX 12.10), the exact mode of KAYROS 1.7.0 alone with CPLEX, the same with HiGHS 1.14.0, the heuristic mode of KAYROS alone, and the full solver (15 s of heuristic search, then the warm-started exact mode with CPLEX). Each arm runs 5 trials on each instance, 1,400 runs in total, each with 7,200 s from process launch, one pinned core and an address space limited to 16 GiB, with 10 concurrent runs per node on the grvingt cluster of the Grid'5000 testbed. The heuristic and full arms use 5 paired seeds. KAYROS runs used commit 25d8f0088337b9667956f07fe365c749def9894f of https://github.com/0nyr/kayros , released as version 1.7.0. The sources of the repaired baseline are also public, as the tag component-study-as-run of https://github.com/0nyr/lera-tdvrptw-bpc-repaired . Contents. cells/ holds one directory per run with the run summary (cell.json), the timestamped stream of incumbents, lower bounds and closures (events.jsonl), the native solver result (native.json, absent for the 185 runs ended by the memory limit or killed after the budget), the solver standard error (stderr.log) and the claim record (claim.json). plan.json is the plan of the 1,400 runs, runners/ the runner and job logs, scripts/ the frozen runner scripts. analysis/ holds the analysis of record (final-summary.json, which re-checks every route set with the reference checker mamut-routing-lib 0.11.0), the main and per-instance tables, and a comparison of the proofs with the stored optimality certificates. code/ holds the experiment harness, the analysis scripts, the frozen best-known-solution snapshot used as reference, the script that produces the tables and figures of the appendix, and the 3 patches of the baseline. Accepted proofs: 165 of 280 runs for the repaired baseline, 172 for the exact mode of KAYROS with CPLEX, 135 with HiGHS (5 proofs rejected because a priced column fails the checker), 171 for the full solver, and none for the heuristic arm, which cannot prove optimality. summary: We study time-fractional diffusion on real hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$, $n\ge2$, with Caputo order $0<α<1$. We establish global two-sided pointwise estimates for the homogeneous fundamental kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$ and the inhomogeneous (Duhamel) kernel $Y_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$, uniformly over all $t>0$ and positive geodesic distances $r$. By combining inverse-stable subordination with global bounds for the hyperbolic heat kernel, we distinguish a short-time local regime, a large-time interior region, and an exterior region governed by a saddle-point problem with parameter $r/t$. Both kernels have the same exterior exponential rate, while their amplitudes are related by an explicit saddle-point factor. The estimates are uniformly comparable on the interfaces between regimes, recover the Euclidean time-fractional singularities at small scales, and identify the influence of hyperbolic geometry on large-scale decay. The kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}$ also describes the one-time marginal density of hyperbolic Brownian motion under an independent inverse stable clock. This representation yields a radial limit law, moment and quantile asymptotics, and a change in the mean square displacement from order $t^α$ at small times to order $t^{2α}$ at large times.

summary: We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. summary: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and schedule
title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA

summary: Current research in the food industry highlights the importance of alternative protein sources in the context of global population growth and the need to reduce the negative impact of raising animals, producing animal proteins, on the environment. Plant proteins represent a sustainable, affordable and beneficial option for health, with high potential to replace animal proteins in the food industry. Plant sources rich in protein include legumes, cereals, pseudocereals, oilseeds, green leaves, algae and, more recently, insects. They differ considerably in protein content and amino acid profile, and their strategic combination can ensure a balanced intake of essential nutrients. Legumes offer high protein content, but are deficient in sulfur amino acids. Cereals, although lower in protein, bring technological benefits and can complement the amino acids missing from legumes. Pseudocereals have a higher nutritional value than conventional cereals, while green leaves and algae offer a high proteins intake and compounds with antioxidant potential, although they require advanced technologies to overcome extraction limitations. Extraction methods play a decisive role in the yield and quality of plant proteins. Conventional techniques are efficient but can cause denaturation and provide low yields. On the other hand, emerging methods allow the recovery of proteins in larger quantities, preserving their functional and technological properties.
title: Plant-based proteins: sources, extraction methods and functional perspectives for the sustainable food industry

summary: Simultaneous tolerance certification asks whether every component of a dense latent vector lies within its prescribed range. This preprint studies noisy unit-norm linear measurements under pathwise resource budgets, with tolerances calibrated to a fixed prior membership probability. For independent Gaussian priors, every fixed linear channel is uniformly asymptotically equivalent, for the membership decision, to a coordinate-precision design at no greater total precision. A marked Poisson limit characterizes the complete family of feasible limiting experiments. The resulting allocation theory gives exact Brier-optimal designs and proves that every classification-optimal allocation has zero plus at most one positive normalized precision level. The global classification problem therefore reduces to a one-dimensional coverage choice. At low budgets, no allocation is most informative for every decision loss. At fixed row precision, adaptive screening yields a squared-logarithmic reduction in the order of measurements required for prescribed positive decision gain. For classification, sharp high-accuracy constants distinguish the inverse-square risk dependence of fixed designs from the logarithmic dependence of adaptive acquisition. Bounded-spectrum Gaussian dependence preserves the fixed-design frontier. Matching resource orders extend to exponential-power priors, including Laplace and lighter tails. A frozen Gaussian simulation, combined with certified deterministic bounds, establishes a finite-dimensional advantage over all fixed linear designs under the same affine acquisition budget, with one-sided 95% Monte Carlo confidence. This record contains the preprint, proof supplement, editable LaTeX sources, and a reproducibility archive with programs, experimental protocols, and saved results. summary: This record accompanies Working Paper No. 9 of the Independent FAIR Evaluation Series of the ATLAS Framework , entitled Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation . The study examines the concentration of computational AACF susceptibility profiles derived from frozen PaccMann and DRPreter predictions for 95 unique registered configurations across 970 matched cancer cell-line profiles . Scores are transformed into normalized weights using a softmax transformation favouring lower AACF indices, with fixed model-specific reference scales. Profile characterization includes Shannon entropy, normalized entropy, effective configuration counts, and leading configuration weights. The evaluation addresses five normalization-scale multipliers, the effect of retaining 97 registered labels instead of 95 unique configurations, lineage comparisons covering 953 profiles in 21 groups, and variability across ten DRPreter checkpoints. It also distinguishes entropy calculated after median index aggregation from the median of checkpoint-wise entropies. At the reference scales, median normalized entropy was 0.9346 for PaccMann and 0.9528 for the DRPreter median consensus . These aggregate differences coexisted with weak cross-model agreement in cell-line entropy rankings ( Spearman ρ = −0.0788 ) and only six shared profiles among the 97 most concentrated profiles identified by each model. Normalization and checkpoint aggregation affected concentration summaries and rankings, demonstrating that entropy requires an explicitly specified computational representation. The accompanying computational materials document the six-stage workflow through analysis scripts, frozen input resources, configuration and profile mappings, normalization policies, numerical tables and arrays, saved bootstrap draws, and provenance and validation records. A README explains the directory structure, principal outputs, reproduction workflow, and interpretation limits. Resources inherited from ATLAS Working Papers 06–08 retain their upstream licensing and attribution requirements. The final technical audit recorded 2,363 passed checks and no failed checks , reviewing 206 distinct files in the selected analysis chain. This audit supports technical consistency and traceability within the implemented checks; it does not constitute independent experimental or clinical validation. The results establish entropy as a conditional descriptor of computational profile concentration . They do not establish therapeutic efficacy, measured mixture responses, biological mechanisms, or malignant-versus-normal selectivity. The materials support transparent inspection, reanalysis, and further methodological evaluation of the ATLAS framework.

summary: Resilience in psychology and public health is usually assessed through recovery or maintained functioning, outcomes that do not reveal whether desirable states have become self-maintaining or still depend on external support. Drawing on coerced-regime theory from social-ecological systems research, we develop aided mental health resilience (AMHR), a framework for desirable mental health states established or maintained through external inputs of resources, organisation, political capital and trust. We make three contributions. First, we frame population mental health as a dimension of social-ecological system states and define the external maintenance subsidy required to sustain desirable conditions. Second, using a dialectical reading of regime change, we distinguish reversion, permanent subsidy and sublation, in which the function initially supplied by aid becomes reproduced through reorganised capacities, practices or institutions. Displacement of harm is treated as a cross-cutting failure mode. Four cases illustrate these dynamics and their limits. Third, drawing on strange loop ethics, we argue that paradoxical outcomes should trigger review not only of intervention instruments but also of the premises that define desirable states and authorise intervention. We outline disconfirmation conditions and a research agenda centred on longitudinal evaluation, subsidy accounting, displacement monitoring and recursive premise review.
title: Aided mental health resilience: governing desirable states that cannot sustain themselves

Operational resilience must therefore be accompanied by epistemic resilience: the capacity of the infrastructure to preserve the conditions that make digital resources and computational processes trustworthy, interpretable, and scientifically reusable.  The relationship between cultural memory and machine memory provides a particularly relevant perspective for this discussion. As cultural knowledge is increasingly encoded into structured datasets and processed through automated and AI-supported environments, research infrastructures mediate between human interpretations of cultural memory and their computational representations. Starting at an architectural level, the outlined framework requires investigating how geographically distributed resources can evolve from a set of interconnected nodes into a resilient federated infrastructure. Relevant mechanisms include containerised microservices, multi-cluster orchestration, service meshes, zero-trust API gateways, OAuth2/OIDC and mTLS, secure CI/CD pipelines, immutable backups, distributed replication, and business continuity and disaster recovery procedures. The central problem is therefore one of controlled interdependence: designing a federation in which services and resources can cooperate while preventing individual failures from propagating across the wider ecosystem. A complementary dimension concerns the resilience of scientific workflows. Workflows create dependencies that span services, datasets, computational environments, authentication mechanisms and external resources. Their resilience therefore requires reproducible execution environments, explicit dependency management, provenance tracking, continuous monitoring and mechanisms to detect and respond to anomalous behaviour. The evolution of the DARIAH-IT orchestration environment towards native containerised and distributed execution provides an experimental context for the study of adaptive workflows, anomaly detection, agent-based orchestration, federated learning and semi-automatic recovery mechanisms. For SSH infrastructures, however, operational continuity alone is not sufficient. A technically successful failover or recovery may still constitute a scientific failure if provenance, authenticity, semantic consistency, reproducibility or reliability are compromised. summary: This repository provides the data, spatial analysis polygons, statistical outputs and reproducible Python workflows associated with the manuscript “Satellite-based aftercare screening for data-scarce landfills: 27 years of vegetation trajectories and baseline sensitivity in Vietnam”. The study examines six Vietnamese landfill sites represented by eight analysis polygons over 1999–2025. The archive includes date-level Landsat Collection 2 observations and Sentinel-2 cross-check exports; approximate site and sector polygons; controlled interrupted time-series analysis; recovery and repeated-parity metrics; Kieu Ky within-site contrasts and baseline-length sensitivity; Typhoon Yagi relative vegetation departures; and supplementary results tables B1–B9. The supplied scripts reproduce statistical tables and article figures from the archived exports without requiring Google Earth Engine access. Google Earth Engine scripts and a Colab notebook are included for re-extraction, subject to user credentials and project setup. These observations support first-stage landfill aftercare screening and prioritisation of field inspections; the analysis polygons are interpreted study areas rather than surveyed waste footprints. KEYWORDS: RELATED MANUSCRIPT: Satellite-based aftercare screening for data-scarce landfills: 27 years of vegetation trajectories and baseline sensitivity in Vietnam (Do not invent or enter an article DOI unless already assigned.)

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24146492 . Peer review report: Caetano et al., investigate the diversity of mammalian box C/D small nucleolar RNAs (SNORDs) by combining Fibrillarin- and Snu13-associated RNA sequencing with extensive analysis of publicly available datasets. They identify 21,732 candidate loci, including a large population of unusually short single-stranded RNAs (20-50 nt), termed tiSNORDs. This work is important because it challenges the current annotation of the mammalian snoRNAs and raises fundamental questions about snoRNP biogenesis and the emergence of regulatory RNAs. Particularly convincing are the enrichment of characteristic box C/D sequence signatures, the association of selected candidates with Fibrillarin, and the demonstration that a 36-nt tiSNORD can guide RNA methylation. The observations concerning terminal stem structures, RNA stability and host-gene expression provide further support for the biological relevance of at least a subset of these RNAs. Therefore, the study is interesting and potentially significant. Addressing several methodological and interpretative concerns , particularly regarding library-preparation biases, statistical validation of candidate identification, and the distinction between mature RNAs and RNA fragments would strengthen claims and introduce reproducibility. Major points: 1. RNA library preparation and size-selection bias. Approximately ~70 % of tiSNORDs are 20-50 nt long, yet the size-selection used with the TruSeq small RNA library preparation kit is not specified. Size-dependent recovery and sequence-dependent ligation biases could substantially influence this distribution. The authors acknowledge such biases for SNORD50 and substantial technical variability between datasets. Clarification of the selected insert range and, ideally, independent analysis of RNAs across a broader size range would strengthen this central conclusion. One would be to use splint-ligation library preparation to get 'unbiased' small RNA library for sequencing (e.g. Maguire et al., 2020; PMID: 32496547). 2. Statistical validation of sequence signatures. The identification of tiSNORDs relies heavily on canonical C/D-box motifs, their terminal positions and uridine enrichment (Figures 1C to 1G). However, no explicit null model accounts for the search criteria, meaning that some positional enrichment is expected by construction. Small RNA-seq ligation biases may also influence nucleotide frequencies (Kim et al., 2019; PMID: 30605524). Permutation analyses using length- and composition-matched intronic sequences processed through the same pipeline would help ensure statistical significance and estimate false-positive rates. Potential spike ins would be of use as well. 3. Distinguishing mature tiSNORDs from RNA fragments. Although the authors demonstrate stable endogenous expression of tiSNORD candidate and successful processing of selected ectopically expressed candidates, these findings cannot necessarily be extrapolated to thousands of low-abundance sequences. Examining coverage across candidate loci, overlapping fragments, flanking regions and potential longer precursors would help distinguish independently matured tiSNORDs from RNA processing or degradation/fragmentation products. 4. Confidence in the proposed repertoire. 12% of candidates exceed one count per million, and substantial discrepancies are observed between independent datasets (Supplementary Figure 3). The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations further in the text, but the claim that more than 20,000 loci substantially expand the snoRNA repertoire is a potential since it does not have biochemical validation and mentioning that they are "putative" in the abstract would help the reader to understand the scope of this article. One would be to use splint-ligation library preparation to get 'unbiased' small RNA library for sequencing (e.g. Maguire et al., 2020; PMID: 32496547). 2. Statistical validation of sequence signatures. The identification of tiSNORDs relies heavily on canonical C/D-box motifs, their terminal positions and uridine enrichment (Figures 1C to 1G). However, no explicit null model accounts for the search criteria, meaning that some positional enrichment is expected by construction. Small RNA-seq ligation biases may also influence nucleotide frequencies (Kim et al., 2019; PMID: 30605524). Permutation analyses using length- and composition-matched intronic sequences processed through the same pipeline would help ensure statistical significance and estimate false-positive rates. Potential spike ins would be of use as well. 3. Distinguishing mature tiSNORDs from RNA fragments. Although the authors demonstrate stable endogenous expression of tiSNORD candidate and successful processing of selected ectopically expressed candidates, these findings cannot necessarily be extrapolated to thousands of low-abundance sequences. Examining coverage across candidate loci, overlapping fragments, flanking regions and potential longer precursors would help distinguish independently matured tiSNORDs from RNA processing or degradation/fragmentation products. 4. Confidence in the proposed repertoire. 12% of candidates exceed one count per million, and substantial discrepancies are observed between independent datasets (Supplementary Figure 3). The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations further in the text, but the claim that more than 20,000 loci substantially expand the snoRNA repertoire is a potential since it does not have biochemical validation and mentioning that they are "putative" in the abstract would help the reader to understand the scope of this article. Stratification by abundance, reproducibility and independent experimental evidence wou

summary: Data and code to reproduce all tables and figures in "Priced In, Not Zoned Out: Social Capital, Land-Use Regulation, and US Housing Prices." The package tests whether bridging social capital lowers housing prices through trust, or civic and bonding social capital raises them by restricting supply. It contains: - County data (1,747 counties): FHFA residential land prices per acre (Davis, Larson, Oliner and Shui 2021), Social Capital Atlas measures (Chetty et al. 2022), Census building permits 2012-2024, and Wharton WRLURI 2018 metropolitan means. - Metropolitan data (530 CBSAs): WRLURI 2018 and population-weighted social capital. - State panel, 1975-2019: OECD regional house price indices (FHFA), BEA per-capita income and population (SAINC4), CPI-U; 51-unit and 50-state (DC excluded) versions. - Stata 19.5 do-files: CD, CIPS, Westerlund bootstrap cointegration, PMG/MG, CS-ARDL, CS-DL, CCE-MG, Driscoll-Kraay, Mundlak CRE, MMQR, and county/metro fixed-effects models. - Python scripts: 50-state estimates, MMQR with state-cluster bootstrap, density interactions, and robustness checks. - Codebook, README with sources and terms of use, and Figures 1-2. WRLURI survey microdata are not redistributed; only metropolitan-area means derived from them are included.
title: Replication package: Priced In, Not Zoned Out: Social Capital, Land-Use Regulation, and US Housing Prices

summary: R code to reproduce all estimates in the article "Gateway or add-on? Prepaid cards and banking depth in Chilean households". The script uses the 2024 Chilean Household Finance Survey (Encuesta Financiera de Hogares, EFH 2024) of the Central Bank of Chile. It estimates survey-weighted probit models of prepaid card use (EFH item u_tprepago) as a function of banking depth (unbanked, demand account only, current account), non-bank credit, and respondent and household characteristics. Models are estimated separately in each of the 30 implicates, variances are computed with the 1,000 EFH bootstrap replicate weights, and estimates are combined with Rubin's rules. The script reports average marginal effects, contrast models for prepaid vouchers and any prepaid use, interaction analyses (current account x income stratum, age x gender), regressions for a digital financial inclusion index, and Oster (2019) bounds. Results are exported to an Excel workbook. The EFH microdata are not included. They are available from the Central Bank of Chile upon registration. See README.md for data access, software requirements, run instructions and the mapping between output sheets and the article's tables.
title: Replication code for: Gateway or add-on? Prepaid cards and banking depth in Chilean households

summary: Abstract Generative visual AI is increasingly used in early-stage design to produce sketches, concept renderings and alternative visual directions. However, visually convincing outputs do not necessarily constitute traceable or justified design decisions. In human–AI co-creation, generated images may remain weakly connected to design intent, evaluation criteria, evidence and design rationale, making the creative process difficult to review, reuse, and, where applicable, assess consistently. This paper proposes a process-level methodological framework for human–AI co-creation with generative visual AI systems. The framework is conceived as a lightweight traceability schema linking design problem, design intent, evaluation criteria, generative input, AI output, selected and rejected features, specifications, evidence, design decisions and iteration records. Its purpose is not to explain the internal behaviour of the generative model, but to document the human interpretation and decision-making process around generated visual artefacts. The proposal is illustrated through a postgraduate conceptual product design case in which generative visual AI was introduced after a systemic intent-structuring phase. The case provides evidence of feasibility for reconstructing the relationship between prior intent, generated outputs, and design decisions, but it is not presented as a controlled validation. The paper contributes to creative AI and human–AI interaction by reframing generated outputs as intermediate artefacts that require explicit links to intent, evidence and accountable design decisions.
title: From Generative Output to Traceable Design Decisions: A Process-Level Framework for Human–AI Co-Creation in Conceptual Design

summary: The triangular Lagrange point of the restricted three-body problem and the radial motion of a charged particle in a Penning trap are both equilibria held at a maximum of an effective potential by a gyroscopic force. Each possesses one mode of negative energy, and each loses linear stability when its two frequencies collide—one at Routh’s mass ratio, the other at the trapping limit. Both systems belong to a single family of planar gyroscopic Hamiltonians. On every level of the conserved angular-momentum invariant, the degree-four normal form of any member at such a collision coincides with the reduced Hamiltonian of an axisymmetric Penning trap whose detuning is shifted by a term proportional to the invariant and whose quartic coefficient is fixed by a single normal-form invariant. On the level containing orbits that start at rest, this reduction yields closed-form laws for the largest excursion, the escape threshold, and the escape time. These laws depend only on the sign of the quartic coefficient and on scaled variables. At the triangular point the coefficient is positive, placing the collision in the soft class: orbits remain confined after stability is lost, with an excursion that grows like the square root of the distance past the critical value. Direct integration confirms the soft law to a fraction of a percent at the smallest detunings tested. Two traps whose quartic coefficient matches that of the triangular point reproduce the same law. Traps with the opposite sign escape at the predicted threshold and in the predicted times. A randomized ensemble of members confirms the classification by the sign of the coefficient. Two further results hold for every member of the family. Before the collision the linear transient gain is exactly the inverse square root of the frequency splitting. With isotropic velocity damping the first-order growth rates depend only on the undamped frequencies, and at the collision they scale with the square root of the damping rate. The first of these explains earlier reports of apparent escape just below Routh’s value as ordinary linear transients that reach a fixed radius. The second recovers the classical magnetron-instability formula as a special case. The results are local, planar, and classical. What transfers between the asteroid and the trap is the normal-form dynamics on each level of the invariant, the transient gain, and the damped linear rates. What does not transfer without further work is the behaviour beyond the normal-form neighbourhood, where the gravitational terms of every order cause the triangular point to deviate from any purely quartic trap.
title: An Asteroid in a Penning Trap

summary: Heterogeneous evidence systems frequently combine observations that differ in measurement process, provenance, semantic representation, reliability, temporal coverage, spatial resolution, and statistical dependence. Naive aggregation can consequently amplify duplicated sources, conceal systematic bias, misrepresent uncertainty, and force consensus across claims that are not genuinely comparable. This manuscript proposes Cross-Domain Evidence-Constrained State Reconstruction (CDECSR), a research architecture whose default mechanism is Provenance-Aware, Uncertainty-Preserving State Reconstruction (PAUSR). The architecture preserves four macro-stages: taxonomic and semantic anchoring; error, dependence, and reliability parameterization: triangulation, robust fusion, and contradiction management; and latent-state estimation, validation, and controlled revision. These stages are operationalized through fourteen layers. The formal framework distinguishes the underlying target state from observations and model-dependent estimates. It represents heterogeneous observations through source-specific measurement models, accounts for shared provenance and correlated errors, and treats source reliability as a conditional quantity rather than a direct measure of truth. The proposed output is a state estimate or posterior distribution accompanied by uncertainty, provenance, unresolved contradictions, assumptions, validation results, and a reproducibility record. The architecture is specified through the Conflicting Reports in an Environmental Crisis (CREC), a structured primary case in which field reports and other observations may disagree about event location, timing, intensity, extent, and progression. The manuscript also defines a falsifiable research program, conditional mathematical results, counterexamples, simulation requirements, validation protocols, and a fourteen-step pathway toward a research paper.

title: Cross-Domain Evidence-Constrained State Reconstruction Theory

summary: Abstract This paper proposes the Reference-Standard Inference-to-Fact Escalation Principle (RSIFEP), a general theoretical framework for analysing how a reasonable default inference about an object, individual, event, process, model, or system may be presented with a stronger epistemic status than its available justification warrants. The framework distinguishes the basis used to construct an inference from the inference itself, the evidence supporting it, the status assigned to it, the scope within which it is. asserted, and the role it plays in an operational system. A reference standard may consist of a statistical base rate, a measure of central tendency, an operational default, a validated baseline, a normative or formal standard, or a model-based analogy. These categories are related but not interchangeable. The central proposition is conditional. A default inference may be reasonable and useful without being an established fact. A status-escalation error may arise when an inference is promoted to the status of an established fact, objective description, or necessary system condition without adequate evidential, logical, or formal warrant. Such an error does not automatically produce a contradiction, paradox, dilemma, or operational failure. Those outcomes require independent definitions and additional conditions. The paper develops a six-class reference-standard taxonomy, a formal representation of reasonable reference-standard inference, a seven-stage-or-more process architecture, a twelve-category outcome taxonomy, seven theoretical propositions, a general mathematical specification, and a research programme centred on the social-media newcomer purpose-projection case. The framework also specifies its boundaries, alternative explanations, potential falsifiers, measurement requirements, and route to empirical validation. RSIFEP is presented as a proposed theoretical contribution rather than an established uni- versal law. Its novelty, explanatory advantage, measurement validity, and domain generality remain questions for literature comparison, formal analysis, and empirical testing. Keywords: reference standards; reasonable inference; default reasoning; epistemic status; status escalation; evidential warrant; scope overextension; contradiction; paradox; system-level outcomes.

title: The Reference-Standard Inference-to-Fact Escalation Principle (RSIFEP): A General Framework for Reasonable Default Inference, Epistemic Status Escalation, and System-Level Outcomes

summary: This paper proposes the Representational-Operational State-Inversion Principle (ROSIP), a candidate framework for describing cases in which an internal representation assigns a state that is the formally defined inverse of a corresponding operational state, while the operational state itself need not undergo a physical reversal. The motivating case is a false awakening: a person is asleep according to an independent physiological reference while the person's dream represents the self as awake. The proposed framework generalizes this contrast by separating the operational state of a system, the internal state of its model, the represented proposition about a shared referent, the inverse relation between comparable state features, and the attribution of the represented state as current reality. The paper defines a common semantic comparison space, an involutive inverse-state mapping, a state-divergence measure, an inversion-fit score, and a gated event-classification rule. It distinguishes representational inversion from ordinary mismatch, stale information, hypothetical simulation, false reporting, and actual reversal of physical dynamics. Eight proposed mechanism stages and fourteen analytical layers organize the framework. The manuscript identifies five foundational domains, a primary sleep-science validation pro- gram, six exploratory application domains, seven testable hypotheses, alternative explanations, falsification criteria, methodological requirements, and a fourteen-stage research roadmap. The framework's central contribution is presented as a testable formalization proposal, not as an established discovery. Its explanatory value depends on construct validity, temporal alignment, reliable measurement, independent replication, and evidence of incremental value over existing explanations. Representational state; operational state; state inversion; internal model; cybernetics; dynamical systems; state estimation; information theory; false awakening; cross-domain modeling.

title: The Representational-Operational State-Inversion Principle (ROSIP): A Proposed Formal Framework for Inverse State Representation, Functional Attribution, and Apparent Cross-Level Paradox

summary: This paper proposes the Representational-Operational State-Inversion Principle (ROSIP), a candidate framework for describing cases in which an internal representation assigns a state that is the formally defined inverse of a corresponding operational state, while the operational state itself need not undergo a physical reversal. The motivating case is a false awakening: a person is asleep according to an independent physiological reference while the person's dream represents the self as awake. The proposed framework generalizes this contrast by separating the operational state of a system, the internal state of its model, the represented proposition about a shared referent, the inverse relation between comparable state features, and the attribution of the represented state as current reality. The paper defines a common semantic comparison space, an involutive inverse-state mapping, a state-divergence measure, an inversion-fit score, and a gated event-classification rule. It distinguishes representational inversion from ordinary mismatch, stale information, hypothetical simulation, false reporting, and actual reversal of physical dynamics. Eight proposed mechanism stages and fourteen analytical layers organize the framework. The manuscript identifies five foundational domains, a primary sleep-science validation pro- gram, six exploratory application domains, seven testable hypotheses, alternative explanations, falsification criteria, methodological requirements, and a fourteen-stage research roadmap. The framework's central contribution is presented as a testable formalization proposal, not as an established discovery. Its explanatory value depends on construct validity, temporal alignment, reliable measurement, independent replication, and evidence of incremental value over existing explanations. summary: Abstract This paper proposes the Functional Direction-Purpose Mismatch Framework (FDPMF), a goal-relative framework for analyzing operations whose functional direction may not correspond to an agent's specified purpose. The framework distinguishes structural direction- purpose relations from measured direct utility, capability acquisition from execution, and direct utility from broader functional value. The mathematical core defines incremental direct utility as a difference between expected goal-related outcomes under an operation and a specified baseline. This definition enables conditional statements about positive, zero, or negative contribution while avoiding the unsupported inference that a mismatch automatically makes an operation universally useless. A separate Signal-Identity Inference Module (SIIM) examines how an observed event is used to infer an agent's identity or motive. Bayesian notation is used to formalize the evidential relationship between an observation and competing hypotheses. The framework does not treat any single learned or performed behavior as a deterministic indicator of sexual orientation. The primary illustrative case concerns a heterosexual self-identified male learner being taught a sexual behavior directed toward a male recipient, where the intended use is excluded from the learner's explicitly specified personal sexual goal. The case is conditional on these assumptions and is distinguished from a control case in which the target of the learned operation is consistent with the learner's stated goal. The paper defines the framework's ontology, terminology, mathematical variables, core mechanism, propositions, boundary conditions, operationalization protocol, empirical hy- potheses, research domains, falsification criteria, and manuscript-development roadmap. No empirical results are claimed. The paper concludes that the framework is conceptually specified for investigation, while its empirical validity and novelty remain open. Keywords: functional direction; purpose congruence; goal-relative utility; causal inference; capability acquisition; signaling theory; identity inference; operationalization; theoretical model

summary: Observations of a common physical event may differ across sensors because the sensors operate at different elevations, coordinate frames, reference times, sampling rates, calibration states, response functions, and uncertainty regimes. Raw disagreement does not, by itself, establish a physical contradiction, a sensor failure, or the existence of a new physical phenomenon. It may arise from frame misregistration, clock offsets, distinct measurands, correlated errors, genuine event dynamics, model misspecification, or insufficient observability. This paper specifies the Unified Cross-Frame Information Convergence Architecture (UCFICA), a modular framework for diagnosing and reconciling multisource observations before reconstructing a target system state. Its operational estimation core is the Reference-Conditioned Multisource State Reconstruction Architecture (RCMSRA). The framework preserves the Multi-Elevation Spatial Observation Discrepancy (MESOD) as its primary case, the Reference-Conditioned State Reconstruction Mechanism (RCSRM) as its default mechanism, and the Cross-Dimensional State Realization Protocol (CD-SRP) as its named operational protocol. The manuscript formalizes heterogeneous measurement models, coordinate and time registration, uncertainty propagation, linear-Gaussian information-form fusion, nonlinear estimation alternatives, unknown-correlation handling, residual diagnostics, and explicit rules for unresolved or incompatible observations. It preserves the original five conceptual levels while mapping them to nine operational layers. Relativistic corrections, quantum measurement theory, and holographic or cosmological hypotheses are retained as conditional research branches rather than assumed components of every fusion problem. Conditional propositions establish the mathematical circumstances under which familiar Bayesian and linear-estimation results apply. In particular, the paper does not assume that increasing the number of sensors necessarily drives estimation covariance to zero. It defines falsifiable hypotheses, controlled simulation scenarios, empirical validation requirements, counterexamples, and a staged reproducibility protocol. No simulation or empirical result is claimed to have been obtained in this manuscript.

summary: We compare neural networks, exact Matérn kernel regression and their combinations as emulators of a six-dimensional radiative-transfer table on the 285-band EMIT grid, and we study how their forward accuracy carries over to reflectance retrieval. Over ten partitions of 23{,}313 states, a kernel with one length scale per input reaches $0.095\%$ mean relative radiance error and a network $0.387\%$; a kernel on the concatenated hidden features of five networks reaches $0.076\%$. Forward and inverse rankings disagree. A convex stack improves on a wide feature kernel by only $0.0006$ radiance percentage points, yet its 95th-percentile reflectance error is larger at every partition, three times larger on average. We prove that on the physical domain the constrained retrieval error is at most the retrieval-weighted component error divided by the transmission, with constant one, that the rate this implies is sharp, and that errors proportional to the transmission lose no rate. The reversal persists on the physical domain of the retrieval and when every family is retrained on physically admissible targets only; on a second radiative-transfer code, whose transmissions stay away from zero outside one opaque band, it is much weaker.
title: Learned representations and kernel corrections for radiative-transfer emulation

summary: Harmonized snATAC-seq / snMultiome atlas across 10 published GBM cohorts (67 patients with >=50 cells per label group, ~1.65M nuclei, 2,085,175 union peaks), scored per cell type with specificity (log2FC across 10 primary cell types or 13 cell types with Neftel subtype split) and strength (fragments per cell at the peak, patient-averaged, width-normalized). v2026-11-10d correctness patch: re-applies the 60% patient-detection hard floor on top-1000 selection, after the v7 pipeline rewrite silently dropped it at v2026-11-10. scripts/scoring_config.py gains MIN_DETECTION_RATE=0.60 and MIN_CELLS_EVALUABLE=50 constants, plus an assert_filters() guard that fails at import time if downstream scripts disagree. Both the regen_top1000_v7 and build_atlas_v4_html scripts now import and enforce the floor. v4_master_scores.parquet unchanged (byte-identical to v10c). Impact: malignant top-1000 min detection rose from 33% to 60%; several high-detection peaks (SEC61G-DT, EGFR-AS1, etc.) are back in the top-1000 as they were pre-v10. Deliverables: self-contained interactive HTML viewer with 15 cell-type tabs, per-peak UCSC links, per-patient fragment-density grids and per-cohort replication chips; 15 per-cell-type top-1000 TSV tables (now filtered to patient_detection_rate >= 0.60); full peak-level master score parquet (2.09M peaks x 153 columns); underlying 430-pseudobulk matrix.
title: A harmonized human glioblastoma chromatin accessibility atlas (snATAC-seq, 67 patients, 10 cohorts, ~1.65M nuclei)

summary: FAIR metadata (Schema.org, Bioschemas and MLCommons Croissant) for the ELIXIR 3D-BioInfo benchmark of 1,677 homodimer interfaces from 1,645 protein crystal structures, together with the structure files (PDB and mmCIF), an in-repository snapshot of the PDB metadata of every entry, and the documentation of the label curation. The benchmark was published by Schweke et al. (2023, Proteomics 23(17):e2200323, doi:10.1002/pmic.202200323; 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces). This package uses the curated annotation file of the benchmark authors (844 physiological and 833 non-physiological interfaces; 16 labels revised, 20 interfaces flagged ambiguous and 6 flagged for deletion). Every interface carries both the curated label and the published label ( PublishedPhysio ). See data/curation/README.md . Please cite the original publication as well as this package.
title: ELIXIR - Protein-Protein Interface Benchmark - FAIR Metadata

It contains the campaign runner and the coverage tool, the protocol of the 2026 campaigns, the analysis of the revised evaluation, the archived and the corrected OpenAPI specifications of the CMDE API, and the raw data of the initial study (2025). The raw data of the 2026 campaigns are published separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24148473 .
title: Replication package: Automatic Test Data Generation for RESTful APIs: A Case Study on a Governmental System

summary: The ELIXIR 3D-BioInfo community benchmark for discriminating physiological from non-physiological protein–protein interfaces (Schweke et al., Proteomics 2023) contains 1,677 homodimer interfaces from 1,645 PDB entries. We describe the FAIRification of this benchmark, carried out by the University of Bologna ELIXIR node within the ELIXIR Tools Platform. The benchmark is described with Bioschemas/schema.org JSON-LD: every interface is annotated with its label, chains, structural features, sequence-cluster assignment, provenance and licence, and linked to the PDB structure files and to snapshots of the RCSB PDB metadata. The first version of the package was audited against the publication and the source repository, and the errors found were corrected. A lightweight design removed the need for Git LFS and for duplicated metadata. The post-publication curation of the labels (844 physiological and 833 non-physiological interfaces, compared with 836 and 841 in the publication) is documented, and three entries superseded in the PDB are linked to their replacements. A reference machine-learning script with cluster-aware cross-validation is included. Data, scripts and a web portal are available on GitHub under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence, with full attribution to the original work.
title: FAIRification of the ELIXIR 3D-Bioinfo Protein-Protein Interface Benchmark

summary: Raw data of the revised evaluation of the paper "Automatic Test Data Generation for RESTful APIs: A Case Study on a Governmental System". Two campaigns ran four techniques implemented in EvoMaster 6.2.0 (MIO, RANDOM, WTS, and SMARTS) in black-box mode against a local deployment of the CMDE API with fictitious records. official-6.2.0.tar.gz : main campaign, 30 blocks × 4 techniques (120 executions), 30-minute search budget. low-budget-6.2.0.tar.gz : low-budget campaign, 10 blocks × 4 techniques (40 executions), limited to 20 requests per minute. Each execution directory holds the generated test suite, EvoMaster's statistics, the coverage of each criterion, the HTTP traffic of two re-executions of the suite, and the API's logs. MANIFEST-*.txt give the SHA-256 of every file in each archive, and SHA256SUMS the SHA-256 of the archives. The API keys were replaced with REDACTED_API_KEY . The records of people in the deployment are fictitious. The code, the protocol of the campaigns, and the analysis scripts are in the replication package ( https://github.com/vilelaricardo/cmde-restapi-replication-package , archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22112783 ). To reproduce the analysis, extract the archives and set CMDE_DATA to the extracted directory (see analysis/jss-revision/README.md in the package).
title: Raw data of the 2026 campaigns: automatic test data generation for the CMDE RESTful API (EvoMaster 6.2.0)

summary: This article develops a mathematical reconstruction of a conceptual proposal called the fixed attractor. The proposal starts from a question in the philosophy of social order: why do human societies repeatedly produce forms of cooperation and coordination without converging either to a permanently unified condition or to uninterrupted, system-wide disintegration? The article approaches this question through a deliberately limited dialogue between Qur’anic concepts and stochastic dynamical systems. Five conceptual motifs are examined: persistent human difference (ikhtilaf ), countervailing action (daf ), a boundary or separator (barzakh), the regularity of social processes (sunnat Allah), and the presence of morally exceptional minorities. These motifs are treated as interpretive prompts for model construction, not as mathematical theorems contained verbatim in scripture. The formal model describes a vector of normalized social indicators evolving in an open, bounded state space. Its drift combines mean-reverting forces with cross-domain coupling; its diffusion is state-dependent and vanishes at the boundary; and its finite-activity jump component represents shocks whose state-dependent impact preserves the interior. The article corrects and makes explicit several conditions that are necessary for the model to work: uniform inward-pointing drift at every face of the state domain, a stable coupling matrix, and a jump map that preserves the domain. Under these assumptions, a logarithmic barrier function establishes non-attainment of the boundary in finite time. Additional Lyapunov, Feller, and irreducibility conditions yield existence and uniqueness of an invariant probability distribution. When the drift is centered and the jump marks have zero mean, the invariant mean equals the model’s interior reference point, while non-degenerate interior diffusion produces persistent stationary variation. A three-dimensional example is specified for political, economic, and cultural indicators. A reproducible Euler–Maruyama/compound-Poisson experiment, reconstructed from the supplied source manuscript with a consistent parameter matrix, gives illustrative sample means close to the reference point and non-zero dispersion. These computations verify the numerical behavior of the chosen model implementation; they do not constitute empirical evidence that actual societies obey it. The article therefore separates three claims that are often conflated: a theological reading, a mathematical implication conditional on assumptions, and an empirical hypothesis requiring operational definitions and historical data. Its contribution is a transparent bounded-dynamics framework and a research programme for testing it, rather than a proof of a universal law of history.
tags: social dynamics; bounded stochastic processes; invariant distribution; boundary non- attainment; coupled systems; jump–diffusion; Qur'anic concepts; social order; resilience; model validation
title: The Fixed Attractor: A Bounded Stochastic Framework for the Dynamics of Human Social Order

The formal model describes a vector of normalized social indicators evolving in an open, bounded state space. Its drift combines mean-reverting forces with cross-domain coupling; its diffusion is state-dependent and vanishes at the boundary; and its finite-activity jump component represents shocks whose state-dependent impact preserves the interior. The article corrects and makes explicit several conditions that are necessary for the model to work: uniform inward-pointing drift at every face of the state domain, a stable coupling matrix, and a jump map that preserves the domain. Under these assumptions, a logarithmic barrier function establishes non-attainment of the boundary in finite time. Additional Lyapunov, Feller, and irreducibility conditions yield existence and uniqueness of an invariant probability distribution. When the drift is centered and the jump marks have zero mean, the invariant mean equals the model’s interior reference point, while non-degenerate interior diffusion produces persistent stationary variation. A three-dimensional example is specified for political, economic, and cultural indicators. A reproducible Euler–Maruyama/compound-Poisson experiment, reconstructed from the supplied source manuscript with a consistent parameter matrix, gives illustrative sample means close to the reference point and non-zero dispersion. These computations verify the numerical behavior of the chosen model implementation; they do not constitute empirical evidence that actual societies obey it. The article therefore separates three claims that are often conflated: a theological reading, a mathematical implication conditional on assumptions, and an empirical hypothesis requiring operational definitions and historical data. Its contribution is a transparent bounded-dynamics framework and a research programme for testing it, rather than a proof of a universal law of history.

summary: Freestanding thin films of quantum materials naturally develop sub-micrometer, nonuniform strain fields that strongly affect their electronic, magnetic, and structural properties in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium conditions. However, current methods to quantitatively resolve these mesoscopic features are primarily restricted to scanning probes, making it challenging for dynamical measurements such as single-shot imaging and femtosecond microscopy. Here, we present a new computational framework which we denote as bend contour electron tomography (BCET), which efficiently converts bend contours in transmission electron microscope images into quantitative two-dimensional maps of strain and topography. By iteratively minimizing a designed loss function between experimental and simulated bend contour images, BCET retrieves both surface morphology and in-plane strain tensor fields without requiring scanning or diffraction mapping. We applied BCET to freestanding SrTiO 3 thin films, demonstrating the successful reconstruction of the local strain distribution and curvature field with high fidelity. Our approach provides a quantitative framework for characterizing mesoscale structures in freestanding films using wide-field imaging, opening new avenues to investigate how spatial inhomogeneity governs phase transitions and nonequilibrium dynamics in two-dimensional quantum materials.
title: Bend Contour Electron Tomography (BCET): Quantitative strain and topography mapping

summary: This record provides the derived dataset, analysis code snapshot, and complete supporting analysis archive for research on recorded wildfire fireline outcomes. The retained dataset contains 304,143 fireline units from 381 fires in 2020–2024. Each unit contains at most 250 m of total mapped fireline length. Recorded outcomes comprise 205,926 Held units and 98,217 Burned Over units. NIFC fireline records are linked with NIROPS timing evidence, weather forecasts, terrain, and vegetation. The package includes a selection audit covering 572,200 candidate fireline units, 803 designated modeling predictors, data dictionaries, evaluation folds, saved predictions, supporting results, figure-generation inputs, and the complete analysis archive. The code supports verification of saved results and reproduction of documented figures. Full reconstruction of the historical extraction and training workflow requires additional inputs described in the documentation. Fireline-unit selection was retrospective. The analyses describe relationships with recorded outcomes and do not establish the causal effect of constructing a fireline or reliability for operational suppression decisions. summary: Purpose This record documents a two-sample summary-data Mendelian randomization study designed to test whether genetic liability to cirrhosis, and to liver fibrosis, is causally related to cardiovascular disease. People with fibrotic liver disease carry a substantial excess of cardiovascular events, but whether that excess reflects a direct vascular effect of fibrosis or the metabolic disturbance that accompanies it is difficult to separate in observational data, where both are entangled with shared risk factors and with reverse causation. The study uses common genetic variants as instruments to break that entanglement, and asks two questions in sequence: whether the exposure is causally associated with five cardiovascular outcomes, and, if the association is absent or heterogeneous, which component of the exposure carries such association as exists. Contents The deposit holds the complete analytical record rather than selected outputs. It comprises 44 analysis scripts; 6 typesetting scripts retained for transparency but not runnable in isolation; 105 analysis-ready input files derived from public summary statistics, including a rebuilt LD score panel; 56 result files, one per analysis; the thirteen numbered tables of the companion article as CSV, with a companion legends file; Figures 1–3 as submitted; and a manifest giving dataset provenance for each of the eleven source datasets, a file-level inventory with SHA-256 checksums, a crosswalk between pipeline and article table numbering, and the recorded software environment. ANALYSIS_PLAN.md is the English rendering of the study protocol, together with a record of how each provision was implemented and a twelve-item register of departures from that protocol. Two of those departures, and two analyses added after first submission, are documented there rather than left implicit in the code. Methods Instruments were constructed from eleven public datasets — ten studies from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog and one FinnGen release — for cirrhosis liability as the primary exposure and liver fibrosis as the replication exposure, against coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ischaemic stroke and arterial stiffness, with four metabolic traits considered as candidate mediators. Estimates were obtained from six estimators: inverse-variance weighted with multiplicative random effects, MR-Egger with SIMEX correction, weighted median, weighted mode, MR-PRESSO and the contamination mixture. These are read alongside Cochran's Q and I²_GX, leave-one-out analysis, reverse-direction Mendelian randomization, overlap correction by MRlap, multivariable Mendelian randomization with conditional F statistics, two-step mediation, stratification by each variant's effect on LDL cholesterol, and colocalisation by coloc.abf . A positive control, LDL cholesterol against coronary disease, is included to show that the pipeline recovers a known effect. Use Three entry points are supported, at increasing cost. A published estimate can be checked from the deposited harmonised per-variant effects alone, without any download, by passing four columns to the estimator functions in mrlib.py . Every numbered table can be regenerated from the deposited results with a single script; the regenerated sources for the two tables carrying the primary estimates were verified byte-identical to those that produced the submitted tables. A full re-run from raw data is possible once the third-party summary statistics are placed under data/ in accordance with the registry in datasets.py , from which the driver run_all.py executes the stages in order. Every stochastic estimator is seeded and its resampling counts are fixed, so a re-run reproduces the deposited numbers exactly rather than within Monte Carlo error. Reuse and value The deposit is constructed to be reusable beyond the study that produced it. mrlib.py implements each estimator from its published description and is self-contained, so
title: Genetic Liability to Cirrhosis and Cardiovascular Disease: A Mendelian Randomization Study of Dyslipidemia, Not Fibrosis

summary: The YiPEE cluster-randomised controlled trial was conducted in Chennai, India, in 2024-2025 evaluating a school-based intervention aiming to improve adolescent mental health and well-being. This dataset includes quantitative data from 30 schools with approximately 2,800 seventh grade students. Baseline and endline data were collected using pen and paper surveys. Variables include adolescents' self-reported anxiety and depression symptoms, suicide thoughts and behaviors, scales on well-being, school cohesion, hope, gratitude, belonging, resilience, connectedness, and school kindness. There is also data from approximately 200 teachers at baseline and endline which includes self-reported well-being. Cross-sectional data was collected from school-going adolescents in seventh grade in Stockholm, Sweden in 2025. Variables include symptoms of anxiety and depression, suicide thoughts and behaviors, scales on well-being, hope, belonging, and participation. Cross-sectional data was collected from 373 school-going adolescents in Nairobi, Kenya in 2025. Students ages 12-15 years completed pen-and-paper questionnaires on well-being, connectedness, gratitude, school kindness, hope, resilience, self-esteem and school climate.  Data access: Data are available upon request and will be made publicly available once the articles using the data are published.
title: Data for: Youth co-Production for sustainable Engagement and Empowerment in health (YiPEE)

summary: Overview Songdo Vision OBB is the oriented bounding box (OBB) counterpart of the Songdo Vision dataset. It provides the same 5,419 high-resolution 4K RGB frames (3840×2160) captured over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea , with every one of the 274,190 vehicle annotations expressed as a rotated rectangle instead of an axis-aligned box, across the same four classes : Car (including vans and light-duty vehicles) Bus Truck Motorcycle Horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) are a poor fit for high-altitude bird's-eye-view (BeV) imagery, where vehicles appear at arbitrary in-plane orientations. A diagonally traveling or parked vehicle fills a small fraction of its axis-aligned box, and the rest is road surface, lane markings, or a neighboring vehicle. Songdo Vision OBB replaces those boxes with tight oriented ones, so the dataset can serve as a benchmark for oriented aerial vehicle detection and as a source of vehicle heading for downstream traffic analysis. The images are byte-identical to those of Songdo Vision, and the annotations are derived one-to-one from Songdo Vision v2 , so the two records can be used together or interchangeably. Alongside the converted annotations, the release ships the 50 manually annotated OBB frames that were used to tune and validate the conversion. A full dataset card with usage instructions and download guidance is available on Hugging Face . 📌 Citation: if you use this dataset in your work, please cite the paper that introduces it, which is the preferred citation: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis (2026). Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes. arXiv: XXXX.XXXXX. Please also cite the article behind the imagery and the source annotations [1] . BibTeX entries for both, and the dataset's own archival citation, are in Citation & Attribution. 🔗 Related datasets: the source HBB annotations are Songdo Vision v2: 10.5281/zenodo.21728430 . For precisely georeferenced vehicle trajectories extracted from the same large-scale multi-drone experiment, see Songdo Traffic (latest version): 10.5281/zenodo.13828383 . The benchmark paper that introduces this dataset annotates its own data at the conversion settings selected here: see its software, stabilo-benchmark ( 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX , GitHub: rfonod/stabilo-benchmark ), and its data record ( 10.5281/zenodo.23623540 ). 🛠️ Conversion tool: the oriented boxes were produced with HBB2OBB v1.10.0 ( 10.5281/zenodo.22664151 , GitHub: rfonod/hbb2obb ), the exact version recorded in each subset's PROVENANCE.txt . See How the OBBs Were Produced. Motivation Axis-aligned boxes discard orientation, which in aerial imagery is both information the sensor genuinely captured and information downstream tasks need: Loose spatial support. A vehicle at 45° occupies roughly half of its axis-aligned box; the remainder is background that a detector must learn to ignore, and that an instance-level consumer cannot separate from the vehicle. Neighbor bleed. In dense parking rows and at intersection approaches, the axis-aligned box of one diagonally oriented vehicle routinely overlaps, and sometimes fully contains, its neighbors. Songdo Vision v2 documents 104 such pairs at IoU 0.3 to 0.5 that are correct yet unavoidable with HBBs. No heading. Vehicle orientation has to be inferred from tracking, which is fragile for stationary or slow-moving vehicles. Cost of re-annotation. Producing OBBs by hand at this scale, roughly 274k instances, is not practical. Songdo Vision OBB addresses this by converting the existing, human-verified HBBs into OBBs with a segmentation-based method, rather than by re-annotating from scratch. Every OBB inherits the class label and the provenance of the HBB it came from, so the annotation quality work done for Songdo Vision v2 carries over intact. Dataset Composition The dataset keeps the training (80%) and test (20%) split of Songdo Vision, frame for frame. Conversion is one-to-one, so

summary: Human dermo-epidermal skin equivalents (DE) comprising  in vitro  expanded autologous keratinocytes and fibroblasts are a good option for massive burn treatment. However, the lengthy expansion time required to obtain sufficient surface to cover an extensive burn together with the challenging surgical procedure limits their clinical use. The integration of DE and biodegradable scaffolds has been proposed in an effort to enhance their mechanical properties. Here, it is shown that poly(hydroxybutyrate) electrospun scaffolds (PHB) present good biocompatibility both  in vitro  and  in vivo  and are superior to poly-ε-caprolactone electrospun scaffolds as a substrate for skin reconstruction. Implantation of PHB scaffolds in healthy rats polarized macrophages to an M2-type that promoted constructive  in vivo remodelling. Moreover, implantation of DE-PHB composites in a NOD/SCID mouse xenograft model resulted in engraftment accompanied by an increase in angiogenesis that favoured the survival of the human graft. Thus, PHB scaffolds are an attractive substrate for further exploration in skin reconstruction procedures, probably due in part to their greater angiogenic and M2 macrophage polarization properties

title: Electrospun poly(hydroxybutyrate) scaffolds promote engraftment of human skin equivalents via macrophage M2 polarization and angiogenesis
