summary: Run records, analysis of record and code of the component study reported in the appendix "Design, Provenance and Component Study of KAYROS" of the PhD thesis of Florian Rascoussier, "Improving Anytime Resolution of Large-Scale VRPTW and its Time-Dependent Extension" (ED SPIN, IMT Atlantique and INSA Lyon). Every table, figure and number of the component-study section of that appendix is computed from the files of this dataset. KAYROS is an exact and anytime solver for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with time windows (TDVRPTW) under the Duration objective. Its exact mode is a branch-price-and-cut derived from the open-source solver of Lera-Romero, Miranda-Bront and Soulignac (Networks, 2020), and its heuristic mode is an iterated local search. The study asks 3 questions: whether the exact mode of KAYROS still performs as the solver it comes from once embedded, repaired and extended, what the open LP backend HiGHS costs compared with CPLEX, and what the heuristic and exact modes bring to each other. Design. The panel is the complete set of 56 Dabia et al. (2013) TDVRPTW instances with 100 customers, as distributed by MAMUT-routing. The 5 arms are the repaired baseline (the solver of Lera-Romero et al. at its public commit cabc56a plus 3 patches, with CPLEX 12.10), the exact mode of KAYROS 1.7.0 alone with CPLEX, the same with HiGHS 1.14.0, the heuristic mode of KAYROS alone, and the full solver (15 s of heuristic search, then the warm-started exact mode with CPLEX). Each arm runs 5 trials on each instance, 1,400 runs in total, each with 7,200 s from process launch, one pinned core and an address space limited to 16 GiB, with 10 concurrent runs per node on the grvingt cluster of the Grid'5000 testbed. The heuristic and full arms use 5 paired seeds. KAYROS runs used commit 25d8f0088337b9667956f07fe365c749def9894f of https://github.com/0nyr/kayros , released as version 1.7.0. The sources of the repaired baseline are also public, as the tag component-study-as-run of https://github.com/0nyr/lera-tdvrptw-bpc-repaired . Contents. cells/ holds one directory per run with the run summary (cell.json), the timestamped stream of incumbents, lower bounds and closures (events.jsonl), the native solver result (native.json, absent for the 185 runs ended by the memory limit or killed after the budget), the solver standard error (stderr.log) and the claim record (claim.json). plan.json is the plan of the 1,400 runs, runners/ the runner and job logs, scripts/ the frozen runner scripts. analysis/ holds the analysis of record (final-summary.json, which re-checks every route set with the reference checker mamut-routing-lib 0.11.0), the main and per-instance tables, and a comparison of the proofs with the stored optimality certificates. code/ holds the experiment harness, the analysis scripts, the frozen best-known-solution snapshot used as reference, the script that produces the tables and figures of the appendix, and the 3 patches of the baseline. The bundled README.md decodes the layout, the record fields, the acceptance rule of a proof and the integrity hashes. Main results. Accepted proofs: 165 of 280 runs for the repaired baseline, 172 for the exact mode of KAYROS with CPLEX, 135 with HiGHS (5 proofs rejected because a priced column fails the checker), 171 for the full solver, and none for the heuristic arm, which cannot prove optimality. Restricted mean time to proof: 3,295.0 s, 3,181.3 s, 4,256.3 s and 3,197.5 s. Mean anytime score: 0.37914, 0.35880, 0.49777, 0.00238 for the heuristic arm and 0.00644 for the full solver. 177 runs end at the memory limit, on 13 instances that no arm proves. Limits. The baseline is the repaired solver, not the published one. The pricing changes of KAYROS 1.7.0 were selected on this same panel. The panel is one family at one size, run on one machine type. The proofs are computational closures of single runs, checked for consistency, and not independent certificates. The records keep their original Grid
title: Component Study of KAYROS on the Dabia2013 TDVRPTW Instances with 100 Customers: Run Records and Analysis

summary: Code, data and model outputs of the study "Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference". The study fine-tunes small language models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Phi-4-mini-instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) to estimate twelve structural properties of a graph from its text serialization, and maps where this generalizes and where it fails: across graph sizes, graph families, vertex numberings, serializations and real-world domains. Files graph-structural-inference-slm.zip - the code of the study: generation of every evaluation set, fine-tuning, constrained-decoding evaluation, audits, statistical analyses and the scripts that produce every table and figure of the article, together with every model prediction (one record per graph and evaluation). Code under the MIT licence, predictions under CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-evaluation-sets.zip - 10,320 synthetic evaluation graphs (twelve size ranges beyond the training size and a second size series up to 300 vertices, seven further graph families, renumbered copies, seven serializations, and the test graphs rewired with every vertex degree kept) and two further samples of 1,200 training graphs, with exact labels, provenance and checksums. CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-adapters-main.zip - the 18 LoRA adapters behind the in-distribution results (three base models, adjacency list and edge list, seeds 42, 43 and 44), with their base models, seeds and checksums. Each adapter is subject to the licence of its base model (Llama 3.2 Community License, MIT, Qwen Research License). Built with Llama. Built with Qwen. The training and test graphs of the study are those of the TinyGraphEstimator dataset. The real-world datasets (ENZYMES, IMDB-BINARY, NCI1, ogbg-moltox21) are not redistributed: the code rebuilds the sets of the study from their original sources.
title: Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference: code, predictions, evaluation sets and fine-tuned adapters

summary: Code, runner kits and measurements of ParityRT, a method for comparing hardware ray tracing cost across Apple GPUs (Metal) and PC GPUs (Vulkan). One renderer runs the same workloads on both APIs through inline ray queries in compute passes, times every ray-traced effect as its own pass, and withholds timings from any backend that fails the image-parity, ray-count and depth-correctness gates. The record holds the source code (C++20 engine, Slang shaders, scenes, workload files, analysis scripts), runner kits for macOS and Windows, and the 18 result bundles of the measurements: an Apple M5 (fanless), an Apple M5 Max and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti as measured devices, and an AMD Radeon 660M, an Intel Arc 140T, an Intel Arc (Core Ultra 7 155H) and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2050 as validation-only devices run by outside runners. DATA_README.md describes every file and how to re-analyse the bundles. Computer names and home-folder paths are redacted.
title: ParityRT: a cross-vendor hardware ray tracing benchmark for Metal and Vulkan GPUs: code, runner kits and result bundles

summary: Version 3.1 (12 November 2026) of "The Standard Model and gravity as effective LdGS". The Standard Model and gravity as a reference effective theory with a matching programme toward a single Landau–de Gennes–Skyrme (LdGS) tensor field. Version 3.0 established the reading used throughout (classical configurations as leading order, quantized ensembles as physical objects, experiment as the final judge), milestones stated by experiment across atomic, nuclear, particle, gravity and cosmology, and atomic-scale bounds on LdGS-specific effects. New in 3.1: • First steps toward a derived hadronic action: the winding field and the record frame form an SO(4) frame with the hidden-local-symmetry parametrization (a composite connection, not yet a dynamical ρ); unfitted soliton numbers with physical meson inputs reproduce the known soliton systematics; a parent-induced vector response computed, with the timelike control showing what remains to be calculated (pole, residue, decay vertex). • A corrected account of the native Card C: the record enters the matter tensor and couples to the winding field through an exact positive cross term of order 1/230, with a coefficient-free ablation defined. • External replication through frozen packets (manifests, SHA-256 checksums, plans before numbers): the string tension of the fractional-charge strand with its width and stress profile against archived lattice data is the first LdGS-specific test, taken by an external team; then the W multi-baryon pipeline and the photon-point comparison with and without the record. • Reviews by several AI systems folded in, including corrections of earlier statements, recorded in the version history. Sharpest external test remains the rank-two seesaw's Σmν = 58.69 meV (normal ordering, m1 = 0), at the edge of DESI's Bayesian ΛCDM limits and in tension with its Feldman–Cousins limit, as every oscillation-compatible spectrum is. Version 4.0 is reserved for the first native LdGS prediction confirmed against data it was not fitted to, in any domain. summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies the manuscript “Disentangling analytical sensitivity and donor influence in single-nucleus depression data”. Version 2.0.0 contains author-derived aggregate results, gene-level result summaries, figure source tables, analysis code, source fingerprints, documentation, and executable statistical and plotting checks supporting six main figures and eight supplementary figures. The study examines analytical-component sensitivity, donor influence, conditional calibration, sample planning, modern statistical methods, and independent disease evaluations. The internally stable 68-gene catalogue did not meet the evaluated external replication criteria. Fine-subtype annotation qualification failed, and the planned target fine-subtype disease analysis was not performed. The portable workflow supports aggregate statistical checks and figure reconstruction. Full count-model reruns require separately obtained source matrices, permitted metadata, and the documented dependencies. Third-party count matrices, individual clinical records, installed environments, and complete third-party gene-set libraries are excluded. Author-owned analysis code is licensed under the MIT License. Original derived aggregate results and documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Third-party inputs and software remain subject to their original terms. Funding: General Project of the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Education, China, grant Y202559996; Basic Scientific Research Project of the Wenzhou Science and Technology Bureau, China, grant YC20250576.

summary: This repository provides data and Python code supporting the manuscript “Estimating Depth-Integrated Suspended-Sediment Flux During Floods Using Hyperspectral CCTV.” The study combines hyperspectral estimates of surface suspended-sediment concentration (SSC) and image-derived surface velocity with a Rouse–flux model to estimate depth-integrated sediment transport per unit channel width. The archive includes: SSC training data and models: 342 matchups for the unified model, comprising 127 baseline observations and 215 flood observations, and 211 matchups for the tracer model. Reflectance data, concentration targets, feature-selection information, model parameters, and code for model fitting and 5-fold cross-validation are provided. Vertical-profile and flux data: Processed SSC and velocity profiles from 27 field casts, together with code for vertical-profile reconstruction and flux correction. Camera-input comparisons: Nine comparison records, including seven with paired camera-derived SSC and velocity estimates. STIV example: One preprocessed space-time image from a flood observation, with code for surface-velocity estimation. Summary results for all nine STIV validation scans are also included. Supporting information: Hourly hydrological data, archived comparison results, a data dictionary, dependency specifications, and numerical reproduction checks. The archive starts from processed observation tables and a preprocessed space-time image. Raw hyperspectral cubes and complete spatial SSC, velocity, and flux maps are outside its scope. The tracer training table preserves the original processed concentration target and provides all-size LISST concentration separately. Target definitions, wavelength conventions, evaluation procedures, and calibration dependencies are documented in the accompanying files. Run python run_all.py to execute the included analyses and reproduction checks. See README.txt for installation and usage instructions and DATA_DICTIONARY.txt for variable definitions and units. Data, documentation, and results are provided under CC BY 4.0 , and Python code is provided under the MIT License . Please cite this dataset and the associated paper when using these materials.

summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) presents significant clinical heterogeneity in cognitive decline. Neuroimaging profiles and peripheral biomarkers, such as plasma oxidative stress biomarkers could provide information on AD progression. This study evaluates the contribution of baseline neuroimaging features and plasma lipid peroxidation biomarkers to modelling cognitive decline trajectories in early AD. Data were collected from patients with early AD (n = 195), and they were neuropsychologically evaluated to assess their progression. Baseline data included demographics, neuropsychological evaluations, neuroimaging measures and plasma lipid peroxidation levels. Follow-up neuropsychological evaluations were conducted biennially. Individual cognitive decline trajectories were estimated using MMSE and CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. Multivariate modelling and hierarchical clustering analyses were applied to identify prognostic signatures and patient subgroups. Baseline neuroimaging variables showed significant associations with longitudinal cognitive trajectories, as reflected in MMSE and CDR Sum of Boxes slopes, whereas plasma lipid peroxidation biomarkers did not. Multivariate models based on neuroimaging features demonstrated substantial predictive contribution (conditional R 2 0.825 for MMSE and 0.808 for CDR Sum of Boxes). Hierarchical clustering identified four distinct groups, primarily driven by left Koedam scores, enlarged perivascular spaces, and Fazekas scores. These clusters were significantly associated with differential rates of cognitive decline, particularly for MMSE. In conclusion, structural neuroimaging measures at baseline are robust indicators of cognitive decline in early AD, supporting its utility for individualized prognosis in early AD.

summary: Industrial motors are widely used in manufacturing plants, pumps, conveyors, compressors and other industrial equipment. Unexpected motor failure can interrupt production, increase maintenance costs and create safety risks. Routine maintenance and reactive repair may not identify developing faults early enough. This project presents an embedded-system-based predictive maintenance system for industrial motors that monitors operating parameters and provides early warnings when abnormal conditions are detected. The proposed system uses an ESP32 microcontroller with a DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, an SW-420 vibration sensor and an ACS712 current sensor. Sensor readings are processed by the controller to identify conditions such as excessive temperature, abnormal vibration and unusual current consumption. An LCD with an I2C interface displays the operating status, while LEDs and a buzzer provide local fault alerts. The ESP32 can also transmit readings to an IoT dashboard for remote monitoring. An AI prediction layer can be added by collecting labelled operating data and training a classification or anomaly-detection model to estimate motor condition. In a small-scale implementation, threshold-based alerts provide the baseline, while the AI model can be evaluated separately using recorded data. The project demonstrates how embedded sensing, IoT communication and data-driven analysis can support condition monitoring and reduce unplanned downtime. The system is intended as an educational demonstrator and requires industrial-grade sensors, isolation and validation before deployment on production equipment.

summary: Abstract : Background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global public-health problem and an important cause of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. Although nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy has substantially improved management, antiviral resistance-associated mutations may occasionally be detected before treatment exposure. Objective: To systematically determine the prevalence and distribution of established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations among treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection and to estimate the pooled prevalence of patients carrying at least one established primary resistance mutation. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using a patient-level endpoint defined as the presence of at least one established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutation in a unique treatment-naïve patient. Secondary or compensatory mutations were not counted as primary resistance when occurring alone. Studies using highly sensitive assays, including mutation-specific PCR and next-generation sequencing, were considered separately where appropriate. The review was structured according to PRISMA 2020. Results: The current primary quantitative dataset comprised 42 cohorts involving 9,811 evaluable treatment-naïve participants, of whom 417 carried at least one qualifying primary resistance-associated mutation, giving a crude prevalence of 4.25%. The current random-effects synthesis estimated an overall pooled prevalence of 1.80% (95% CI, 1.04–3.09%). Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=93.3%; τ²=2.541; Q=616.02). The approximate 95% prediction interval was 0.08–30.41%. Conclusion: Naturally occurring primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations are detectable in a minority of treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection, but reported prevalence varies substantially according to population, geography, genotype, study design, and assay sensitivity. The pooled estimate should therefore not be interpreted as a universal prevalence applicable to every clinical setting.

summary: Abstract : Background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global public-health problem and an important cause of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. Although nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy has substantially improved management, antiviral resistance-associated mutations may occasionally be detected before treatment exposure. Objective: To systematically determine the prevalence and distribution of established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations among treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection and to estimate the pooled prevalence of patients carrying at least one established primary resistance mutation. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using a patient-level endpoint defined as the presence of at least one established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutation in a unique treatment-naïve patient. Secondary or compensatory mutations were not counted as primary resistance when occurring alone. Studies using highly sensitive assays, including mutation-specific PCR and next-generation sequencing, were considered separately where appropriate. The review was structured according to PRISMA 2020. Results: The current primary quantitative dataset comprised 42 cohorts involving 9,811 evaluable treatment-naïve participants, of whom 417 carried at least one qualifying primary resistance-associated mutation, giving a crude prevalence of 4.25%. The current random-effects synthesis estimated an overall pooled prevalence of 1.80% (95% CI, 1.04–3.09%). Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=93.3%; τ²=2.541; Q=616.02). The approximate 95% prediction interval was 0.08–30.41%. Conclusion: Naturally occurring primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations are detectable in a minority of treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection, but reported prevalence varies substantially according to population, geography, genotype, study design, and assay sensitivity. The pooled estimate should therefore not be interpreted as a universal prevalence applicable to every clinical setting.

A polyphenol that survives separation may still be degraded by oxygen. A stable flavonoid can compete for the same carrier interface that an identified terpenoid requires. A polysaccharide fraction may alter viscosity and transport while also changing what an instrument can recover. And a pleasing co-delivery curve might still conceal a failure of the weakest component. This notebook studies the bridges, not merely the isolated accomplishments of each chemistry. The F001 to F005 sequence should be regarded as a chain of evidence. A specimen passport precedes the chromatographic result; a parent-product chemical balance precedes any stability claim; a measured free-active pool precedes an encapsulation claim; a distribution-aware fraction analysis precedes a structure-property claim; and a component-specific conservation ledger precedes any assertion about a combined formulation. These contracts can fail independently. The result is a discipline that refuses to let one beautiful plot pay for another missing measurement. The Ben Cao Gang Mu enters here as intellectual history and a question-forming tradition. Classification, preparation, relationships among materials, and care over identity can inspire what modern scientists decide to separate or compare. A research atlas that contains 819 pages may be useful as a navigable inventory of proposed investigations, yet its scale does not convert hypotheses into results. summary: Protein sequences change over time due to the accumulation of mutations in the genes that encode them. Nonetheless, accurately identifying the most probable evolutionary pathways and more efficient trajectories between an ancestral and a derived sequence remains a challenge. This difficulty stems from a limited understanding of the critical factors that drive the evolutionary process. This study aims to address this issue by validating a newly proposed mechanistic model (grounded on the principle of least action) for analyzing protein evolution, using beta-lactamase as an empirically characterized evolutionary model. The initial findings indicate that, after accounting for how mutations and the context-dependent interactions between them (epistasis) affect protein stability and, hence, the kinetics of protein folding, a resort to the principle of least action allows us to simultaneously identify the most probable pathways and the most efficient trajectories swiftly and accurately. These findings also suggest that the most probable evolutionary protein pathways are the ones that exhibit the most efficient trajectories. All in all, our study addresses several unanswered questions regarding the main factors that govern how protein evolves at the molecular level (under constant selection pressure) and outlines directions for future research in key fields such as directed evolution and ancestral sequence reconstruction.
title: Analyzing \b{eta}-Lactamase Evolution from the Principle of Least Action Perspective

summary: Assuming that mutation and fixation processes are reversible Markov processes, we prove that the equilibrium ensemble of sequences obeys a Boltzmann distribution with $\exp(4N_e m(1 - 1/(2N)))$, where $m$ is Malthusian fitness and $N_e$ and $N$ are effective and actual population sizes. On the other hand, the probability distribution of sequences with maximum entropy that satisfies a given amino acid composition at each site and a given pairwise amino acid frequency at each site pair is a Boltzmann distribution with $\exp(-ψ_N)$, where $ψ_N$ is represented as the sum of one body and pairwise potentials. A protein folding theory indicates that homologous sequences obey a canonical ensemble characterized by $\exp(-ΔG_{ND}/k_B T_s)$ or by $\exp(- G_{N}/k_B T_s)$ if an amino acid composition is kept constant, where $ΔG_{ND} \equiv G_N - G_D$, $G_N$ and $G_D$ are the native and denatured free energies, and $T_s$ is selective temperature. Thus, $4N_e m (1 - 1/(2N))$, $-Δψ_{ND}$, and $-ΔG_{ND}/k_B T_s$ must be equivalent to each other. Based on the analysis of the changes ($Δψ_N$) of $ψ_N$ due to single nucleotide nonsynonymous substitutions, $T_s$, and then glass transition temperature $T_g$, and $ΔG_{ND}$ are estimated with reasonable values for 14 protein domains. In addition, approximating the probability density function (PDF) of $Δψ_N$ by a log-normal distribution, PDFs of $Δψ_N$ and $K_a/K_s$, which is the ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate per site, in all and in fixed mutants are estimated. It is confirmed that $T_s$ negatively correlates with the mean of $K_a/K_s$. Stabilizing mutations are significantly fixed by positive selection, and balance with destabilizing mutations fixed by random drift. Supporting the nearly neutral theory, neutral selection is not significant.
title: Selection originating from protein stability/foldability: Relationships between protein folding free energy, sequence ensemble, and fitness

summary: The four-component (T, I, N, F) neutrosophic representation distinguishes pure indeterminacy I from neutrality N, in addition to truth T and falsehood F. Existing neutrosophic-graph research mainly assigns uncertain values to vertices or edges and studies the resulting graph structure. This paper addresses a different problem: a fixed weighted network is given, while a (T, I, N, F) assessment is the signal carried by each vertex. A benefit-coordinate embedding converts the semantic order into the standard product order and permits graph-Laplacian methods without merging neutrality and indeterminacy. For continuous-time heat diffusion, we prove preservation of the TINF cube, semantic order, component means, complement symmetry, and a maximum principle. A weighted Dirichlet energy is shown to decay monotonically, with exponential convergence governed by the algebraic connectivity. A stable discrete-time scheme and a soft-anchor graph filter are also established. For partially observed signals, the TINF harmonic extension is characterized simultaneously as the unique Dirichlet-energy minimizer and as a convex combination of boundary assessments. This yields complement equivariance, a semantic maximum principle, nonexpansive dependence on boundary data, and an explicit topology-perturbation bound. Complement-paired TINF prototypes are then introduced for four-state semi-supervised inference. They form a regular simplex in benefit coordinates, and nearest-prototype TINF classification is proved exactly equivalent to classical multiclass harmonic label propagation when anchors use the prototypes. In contrast, a symmetric three-component collapse makes neutrality and pure indeterminacy non-identifiable. An exact cycle example and Monte Carlo stochastic-block experiments confirm the equivalence numerically and demonstrate the information loss caused by collapse. The framework provides a mathematically auditable route for propagating four-component information over social, sensor, and knowledge networks.
title: TINF Signals on Networks: Complement-Equivariant Graph Diffusion, Harmonic Extension, and Semi-Supervised Inference

summary: The ELIXIR 3D-BioInfo community benchmark for discriminating physiological from non-physiological protein–protein interfaces (Schweke et al., Proteomics 2023) contains 1,677 homodimer interfaces from 1,645 PDB entries. We describe the FAIRification of this benchmark, carried out by the University of Bologna ELIXIR node within the ELIXIR Tools Platform. The benchmark is described with Bioschemas/schema.org JSON-LD: every interface is annotated with its label, chains, structural features, sequence-cluster assignment, provenance and licence, and linked to the PDB structure files and to snapshots of the RCSB PDB metadata. The first version of the package was audited against the publication and the source repository, and the errors found were corrected. A lightweight design removed the need for Git LFS and for duplicated metadata. The post-publication curation of the labels (844 physiological and 833 non-physiological interfaces, compared with 836 and 841 in the publication) is documented, and three entries superseded in the PDB are linked to their replacements. A reference machine-learning script with cluster-aware cross-validation is included. Data, scripts and a web portal are available on GitHub under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence, with full attribution to the original work.
title: FAIRification of the ELIXIR 3D-Bioinfo Protein-Protein Interface Benchmark

summary: Purpose This record documents a two-sample summary-data Mendelian randomization study designed to test whether genetic liability to cirrhosis, and to liver fibrosis, is causally related to cardiovascular disease. People with fibrotic liver disease carry a substantial excess of cardiovascular events, but whether that excess reflects a direct vascular effect of fibrosis or the metabolic disturbance that accompanies it is difficult to separate in observational data, where both are entangled with shared risk factors and with reverse causation. The study uses common genetic variants as instruments to break that entanglement, and asks two questions in sequence: whether the exposure is causally associated with five cardiovascular outcomes, and, if the association is absent or heterogeneous, which component of the exposure carries such association as exists. Contents The deposit holds the complete analytical record rather than selected outputs. It comprises 44 analysis scripts; 6 typesetting scripts retained for transparency but not runnable in isolation; 105 analysis-ready input files derived from public summary statistics, including a rebuilt LD score panel; 56 result files, one per analysis; the thirteen numbered tables of the companion article as CSV, with a companion legends file; Figures 1–3 as submitted; and a manifest giving dataset provenance for each of the eleven source datasets, a file-level inventory with SHA-256 checksums, a crosswalk between pipeline and article table numbering, and the recorded software environment. ANALYSIS_PLAN.md is the English rendering of the study protocol, together with a record of how each provision was implemented and a twelve-item register of departures from that protocol. Two of those departures, and two analyses added after first submission, are documented there rather than left implicit in the code. Methods Instruments were constructed from eleven public datasets — ten studies from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog and one FinnGen release — for cirrhosis liability as the primary exposure and liver fibrosis as the replication exposure, against coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ischaemic stroke and arterial stiffness, with four metabolic traits considered as candidate mediators. Estimates were obtained from six estimators: inverse-variance weighted with multiplicative random effects, MR-Egger with SIMEX correction, weighted median, weighted mode, MR-PRESSO and the contamination mixture. These are read alongside Cochran's Q and I²_GX, leave-one-out analysis, reverse-direction Mendelian randomization, overlap correction by MRlap, multivariable Mendelian randomization with conditional F statistics, two-step mediation, stratification by each variant's effect on LDL cholesterol, and colocalisation by coloc.abf . A positive control, LDL cholesterol against coronary disease, is included to show that the pipeline recovers a known effect. Use Three entry points are supported, at increasing cost. A published estimate can be checked from the deposited harmonised per-variant effects alone, without any download, by passing four columns to the estimator functions in mrlib.py . Every numbered table can be regenerated from the deposited results with a single script; the regenerated sources for the two tables carrying the primary estimates were verified byte-identical to those that produced the submitted tables. A full re-run from raw data is possible once the third-party summary statistics are placed under data/ in accordance with the registry in datasets.py , from which the driver run_all.py executes the stages in order. Every stochastic estimator is seeded and its resampling counts are fixed, so a re-run reproduces the deposited numbers exactly rather than within Monte Carlo error. Reuse and value The deposit is constructed to be reusable beyond the study that produced it. mrlib.py implements each estimator from its published description and is self-contained, so
title: Genetic Liability to Cirrhosis and Cardiovascular Disease: A Mendelian Randomization Study of Dyslipidemia, Not Fibrosis

summary: Overview Songdo Vision OBB is the oriented bounding box (OBB) counterpart of the Songdo Vision dataset. It provides the same 5,419 high-resolution 4K RGB frames (3840×2160) captured over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea , with every one of the 274,190 vehicle annotations expressed as a rotated rectangle instead of an axis-aligned box, across the same four classes : Car (including vans and light-duty vehicles) Bus Truck Motorcycle Horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) are a poor fit for high-altitude bird's-eye-view (BeV) imagery, where vehicles appear at arbitrary in-plane orientations. A diagonally traveling or parked vehicle fills a small fraction of its axis-aligned box, and the rest is road surface, lane markings, or a neighboring vehicle. Songdo Vision OBB replaces those boxes with tight oriented ones, so the dataset can serve as a benchmark for oriented aerial vehicle detection and as a source of vehicle heading for downstream traffic analysis. The images are byte-identical to those of Songdo Vision, and the annotations are derived one-to-one from Songdo Vision v2 , so the two records can be used together or interchangeably. Alongside the converted annotations, the release ships the 50 manually annotated OBB frames that were used to tune and validate the conversion. A full dataset card with usage instructions and download guidance is available on Hugging Face . 📌 Citation: if you use this dataset in your work, please cite the paper that introduces it, which is the preferred citation: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis (2026). Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes. arXiv: XXXX.XXXXX. Please also cite the article behind the imagery and the source annotations [1] . BibTeX entries for both, and the dataset's own archival citation, are in Citation & Attribution. 🔗 Related datasets: the source HBB annotations are Songdo Vision v2: 10.5281/zenodo.21728430 . For precisely georeferenced vehicle trajectories extracted from the same large-scale multi-drone experiment, see Songdo Traffic (latest version): 10.5281/zenodo.13828383 . The benchmark paper that introduces this dataset annotates its own data at the conversion settings selected here: see its software, stabilo-benchmark ( 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX , GitHub: rfonod/stabilo-benchmark ), and its data record ( 10.5281/zenodo.23623540 ). 🛠️ Conversion tool: the oriented boxes were produced with HBB2OBB v1.10.0 ( 10.5281/zenodo.22664151 , GitHub: rfonod/hbb2obb ), the exact version recorded in each subset's PROVENANCE.txt . See How the OBBs Were Produced. Motivation Axis-aligned boxes discard orientation, which in aerial imagery is both information the sensor genuinely captured and information downstream tasks need: Loose spatial support. A vehicle at 45° occupies roughly half of its axis-aligned box; the remainder is background that a detector must learn to ignore, and that an instance-level consumer cannot separate from the vehicle. Neighbor bleed. In dense parking rows and at intersection approaches, the axis-aligned box of one diagonally oriented vehicle routinely overlaps, and sometimes fully contains, its neighbors. Songdo Vision v2 documents 104 such pairs at IoU 0.3 to 0.5 that are correct yet unavoidable with HBBs. No heading. Vehicle orientation has to be inferred from tracking, which is fragile for stationary or slow-moving vehicles. Cost of re-annotation. Producing OBBs by hand at this scale, roughly 274k instances, is not practical. Songdo Vision OBB addresses this by converting the existing, human-verified HBBs into OBBs with a segmentation-based method, rather than by re-annotating from scratch. Every OBB inherits the class label and the provenance of the HBB it came from, so the annotation quality work done for Songdo Vision v2 carries over intact. summary: Run records, analysis of record and code of the component study reported in the appendix "Design, Provenance and Component Study of KAYROS" of the PhD thesis of Florian Rascoussier, "Improving Anytime Resolution of Large-Scale VRPTW and its Time-Dependent Extension" (ED SPIN, IMT Atlantique and INSA Lyon). Every table, figure and number of the component-study section of that appendix is computed from the files of this dataset. KAYROS is an exact and anytime solver for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with time windows (TDVRPTW) under the Duration objective. Its exact mode is a branch-price-and-cut derived from the open-source solver of Lera-Romero, Miranda-Bront and Soulignac (Networks, 2020), and its heuristic mode is an iterated local search. The study asks 3 questions: whether the exact mode of KAYROS still performs as the solver it comes from once embedded, repaired and extended, what the open LP backend HiGHS costs compared with CPLEX, and what the heuristic and exact modes bring to each other. Design. The panel is the complete set of 56 Dabia et al. (2013) TDVRPTW instances with 100 customers, as distributed by MAMUT-routing. The 5 arms are the repaired baseline (the solver of Lera-Romero et al. at its public commit cabc56a plus 3 patches, with CPLEX 12.10), the exact mode of KAYROS 1.7.0 alone with CPLEX, the same with HiGHS 1.14.0, the heuristic mode of KAYROS alone, and the full solver (15 s of heuristic search, then the warm-started exact mode with CPLEX). Each arm runs 5 trials on each instance, 1,400 runs in total, each with 7,200 s from process launch, one pinned core and an address space limited to 16 GiB, with 10 concurrent runs per node on the grvingt cluster of the Grid'5000 testbed. The heuristic and full arms use 5 paired seeds. KAYROS runs used commit 25d8f0088337b9667956f07fe365c749def9894f of https://github.com/0nyr/kayros , released as version 1.7.0. The sources of the repaired baseline are also public, as the tag component-study-as-run of https://github.com/0nyr/lera-tdvrptw-bpc-repaired . Contents. cells/ holds one directory per run with the run summary (cell.json), the timestamped stream of incumbents, lower bounds and closures (events.jsonl), the native solver result (native.json, absent for the 185 runs ended by the memory limit or killed after the budget), the solver standard error (stderr.log) and the claim record (claim.json). plan.json is the plan of the 1,400 runs, runners/ the runner and job logs, scripts/ the frozen runner scripts. analysis/ holds the analysis of record (final-summary.json, which re-checks every route set with the reference checker mamut-routing-lib 0.11.0), the main and per-instance tables, and a comparison of the proofs with the stored optimality certificates. code/ holds the experiment harness, the analysis scripts, the frozen best-known-solution snapshot used as reference, the script that produces the tables and figures of the appendix, and the 3 patches of the baseline. The bundled README.md decodes the layout, the record fields, the acceptance rule of a proof and the integrity hashes. Main results. Accepted proofs: 165 of 280 runs for the repaired baseline, 172 for the exact mode of KAYROS with CPLEX, 135 with HiGHS (5 proofs rejected because a priced column fails the checker), 171 for the full solver, and none for the heuristic arm, which cannot prove optimality. Restricted mean time to proof: 3,295.0 s, 3,181.3 s, 4,256.3 s and 3,197.5 s. Mean anytime score: 0.37914, 0.35880, 0.49777, 0.00238 for the heuristic arm and 0.00644 for the full solver. 177 runs end at the memory limit, on 13 instances that no arm proves. Limits. The baseline is the repaired solver, not the published one. The pricing changes of KAYROS 1.7.0 were selected on this same panel. The panel is one family at one size, run on one machine type. The proofs are computational closures of single runs, checked for consistency, and not independent certificates. The records keep their original Grid
title: Component Study of KAYROS on the Dabia2013 TDVRPTW Instances with 100 Customers: Run Records and Analysis

summary: Code, data and model outputs of the study "Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference". The study fine-tunes small language models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Phi-4-mini-instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) to estimate twelve structural properties of a graph from its text serialization, and maps where this generalizes and where it fails: across graph sizes, graph families, vertex numberings, serializations and real-world domains. Files graph-structural-inference-slm.zip - the code of the study: generation of every evaluation set, fine-tuning, constrained-decoding evaluation, audits, statistical analyses and the scripts that produce every table and figure of the article, together with every model prediction (one record per graph and evaluation). Code under the MIT licence, predictions under CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-evaluation-sets.zip - 10,320 synthetic evaluation graphs (twelve size ranges beyond the training size and a second size series up to 300 vertices, seven further graph families, renumbered copies, seven serializations, and the test graphs rewired with every vertex degree kept) and two further samples of 1,200 training graphs, with exact labels, provenance and checksums. CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-adapters-main.zip - the 18 LoRA adapters behind the in-distribution results (three base models, adjacency list and edge list, seeds 42, 43 and 44), with their base models, seeds and checksums. Each adapter is subject to the licence of its base model (Llama 3.2 Community License, MIT, Qwen Research License). Built with Llama. Built with Qwen. The training and test graphs of the study are those of the TinyGraphEstimator dataset. The real-world datasets (ENZYMES, IMDB-BINARY, NCI1, ogbg-moltox21) are not redistributed: the code rebuilds the sets of the study from their original sources.
title: Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference: code, predictions, evaluation sets and fine-tuned adapters

summary: Version 3.1 (12 November 2026) of "The Standard Model and gravity as effective LdGS". The Standard Model and gravity as a reference effective theory with a matching programme toward a single Landau–de Gennes–Skyrme (LdGS) tensor field. Version 3.0 established the reading used throughout (classical configurations as leading order, quantized ensembles as physical objects, experiment as the final judge), milestones stated by experiment across atomic, nuclear, particle, gravity and cosmology, and atomic-scale bounds on LdGS-specific effects. New in 3.1: • First steps toward a derived hadronic action: the winding field and the record frame form an SO(4) frame with the hidden-local-symmetry parametrization (a composite connection, not yet a dynamical ρ); unfitted soliton numbers with physical meson inputs reproduce the known soliton systematics; a parent-induced vector response computed, with the timelike control showing what remains to be calculated (pole, residue, decay vertex). • A corrected account of the native Card C: the record enters the matter tensor and couples to the winding field through an exact positive cross term of order 1/230, with a coefficient-free ablation defined. • External replication through frozen packets (manifests, SHA-256 checksums, plans before numbers): the string tension of the fractional-charge strand with its width and stress profile against archived lattice data is the first LdGS-specific test, taken by an external team; then the W multi-baryon pipeline and the photon-point comparison with and without the record. • Reviews by several AI systems folded in, including corrections of earlier statements, recorded in the version history. Sharpest external test remains the rank-two seesaw's Σmν = 58.69 meV (normal ordering, m1 = 0), at the edge of DESI's Bayesian ΛCDM limits and in tension with its Feldman–Cousins limit, as every oscillation-compatible spectrum is. Version 4.0 is reserved for the first native LdGS prediction confirmed against data it was not fitted to, in any domain. AI-assisted research: computations and reviews by several AI systems (Claude, ChatGPT/Sol and others), contributions listed in the paper; hypotheses and responsibility are the author's. Not externally peer reviewed. Source, scripts, frozen-packet definitions and review documents are in the accompanying archive.

summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies the manuscript “Disentangling analytical sensitivity and donor influence in single-nucleus depression data”. Version 2.0.0 contains author-derived aggregate results, gene-level result summaries, figure source tables, analysis code, source fingerprints, documentation, and executable statistical and plotting checks supporting six main figures and eight supplementary figures. The study examines analytical-component sensitivity, donor influence, conditional calibration, sample planning, modern statistical methods, and independent disease evaluations. The internally stable 68-gene catalogue did not meet the evaluated external replication criteria. Fine-subtype annotation qualification failed, and the planned target fine-subtype disease analysis was not performed. The portable workflow supports aggregate statistical checks and figure reconstruction. Full count-model reruns require separately obtained source matrices, permitted metadata, and the documented dependencies. Third-party count matrices, individual clinical records, installed environments, and complete third-party gene-set libraries are excluded. Author-owned analysis code is licensed under the MIT License. Original derived aggregate results and documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Third-party inputs and software remain subject to their original terms. Funding: General Project of the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Education, China, grant Y202559996; Basic Scientific Research Project of the Wenzhou Science and Technology Bureau, China, grant YC20250576.
title: Disentangling analytical sensitivity and donor influence in single-nucleus depression data

summary: This repository provides data and Python code supporting the manuscript “Estimating Depth-Integrated Suspended-Sediment Flux During Floods Using Hyperspectral CCTV.” The study combines hyperspectral estimates of surface suspended-sediment concentration (SSC) and image-derived surface velocity with a Rouse–flux model to estimate depth-integrated sediment transport per unit channel width. The archive includes: SSC training data and models: 342 matchups for the unified model, comprising 127 baseline observations and 215 flood observations, and 211 matchups for the tracer model. Reflectance data, concentration targets, feature-selection information, model parameters, and code for model fitting and 5-fold cross-validation are provided. Vertical-profile and flux data: Processed SSC and velocity profiles from 27 field casts, together with code for vertical-profile reconstruction and flux correction. Camera-input comparisons: Nine comparison records, including seven with paired camera-derived SSC and velocity estimates. STIV example: One preprocessed space-time image from a flood observation, with code for surface-velocity estimation. Summary results for all nine STIV validation scans are also included. Supporting information: Hourly hydrological data, archived comparison results, a data dictionary, dependency specifications, and numerical reproduction checks. The archive starts from processed observation tables and a preprocessed space-time image. Raw hyperspectral cubes and complete spatial SSC, velocity, and flux maps are outside its scope. The tracer training table preserves the original processed concentration target and provides all-size LISST concentration separately. Target definitions, wavelength conventions, evaluation procedures, and calibration dependencies are documented in the accompanying files. Run python run_all.py to execute the included analyses and reproduction checks. See README.txt for installation and usage instructions and DATA_DICTIONARY.txt for variable definitions and units. Data, documentation, and results are provided under CC BY 4.0 , and Python code is provided under the MIT License . Please cite this dataset and the associated paper when using these materials.
title: Data and code for HISST-FLUX: estimating depth-averaged suspended-sediment flux using hyperspectral CCTV

summary: Description This record contains the datasets collected via TuniCo, along with the computational scripts, diachronic text corpora, and documentation associated with the comparative analysis of trilingual code-switching (Tunisian Arabic, French, and Italian/Sicilian). The materials are structured to ensure full reproducibility and transparency in alignment with Open Science and FAIR data principles. Contents of the Record: dataset/ : Primary corpora extracted via TuniCo (alongside historical comparative materials such as the Simpaticuni press corpus, 1911–1933), including processed textual data, metadata, and tokenized structures. scripts/ : Executable Python scripts, Jupyter Notebooks, and configuration modules utilized for text mining, topic modeling, semantic network analysis, and the evaluation of translation and code-switching strategies. documentation/ : Methodological notes, metadata schemas, and validation reports detailing the workflow parameters, data provenance, and analytical frameworks. Methodological Framework: The analyses combine close reading with quantitative text-mining methodologies, diachronic variance tracking, and structural network metrics to evaluate language contact, lexical borrowing, and the mediating role of French between historical Italian and Tunisian Arabic. All computational workflows are scripted to allow independent verification and secondary reuse by researchers, academic staff, and citizen science initiatives. summary: Abstract : Background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global public-health problem and an important cause of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. Although nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy has substantially improved management, antiviral resistance-associated mutations may occasionally be detected before treatment exposure. Objective: To systematically determine the prevalence and distribution of established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations among treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection and to estimate the pooled prevalence of patients carrying at least one established primary resistance mutation. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using a patient-level endpoint defined as the presence of at least one established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutation in a unique treatment-naïve patient. Secondary or compensatory mutations were not counted as primary resistance when occurring alone. Studies using highly sensitive assays, including mutation-specific PCR and next-generation sequencing, were considered separately where appropriate. The review was structured according to PRISMA 2020. Results: The current primary quantitative dataset comprised 42 cohorts involving 9,811 evaluable treatment-naïve participants, of whom 417 carried at least one qualifying primary resistance-associated mutation, giving a crude prevalence of 4.25%. The current random-effects synthesis estimated an overall pooled prevalence of 1.80% (95% CI, 1.04–3.09%). Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=93.3%; τ²=2.541; Q=616.02). The approximate 95% prediction interval was 0.08–30.41%. Conclusion: Naturally occurring primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations are detectable in a minority of treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection, but reported prevalence varies substantially according to population, geography, genotype, study design, and assay sensitivity. The pooled estimate should therefore not be interpreted as a universal prevalence applicable to every clinical setting.
tags: antiviral resistance, Chronic Hepatitis B, hepatitis B virus, resistance-associated mutations, reverse transcriptase, treatment-naïve.
title: Prevalence and Distribution of Naturally Occurring Antiviral Resistance-Associated Mutations in Treatment-Naïve Chronic Hepatitis B: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: STARLI RESEARCH CIVILIZATION Five Botanical Research Mechanisms, One Scientific Inheritance F001–F005  |  Integrated English Scientific and Technical Notebook A companion to the 819-page STARLI Botanical Family 01 research atlas. A continuous, three-part scientific essay corresponding to all 82 research chapters; it does not duplicate the PDF chapter paragraphs. F001  /  BOTANICAL POLYPHENOL ISOLATION AND PURIFICATION F002  /  BOTANICAL FLAVONOID MOLECULAR STABILIZATION F003  /  BOTANICAL TERPENOID ACTIVE NANOENCAPSULATION F004  /  BOTANICAL POLYSACCHARIDE MOLECULAR-WEIGHT FRACTIONATION F005  /  MULTIBOTANICAL ACTIVE NANO-CODELIVERY Status: prospective research design and counterfactual scientific commentary. Mathematical surfaces are synthetic demonstrations, not experimental or human efficacy data.     Research position: a scientific book rather than five adjacent brochures Five research flags can be placed on five shelves, but the scientific difficulty begins when the shelves are removed. A polyphenol that survives separation may still be degraded by oxygen. A stable flavonoid can compete for the same carrier interface that an identified terpenoid requires. A polysaccharide fraction may alter viscosity and transport while also changing what an instrument can recover. And a pleasing co-delivery curve might still conceal a failure of the weakest component. This notebook studies the bridges, not merely the isolated accomplishments of each chemistry. The F001 to F005 sequence should be regarded as a chain of evidence. A specimen passport precedes the chromatographic result; a parent-product chemical balance precedes any stability claim; a measured free-active pool precedes an encapsulation claim; a distribution-aware fraction analysis precedes a structure-property claim; and a component-specific conservation ledger precedes any assertion about a combined formulation. These contracts can fail independently. The result is a discipline that refuses to let one beautiful plot pay for another missing measurement. The Ben Cao Gang Mu enters here as intellectual history and a question-forming tradition. Classification, preparation, relationships among materials, and care over identity can inspire what modern scientists decide to separate or compare. Nothing about that historical inspiration proves a molecule, a nanostructure, a biological effect or a medical outcome. The proper crossing from classical material thought to contemporary science is a testable hypothesis with a rival explanation and an explicit right to fail. A research atlas that contains 819 pages may be useful as a navigable inventory of proposed investigations, yet its scale does not convert hypotheses into results. Figures drawn from deterministic equations only show what the equations imply in the declared range. An external laboratory would need to establish whether those equations describe any particular botanical material. This notebook therefore uses an open-ended three-part form: mechanistic origin, extreme counterfactual, and a successor experiment that could be rebuilt independently. summary: Protein sequences change over time due to the accumulation of mutations in the genes that encode them. Nonetheless, accurately identifying the most probable evolutionary pathways and more efficient trajectories between an ancestral and a derived sequence remains a challenge. This difficulty stems from a limited understanding of the critical factors that drive the evolutionary process. This study aims to address this issue by validating a newly proposed mechanistic model (grounded on the principle of least action) for analyzing protein evolution, using beta-lactamase as an empirically characterized evolutionary model. The initial findings indicate that, after accounting for how mutations and the context-dependent interactions between them (epistasis) affect protein stability and, hence, the kinetics of protein folding, a resort to the principle of least action allows us to simultaneously identify the most probable pathways and the most efficient trajectories swiftly and accurately. These findings also suggest that the most probable evolutionary protein pathways are the ones that exhibit the most efficient trajectories. All in all, our study addresses several unanswered questions regarding the main factors that govern how protein evolves at the molecular level (under constant selection pressure) and outlines directions for future research in key fields such as directed evolution and ancestral sequence reconstruction.
title: Analyzing \b{eta}-Lactamase Evolution from the Principle of Least Action Perspective

No manual map shift or pre-projection/resampling of complex images is required. PHASE v7.1.15 Refuse CSK resume when existing master/slave crops were created for a different AOI; preserve original graph provenance and explain when Step 1 with master processing is required. Retain ten decimal places when writing AOI bounds. Read the external GeoTIFF DEM's declared GDAL NoData value (Classic TIFF/BigTIFF, both byte orders) and propagate it to CSK interferogram, topographic phase removal and terrain correction operators. Log an explicit warning when no value is declared. Exclude invalid/NoData SNAP geolocation from full-area PSI preparation through the native StaMPS mask, as already done for polygon processing. Refuse resuming old candidates with invalid coordinates; do not change valid source rasters or scientific selection thresholds. Preserve no-PS flags saved by StaMPS selection/weeding steps. Report empty patch merges and insufficient triangulation points explicitly instead of array-bound or Delaunay exceptions. Propagate failed CSK SNAP stages and retain their output in logs; stop Windows slave pipelines after failed stages. Verify MATLAB resume/mask/StaMPS control-flow regressions and Python NoData/error propagation. Real-data CSK reprocessing is required to validate coverage and coherence; these fixes do not guarantee PS retention or recover missing DEM data. summary: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Data governance (access rules, purpose limits, obligations, and claims about what data means) is enforced where data is stored and served, but derived data rarely inherits it. Query results, aggregates, and reports written by large language models (LLMs) leave the system that governed their inputs, and downstream consumers cannot tell which rules still bind them. TN represents a value together with its source policies. A calculation on governed inputs produces another governed value carrying their policies. Signed claims retain their original authors and subjects. Each receiving endpoint verifies the policies bound to the result and decides the proposed use under its own authorities and keys. An analyst joins two tables to prepare a financial report. The query filters on companies.active and returns the selected amounts. Although the active flag is absent from the result, those amounts carry the internal-use policy on companies. A dataframe aggregate computed from them inherits that policy. When an application supplies a governed value to an inference server, the server puts its policies and claims in the model's prompt before the model can request a protected field. Immediately before generation, the runtime checks that the scheduled input tokens and settings match the task it authorized. TN is a wire protocol for exchanging governed values between applications. Its adapters let developers use ordinary SQL queries, Polars expressions, Python operators, and calls to an inference server. As long as the application passes governed values through these interfaces, the adapters package each result with its policies and claims automatically. In our evaluation, Qwen3-4B generated an HTML report from data queried in SQL, aggregated in Polars, and formatted in Python. The report retained the source policies and original claims.
title: TN: Data Governance That Travels Through SQL, Dataframe, and LLM Pipelines

summary: Fibonacci -Spiral Nanophotonic Cavity and Symmetry-Modulated Ly Lattice Quantum Key Distribution C. J Tully and collaborators Ly-Design Engine / NOUS-ONE Lattice Continuity Project https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332   13 November 2026 We present a dual construction that maps the linear amino-acid sequence of Gen4_Variant_04 onto a Fibonacci -spiral coordinate matrix for a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) nanophotonic cavity and embeds the same algebraic grading into a high-dimensional quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. The cavity uses a base lattice pitch and selectively etches air holes at the five basic residues (K, R, H), targeting a localized resonance near . The QKD protocol encodes blocks into one of five cyclic algebraic sectors , applies non-commutative forward and inverse matrices, and employs center-invariant checking states protected by the golden-ratio operator . Intercept-resend attacks by the designated party Eav produce detectable deviations from the degree-conservation law modulo 5. The resulting GDSII stream is provided for mask fabrication, and the protocol is ready for numerical evaluation of the quantum bit error rate under Eav’s attack.

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.

F036: A chemical fingerprint is an argument about identity Untargeted metabolomics produces an enormous chemical landscape, but feature abundance alone is not independent chemical discovery. One ion can produce multiple adducts, fragments and isotope patterns; one matrix shift can suppress many ion signals at once. Fermented material should be compared using authenticated botanical lots, inoculum identity, predeclared sampling windows and matrix-spiked standard recovery. Named products require authentic standards or orthogonal structural evidence and metabolite annotations must carry confidence. Source-to-source variance must remain visible rather than pooled into a flattering heat map. In the strongest design an external laboratory receives a blinded source and a new culture batch. The fingerprint is meaningful only if competing explanations such as abiotic acid treatment, biomass-associated peaks and analytical drift cannot reproduce its claimed transformation. F037: Enzymes can reveal, transform, and destroy Fermentation can liberate an existing phenolic from a plant cell wall, hydrolyze a glycoside into an aglycone or convert a released compound into smaller downstream products. These are different processes with different mass ledgers. A purified beta-glucosidase may alter a named glycosidic bond, but a crude culture may also change pH, solvent exposure and degradation simultaneously. One should preserve absolute parent moles, identified intermediate moles, product moles and the unrecovered fraction. Reaction rates require independent enzyme activity and defensible substrate concentration; saturation models should not be trusted when particle diffusion or enzyme inactivation dominates. The scientific success is not the largest product peak. It is the ability to identify which molecular bond changed, where its atoms went and which comparator could recreate that pattern without the proposed enzyme. F038: Why molecular weight, structure and viscosity disagree A fermented polysaccharide cannot be characterized from one high viscosity number. A polymer chain may shorten through hydrolase cleavage, become compact through ionic screening, associate with a peptide, or be replaced by newly produced microbial exopolysaccharide. All can generate contradictory relationships between apparent molar mass, diffusivity and the feel of a gel. Size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, monomer composition, linkage analysis and calibrated wet-state rheology ask different questions. Even SEC-MALS requires attention to aggregates, optical parameters and sample recovery. A claim about botanical polymer remodeling should not be made when the measured high-mass fraction originates from microbial material. The pathway from polymer molecular structure to a future carrier must be preserved rather than simplified into a claim that all fermentation increases hydration. F039: A nanoscale carrier is not proof of delivered benefit Ferment extracts include many chemically distinct products; not every fraction is carried into a lipid or polymer nanostructure in the same way. DLS size and polydispersity describe a scattering-weighted population, not the chemical identity of material inside the droplet. Free cargo, micelle-bound cargo, vessel-wall loss, carrier-associated cargo and degraded cargo need separate inventories. Residual enzymes can weaken a shell while fermentation acids alter emulsifier charge, so a formulation that looks stable on preparation day can change after storage. Release tests must distinguish actual molecular diffusion from dialysis membrane retention. A useful crossover experiment tests the same chemically named cargo both with and without the carrier, matching total mass and vehicle conditions. The model asks whether a reproducible material state was formed, not whether a new cosmetic product has already been proven. F040: Safety is the constraint that cannot be paid away Fermentation can create attractive chemical diversity while introducing hazards that cannot be inferred from the name of the microbe or the absence of visible mold. Biogenic amines, solvent residues, unintended microbial metabolites, active residual enzymes, contamination and extraction impurities need explicit risk-based decisions. Microfiltration removes some physical particles, but dissolved hazards can pass through untouched. Adsorption may reduce a hazard while destroying the named botanical cargo; purification must therefore have an identifiable mass balance and a noncompensatory safety gate. Dark extracts can interfere with reconstructed epidermis assays and should be subjected to validated blanks. OECD TG 439 concerns a defined irritation hazard and is not human tolerance or product efficacy proof. The Ben Cao Gang Mu tradition invites care in preparation, provenance and proportion; scientific inheritance requires that care to be expressed as testable identities, transparent failures and safe stopping conditions.

summary: A companion paper argued that biological memory is a record that is rewritten by its own consultation, and wrote this as a readout-write channel that preserves the index of a record and revises its content. That treatment assumed the codes addressing different records do not overlap, which is the one assumption the distributed, superposed memories of the holographic lineage never make. We relax it. In a mushroom-body layer where odour codes overlap, every write has the same form, addressed by the code of the record being read, and one line of algebra gives an identity: the change a revision of record a produces in the readout of record b is the code overlap times the change it produces in a. Because training is a write of that form too, the fraction of a revision that transfers to b and the fraction of training that generalises to b are the same number, and it cancels. The prediction has no free parameter and no measurement of overlap: transfer of revision equals generalisation of training. Four consequences follow. Leakage splits into a term set by mean overlap and a term set by the fluctuation in overlap that does not fall with sparseness, so there is a floor at a coding level of 1/√N, about two per cent in the fly. Trading read noise against leakage gives an optimal coding level that falls as the revision load rises. Leakage inherits the window of the companion paper, so a record can be protected by timing alone. And in the quantum layer, index invariance turns out to be a conservation law, one charge per record, belonging to an abelian symmetry of the channel; overlap breaks that symmetry, and the index charge moves only at second order in the overlap while content moves at first, so the objectivity result degrades more slowly than the content does. We then show that the two classic results that look like confinement, synapse-specific reconsolidation and the protection of indirectly reactivated memories, are both compatible with leakage, because neither tests two records that share synapses. The fly is where that case can be tested, and we give the experiment, its controls and its power.   Spanish version included in this record: "Lo que toca una revisión: reescritura en la lectura en una memoria superpuesta". The English version is the reference text.

summary: This is a big release, jam-packed with lots of new features in our GUI, a more streamlined saving interface, and many new kinematic measures. [!important] This release contains minor breaking changes to the saving functions, to the nan_policy options of path metrics, and to the default behaviour of filter_by_confidence() . Please read the notes below before updating. To update movement to the latest version, see the update guide . What's Changed ⚡️ Highlight: Edit pose tracks in the GUI Pose estimation models often produce errors, such as mis-localised keypoints or false-positive detections in the background. movement.filtering offers several post-processing options, but not all errors can be dealt with automatically. You can now correct these stubborn errors by hand, directly in the movement GUI. This feature is the result of @anna-teruel's Google Summer of Code 2026 project . A huge thank you to Anna for designing and building it, and congratulations on joining the movement team! We're also grateful to @sfmig, who co-mentored the project and made the GUI's layer callbacks and frame slider more robust. Thanks also to @SahilKumar75 and @devanshc777 for contributing the reset controls and a re-export fix. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/10cba1ff-998b-4931-842a-0a84d5be940e Once you load tracked data into the GUI, you can: Move keypoints by dragging them to the correct position, or remove them altogether. See which frames you have edited on the edit timeline , optionally split by individual, and click on it to jump to an edited frame. Reset edits in the current frame or across all frames. Save the corrected dataset in movement 's native netCDF format, and load it again later to pick up where you left off. The tracks layer stays in sync with the edited keypoints, and edited keypoints are shown as rings. The saved dataset has an additional boolean edited data variable, which records which keypoints were edited by hand. You can use it in your analysis, for example to report how many keypoints were corrected. See the Edit tracked data section of the GUI guide for details. What's next? Editing currently works one frame at a time and supports moving and removing keypoints in poses datasets, with saving to netCDF only. Planned extensions include: editing across a range of frames, addition of missing keypoints, correction of identity swaps between individuals or keypoints, support for editing bounding boxes datasets, and saving to third-party formats. [!WARNING] The confidence of edited keypoints is set to NaN , since the model's score no longer applies. summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative learning on Internet of Things (IoTs) without sharing raw data, yet deployment remains challenging due to Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) local distributions, intermittent participation, and evolving environmental conditions. Resource-constrained devices such as zero-energy devices (ZEDs) further require communication-efficient training and lightweight models. This work examines whether tiny Machine Learning (tinyML) -oriented FL , hereafter Lightweight Federated Learning (LWFL) , is practical under these constraints. We evaluate three LWFL aggregators ( FedAvg , FedNova, and FAdamGC ) under heterogeneous non-IID settings with client participation rates of 10%, 90%, and 100%. To reduce communication overhead, we apply three Quantization/Compression (Q/C) schemes to client–server payloads. We also study two distribution-shift scenarios: intra-dataset distribution (intraDD) (redistribution of class subsets among clients) and interdataset distribution (inter-DD) (label space replaced by a disjoint dataset). Under extreme heterogeneity (three clients, one shared class), every aggregator roughly doubles the heldout accuracy of the Local baseline (Local) , with FedNova highest and the spread among aggregators below 0 . 013 . With 20 clients, even simple averaging is competitive. All FL methods converge to high accuracy. FAdamGC performs best at 10% participation due to drift correction but degrades sharply under inter-DD . FedNova attains the highest accuracy in the two most demanding conditions, extreme heterogeneity and interDD shift, and stays within 0 . 016 of the best method under sparse participation, lossy communication, and intra-DD shift. Q/C methods reduce payload size with negligible accuracy loss, among which quantization offers the best balance of simplicity, speed, and fidelity. Overall, the results show LWFL , particularly FedNova with compression, can deliver robust and adaptive learning in resource-constrained environments.
title: Lightweight Federated Learning for Environmental Resiliency in TinyML-IoT Ecosystems

summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative learning on Internet of Things (IoTs) without sharing raw data, yet deployment remains challenging due to Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) local distributions, intermittent participation, and evolving environmental conditions. Overall, the results show LWFL , particularly FedNova with compression, can deliver robust and adaptive learning in resource-constrained environments.

summary: KenyaESG is a sentence-level dataset for three independent binary ESG classification tasks (Environmental, Social, Governance) built from the annual, integrated, and sustainability reports of firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), 2010–2024, combined with reference sentences from Schimanski et al. (2024). For each pillar, the dataset provides a fine-tuning set of 3,900 sentences and a disjoint held-out human evaluation set of 300 sentences. Each evaluation sentence carries the judgments of two independent annotators and an adjudicated reference label. Training and evaluation sentences share no sentence (exact match after normalisation), which prevents leakage. Version 2 (November 2026) changes: (1) the evaluation sets were extended from 100 to 300 sentences per pillar, the 200 new sentences being drawn at random from Kenyan reports outside the training pool and balanced across sectors; (2) all Kenya-sourced training labels were re-read against an explicit, meaning-based annotation guideline (45 E, 80 S and 124 G labels changed, all documented); (3) an adjudicated evaluation label was added, with agreement between the adjudicated label and annotators A/B of κ = 0.79/0.81 (E), 0.66/0.68 (S) and 0.70/0.72 (G); (4) the companion models were retrained, reaching F1 against the adjudicated label of 0.926 (E), 0.886 (S) and 0.918 (G); (5) precision, recall, confusion matrices, bootstrap confidence intervals and full training details are reported in the dataset card. Training labels for the Kenya-sourced sentences are keyword-derived and reviewed, not fully manually annotated, so the human-annotated evaluation sets are the appropriate benchmark for performance estimates. The dataset captures disclosure intensity rather than disclosure quality. The corpus is predominantly English but retains a small number of Swahili and OCR-degraded sentences, reflecting the original NSE reports. Company names and personal names have been masked in the text field ([COMPANY] and [PERSON]) in line with the anonymisation principles of the Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019) and Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR). Masking is semi-automatic and not guaranteed to be exhaustive. A small number of false-positive masks on common words (e.g. “equity”, “equality”, “Standard”) were subsequently restored, as documented in the correction log. The dataset must not be used to attempt re-identification of individuals or firms.
