summary: Eleven burnt areas from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (EMS) Rapid Mapping activations for forest fires in 2025 (Spain, Greece, Montenegro). Each area of interest (AOI) pairs a pre-event Sentinel-2 L1C image (bands B2, B3, B4, B8) with a post-event Sentinel-1 GRD image (VV, VH, dB) and the EMS burnt-area map as reference, on a common 10 m UTM grid, with a validity mask and the reason of every excluded pixel. The benchmark was built for heterogeneous (optical-to-SAR) change detection: 18.9 million evaluated pixels, 11.9 % burnt (3.7 % to 32.5 % per AOI), 3 to 14 days between the two images. See README.md for the file layout, the selection rules and the known limitations. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025. Contains modified Copernicus Service information 2025. Burnt-area references derived from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (© 2025 European Union) Rapid Mapping products; the per-AOI product citations are listed in ATTRIBUTION.txt.

Each area of interest (AOI) pairs a pre-event Sentinel-2 L1C image (bands B2, B3, B4, B8) with a post-event Sentinel-1 GRD image (VV, VH, dB) and the EMS burnt-area map as reference, on a common 10 m UTM grid, with a validity mask and the reason of every excluded pixel. The benchmark was built for heterogeneous (optical-to-SAR) change detection: 18.9 million evaluated pixels, 11.9 % burnt (3.7 % to 32.5 % per AOI), 3 to 14 days between the two images. See README.md for the file layout, the selection rules and the known limitations. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025. Contains modified Copernicus Service information 2025. Burnt-area references derived from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (© 2025 European Union) Rapid Mapping products; the per-AOI product citations are listed in ATTRIBUTION.txt.

summary: This versioned research dataset accompanies the manuscript "Does Downhole Seismic Information Add Value to Pressuremeter-Modulus Prediction? Borehole-Held-Out Evidence from Isfahan Metro Line 2". It contains a coordinate-free, pseudonymized cohort of 41 support-matched Ménard pressuremeter and downhole seismic analytical observations from 21 borehole groups on Isfahan Metro Line 2, a data dictionary, retained out-of-borehole model predictions, scripts that independently reconstruct B0–B3 nested grouped predictions, whole-borehole bootstrap calculations, and secondary robustness diagnostics. The dataset field Es_MPa denotes the Ménard pressuremeter modulus E_m in MPa, as explicitly confirmed by the responsible author; original computational field names are retained for traceability. B4-CA is supplied as a frozen-output sensitivity, not a fully reconstructed original fitting pipeline. Positive controls are synthetic and clearly distinguished from empirical observations. The package does not contain original third-party geotechnical reports, direct borehole coordinates, unmasked site identifiers, source workbooks, or external-site/Tabriz data. There is no calibrated tunnel-settlement finite-element prediction or demonstrated independent-site transportability in this archive. Data, derived results and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; original code files under the MIT License.
title: Isfahan Metro Line 2: pseudonymized pressuremeter–downhole seismic benchmark and reproducibility code

summary: Changes since v1.0.0 Optimizer (MATLAB HSSR_Optimizer.m and Python optimizer.py) Fixed the Akaike information criterion used to choose between the normal and gamma regression models (2k - 2 log-likelihood). Responses fitted with the gamma (log-link) model are now back-transformed before the desirability is computed, so that all responses are on the scale of the measurements. Data Updated the sensitivity analysis results (data/Sensitivity_Analysis_PPGDalia.xlsx, data/Sensitivity_Analysis_WESAD.xlsx, data/sensitivity_walking.csv): the limits of agreement are now obtained from Bland-Altman analysis on log-transformed PPG/ECG ratios and stored as the natural logarithm of the limit of agreement width. Examples robustness_importance (MATLAB and Python) updated with the parameters selected in the revised paper; it reproduces Supplementary Table 5. The HSSR-SLOPE algorithm (HSSR_SLOPE.m, SSA.m, PPG_FPDetection_Slope.m and the Python counterparts) is unchanged.
title: HSSR-SLOPE: PPG waveform reconstruction and beat detection for heart rate variability analysis

summary: This repository provides analysis code, aggregate results and supporting documentation for the manuscript “Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana.” The study uses Ghana Living Standards Survey Round 7 (GLSS 7), conducted in 2016/17, to examine associations between earnings, observable employment conditions and employment-change intentions across Ghana’s ten survey-era regions. Employment-change intentions distinguish wanting to change jobs, take an additional job or change current-job conditions. The materials include Stata scripts for survey-weighted earnings, job-quality, binary-logit and multinomial-logit models; regional interaction analyses; and Python scripts for data construction and machine-learning prediction. The repository also contains aggregate statistical tables, figures, variable documentation, sample-construction summaries, reproduction instructions and file checksums. Respondent-level survey data and individual prediction records are excluded. Researchers must obtain the underlying GLSS 7 data from the Ghana Statistical Service under its applicable access conditions. The supplied code and results are preserved without re-estimation. Reproduction requirements and outstanding limitations including unavailable original software-version information and two inventory files required for raw-data reconstruction are documented in the package. The findings describe conditional associations and predictive relationships, not causal effects.
title: Replication Materials for Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana

Employment-change intentions distinguish wanting to change jobs, take an additional job or change current-job conditions. The materials include Stata scripts for survey-weighted earnings, job-quality, binary-logit and multinomial-logit models; regional interaction analyses; and Python scripts for data construction and machine-learning prediction. The repository also contains aggregate statistical tables, figures, variable documentation, sample-construction summaries, reproduction instructions and file checksums. Respondent-level survey data and individual prediction records are excluded. Researchers must obtain the underlying GLSS 7 data from the Ghana Statistical Service under its applicable access conditions. The supplied code and results are preserved without re-estimation. Reproduction requirements and outstanding limitations including unavailable original software-version information and two inventory files required for raw-data reconstruction are documented in the package. The findings describe conditional associations and predictive relationships, not causal effects.

F046: From oil chemistry to an accountable oil-water interface A droplet cannot be defined by a photograph alone. It exists through competition among free-energy cost, oil composition, interface coverage and imposed mixing work. A low-energy phase inversion route and an energy-intensive emulsification process may produce similar early hydrodynamic diameters while leaving different residues, oxygen histories and molecular degradation. The experimental challenge is to keep an oil chemical ledger and a process energy ledger simultaneously. A strong oil-matched control can reveal that supposed botanical superiority originated in a residual cosolvent or in surfactant concentration. An independent laboratory must be able to identify the same marker molecules before accepting the morphology. F047: A mean radius is a poor description of a diverse droplet world An intensity-weighted DLS peak can be ruled by a small number of large scatterers. Number-weighted counts and volume-weighted oil fractions answer different questions. The same mean hydrodynamic diameter can belong to two populations with different rare large-droplet tails, different oil mass distribution and different stability trajectories. This is why the tenth family refuses a one-number specification. A richer experiment defines the droplet population at the moment of collection, after a controlled dilution, and after thermal aging. An unblinded analyst can always find the prettiest distribution. A credible research method should make a high-tail or poorly fitting distribution visible even when it defeats the preferred recipe. F048: The useful interface and the hazardous excess may coexist A surfactant occupies the oil-water interface, exchanges with water and may assemble into micelles at concentrations above its relevant critical aggregation threshold. Shrinking droplets increases total interface area. Yet simply adding more surfactant can increase the bioavailable free fraction without ensuring superior film coverage. A formulation might therefore look beautiful and remain unsuitable for a qualified reconstructed epidermis comparison. The laboratory must measure adsorbed, dissolved, micellar, degraded and container-associated amounts. Co-solvent and preservative must enter the competition as separate interventions. A safe-looking numerical stability frontier cannot overrule a failed nonclinical exposure gate. F049: Temperature is a history, not just a number on a shelf Heating and cooling can rearrange interfacial films, drive oil oxidation, change phase densities, reveal cloud transitions and make small droplets feed large ones by differential solubility. A single elevated-temperature hold cannot be treated as a certificate of ambient shelf life. Repeated heating-cooling loops can generate hysteresis even when they return to an identical endpoint temperature. The mechanistic rivals include droplet coalescence, reversible flocculation, Ostwald ripening, packaging sorption and loss of the original botanical marker. Each produces a different laboratory question. At least one independent real-time lot is needed to test whether accelerated aging forecasts actual storage behavior. F050: Nonclinical skin compatibility is an evidence contract A reconstructed human epidermis model is a defined surrogate, not a human wearer. Botanical pigments, reducing molecules and surfactants can distort common viability assays. The proper design uses a matched oil-and-surfactant vehicle, an independent exposure dose per tissue area, qualified tissue integrity, color interference controls and noncompensatory refusal conditions. A lower cytokine concentration can arise from fewer living cells. A higher local skin-associated chemical signal may arise from barrier injury or unwashed surface material. Even a fully qualified irritation hazard test cannot rule out sensitization, repeated-use intolerance or clinical treatment effects. All these boundaries should be visible on the first reading.

The same mean hydrodynamic diameter can belong to two populations with different rare large-droplet tails, different oil mass distribution and different stability trajectories. This is why the tenth family refuses a one-number specification. A richer experiment defines the droplet population at the moment of collection, after a controlled dilution, and after thermal aging. An unblinded analyst can always find the prettiest distribution. A credible research method should make a high-tail or poorly fitting distribution visible even when it defeats the preferred recipe. F048: The useful interface and the hazardous excess may coexist A surfactant occupies the oil-water interface, exchanges with water and may assemble into micelles at concentrations above its relevant critical aggregation threshold. Shrinking droplets increases total interface area. Yet simply adding more surfactant can increase the bioavailable free fraction without ensuring superior film coverage. A formulation might therefore look beautiful and remain unsuitable for a qualified reconstructed epidermis comparison. The laboratory must measure adsorbed, dissolved, micellar, degraded and container-associated amounts. Co-solvent and preservative must enter the competition as separate interventions. A safe-looking numerical stability frontier cannot overrule a failed nonclinical exposure gate. F049: Temperature is a history, not just a number on a shelf Heating and cooling can rearrange interfacial films, drive oil oxidation, change phase densities, reveal cloud transitions and make small droplets feed large ones by differential solubility. A single elevated-temperature hold cannot be treated as a certificate of ambient shelf life. Repeated heating-cooling loops can generate hysteresis even when they return to an identical endpoint temperature. The mechanistic rivals include droplet coalescence, reversible flocculation, Ostwald ripening, packaging sorption and loss of the original botanical marker. Each produces a different laboratory question. At least one independent real-time lot is needed to test whether accelerated aging forecasts actual storage behavior. F050: Nonclinical skin compatibility is an evidence contract A reconstructed human epidermis model is a defined surrogate, not a human wearer. Botanical pigments, reducing molecules and surfactants can distort common viability assays. The proper design uses a matched oil-and-surfactant vehicle, an independent exposure dose per tissue area, qualified tissue integrity, color interference controls and noncompensatory refusal conditions. A lower cytokine concentration can arise from fewer living cells. A higher local skin-associated chemical signal may arise from barrier injury or unwashed surface material. Even a fully qualified irritation hazard test cannot rule out sensitization, repeated-use intolerance or clinical treatment effects. All these boundaries should be visible on the first reading.

summary: Purpose This record documents a two-sample summary-data Mendelian randomization study designed to test whether genetic liability to cirrhosis, and to liver fibrosis, is causally related to cardiovascular disease. People with fibrotic liver disease carry a substantial excess of cardiovascular events, but whether that excess reflects a direct vascular effect of fibrosis or the metabolic disturbance that accompanies it is difficult to separate in observational data, where both are entangled with shared risk factors and with reverse causation. The study uses common genetic variants as instruments to break that entanglement, and asks two questions in sequence: whether the exposure is causally associated with five cardiovascular outcomes, and, if the association is absent or heterogeneous, which component of the exposure carries such association as exists. Contents The deposit holds the complete analytical record rather than selected outputs. It comprises 44 analysis scripts; 6 typesetting scripts retained for transparency but not runnable in isolation; 105 analysis-ready input files derived from public summary statistics, including a rebuilt LD score panel; 56 result files, one per analysis; the thirteen numbered tables of the companion article as CSV, with a companion legends file; Figures 1–3 as submitted; and a manifest giving dataset provenance for each of the eleven source datasets, a file-level inventory with SHA-256 checksums, a crosswalk between pipeline and article table numbering, and the recorded software environment. ANALYSIS_PLAN.md is the English rendering of the study protocol, together with a record of how each provision was implemented and a twelve-item register of departures from that protocol. Two of those departures, and two analyses added after first submission, are documented there rather than left implicit in the code. Methods Instruments were constructed from eleven public datasets — ten studies from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog and one FinnGen release — for cirrhosis liability as the primary exposure and liver fibrosis as the replication exposure, against coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ischaemic stroke and arterial stiffness, with four metabolic traits considered as candidate mediators. Estimates were obtained from six estimators: inverse-variance weighted with multiplicative random effects, MR-Egger with SIMEX correction, weighted median, weighted mode, MR-PRESSO and the contamination mixture. These are read alongside Cochran's Q and I²_GX, leave-one-out analysis, reverse-direction Mendelian randomization, overlap correction by MRlap, multivariable Mendelian randomization with conditional F statistics, two-step mediation, stratification by each variant's effect on LDL cholesterol, and colocalisation by coloc.abf . A positive control, LDL cholesterol against coronary disease, is included to show that the pipeline recovers a known effect. Use Three entry points are supported, at increasing cost. A published estimate can be checked from the deposited harmonised per-variant effects alone, without any download, by passing four columns to the estimator functions in mrlib.py . Every numbered table can be regenerated from the deposited results with a single script; the regenerated sources for the two tables carrying the primary estimates were verified byte-identical to those that produced the submitted tables. A full re-run from raw data is possible once the third-party summary statistics are placed under data/ in accordance with the registry in datasets.py , from which the driver run_all.py executes the stages in order. Every stochastic estimator is seeded and its resampling counts are fixed, so a re-run reproduces the deposited numbers exactly rather than within Monte Carlo error. Reuse and value The deposit is constructed to be reusable beyond the study that produced it. mrlib.py implements each estimator from its published description and is self-contained, so
title: Genetic Liability to Cirrhosis and Cardiovascular Disease: A Mendelian Randomization Study of Dyslipidemia, Not Fibrosis

summary: Overview Songdo Vision OBB is the oriented bounding box (OBB) counterpart of the Songdo Vision dataset. It provides the same 5,419 high-resolution 4K RGB frames (3840×2160) captured over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea , with every one of the 274,190 vehicle annotations expressed as a rotated rectangle instead of an axis-aligned box, across the same four classes : Car (including vans and light-duty vehicles) Bus Truck Motorcycle Horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) are a poor fit for high-altitude bird's-eye-view (BeV) imagery, where vehicles appear at arbitrary in-plane orientations. A diagonally traveling or parked vehicle fills a small fraction of its axis-aligned box, and the rest is road surface, lane markings, or a neighboring vehicle. Songdo Vision OBB replaces those boxes with tight oriented ones, so the dataset can serve as a benchmark for oriented aerial vehicle detection and as a source of vehicle heading for downstream traffic analysis. The images are byte-identical to those of Songdo Vision, and the annotations are derived one-to-one from Songdo Vision v2 , so the two records can be used together or interchangeably. Alongside the converted annotations, the release ships the 50 manually annotated OBB frames that were used to tune and validate the conversion. A full dataset card with usage instructions and download guidance is available on Hugging Face . 📌 Citation: if you use this dataset in your work, please cite the paper that introduces it, which is the preferred citation: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis (2026). Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes. arXiv: XXXX.XXXXX. Please also cite the article behind the imagery and the source annotations [1] . BibTeX entries for both, and the dataset's own archival citation, are in Citation & Attribution. 🔗 Related datasets: the source HBB annotations are Songdo Vision v2: 10.5281/zenodo.21728430 . For precisely georeferenced vehicle trajectories extracted from the same large-scale multi-drone experiment, see Songdo Traffic (latest version): 10.5281/zenodo.13828383 . The benchmark paper that introduces this dataset annotates its own data at the conversion settings selected here: see its software, stabilo-benchmark ( 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX , GitHub: rfonod/stabilo-benchmark ), and its data record ( 10.5281/zenodo.23623540 ). 🛠️ Conversion tool: the oriented boxes were produced with HBB2OBB v1.10.0 ( 10.5281/zenodo.22664151 , GitHub: rfonod/hbb2obb ), the exact version recorded in each subset's PROVENANCE.txt . See How the OBBs Were Produced. Motivation Axis-aligned boxes discard orientation, which in aerial imagery is both information the sensor genuinely captured and information downstream tasks need: Loose spatial support. A vehicle at 45° occupies roughly half of its axis-aligned box; the remainder is background that a detector must learn to ignore, and that an instance-level consumer cannot separate from the vehicle. Neighbor bleed. In dense parking rows and at intersection approaches, the axis-aligned box of one diagonally oriented vehicle routinely overlaps, and sometimes fully contains, its neighbors. Songdo Vision v2 documents 104 such pairs at IoU 0.3 to 0.5 that are correct yet unavoidable with HBBs. No heading. Vehicle orientation has to be inferred from tracking, which is fragile for stationary or slow-moving vehicles. Cost of re-annotation. Producing OBBs by hand at this scale, roughly 274k instances, is not practical. Songdo Vision OBB addresses this by converting the existing, human-verified HBBs into OBBs with a segmentation-based method, rather than by re-annotating from scratch. Every OBB inherits the class label and the provenance of the HBB it came from, so the annotation quality work done for Songdo Vision v2 carries over intact. Dataset Composition The dataset keeps the training (80%) and test (20%) split of Songdo Vision, frame for frame. Conversion is one-to-one, so
title: Songdo Vision OBB: Oriented Bounding-Box Vehicle Annotations from High-Altitude BeV Drone Imagery in a Smart City

summary: Run records, analysis of record and code of the component study reported in the appendix "Design, Provenance and Component Study of KAYROS" of the PhD thesis of Florian Rascoussier, "Improving Anytime Resolution of Large-Scale VRPTW and its Time-Dependent Extension" (ED SPIN, IMT Atlantique and INSA Lyon). Every table, figure and number of the component-study section of that appendix is computed from the files of this dataset. KAYROS is an exact and anytime solver for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with time windows (TDVRPTW) under the Duration objective. Its exact mode is a branch-price-and-cut derived from the open-source solver of Lera-Romero, Miranda-Bront and Soulignac (Networks, 2020), and its heuristic mode is an iterated local search. The study asks 3 questions: whether the exact mode of KAYROS still performs as the solver it comes from once embedded, repaired and extended, what the open LP backend HiGHS costs compared with CPLEX, and what the heuristic and exact modes bring to each other. Design. The panel is the complete set of 56 Dabia et al. (2013) TDVRPTW instances with 100 customers, as distributed by MAMUT-routing. The 5 arms are the repaired baseline (the solver of Lera-Romero et al. at its public commit cabc56a plus 3 patches, with CPLEX 12.10), the exact mode of KAYROS 1.7.0 alone with CPLEX, the same with HiGHS 1.14.0, the heuristic mode of KAYROS alone, and the full solver (15 s of heuristic search, then the warm-started exact mode with CPLEX). Each arm runs 5 trials on each instance, 1,400 runs in total, each with 7,200 s from process launch, one pinned core and an address space limited to 16 GiB, with 10 concurrent runs per node on the grvingt cluster of the Grid'5000 testbed. The heuristic and full arms use 5 paired seeds. KAYROS runs used commit 25d8f0088337b9667956f07fe365c749def9894f of https://github.com/0nyr/kayros , released as version 1.7.0. The sources of the repaired baseline are also public, as the tag component-study-as-run of https://github.com/0nyr/lera-tdvrptw-bpc-repaired . Contents. cells/ holds one directory per run with the run summary (cell.json), the timestamped stream of incumbents, lower bounds and closures (events.jsonl), the native solver result (native.json, absent for the 185 runs ended by the memory limit or killed after the budget), the solver standard error (stderr.log) and the claim record (claim.json). plan.json is the plan of the 1,400 runs, runners/ the runner and job logs, scripts/ the frozen runner scripts. analysis/ holds the analysis of record (final-summary.json, which re-checks every route set with the reference checker mamut-routing-lib 0.11.0), the main and per-instance tables, and a comparison of the proofs with the stored optimality certificates. code/ holds the experiment harness, the analysis scripts, the frozen best-known-solution snapshot used as reference, the script that produces the tables and figures of the appendix, and the 3 patches of the baseline. The bundled README.md decodes the layout, the record fields, the acceptance rule of a proof and the integrity hashes. Main results. Accepted proofs: 165 of 280 runs for the repaired baseline, 172 for the exact mode of KAYROS with CPLEX, 135 with HiGHS (5 proofs rejected because a priced column fails the checker), 171 for the full solver, and none for the heuristic arm, which cannot prove optimality. Restricted mean time to proof: 3,295.0 s, 3,181.3 s, 4,256.3 s and 3,197.5 s. Mean anytime score: 0.37914, 0.35880, 0.49777, 0.00238 for the heuristic arm and 0.00644 for the full solver. 177 runs end at the memory limit, on 13 instances that no arm proves. Limits. The baseline is the repaired solver, not the published one. The pricing changes of KAYROS 1.7.0 were selected on this same panel. The panel is one family at one size, run on one machine type. The proofs are computational closures of single runs, checked for consistency, and not independent certificates. The records keep their original Grid
title: Component Study of KAYROS on the Dabia2013 TDVRPTW Instances with 100 Customers: Run Records and Analysis

summary: Code, data and model outputs of the study "Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference". The study fine-tunes small language models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Phi-4-mini-instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) to estimate twelve structural properties of a graph from its text serialization, and maps where this generalizes and where it fails: across graph sizes, graph families, vertex numberings, serializations and real-world domains. Files graph-structural-inference-slm.zip - the code of the study: generation of every evaluation set, fine-tuning, constrained-decoding evaluation, audits, statistical analyses and the scripts that produce every table and figure of the article, together with every model prediction (one record per graph and evaluation). Code under the MIT licence, predictions under CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-evaluation-sets.zip - 10,320 synthetic evaluation graphs (twelve size ranges beyond the training size and a second size series up to 300 vertices, seven further graph families, renumbered copies, seven serializations, and the test graphs rewired with every vertex degree kept) and two further samples of 1,200 training graphs, with exact labels, provenance and checksums. CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-adapters-main.zip - the 18 LoRA adapters behind the in-distribution results (three base models, adjacency list and edge list, seeds 42, 43 and 44), with their base models, seeds and checksums. Each adapter is subject to the licence of its base model (Llama 3.2 Community License, MIT, Qwen Research License). Built with Llama. Built with Qwen. The training and test graphs of the study are those of the TinyGraphEstimator dataset. The real-world datasets (ENZYMES, IMDB-BINARY, NCI1, ogbg-moltox21) are not redistributed: the code rebuilds the sets of the study from their original sources.
title: Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference: code, predictions, evaluation sets and fine-tuned adapters

summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies the manuscript “Disentangling analytical sensitivity and donor influence in single-nucleus depression data”. Version 2.0.0 contains author-derived aggregate results, gene-level result summaries, figure source tables, analysis code, source fingerprints, documentation, and executable statistical and plotting checks supporting six main figures and eight supplementary figures. The study examines analytical-component sensitivity, donor influence, conditional calibration, sample planning, modern statistical methods, and independent disease evaluations. The internally stable 68-gene catalogue did not meet the evaluated external replication criteria. Fine-subtype annotation qualification failed, and the planned target fine-subtype disease analysis was not performed. The portable workflow supports aggregate statistical checks and figure reconstruction. Full count-model reruns require separately obtained source matrices, permitted metadata, and the documented dependencies. Third-party count matrices, individual clinical records, installed environments, and complete third-party gene-set libraries are excluded. Author-owned analysis code is licensed under the MIT License. Original derived aggregate results and documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Third-party inputs and software remain subject to their original terms. Funding: General Project of the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Education, China, grant Y202559996; Basic Scientific Research Project of the Wenzhou Science and Technology Bureau, China, grant YC20250576.
title: Disentangling analytical sensitivity and donor influence in single-nucleus depression data

summary: Description This record contains the datasets collected via TuniCo, along with the computational scripts, diachronic text corpora, and documentation associated with the comparative analysis of trilingual code-switching (Tunisian Arabic, French, and Italian/Sicilian). The materials are structured to ensure full reproducibility and transparency in alignment with Open Science and FAIR data principles. Contents of the Record: dataset/ : Primary corpora extracted via TuniCo (alongside historical comparative materials such as the Simpaticuni press corpus, 1911–1933), including processed textual data, metadata, and tokenized structures. scripts/ : Executable Python scripts, Jupyter Notebooks, and configuration modules utilized for text mining, topic modeling, semantic network analysis, and the evaluation of translation and code-switching strategies. documentation/ : Methodological notes, metadata schemas, and validation reports detailing the workflow parameters, data provenance, and analytical frameworks. Methodological Framework: The analyses combine close reading with quantitative text-mining methodologies, diachronic variance tracking, and structural network metrics to evaluate language contact, lexical borrowing, and the mediating role of French between historical Italian and Tunisian Arabic. All computational workflows are scripted to allow independent verification and secondary reuse by researchers, academic staff, and citizen science initiatives. Technical Specifications & Reuse: Programming Language: Python Key Dependencies: spaCy, scikit-learn, NetworkX, pandas, NumPy License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0) or GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPL-3.0) (modificare in base alla preferenza di rilascio)
title: Python-Based Computational Pipeline for Diachronic Text Corpus Analysis and High-Resolution Plotting

summary: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Data governance (access rules, purpose limits, obligations, and claims about what data means) is enforced where data is stored and served, but derived data rarely inherits it. Query results, aggregates, and reports written by large language models (LLMs) leave the system that governed their inputs, and downstream consumers cannot tell which rules still bind them. TN represents a value together with its source policies. A calculation on governed inputs produces another governed value carrying their policies. Signed claims retain their original authors and subjects. Each receiving endpoint verifies the policies bound to the result and decides the proposed use under its own authorities and keys. An analyst joins two tables to prepare a financial report. The query filters on companies.active and returns the selected amounts. Although the active flag is absent from the result, those amounts carry the internal-use policy on companies. A dataframe aggregate computed from them inherits that policy. When an application supplies a governed value to an inference server, the server puts its policies and claims in the model's prompt before the model can request a protected field. Immediately before generation, the runtime checks that the scheduled input tokens and settings match the task it authorized. TN is a wire protocol for exchanging governed values between applications. Its adapters let developers use ordinary SQL queries, Polars expressions, Python operators, and calls to an inference server. As long as the application passes governed values through these interfaces, the adapters package each result with its policies and claims automatically. In our evaluation, Qwen3-4B generated an HTML report from data queried in SQL, aggregated in Polars, and formatted in Python. The report retained the source policies and original claims.
title: TN: Data Governance That Travels Through SQL, Dataframe, and LLM Pipelines

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FHR File Converter

The fingerprint is meaningful only if competing explanations such as abiotic acid treatment, biomass-associated peaks and analytical drift cannot reproduce its claimed transformation. It is the ability to identify which molecular bond changed, where its atoms went and which comparator could recreate that pattern without the proposed enzyme. A polymer chain may shorten through hydrolase cleavage, become compact through ionic screening, associate with a peptide, or be replaced by newly produced microbial exopolysaccharide. summary: This versioned research dataset accompanies the manuscript "Does Downhole Seismic Information Add Value to Pressuremeter-Modulus Prediction? Borehole-Held-Out Evidence from Isfahan Metro Line 2". It contains a coordinate-free, pseudonymized cohort of 41 support-matched Ménard pressuremeter and downhole seismic analytical observations from 21 borehole groups on Isfahan Metro Line 2, a data dictionary, retained out-of-borehole model predictions, scripts that independently reconstruct B0–B3 nested grouped predictions, whole-borehole bootstrap calculations, and secondary robustness diagnostics. The dataset field Es_MPa denotes the Ménard pressuremeter modulus E_m in MPa, as explicitly confirmed by the responsible author; original computational field names are retained for traceability. B4-CA is supplied as a frozen-output sensitivity, not a fully reconstructed original fitting pipeline. Positive controls are synthetic and clearly distinguished from empirical observations. The package does not contain original third-party geotechnical reports, direct borehole coordinates, unmasked site identifiers, source workbooks, or external-site/Tabriz data. There is no calibrated tunnel-settlement finite-element prediction or demonstrated independent-site transportability in this archive. Data, derived results and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; original code files under the MIT License.
title: Isfahan Metro Line 2: pseudonymized pressuremeter–downhole seismic benchmark and reproducibility code

summary: Coal Mine Overburden Waste (CMOW) material in the coal mining industry possesses serious environmental risk through the leaching of hazardous and toxic heavy metals along with geotechnical constraints because of the low strength. Hence, the primary objective of the present study is to examine the efficacy of Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) technique to immobilize the metal ions present in the CMOW and simultaneously to investigate the enhancement in the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS). Leaching tests along with highly advanced Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) have been performed to examine the immobilization potential of MICP treated CMOW samples. ICP-MS analysis indicated that MICP treatment resulted in more than 90% immobilisation of several investigated metal ions, based on comparison of their initial concentrations in untreated CMOW obtained by direct digestion with their concentrations detected in the leachate following MICP treatment. However, the extent of immobilization was more pronounced in metals due to changes in the pH, controlling precipitation of calcite and thereby ionic exchange.   Further, UCS test of CMOW has achieved significant improvement in the average strength i.e., 437.76 kPa, 324.46 kPa and 141.83 kPa due to corresponding average precipitation of calcite is 7.46%, 6.06%, and 4.15% and thereby enhancement in particles bonding using bacterial strains (SP79, SP77 and SP78), respectively. Further, PFC(2D) based discrete element modelling was performed by calibrating particle-scale stiffness, friction, and parallel-bond strength parameters to reproduce the experimental stress–strain response of the MICP-treated CMOW samples, with UCS deviations of less than 4% for all three bacterial strains. The calibrated models further captured the development of bond failure and localized fracture patterns, which are consistent with the strain localization and shear-band evolution observed using Digital Image Correlation (DIC). This pronounces that the process is switched to localized brittle failure as cementation increased. In addition, FESEM examination has confirmed the presence of calcite between the particles, validating the results of XRD analysis. Finally, MICP technique is established to be used for heavy metal ions immobilization and improvement in strength of CMOW materials.
title: Metal Ions Immobilization and Strength Behaviour of Coal Mine Overburden Waste Materials Treated with Microbial Induced Calcite Precipitate Technique – Experimental and DEM Analyses

summary: Technical Report S-A-R-v2.2-ORIGIN traces the historical genealogy and software engineering architecture of Curriculum-as-Code (CaC) across three distinct generations (2018–2026) and establishes the canonical S-A-R Standard v2.2 (Scalable / Auditable / Repeatable) reference architecture deployed across higher education and clinical kinesiology / nutrition cohorts. Generation 1 (2018–2020) originated in network infrastructure emulation (NRE Labs / Antidote Kubernetes container laboratories), proving that interactive technical instruction could be version-controlled in Git and compiled reproducibly. Generation 2 (2021–2024) adapted plain-text Single Sources of Truth (Markdown / LaTeX), early GitHub AI Co-Pilot workflows, Python federal data APIs, and Continuous Integration (CI/CD) pipelines to public planning and open textbooks—demonstrating version control and accessible HTML generation while remaining limited to flat document trees without pedagogical graph semantics or civil-rights compliance gates. Generation 3 (2025–2026, S-A-R Standard v2.2 — originated by Alan Lee Pruitt at Webcognita LLC and Arizona Western College) advances Curriculum-as-Code from flat Docs-as-Code into neuro-symbolic clinical pedagogy and upstream Compliance-as-Code. The architecture unites: (1) a 3,265-node DOM GraphRAG knowledge graph preserving heading hierarchy, learning outcomes, and primary federal Sources of Truth (HHS PAGA 2018 2nd Ed., 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, ACSM 12th Ed., NASM OPT, and U.S. DOL ETA Advisory TEN No. 07-25 AI Literacy); (2) W3C PROV-O SHA-256 cryptographic provenance receipts and W3C SKOS bilingual (English / Norteño-Spanish) clinical ontologies; (3) automated pre-commit ADA Title II (28 CFR Part 35), WCAG 2.2 AA (9:1 Double-Contrast Guard), and WCAG 3.0 APCA accessibility linters verified at 0 open issues across 419+ production Canvas LMS pages; and (4) air-gapped Apple Silicon Edge AI inference preserving 100% FERPA and HIPAA data sovereignty under The Centaur Protocol and The Clinical Framing Protocol (Pattern / Rule / Solve).   Canonical Web Edition: https://alanpruitt.com/curriculum-as-code/ Institutional & Federal Partner Portal: https://www.webcognita.com/

summary: This record contains the Python analysis scripts, generated CSV data files, and environment specification used in the manuscript "Feasibility Bounds and Uncertainty Breakdown Near the Effectiveness Limit in Shell-and-Tube Exchangers" by Majid Esfandiari and Mustafa Omranshobi. Contents: - run_analysis.py: generates the agreement loci and area fractions (Fig. 2, Tables 1–3) - verify_levelA.py: verifies the effectiveness relation against the numerical ODE solution (Table 4) - uncertainty_compare.py: performs the Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis (Tables 6–9, Fig. 3) - ntu_crossflow_screening.py: compares cross-flow effectiveness relations for the Kang et al. measured case (Table 10) - fthx_model_margins.py: calculates the loose bounds from the reported effectiveness range - fig1.py: generates the schematic of the one-shell-pass/two-tube-pass exchanger (Fig. 1) - Generated CSV files corresponding to the tables and figures in the manuscript - requirements.txt: Python package versions - README.md: brief instructions for reproducing the results The Monte Carlo analysis uses 4 × 10^5 realizations per point with seed 7. This record is deposited to support reproducibility; the manuscript itself is not included in this record.

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. As a result, some sites have WAV files with 0 bytes of data or timestamps outside the range of probable recording times. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. Data with 0 bytes of data were included for completeness. When possible, all site-specific files, including the audio files, are included in a single zip file for ease of download. If a single zip file upload was not possible due to upload or bandwidth limitations, audio files are included in multiple zip files based on the day of the observation. Data Site location information: Latitude: 39.836701  Longitude:  -84.838096 Local Eclipse Type: Total Solar Eclipse Eclipse Percent (%): 100 WAV files Time & Date Settings: Set with Automated AudioMoth Time Chime (More information on TimeStamp Setting below) Data Collector Start Time Notes: N/A Included Data: Audio files in WAV format  with the date and time in UTC within the file name: YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS meaning YearMonthDay_HourMinuteSecond For example, 20240411_141600.WAV means that this audio file starts on April 11, 2024 at 14:16:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) CONFIG Text file:  Includes AudioMoth device setting information, such as sample rate in Hertz (Hz), gain, firmware, etc.  README.md:  Markdown formatted file with information about the recording and recording site. file_list.csv:  A machine and human file that gives the following information on each file in the record: File Name, File Type, Description, File Size in kilobytes, Name of Associated Data Dictionary with the file, calculated SHA-512 Hash of the file as a unique identifier to insure data integrity during transfer and compression. total_eclipse_data.csv:  A machine and human readable file that gives the following information about the site where the audio data recording was taken: ESID#, Latitude, Longitude, Eclipse_type, CoveragePercent, Eclipse Start UTC (1st contact), Totality Start UTC (2nd contact), Totality End UTC (3rd Contact), Eclipse End UTC (4th Contact), Max Eclipse Time UTC License.txt:  A human readable file that explains the terms and conditions under which the data can be used. AudioMoth_Operation_Manual.pdf:  A human readable document that explains the use of an AudioMoth device. The document is current up to the time of the AudioMoth's use in the Eclipse Soundscapes project. file_list_data_dict.csv:  A machine and human data dictionary file that gives information on the variables contained within the file_list.csv file. CONFIG_data_dict.csv:  A machine and human data dictionary file that gives information on the variables contained within the CONFIG.TXT file. eclipse_data_data_dict.csv:  A machine and human data dictionary file that gives information on the variables contained within the total_eclipse_data.csv file. WAV_data_dict.csv:  A machine and human data dictionary file that gives information on the variables contained within the *.WAV files. ES_Data_Management_Pre-Eclipse_Data_Infrastructure_Stage_0.pdf:  PDF document that describes Stage 0 (Pre-Eclipse Infrastructure and Data Stewardship Planning) of the Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) data lifecycle. ES_Data_Management_Receipt_Sorting_and_Metadata_Organization_Stage_1.pdf:  PDF document that describes Stage 1 (Receipt, Sorting, and Metadata Organization) of the Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) data lifecycle. summary: Background: Gut microbiota modulation is a candidate adjunct for childhood obesity therapy, but the metabolic effects of sequential antibiotic–synbiotic strategies remain unknown. Objectives: To evaluate whether rifaximin followed by a synbiotic improves glucose metabolism, inflammation, oxidative stress, and endotoxemia beyond lifestyle modification (LSM) in prepubertal children with obesity and insulin resistance. Methods: In this open-label, randomized proof-of-mechanism pilot trial, 32 prepubertal children with obesity and acanthosis nigricans received 21 days of LSM alone, LSM plus synbiotic, or LSM plus rifaximin followed by synbiotic; 30 completed the trial. Glycemic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, and endotoxemia markers were assessed before and after treatment. Results: HOMA-IR, the primary outcome, fell by 30–44% in all arms without between-arm differences (sequential regimen vs LSM: ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.54 to 1.36), and adiposity and lipids also improved similarly. Among secondary outcomes, the sequential regimen reduced 2-hour glucose more than LSM (−0.79 mmol/L; 95% CI −1.28 to −0.29) and synbiotic (−0.74 mmol/L; 95% CI −1.26 to −0.22), with similar results for glucose area under the curve, and reduced C-reactive protein, TNF-α, formazan, and carbonyl groups more than both. Lipopolysaccharide fell similarly in all arms. In exploratory analyses, biomarker changes were not associated with the glycemic response independently of treatment, and the glycemic effect was attenuated in children with greater baseline severity. Conclusions: Adding rifaximin followed by a synbiotic to LSM did not reduce HOMA-IR beyond LSM alone, but it improved postprandial glucose handling and lowered markers of inflammation and protein oxidation. This sequential approach to microbiota modulation should be tested as an early metabolic intervention for childhood obesity in longer, adequately powered trials that characterize the microbiota.

summary: This dataset contains hydrological model inputs, simulation outputs, spatial data, analysis code and reproducibility materials for the Mandena coastal mineral-sand mining basin near Taolagnaro, southeastern Madagascar. The SWAT+ simulation period covers 1987–2022, including a warm-up period of 1987–1992. The principal analysis covers 1993–2022, with an additional analysis window ending in 2020. Auxiliary source datasets may extend beyond these periods. The archive includes basin, mining-area, reference-area and hydrological response unit geometries; elevation, land-cover and soil-class rasters; meteorological inputs and rainfall-processing materials; model configuration files; annual and monthly hydrological outputs; scenario definitions; numerical results; scientific figures; and documentation describing data structures, model formulations and analytical methods. Source materials for the independent evapotranspiration comparison include MODIS MOD16A2GF Collection 061 data and associated quality and spatial-support information. The experiment registry defines 35 simulation configurations. These include standard and coupled surface–soil water formulations, static composite parameter-perturbation scenarios, individual parameter-family experiments, rainfall-forcing alternatives, identity experiments and dated synthetic interventions. The parameter families are curve number, overland roughness, leaf area, biomass, residue cover and soil available water capacity. Perturbations target a documented selection of 158 hydrological response units. The dated synthetic intermediate intervention begins on 1 January 2008. Temporal analyses examine simulated mining–reference contrasts using BACI-style and interrupted time-series formulations. The baseline uses static land-cover and soil configurations; its temporal contrasts describe outputs from that configuration. summary: Code, trained models and run data behind every number, table and figure of the article "Matching forecast horizons to actuator dynamics in data-driven supervisory control of wastewater treatment" (D. Voipan and M. Barbu, submitted to the Journal of Process Control). The plant is the open-source bsm2-python implementation (v0.0.16) of Benchmark Simulation Model No. 2 with its official 609-day influent; no other data are needed. Contents - analysis/: recomputes the paper from the included run data. verify.py recomputes every reported value and fails on any drift; make_supp_tables.py and figures/make_figures.py regenerate the supplementary tables and the figures. Requires only NumPy and Matplotlib. - code/: the closed-loop driver, surrogate and policy training, screening experiments and scenario generation, with the launch scripts that record the exact flags of every reported run. - checkpoints/: the trained surrogates and policies the paper reports, including the sixteen arms of the ablation grid. - runs/: the raw full-year runs reduced by the analysis, and the logs of the runs the paper uses. Reproducibility The headline closed-loop results were re-run from this archive alone, in a clean directory, with the commands given in README.md: the recommended release schedule gives 0.2638888889 equivalent days of ammonia violation and the learned schedule with the measured balance target (seed 123) 0.5951388889, both identical to the values in the paper. Environment: Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.3.1 (CUDA 11.8), mamba-ssm 2.2.2, bsm2-python 0.0.16, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.15.3, pandas 2.3.3.

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask whether numerical histories shape generation, whether process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls, and whether learning from construction histories improves the next corpus and the learner trained on it. Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: This software and selected-data release accompanies the manuscript “ Symmetry defects and state-dependent order reduction in Fourier Laplace–rotation splitting ” by Fei Xue and Tianqi Zhang. Version 2.0.0 substantially extends the previous scalar MATLAB release (v1.1.0, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23151617) to provide a unified reproducibility package for scalar and spinor Bose–Einstein condensate dynamics. The package includes: MATLAB implementations of three-dimensional rotational BEC solvers, including explicit Laplace–rotation integrators, merged compact splitting, and full-step forward–method-adjoint (FB) constructions, together with scalar and spinor model components. Python verification tools for the seven-factor (EEI7) and five-operator (EEI5) symmetry-defect certificates, selected spinor subflows, and independent numerical reference calculations. Numerical benchmarks and selected data , including a small-grid matrix-exponential reference test, accuracy-versus-work comparisons, and arbitrary-axis rotation experiments examining the dependence of defect visibility on spatial resolution. Reproducibility documentation , including execution instructions, validation records, file provenance, version comparisons, and SHA-256 checksums. The associated manuscript establishes rigorous fixed-grid symmetry-defect results, analyzes their state-dependent visibility, and develops an adjoint-based implementation that restores the designed temporal order under the stated assumptions. The software provides numerical verification and reproducible examples supporting this analysis. Scope and limitations: The small-grid reference benchmark and selected verification tests have been rerun for this release. Historical large-grid MATLAB production experiments have not been rerun, and some historical terminal-state arrays are not redistributed. The documentation distinguishes independently verified results, archived computations, and derived data. The Python certificate tests are numerical cross-checks rather than substitutes for the mathematical proofs. This release supersedes the scalar-only software distribution while preserving the earlier version in the Zenodo version history.

summary: Heterogeneous evidence systems frequently combine observations that differ in measurement process, provenance, semantic representation, reliability, temporal coverage, spatial resolution, and statistical dependence. Naive aggregation can consequently amplify duplicated sources, conceal systematic bias, misrepresent uncertainty, and force consensus across claims that are not genuinely comparable. This manuscript proposes Cross-Domain Evidence-Constrained State Reconstruction (CDECSR), a research architecture whose default mechanism is Provenance-Aware, Uncertainty-Preserving State Reconstruction (PAUSR). The architecture preserves four macro-stages: taxonomic and semantic anchoring; error, dependence, and reliability parameterization: triangulation, robust fusion, and contradiction management; and latent-state estimation, validation, and controlled revision. These stages are operationalized through fourteen layers. The formal framework distinguishes the underlying target state from observations and model-dependent estimates. It represents heterogeneous observations through source-specific measurement models, accounts for shared provenance and correlated errors, and treats source reliability as a conditional quantity rather than a direct measure of truth. The proposed output is a state estimate or posterior distribution accompanied by uncertainty, provenance, unresolved contradictions, assumptions, validation results, and a reproducibility record. The architecture is specified through the Conflicting Reports in an Environmental Crisis (CREC), a structured primary case in which field reports and other observations may disagree about event location, timing, intensity, extent, and progression. The manuscript also defines a falsifiable research program, conditional mathematical results, counterexamples, simulation requirements, validation protocols, and a fourteen-step pathway toward a research paper.

title: Cross-Domain Evidence-Constrained State Reconstruction Theory

summary: Overview Songdo Vision OBB is the oriented bounding box (OBB) counterpart of the Songdo Vision dataset. It provides the same 5,419 high-resolution 4K RGB frames (3840×2160) captured over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea , with every one of the 274,190 vehicle annotations expressed as a rotated rectangle instead of an axis-aligned box, across the same four classes : Car (including vans and light-duty vehicles) Bus Truck Motorcycle Horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) are a poor fit for high-altitude bird's-eye-view (BeV) imagery, where vehicles appear at arbitrary in-plane orientations. A diagonally traveling or parked vehicle fills a small fraction of its axis-aligned box, and the rest is road surface, lane markings, or a neighboring vehicle. Songdo Vision OBB replaces those boxes with tight oriented ones, so the dataset can serve as a benchmark for oriented aerial vehicle detection and as a source of vehicle heading for downstream traffic analysis. The images are byte-identical to those of Songdo Vision, and the annotations are derived one-to-one from Songdo Vision v2 , so the two records can be used together or interchangeably. Alongside the converted annotations, the release ships the 50 manually annotated OBB frames that were used to tune and validate the conversion. A full dataset card with usage instructions and download guidance is available on Hugging Face . 📌 Citation: if you use this dataset in your work, please cite the paper that introduces it, which is the preferred citation: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis (2026). Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes. arXiv: XXXX.XXXXX. Please also cite the article behind the imagery and the source annotations [1] . BibTeX entries for both, and the dataset's own archival citation, are in Citation & Attribution. 🔗 Related datasets: the source HBB annotations are Songdo Vision v2: 10.5281/zenodo.21728430 . For precisely georeferenced vehicle trajectories extracted from the same large-scale multi-drone experiment, see Songdo Traffic (latest version): 10.5281/zenodo.13828383 . The benchmark paper that introduces this dataset annotates its own data at the conversion settings selected here: see its software, stabilo-benchmark ( 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX , GitHub: rfonod/stabilo-benchmark ), and its data record ( 10.5281/zenodo.23623540 ). 🛠️ Conversion tool: the oriented boxes were produced with HBB2OBB v1.10.0 ( 10.5281/zenodo.22664151 , GitHub: rfonod/hbb2obb ), the exact version recorded in each subset's PROVENANCE.txt . See How the OBBs Were Produced. Motivation Axis-aligned boxes discard orientation, which in aerial imagery is both information the sensor genuinely captured and information downstream tasks need: Loose spatial support. A vehicle at 45° occupies roughly half of its axis-aligned box; the remainder is background that a detector must learn to ignore, and that an instance-level consumer cannot separate from the vehicle. Neighbor bleed. In dense parking rows and at intersection approaches, the axis-aligned box of one diagonally oriented vehicle routinely overlaps, and sometimes fully contains, its neighbors. Songdo Vision v2 documents 104 such pairs at IoU 0.3 to 0.5 that are correct yet unavoidable with HBBs. No heading. Vehicle orientation has to be inferred from tracking, which is fragile for stationary or slow-moving vehicles. Cost of re-annotation. Producing OBBs by hand at this scale, roughly 274k instances, is not practical. Songdo Vision OBB addresses this by converting the existing, human-verified HBBs into OBBs with a segmentation-based method, rather than by re-annotating from scratch. Every OBB inherits the class label and the provenance of the HBB it came from, so the annotation quality work done for Songdo Vision v2 carries over intact. summary: Code, runner kits and measurements of ParityRT, a method for comparing hardware ray tracing cost across Apple GPUs (Metal) and PC GPUs (Vulkan). One renderer runs the same workloads on both APIs through inline ray queries in compute passes, times every ray-traced effect as its own pass, and withholds timings from any backend that fails the image-parity, ray-count and depth-correctness gates. The record holds the source code (C++20 engine, Slang shaders, scenes, workload files, analysis scripts), runner kits for macOS and Windows, and the 18 result bundles of the measurements: an Apple M5 (fanless), an Apple M5 Max and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti as measured devices, and an AMD Radeon 660M, an Intel Arc 140T, an Intel Arc (Core Ultra 7 155H) and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2050 as validation-only devices run by outside runners. DATA_README.md describes every file and how to re-analyse the bundles. Computer names and home-folder paths are redacted.
title: ParityRT: a cross-vendor hardware ray tracing benchmark for Metal and Vulkan GPUs: code, runner kits and result bundles

summary: Version 3.1 (12 November 2026) of "The Standard Model and gravity as effective LdGS". The Standard Model and gravity as a reference effective theory with a matching programme toward a single Landau–de Gennes–Skyrme (LdGS) tensor field. Version 3.0 established the reading used throughout (classical configurations as leading order, quantized ensembles as physical objects, experiment as the final judge), milestones stated by experiment across atomic, nuclear, particle, gravity and cosmology, and atomic-scale bounds on LdGS-specific effects. New in 3.1: • First steps toward a derived hadronic action: the winding field and the record frame form an SO(4) frame with the hidden-local-symmetry parametrization (a composite connection, not yet a dynamical ρ); unfitted soliton numbers with physical meson inputs reproduce the known soliton systematics; a parent-induced vector response computed, with the timelike control showing what remains to be calculated (pole, residue, decay vertex). • A corrected account of the native Card C: the record enters the matter tensor and couples to the winding field through an exact positive cross term of order 1/230, with a coefficient-free ablation defined. • External replication through frozen packets (manifests, SHA-256 checksums, plans before numbers): the string tension of the fractional-charge strand with its width and stress profile against archived lattice data is the first LdGS-specific test, taken by an external team; then the W multi-baryon pipeline and the photon-point comparison with and without the record. • Reviews by several AI systems folded in, including corrections of earlier statements, recorded in the version history. Sharpest external test remains the rank-two seesaw's Σmν = 58.69 meV (normal ordering, m1 = 0), at the edge of DESI's Bayesian ΛCDM limits and in tension with its Feldman–Cousins limit, as every oscillation-compatible spectrum is. Version 4.0 is reserved for the first native LdGS prediction confirmed against data it was not fitted to, in any domain. AI-assisted research: computations and reviews by several AI systems (Claude, ChatGPT/Sol and others), contributions listed in the paper; hypotheses and responsibility are the author's. Not externally peer reviewed. Source, scripts, frozen-packet definitions and review documents are in the accompanying archive.

summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies the manuscript “Disentangling analytical sensitivity and donor influence in single-nucleus depression data”. Version 2.0.0 contains author-derived aggregate results, gene-level result summaries, figure source tables, analysis code, source fingerprints, documentation, and executable statistical and plotting checks supporting six main figures and eight supplementary figures. The study examines analytical-component sensitivity, donor influence, conditional calibration, sample planning, modern statistical methods, and independent disease evaluations. summary: This repository provides data and Python code supporting the manuscript “Estimating Depth-Integrated Suspended-Sediment Flux During Floods Using Hyperspectral CCTV.” The study combines hyperspectral estimates of surface suspended-sediment concentration (SSC) and image-derived surface velocity with a Rouse–flux model to estimate depth-integrated sediment transport per unit channel width. The archive includes: SSC training data and models: 342 matchups for the unified model, comprising 127 baseline observations and 215 flood observations, and 211 matchups for the tracer model. Reflectance data, concentration targets, feature-selection information, model parameters, and code for model fitting and 5-fold cross-validation are provided. Vertical-profile and flux data: Processed SSC and velocity profiles from 27 field casts, together with code for vertical-profile reconstruction and flux correction. Camera-input comparisons: Nine comparison records, including seven with paired camera-derived SSC and velocity estimates. STIV example: One preprocessed space-time image from a flood observation, with code for surface-velocity estimation. Summary results for all nine STIV validation scans are also included. Supporting information: Hourly hydrological data, archived comparison results, a data dictionary, dependency specifications, and numerical reproduction checks. The archive starts from processed observation tables and a preprocessed space-time image. Raw hyperspectral cubes and complete spatial SSC, velocity, and flux maps are outside its scope. The tracer training table preserves the original processed concentration target and provides all-size LISST concentration separately. Target definitions, wavelength conventions, evaluation procedures, and calibration dependencies are documented in the accompanying files. Run python run_all.py to execute the included analyses and reproduction checks. See README.txt for installation and usage instructions and DATA_DICTIONARY.txt for variable definitions and units. Data, documentation, and results are provided under CC BY 4.0 , and Python code is provided under the MIT License . Please cite this dataset and the associated paper when using these materials.
title: Data and code for HISST-FLUX: estimating depth-averaged suspended-sediment flux using hyperspectral CCTV

summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) presents significant clinical heterogeneity in cognitive decline. Neuroimaging profiles and peripheral biomarkers, such as plasma oxidative stress biomarkers could provide information on AD progression. This study evaluates the contribution of baseline neuroimaging features and plasma lipid peroxidation biomarkers to modelling cognitive decline trajectories in early AD. Data were collected from patients with early AD (n = 195), and they were neuropsychologically evaluated to assess their progression. Baseline data included demographics, neuropsychological evaluations, neuroimaging measures and plasma lipid peroxidation levels. Follow-up neuropsychological evaluations were conducted biennially. Individual cognitive decline trajectories were estimated using MMSE and CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. Multivariate modelling and hierarchical clustering analyses were applied to identify prognostic signatures and patient subgroups. Baseline neuroimaging variables showed significant associations with longitudinal cognitive trajectories, as reflected in MMSE and CDR Sum of Boxes slopes, whereas plasma lipid peroxidation biomarkers did not. Multivariate models based on neuroimaging features demonstrated substantial predictive contribution (conditional R 2 0.825 for MMSE and 0.808 for CDR Sum of Boxes). Hierarchical clustering identified four distinct groups, primarily driven by left Koedam scores, enlarged perivascular spaces, and Fazekas scores. These clusters were significantly associated with differential rates of cognitive decline, particularly for MMSE. In conclusion, structural neuroimaging measures at baseline are robust indicators of cognitive decline in early AD, supporting its utility for individualized prognosis in early AD.
title: Baseline Neuroimaging profiles and predictive modelling for early Alzheimer disease diagnosis

summary: Industrial motors are widely used in manufacturing plants, pumps, conveyors, compressors and other industrial equipment. Unexpected motor failure can interrupt production, increase maintenance costs and create safety risks. Routine maintenance and reactive repair may not identify developing faults early enough. This project presents an embedded-system-based predictive maintenance system for industrial motors that monitors operating parameters and provides early warnings when abnormal conditions are detected. The proposed system uses an ESP32 microcontroller with a DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, an SW-420 vibration sensor and an ACS712 current sensor. Sensor readings are processed by the controller to identify conditions such as excessive temperature, abnormal vibration and unusual current consumption. An LCD with an I2C interface displays the operating status, while LEDs and a buzzer provide local fault alerts. The ESP32 can also transmit readings to an IoT dashboard for remote monitoring. An AI prediction layer can be added by collecting labelled operating data and training a classification or anomaly-detection model to estimate motor condition. In a small-scale implementation, threshold-based alerts provide the baseline, while the AI model can be evaluated separately using recorded data. The project demonstrates how embedded sensing, IoT communication and data-driven analysis can support condition monitoring and reduce unplanned downtime. The system is intended as an educational demonstrator and requires industrial-grade sensors, isolation and validation before deployment on production equipment.
title: Predictive maintenance for industrial motors using embedded system

summary: Abstract : Background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global public-health problem and an important cause of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. Although nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy has substantially improved management, antiviral resistance-associated mutations may occasionally be detected before treatment exposure. Objective: To systematically determine the prevalence and distribution of established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations among treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection and to estimate the pooled prevalence of patients carrying at least one established primary resistance mutation. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using a patient-level endpoint defined as the presence of at least one established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutation in a unique treatment-naïve patient. Secondary or compensatory mutations were not counted as primary resistance when occurring alone. Studies using highly sensitive assays, including mutation-specific PCR and next-generation sequencing, were considered separately where appropriate. The review was structured according to PRISMA 2020. Results: The current primary quantitative dataset comprised 42 cohorts involving 9,811 evaluable treatment-naïve participants, of whom 417 carried at least one qualifying primary resistance-associated mutation, giving a crude prevalence of 4.25%. The current random-effects synthesis estimated an overall pooled prevalence of 1.80% (95% CI, 1.04–3.09%). Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=93.3%; τ²=2.541; Q=616.02). The approximate 95% prediction interval was 0.08–30.41%. Conclusion: Naturally occurring primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations are detectable in a minority of treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection, but reported prevalence varies substantially according to population, geography, genotype, study design, and assay sensitivity. The pooled estimate should therefore not be interpreted as a universal prevalence applicable to every clinical setting.
tags: antiviral resistance, Chronic Hepatitis B, hepatitis B virus, resistance-associated mutations, reverse transcriptase, treatment-naïve.
title: Prevalence and Distribution of Naturally Occurring Antiviral Resistance-Associated Mutations in Treatment-Naïve Chronic Hepatitis B: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Protein sequences change over time due to the accumulation of mutations in the genes that encode them. Nonetheless, accurately identifying the most probable evolutionary pathways and more efficient trajectories between an ancestral and a derived sequence remains a challenge. This difficulty stems from a limited understanding of the critical factors that drive the evolutionary process. This study aims to address this issue by validating a newly proposed mechanistic model (grounded on the principle of least action) for analyzing protein evolution, using beta-lactamase as an empirically characterized evolutionary model. The initial findings indicate that, after accounting for how mutations and the context-dependent interactions between them (epistasis) affect protein stability and, hence, the kinetics of protein folding, a resort to the principle of least action allows us to simultaneously identify the most probable pathways and the most efficient trajectories swiftly and accurately. These findings also suggest that the most probable evolutionary protein pathways are the ones that exhibit the most efficient trajectories. All in all, our study addresses several unanswered questions regarding the main factors that govern how protein evolves at the molecular level (under constant selection pressure) and outlines directions for future research in key fields such as directed evolution and ancestral sequence reconstruction.
title: Analyzing \b{eta}-Lactamase Evolution from the Principle of Least Action Perspective
