summary: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Data governance (access rules, purpose limits, obligations, and claims about what data means) is enforced where data is stored and served, but derived data rarely inherits it. Query results, aggregates, and reports written by large language models (LLMs) leave the system that governed their inputs, and downstream consumers cannot tell which rules still bind them. TN represents a value together with its source policies. A calculation on governed inputs produces another governed value carrying their policies. Signed claims retain their original authors and subjects. Each receiving endpoint verifies the policies bound to the result and decides the proposed use under its own authorities and keys. An analyst joins two tables to prepare a financial report. The query filters on companies.active and returns the selected amounts. Although the active flag is absent from the result, those amounts carry the internal-use policy on companies. A dataframe aggregate computed from them inherits that policy. When an application supplies a governed value to an inference server, the server puts its policies and claims in the model's prompt before the model can request a protected field. Immediately before generation, the runtime checks that the scheduled input tokens and settings match the task it authorized. TN is a wire protocol for exchanging governed values between applications. Its adapters let developers use ordinary SQL queries, Polars expressions, Python operators, and calls to an inference server. As long as the application passes governed values through these interfaces, the adapters package each result with its policies and claims automatically. In our evaluation, Qwen3-4B generated an HTML report from data queried in SQL, aggregated in Polars, and formatted in Python. The report retained the source policies and original claims.
title: TN: Data Governance That Travels Through SQL, Dataframe, and LLM Pipelines

summary: Fibonacci -Spiral Nanophotonic Cavity and Symmetry-Modulated Ly Lattice Quantum Key Distribution C. J Tully and collaborators Ly-Design Engine / NOUS-ONE Lattice Continuity Project https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332   13 November 2026 We present a dual construction that maps the linear amino-acid sequence of Gen4_Variant_04 onto a Fibonacci -spiral coordinate matrix for a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) nanophotonic cavity and embeds the same algebraic grading into a high-dimensional quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. The cavity uses a base lattice pitch and selectively etches air holes at the five basic residues (K, R, H), targeting a localized resonance near . The QKD protocol encodes blocks into one of five cyclic algebraic sectors , applies non-commutative forward and inverse matrices, and employs center-invariant checking states protected by the golden-ratio operator . Intercept-resend attacks by the designated party Eav produce detectable deviations from the degree-conservation law modulo 5. The resulting GDSII stream is provided for mask fabrication, and the protocol is ready for numerical evaluation of the quantum bit error rate under Eav’s attack.
title: Fibonacci -Spiral Nanophotonic Cavity and Symmetry-Modulated Ly Lattice Quantum Key Distribution

Named products require authentic standards or orthogonal structural evidence and metabolite annotations must carry confidence. Source-to-source variance must remain visible rather than pooled into a flattering heat map. In the strongest design an external laboratory receives a blinded source and a new culture batch. The fingerprint is meaningful only if competing explanations such as abiotic acid treatment, biomass-associated peaks and analytical drift cannot reproduce its claimed transformation. F037: Enzymes can reveal, transform, and destroy Fermentation can liberate an existing phenolic from a plant cell wall, hydrolyze a glycoside into an aglycone or convert a released compound into smaller downstream products. A polymer chain may shorten through hydrolase cleavage, become compact through ionic screening, associate with a peptide, or be replaced by newly produced microbial exopolysaccharide. summary: A companion paper argued that biological memory is a record that is rewritten by its own consultation, and wrote this as a readout-write channel that preserves the index of a record and revises its content. That treatment assumed the codes addressing different records do not overlap, which is the one assumption the distributed, superposed memories of the holographic lineage never make. We relax it. In a mushroom-body layer where odour codes overlap, every write has the same form, addressed by the code of the record being read, and one line of algebra gives an identity: the change a revision of record a produces in the readout of record b is the code overlap times the change it produces in a. Because training is a write of that form too, the fraction of a revision that transfers to b and the fraction of training that generalises to b are the same number, and it cancels. The prediction has no free parameter and no measurement of overlap: transfer of revision equals generalisation of training. Four consequences follow. Leakage splits into a term set by mean overlap and a term set by the fluctuation in overlap that does not fall with sparseness, so there is a floor at a coding level of 1/√N, about two per cent in the fly. Trading read noise against leakage gives an optimal coding level that falls as the revision load rises. Leakage inherits the window of the companion paper, so a record can be protected by timing alone. And in the quantum layer, index invariance turns out to be a conservation law, one charge per record, belonging to an abelian symmetry of the channel; overlap breaks that symmetry, and the index charge moves only at second order in the overlap while content moves at first, so the objectivity result degrades more slowly than the content does. We then show that the two classic results that look like confinement, synapse-specific reconsolidation and the protection of indirectly reactivated memories, are both compatible with leakage, because neither tests two records that share synapses. The fly is where that case can be tested, and we give the experiment, its controls and its power.   Spanish version included in this record: "Lo que toca una revisión: reescritura en la lectura en una memoria superpuesta". The English version is the reference text.
title: What a Revision Touches: Rewrite-on-Read in a Superposed Memory

summary: This is a big release, jam-packed with lots of new features in our GUI, a more streamlined saving interface, and many new kinematic measures. [!important] This release contains minor breaking changes to the saving functions, to the nan_policy options of path metrics, and to the default behaviour of filter_by_confidence() . Please read the notes below before updating. To update movement to the latest version, see the update guide . What's Changed ⚡️ Highlight: Edit pose tracks in the GUI Pose estimation models often produce errors, such as mis-localised keypoints or false-positive detections in the background. movement.filtering offers several post-processing options, but not all errors can be dealt with automatically. You can now correct these stubborn errors by hand, directly in the movement GUI. This feature is the result of @anna-teruel's Google Summer of Code 2026 project . A huge thank you to Anna for designing and building it, and congratulations on joining the movement team! We're also grateful to @sfmig, who co-mentored the project and made the GUI's layer callbacks and frame slider more robust. Thanks also to @SahilKumar75 and @devanshc777 for contributing the reset controls and a re-export fix. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/10cba1ff-998b-4931-842a-0a84d5be940e Once you load tracked data into the GUI, you can: Move keypoints by dragging them to the correct position, or remove them altogether. See which frames you have edited on the edit timeline , optionally split by individual, and click on it to jump to an edited frame. Reset edits in the current frame or across all frames. Save the corrected dataset in movement 's native netCDF format, and load it again later to pick up where you left off. The tracks layer stays in sync with the edited keypoints, and edited keypoints are shown as rings. The saved dataset has an additional boolean edited data variable, which records which keypoints were edited by hand. You can use it in your analysis, for example to report how many keypoints were corrected. See the Edit tracked data section of the GUI guide for details. What's next? Editing currently works one frame at a time and supports moving and removing keypoints in poses datasets, with saving to netCDF only. Planned extensions include: editing across a range of frames, addition of missing keypoints, correction of identity swaps between individuals or keypoints, support for editing bounding boxes datasets, and saving to third-party formats. [!WARNING] The confidence of edited keypoints is set to NaN , since the model's score no longer applies. To make sure your corrections survive filtering, filter_by_confidence() now keeps points with NaN confidence by default. This also applies to data proofread in other tools (e.g. SLEAP). Previously, such points were dropped. To restore the old behaviour, set keep_points_with_nan_confidence=False . summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative learning on Internet of Things (IoTs) without sharing raw data, yet deployment remains challenging due to Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) local distributions, intermittent participation, and evolving environmental conditions. Resource-constrained devices such as zero-energy devices (ZEDs) further require communication-efficient training and lightweight models. This work examines whether tiny Machine Learning (tinyML) -oriented FL , hereafter Lightweight Federated Learning (LWFL) , is practical under these constraints. We evaluate three LWFL aggregators ( FedAvg , FedNova, and FAdamGC ) under heterogeneous non-IID settings with client participation rates of 10%, 90%, and 100%. To reduce communication overhead, we apply three Quantization/Compression (Q/C) schemes to client–server payloads. We also study two distribution-shift scenarios: intra-dataset distribution (intraDD) (redistribution of class subsets among clients) and interdataset distribution (inter-DD) (label space replaced by a disjoint dataset). Under extreme heterogeneity (three clients, one shared class), every aggregator roughly doubles the heldout accuracy of the Local baseline (Local) , with FedNova highest and the spread among aggregators below 0 . 013 . With 20 clients, even simple averaging is competitive. All FL methods converge to high accuracy. FAdamGC performs best at 10% participation due to drift correction but degrades sharply under inter-DD . FedNova attains the highest accuracy in the two most demanding conditions, extreme heterogeneity and interDD shift, and stays within 0 . 016 of the best method under sparse participation, lossy communication, and intra-DD shift. Q/C methods reduce payload size with negligible accuracy loss, among which quantization offers the best balance of simplicity, speed, and fidelity. Overall, the results show LWFL , particularly FedNova with compression, can deliver robust and adaptive learning in resource-constrained environments.
title: Lightweight Federated Learning for Environmental Resiliency in TinyML-IoT Ecosystems

summary: KenyaESG is a sentence-level dataset for three independent binary ESG classification tasks (Environmental, Social, Governance) built from the annual, integrated, and sustainability reports of firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), 2010–2024, combined with reference sentences from Schimanski et al. (2024). For each pillar, the dataset provides a fine-tuning set of 3,900 sentences and a disjoint held-out human evaluation set of 300 sentences. Each evaluation sentence carries the judgments of two independent annotators and an adjudicated reference label. Training and evaluation sentences share no sentence (exact match after normalisation), which prevents leakage. Version 2 (November 2026) changes: (1) the evaluation sets were extended from 100 to 300 sentences per pillar, the 200 new sentences being drawn at random from Kenyan reports outside the training pool and balanced across sectors; (2) all Kenya-sourced training labels were re-read against an explicit, meaning-based annotation guideline (45 E, 80 S and 124 G labels changed, all documented); (3) an adjudicated evaluation label was added, with agreement between the adjudicated label and annotators A/B of κ = 0.79/0.81 (E), 0.66/0.68 (S) and 0.70/0.72 (G); (4) the companion models were retrained, reaching F1 against the adjudicated label of 0.926 (E), 0.886 (S) and 0.918 (G); (5) precision, recall, confusion matrices, bootstrap confidence intervals and full training details are reported in the dataset card. Training labels for the Kenya-sourced sentences are keyword-derived and reviewed, not fully manually annotated, so the human-annotated evaluation sets are the appropriate benchmark for performance estimates. The dataset captures disclosure intensity rather than disclosure quality. The corpus is predominantly English but retains a small number of Swahili and OCR-degraded sentences, reflecting the original NSE reports. Company names and personal names have been masked in the text field ([COMPANY] and [PERSON]) in line with the anonymisation principles of the Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019) and Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR). Masking is semi-automatic and not guaranteed to be exhaustive. A small number of false-positive masks on common words (e.g. “equity”, “equality”, “Standard”) were subsequently restored, as documented in the correction log. The dataset must not be used to attempt re-identification of individuals or firms. Files: three training sets (KenyaESG_train_environmental_v2.xlsx, KenyaESG_train_social_v2.xlsx, KenyaESG_train_governance_v2.xlsx); three evaluation sets (KenyaESG_evaluation_environmental_final.xlsx, KenyaESG_evaluation_social_final.xlsx, KenyaESG_evaluation_governance_final.xlsx); the list of revised labels (KenyaESG_train_v2_changes.xlsx); the dataset card (KenyaESG_dataset_card.pdf); the correction log (KenyaESG_correction_log.txt). The dataset is also available on the Hugging Face Hub (DOI 10.57967/hf/11590). The companion fine-tuned classifiers (version 2) are KenyaESG-RoBERTa-env (DOI 10.57967/hf/11591), -soc (10.57967/hf/11592) and -gov (10.57967/hf/11593). Licensed under Apache-2.0. Companion working paper: Agossa, J. (2026). Pricing the Cost of Compliance: Equity Reactions to Mandatory ESG Disclosure in Kenya. SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6933338
title: KenyaESG: A Sentence-level ESG Disclosure Classification Dataset for Nairobi Securities Exchange Corporate Reports

summary: Eleven burnt areas from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (EMS) Rapid Mapping activations for forest fires in 2025 (Spain, Greece, Montenegro). Each area of interest (AOI) pairs a pre-event Sentinel-2 L1C image (bands B2, B3, B4, B8) with a post-event Sentinel-1 GRD image (VV, VH, dB) and the EMS burnt-area map as reference, on a common 10 m UTM grid, with a validity mask and the reason of every excluded pixel. The benchmark was built for heterogeneous (optical-to-SAR) change detection: 18.9 million evaluated pixels, 11.9 % burnt (3.7 % to 32.5 % per AOI), 3 to 14 days between the two images. See README.md for the file layout, the selection rules and the known limitations. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025. Contains modified Copernicus Service information 2025. Burnt-area references derived from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (© 2025 European Union) Rapid Mapping products; the per-AOI product citations are listed in ATTRIBUTION.txt.
title: EMS Wildfires 2025: a pre-event optical / post-event SAR burnt-area benchmark

summary: This versioned research dataset accompanies the manuscript "Does Downhole Seismic Information Add Value to Pressuremeter-Modulus Prediction? Borehole-Held-Out Evidence from Isfahan Metro Line 2". It contains a coordinate-free, pseudonymized cohort of 41 support-matched Ménard pressuremeter and downhole seismic analytical observations from 21 borehole groups on Isfahan Metro Line 2, a data dictionary, retained out-of-borehole model predictions, scripts that independently reconstruct B0–B3 nested grouped predictions, whole-borehole bootstrap calculations, and secondary robustness diagnostics. The dataset field Es_MPa denotes the Ménard pressuremeter modulus E_m in MPa, as explicitly confirmed by the responsible author; original computational field names are retained for traceability. B4-CA is supplied as a frozen-output sensitivity, not a fully reconstructed original fitting pipeline. Positive controls are synthetic and clearly distinguished from empirical observations. The package does not contain original third-party geotechnical reports, direct borehole coordinates, unmasked site identifiers, source workbooks, or external-site/Tabriz data. There is no calibrated tunnel-settlement finite-element prediction or demonstrated independent-site transportability in this archive. Data, derived results and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; original code files under the MIT License.
title: Isfahan Metro Line 2: pseudonymized pressuremeter–downhole seismic benchmark and reproducibility code

summary: Changes since v1.0.0 Optimizer (MATLAB HSSR_Optimizer.m and Python optimizer.py) Fixed the Akaike information criterion used to choose between the normal and gamma regression models (2k - 2 log-likelihood). Responses fitted with the gamma (log-link) model are now back-transformed before the desirability is computed, so that all responses are on the scale of the measurements. Data Updated the sensitivity analysis results (data/Sensitivity_Analysis_PPGDalia.xlsx, data/Sensitivity_Analysis_WESAD.xlsx, data/sensitivity_walking.csv): the limits of agreement are now obtained from Bland-Altman analysis on log-transformed PPG/ECG ratios and stored as the natural logarithm of the limit of agreement width. Examples robustness_importance (MATLAB and Python) updated with the parameters selected in the revised paper; it reproduces Supplementary Table 5. The HSSR-SLOPE algorithm (HSSR_SLOPE.m, SSA.m, PPG_FPDetection_Slope.m and the Python counterparts) is unchanged.
title: HSSR-SLOPE: PPG waveform reconstruction and beat detection for heart rate variability analysis

summary: This repository provides analysis code, aggregate results and supporting documentation for the manuscript “Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana.” The study uses Ghana Living Standards Survey Round 7 (GLSS 7), conducted in 2016/17, to examine associations between earnings, observable employment conditions and employment-change intentions across Ghana’s ten survey-era regions. Employment-change intentions distinguish wanting to change jobs, take an additional job or change current-job conditions. The materials include Stata scripts for survey-weighted earnings, job-quality, binary-logit and multinomial-logit models; regional interaction analyses; and Python scripts for data construction and machine-learning prediction. The repository also contains aggregate statistical tables, figures, variable documentation, sample-construction summaries, reproduction instructions and file checksums. Respondent-level survey data and individual prediction records are excluded. Researchers must obtain the underlying GLSS 7 data from the Ghana Statistical Service under its applicable access conditions. The supplied code and results are preserved without re-estimation. Reproduction requirements and outstanding limitations including unavailable original software-version information and two inventory files required for raw-data reconstruction are documented in the package. The findings describe conditional associations and predictive relationships, not causal effects.
title: Replication Materials for Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana

A nanoemulsion can appear stable while the molecule used to justify its name has migrated, evaporated or degraded. We should then ask whether the oil-phase polarity, viscosity and interfacial tension jointly create droplets or merely change the apparent particle reading. The question is an engineering proposal. It is not a claim that any one plant extract has produced a safer or more effective cosmetic. F046: From oil chemistry to an accountable oil-water interface A droplet cannot be defined by a photograph alone. It exists through competition among free-energy cost, oil composition, interface coverage and imposed mixing work. A low-energy phase inversion route and an energy-intensive emulsification process may produce similar early hydrodynamic diameters while leaving different residues, oxygen histories and molecular degradation. The experimental challenge is to keep an oil chemical ledger and a process energy ledger simultaneously. A strong oil-matched control can reveal that supposed botanical superiority originated in a residual cosolvent or in surfactant concentration. An independent laboratory must be able to identify the same marker molecules before accepting the morphology. F047: A mean radius is a poor description of a diverse droplet world An intensity-weighted DLS peak can be ruled by a small number of large scatterers. Number-weighted counts and volume-weighted oil fractions answer different questions. The same mean hydrodynamic diameter can belong to two populations with different rare large-droplet tails, different oil mass distribution and different stability trajectories. This is why the tenth family refuses a one-number specification. A richer experiment defines the droplet population at the moment of collection, after a controlled dilution, and after thermal aging. An unblinded analyst can always find the prettiest distribution. A credible research method should make a high-tail or poorly fitting distribution visible even when it defeats the preferred recipe. F048: The useful interface and the hazardous excess may coexist A surfactant occupies the oil-water interface, exchanges with water and may assemble into micelles at concentrations above its relevant critical aggregation threshold. Shrinking droplets increases total interface area. Yet simply adding more surfactant can increase the bioavailable free fraction without ensuring superior film coverage. A formulation might therefore look beautiful and remain unsuitable for a qualified reconstructed epidermis comparison. The laboratory must measure adsorbed, dissolved, micellar, degraded and container-associated amounts. Co-solvent and preservative must enter the competition as separate interventions. A safe-looking numerical stability frontier cannot overrule a failed nonclinical exposure gate. F049: Temperature is a history, not just a number on a shelf Heating and cooling can rearrange interfacial films, drive oil oxidation, change phase densities, reveal cloud transitions and make small droplets feed large ones by differential solubility. A single elevated-temperature hold cannot be treated as a certificate of ambient shelf life. Repeated heating-cooling loops can generate hysteresis even when they return to an identical endpoint temperature. The mechanistic rivals include droplet coalescence, reversible flocculation, Ostwald ripening, packaging sorption and loss of the original botanical marker. Each produces a different laboratory question. At least one independent real-time lot is needed to test whether accelerated aging forecasts actual storage behavior. F050: Nonclinical skin compatibility is an evidence contract A reconstructed human epidermis model is a defined surrogate, not a human wearer. Botanical pigments, reducing molecules and surfactants can distort common viability assays. The proper design uses a matched oil-and-surfactant vehicle, an independent exposure dose per tissue area, qualified tissue integrity, color interference controls and noncompensatory refusal conditions. A lower cytokine concentration can arise from fewer living cells. A higher local skin-associated chemical signal may arise from barrier injury or unwashed surface material. Even a fully qualified irritation hazard test cannot rule out sensitization, repeated-use intolerance or clinical treatment effects. All these boundaries should be visible on the first reading.

summary: Coal Mine Overburden Waste (CMOW) material in the coal mining industry possesses serious environmental risk through the leaching of hazardous and toxic heavy metals along with geotechnical constraints because of the low strength. Hence, the primary objective of the present study is to examine the efficacy of Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) technique to immobilize the metal ions present in the CMOW and simultaneously to investigate the enhancement in the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS). Leaching tests along with highly advanced Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) have been performed to examine the immobilization potential of MICP treated CMOW samples. ICP-MS analysis indicated that MICP treatment resulted in more than 90% immobilisation of several investigated metal ions, based on comparison of their initial concentrations in untreated CMOW obtained by direct digestion with their concentrations detected in the leachate following MICP treatment. However, the extent of immobilization was more pronounced in metals due to changes in the pH, controlling precipitation of calcite and thereby ionic exchange.   Further, UCS test of CMOW has achieved significant improvement in the average strength i.e., 437.76 kPa, 324.46 kPa and 141.83 kPa due to corresponding average precipitation of calcite is 7.46%, 6.06%, and 4.15% and thereby enhancement in particles bonding using bacterial strains (SP79, SP77 and SP78), respectively. Further, PFC(2D) based discrete element modelling was performed by calibrating particle-scale stiffness, friction, and parallel-bond strength parameters to reproduce the experimental stress–strain response of the MICP-treated CMOW samples, with UCS deviations of less than 4% for all three bacterial strains. The calibrated models further captured the development of bond failure and localized fracture patterns, which are consistent with the strain localization and shear-band evolution observed using Digital Image Correlation (DIC). This pronounces that the process is switched to localized brittle failure as cementation increased. In addition, FESEM examination has confirmed the presence of calcite between the particles, validating the results of XRD analysis. Finally, MICP technique is established to be used for heavy metal ions immobilization and improvement in strength of CMOW materials.
title: Metal Ions Immobilization and Strength Behaviour of Coal Mine Overburden Waste Materials Treated with Microbial Induced Calcite Precipitate Technique – Experimental and DEM Analyses

summary: Technical Report S-A-R-v2.2-ORIGIN traces the historical genealogy and software engineering architecture of Curriculum-as-Code (CaC) across three distinct generations (2018–2026) and establishes the canonical S-A-R Standard v2.2 (Scalable / Auditable / Repeatable) reference architecture deployed across higher education and clinical kinesiology / nutrition cohorts. Generation 1 (2018–2020) originated in network infrastructure emulation (NRE Labs / Antidote Kubernetes container laboratories), proving that interactive technical instruction could be version-controlled in Git and compiled reproducibly. Generation 2 (2021–2024) adapted plain-text Single Sources of Truth (Markdown / LaTeX), early GitHub AI Co-Pilot workflows, Python federal data APIs, and Continuous Integration (CI/CD) pipelines to public planning and open textbooks—demonstrating version control and accessible HTML generation while remaining limited to flat document trees without pedagogical graph semantics or civil-rights compliance gates. Generation 3 (2025–2026, S-A-R Standard v2.2 — originated by Alan Lee Pruitt at Webcognita LLC and Arizona Western College) advances Curriculum-as-Code from flat Docs-as-Code into neuro-symbolic clinical pedagogy and upstream Compliance-as-Code. The architecture unites: (1) a 3,265-node DOM GraphRAG knowledge graph preserving heading hierarchy, learning outcomes, and primary federal Sources of Truth (HHS PAGA 2018 2nd Ed., 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, ACSM 12th Ed., NASM OPT, and U.S. DOL ETA Advisory TEN No. 07-25 AI Literacy); (2) W3C PROV-O SHA-256 cryptographic provenance receipts and W3C SKOS bilingual (English / Norteño-Spanish) clinical ontologies; (3) automated pre-commit ADA Title II (28 CFR Part 35), WCAG 2.2 AA (9:1 Double-Contrast Guard), and WCAG 3.0 APCA accessibility linters verified at 0 open issues across 419+ production Canvas LMS pages; and (4) air-gapped Apple Silicon Edge AI inference preserving 100% FERPA and HIPAA data sovereignty under The Centaur Protocol and The Clinical Framing Protocol (Pattern / Rule / Solve).   Canonical Web Edition: https://alanpruitt.com/curriculum-as-code/ Institutional & Federal Partner Portal: https://www.webcognita.com/
title: From Infrastructure Automation to Clinical Pedagogy: The Origin and Evolution of Curriculum-as-Code (2018–2026)

summary: This record contains the Python analysis scripts, generated CSV data files, and environment specification used in the manuscript "Feasibility Bounds and Uncertainty Breakdown Near the Effectiveness Limit in Shell-and-Tube Exchangers" by Majid Esfandiari and Mustafa Omranshobi. Contents: - run_analysis.py: generates the agreement loci and area fractions (Fig. 2, Tables 1–3) - verify_levelA.py: verifies the effectiveness relation against the numerical ODE solution (Table 4) - uncertainty_compare.py: performs the Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis (Tables 6–9, Fig. 3) - ntu_crossflow_screening.py: compares cross-flow effectiveness relations for the Kang et al. measured case (Table 10) - fthx_model_margins.py: calculates the loose bounds from the reported effectiveness range - fig1.py: generates the schematic of the one-shell-pass/two-tube-pass exchanger (Fig. 1) - Generated CSV files corresponding to the tables and figures in the manuscript - requirements.txt: Python package versions - README.md: brief instructions for reproducing the results The Monte Carlo analysis uses 4 × 10^5 realizations per point with seed 7. This record is deposited to support reproducibility; the manuscript itself is not included in this record.

summary: Background: Gut microbiota modulation is a candidate adjunct for childhood obesity therapy, but the metabolic effects of sequential antibiotic–synbiotic strategies remain unknown. Objectives: To evaluate whether rifaximin followed by a synbiotic improves glucose metabolism, inflammation, oxidative stress, and endotoxemia beyond lifestyle modification (LSM) in prepubertal children with obesity and insulin resistance. Methods: In this open-label, randomized proof-of-mechanism pilot trial, 32 prepubertal children with obesity and acanthosis nigricans received 21 days of LSM alone, LSM plus synbiotic, or LSM plus rifaximin followed by synbiotic; 30 completed the trial. Glycemic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, and endotoxemia markers were assessed before and after treatment. Results: HOMA-IR, the primary outcome, fell by 30–44% in all arms without between-arm differences (sequential regimen vs LSM: ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.54 to 1.36), and adiposity and lipids also improved similarly. Among secondary outcomes, the sequential regimen reduced 2-hour glucose more than LSM (−0.79 mmol/L; 95% CI −1.28 to −0.29) and synbiotic (−0.74 mmol/L; 95% CI −1.26 to −0.22), with similar results for glucose area under the curve, and reduced C-reactive protein, TNF-α, formazan, and carbonyl groups more than both. Lipopolysaccharide fell similarly in all arms. In exploratory analyses, biomarker changes were not associated with the glycemic response independently of treatment, and the glycemic effect was attenuated in children with greater baseline severity. Conclusions: Adding rifaximin followed by a synbiotic to LSM did not reduce HOMA-IR beyond LSM alone, but it improved postprandial glucose handling and lowered markers of inflammation and protein oxidation. This sequential approach to microbiota modulation should be tested as an early metabolic intervention for childhood obesity in longer, adequately powered trials that characterize the microbiota.
title: Sequential rifaximin-synbiotic therapy, inflammation, oxidative stress and glucose tolerance in prepubertal children with obesity and insulin resistance: a randomized proof-of-mechanism pilot trial

summary: This dataset contains hydrological model inputs, simulation outputs, spatial data, analysis code and reproducibility materials for the Mandena coastal mineral-sand mining basin near Taolagnaro, southeastern Madagascar. The SWAT+ simulation period covers 1987–2022, including a warm-up period of 1987–1992. The principal analysis covers 1993–2022, with an additional analysis window ending in 2020. Auxiliary source datasets may extend beyond these periods. The archive includes basin, mining-area, reference-area and hydrological response unit geometries; elevation, land-cover and soil-class rasters; meteorological inputs and rainfall-processing materials; model configuration files; annual and monthly hydrological outputs; scenario definitions; numerical results; scientific figures; and documentation describing data structures, model formulations and analytical methods. Source materials for the independent evapotranspiration comparison include MODIS MOD16A2GF Collection 061 data and associated quality and spatial-support information. The experiment registry defines 35 simulation configurations. These include standard and coupled surface–soil water formulations, static composite parameter-perturbation scenarios, individual parameter-family experiments, rainfall-forcing alternatives, identity experiments and dated synthetic interventions. The parameter families are curve number, overland roughness, leaf area, biomass, residue cover and soil available water capacity. Perturbations target a documented selection of 158 hydrological response units. The dated synthetic intermediate intervention begins on 1 January 2008. Temporal analyses examine simulated mining–reference contrasts using BACI-style and interrupted time-series formulations. The baseline uses static land-cover and soil configurations; its temporal contrasts describe outputs from that configuration. Dated interventions are imposed numerical experiments rather than reconstructions of historical mining disturbance. The analytical materials include annual step, trend, segmented and ramp regressions; alternative breakpoint and pre-intervention placebo analyses; heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent inference; confidence intervals and Holm multiplicity adjustments; monthly and quarterly analyses; conditional detectability and minimum-detectable-effect calculations; block-bootstrap experiments; residual and influence diagnostics; and sensitivity to reference selection, spatial support, analysis period, forcing and parameter configuration. Spatial analyses document polygon coverage, HRU intersections, shared supports, the representativeness of selected HRUs, and differences in configured soil, vegetation and terrain characteristics. Water-balance diagnostics include annual export-based assessments and high-precision daily coupled-budget checks for the documented diagnostic period. Evapotranspiration comparisons report results under alternative quality and spatial-support filters. The archive provides model source code, Windows AMD64 executables, Python analysis scripts, offline dependency wheels for Python 3.12, experiment-specific inputs and outputs, file inventories, checksum manifests and execution instructions. The main entry point supports file-integrity verification, simulation execution and analysis regeneration. Reproducibility testing completed all 35 registered simulation configurations and confirmed numerical agreement for three designated summary tables using an absolute tolerance of 10⁻⁶ and a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁹. Author-created data and documentation are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. The MIT licence applies to the robust-statistics component identified in the archive. Third-party data, model components and software dependencies retain their respective licences, attribution requirements and copyright notices.
title: Mandena hydrological simulations, data and analysis

summary: Code, trained models and run data behind every number, table and figure of the article "Matching forecast horizons to actuator dynamics in data-driven supervisory control of wastewater treatment" (D. Voipan and M. Barbu, submitted to the Journal of Process Control). The plant is the open-source bsm2-python implementation (v0.0.16) of Benchmark Simulation Model No. 2 with its official 609-day influent; no other data are needed. Contents - analysis/: recomputes the paper from the included run data. verify.py recomputes every reported value and fails on any drift; make_supp_tables.py and figures/make_figures.py regenerate the supplementary tables and the figures. Requires only NumPy and Matplotlib. - code/: the closed-loop driver, surrogate and policy training, screening experiments and scenario generation, with the launch scripts that record the exact flags of every reported run. - checkpoints/: the trained surrogates and policies the paper reports, including the sixteen arms of the ablation grid. - runs/: the raw full-year runs reduced by the analysis, and the logs of the runs the paper uses. Reproducibility The headline closed-loop results were re-run from this archive alone, in a clean directory, with the commands given in README.md: the recommended release schedule gives 0.2638888889 equivalent days of ammonia violation and the learned schedule with the measured balance target (seed 123) 0.5951388889, both identical to the values in the paper. Environment: Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.3.1 (CUDA 11.8), mamba-ssm 2.2.2, bsm2-python 0.0.16, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.15.3, pandas 2.3.3.
title: Code, trained models and run data for "Matching forecast horizons to actuator dynamics in data-driven supervisory control of wastewater treatment"

summary: Code used for the manuscript "EDMORE: Workflow-Constrained LLM Agents for Automated 4D-STEM Ptychography in the SEM" (M. Zhao, A. Gladyshev, J. Müller, S. Shabih, C. T. Koch). The record contains three archives frozen at the commits used for the experiments: EDMORE core (event layer, Triage/Planner/Judge coordination, workflow execution; Apache-2.0), the Nion Swift plugin with the MCP agents, the parameter calculator and the half-dataset FRC verification tool (GPL-3.0), and ptycho_sem for SEM/Timepix3 acquisition (Apache-2.0). See README.md for the commits and licenses. Ptychographic reconstruction uses pypty (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19188656). The 4D-STEM dataset is published separately on NOMAD Version 2: a hard-coded Materials Project API key was removed (provide it via the MP_API_KEY environment variable or in the panel), and notebooks, debug scripts, deprecated modules and build artefacts not used by the workflow were removed..

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask whether numerical histories shape generation, whether process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls, and whether learning from construction histories improves the next corpus and the learner trained on it. Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: This software and selected-data release accompanies the manuscript “ Symmetry defects and state-dependent order reduction in Fourier Laplace–rotation splitting ” by Fei Xue and Tianqi Zhang. Version 2.0.0 substantially extends the previous scalar MATLAB release (v1.1.0, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23151617) to provide a unified reproducibility package for scalar and spinor Bose–Einstein condensate dynamics. The package includes: MATLAB implementations of three-dimensional rotational BEC solvers, including explicit Laplace–rotation integrators, merged compact splitting, and full-step forward–method-adjoint (FB) constructions, together with scalar and spinor model components. Python verification tools for the seven-factor (EEI7) and five-operator (EEI5) symmetry-defect certificates, selected spinor subflows, and independent numerical reference calculations. Numerical benchmarks and selected data , including a small-grid matrix-exponential reference test, accuracy-versus-work comparisons, and arbitrary-axis rotation experiments examining the dependence of defect visibility on spatial resolution. Reproducibility documentation , including execution instructions, validation records, file provenance, version comparisons, and SHA-256 checksums. The associated manuscript establishes rigorous fixed-grid symmetry-defect results, analyzes their state-dependent visibility, and develops an adjoint-based implementation that restores the designed temporal order under the stated assumptions. The software provides numerical verification and reproducible examples supporting this analysis. Scope and limitations: The small-grid reference benchmark and selected verification tests have been rerun for this release. Historical large-grid MATLAB production experiments have not been rerun, and some historical terminal-state arrays are not redistributed. The documentation distinguishes independently verified results, archived computations, and derived data. The Python certificate tests are numerical cross-checks rather than substitutes for the mathematical proofs. This release supersedes the scalar-only software distribution while preserving the earlier version in the Zenodo version history.
title: MATLAB reproducibility package for "Symmetry defects and state-dependent order reduction in Fourier Laplace–rotation splitting"

summary: Replication package for the article "Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service with Language Model Implementations, Seeded Faults and Blind Test Suites" (I. Tiievskyi). The study compares three black-box testing techniques on an executable contract of a learning agreement revision service inspired by the Erasmus Without Paper (EWP) Outgoing Mobility Learning Agreements workflow: example scenarios (EX), random request sequences (RND) and contract-guided breadth-first exploration (SYS). The package contains everything needed to rerun the experiments and recompute the reported numbers. Contents - contract/: the executable contract (ten obligations), a description of which parts of the EWP workflow it covers, the reference implementation REF with ten dependent faults, the fourteen example scenarios (EX) and unit tests. - study/impl_I1, study/impl_I2, study/i3: five implementations in total – REF plus I1 (Python) and I2 (Node.js) written from the contract and interface only, and I3 and I4 written by two further language models from the same brief; implementers' notes on ambiguities and file hashes. - study/faults, study/mutants_ext: 40 seeded mutants (F01–F10, G01–G10, GM01–GM10, PM01–PM10) with their catalogue, exact edits, revealing sequences and seeding briefs. - study/human_faults: ten faults (H01–H10) written by a backend developer without AI tools, together with the task sheet stating the inclusion criteria. - study/blind: ten example suites written by six language models from the contract text alone, the writers' brief, the pre-registered evaluation harness with its hashes, the corrected harness and the results before and after the correction. - study/harness, study/controls, study/robustness: the test bench (EX, RND, SYS, differential oracle), the black-box contract observer, oracle and budget controls, the census of disagreements between implementations, observation-level, pruning, hash-seed and fault-mechanism analyses, and regression tests of the scenario comparator. - Raw results (JSON) for every reported table; README.md maps each table of the article to the script and result file that produce it. Requirements and use Python 3.11 or later and Node.js 18 or later, standard libraries only, no network access. Each script is run from its own folder; a run of 20,000 requests takes about 5 seconds. README.md gives quick checks, the exact commands for the full blind-suite run and the census reproduction, and the random seeds used (RND seeds 1–5, 1–10 for the dependent faults, census seed 1, PYTHONHASHSEED 0 for the robustness analyses). Version 1.1 The census of disagreements now draws the request selected from history from a local generator initialised with the census seed, so the census is fully reproducible. All ten pairwise census runs were repeated; the sets of disagreements and the first detection of each point reported in Table 5 are unchanged. The version 1.0 census results are kept in study/census_v1.0. The main mutant and blind-suite runs are not affected by this change. Provenance The contract, the reference implementation, the example scenarios, the dependent faults, the harness and the analysis scripts were prepared by the author with AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5). I1, I2 and F01–G10 were written by isolated Claude Opus 5.5 agents without access to the tests; I3, I4, GM01–GM10 and PM01–PM10 by GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon from the same briefs; the blind suites by Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.2, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. The archived briefs cover the blind suites, I3/I4, the GM/PM mutants and the developer task; full agent and chat transcripts are not included. The developer agreed to the publication of the faults. Integrity SHA256SUMS lists the SHA-256 checksum of every file in the package (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS in the package root).
title: Replication package: Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service

summary: Replication package for the article "Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service with Language Model Implementations, Seeded Faults and Blind Test Suites" (I. Tiievskyi). The study compares three black-box testing techniques on an executable contract of a learning agreement revision service inspired by the Erasmus Without Paper (EWP) Outgoing Mobility Learning Agreements workflow: example scenarios (EX), random request sequences (RND) and contract-guided breadth-first exploration (SYS). The package contains everything needed to rerun the experiments and recompute the reported numbers. Contents - contract/: the executable contract (ten obligations), a description of which parts of the EWP workflow it covers, the reference implementation REF with ten dependent faults, the fourteen example scenarios (EX) and unit tests. - study/impl_I1, study/impl_I2, study/i3: five implementations in total – REF plus I1 (Python) and I2 (Node.js) written from the contract and interface only, and I3 and I4 written by two further language models from the same brief; implementers' notes on ambiguities and file hashes. - study/faults, study/mutants_ext: 40 seeded mutants (F01–F10, G01–G10, GM01–GM10, PM01–PM10) with their catalogue, exact edits, revealing sequences and seeding briefs. - study/human_faults: ten faults (H01–H10) written by a backend developer without AI tools, together with the task sheet stating the inclusion criteria. - study/blind: ten example suites written by six language models from the contract text alone, the writers' brief, the pre-registered evaluation harness with its hashes, the corrected harness and the results before and after the correction. - study/harness, study/controls, study/robustness: the test bench (EX, RND, SYS, differential oracle), the black-box contract observer, oracle and budget controls, the census of disagreements between implementations, observation-level, pruning, hash-seed and fault-mechanism analyses, and regression tests of the scenario comparator. - Raw results (JSON) for every reported table; README.md maps each table of the article to the script and result file that produce it. Requirements and use Python 3.11 or later and Node.js 18 or later, standard libraries only, no network access. Each script is run from its own folder; a run of 20,000 requests takes about 5 seconds. README.md gives quick checks, the exact commands for the full blind-suite run and the census reproduction, and the random seeds used (RND seeds 1–5, 1–10 for the dependent faults, census seed 1, PYTHONHASHSEED 0 for the robustness analyses). Version 1.1 The census of disagreements now draws the request selected from history from a local generator initialised with the census seed, so the census is fully reproducible. All ten pairwise census runs were repeated; the sets of disagreements and the first detection of each point reported in Table 5 are unchanged. The version 1.0 census results are kept in study/census_v1.0. The main mutant and blind-suite runs are not affected by this change. Provenance The contract, the reference implementation, the example scenarios, the dependent faults, the harness and the analysis scripts were prepared by the author with AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5). I1, I2 and F01–G10 were written by isolated Claude Opus 5.5 agents without access to the tests; I3, I4, GM01–GM10 and PM01–PM10 by GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon from the same briefs; the blind suites by Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.2, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. The archived briefs cover the blind suites, I3/I4, the GM/PM mutants and the developer task; full agent and chat transcripts are not included. The developer agreed to the publication of the faults. Integrity SHA256SUMS lists the SHA-256 checksum of every file in the package (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS in the package root).

summary: Contents This release provides the NN-FF-FD-RA numerical implementation, training and evaluation scripts, selected trained model artifacts, archived evaluation arrays, and reproducibility materials. Included materials comprise: Training dataset and baseline, V3, and original pointwise RA model checkpoints, normalization parameters, and training summaries. Archived evaluation artifacts for TEST28, TEST29, TEST37, and TEST38S. Error-distribution metrics used by the result-export workflow. REPRODUCIBILITY_MANIFEST.csv , including file sizes and SHA-256 checksums. The original pointwise RA lineage is preserved. The separate grouped-split RA candidate is not substituted in this release. Reproducibility scope The archived evaluation arrays provide the inputs used by the result-export script to regenerate the corresponding manuscript tables, figures, and summary. The release also provides selected training data, checkpoints, normalization parameters, and workflows for inspection and use. It does not claim that every experiment or every reported result can be reproduced end-to-end from the released files alone. See README.md for execution instructions and reproducibility limitations. summary: POLYPHENOL-LIPID COUPLING SCIENCE F096-F100 | Family 20 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: molecular interface binding, oil-peroxide kinetics, polyphenol redox depletion, genuine lipid nanocarrier co-loading, and nonclinical barrier/viability evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F096-F100; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of polyphenol-lipid-botanical causation F096 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Interfacial Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint apparent binding constant K_app (L/mol). Fair comparator: free polyphenol alone, free oil/lipid alone, missing-component mixtures and matched blank liposomes. Disqualifying counterexample: surface adsorption, self-quenching, polyphenol autoxidation, incomplete recovery or bilayer disruption masquerading as molecular binding. F097 - Botanical Polyphenol-Plant Oil Antioxidant Coupling at the Limit: primary endpoint plant-oil peroxide formation rate (meq peroxide/kg oil per h). Fair comparator: polyphenol-free oil, oil-free polyphenol, matched vehicle, dark isothermal control and tocopherol reference. Disqualifying counterexample: autooxidation, probe quenching, transient induction-period selection or peroxide breakdown without suppressed secondary oxidation. F098 - Lipid Oxidation and Botanical Polyphenol Activity at the Limit: primary endpoint slope of polyphenol depletion versus lipid oxidation (prespecified native units). Fair comparator: unprotected oil, polyphenol without oil, oxidized-polyphenol spike and matched light-oxygen factorial controls. Disqualifying counterexample: reverse causality, time-confounded oxidation, ion suppression or antioxidant depletion without protection of the lipid phase. F099 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Nano-Codelivery at the Limit: primary endpoint true co-loading fraction (%) of independently qualified polyphenol and lipid compartments. Fair comparator: free botanical in oil, empty carriers, equal-total-mass physically blended carriers and independent single-loaded formulations. Disqualifying counterexample: adsorption to particle surface, unseparated micelles, centrifugation loss or fluorescent overlap mistaken for shared nanocarrier loading. F100 - Barrier Evidence for Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Formulations at the Limit: primary endpoint joint qualified barrier-surrogate effect and RhE viability (%), reported separately. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched control, polyphenol-only, lipid-only, blank carrier and positive reference irritant. Disqualifying counterexample: optical-probe self-quenching, surface occlusion, damaged RhE tissue, dye interference or unmatched vehicle causing false barrier evidence. Methodological introduction F096: apparent interfacial association is not proof of binding Different redox states and lipids require independent molecular identity. A change in fluorescence or oil-water partition can arise from self-quenching, adsorption or photochemical loss. An apparent binding constant must survive reversible washout, recovery checks and a separately measured lipid interface area. F098: oxidative depletion and lipid preservation are different A statistical slope between polyphenol depletion and lipid oxidation is a descriptive estimate, not a causal mechanism. Independently perturb oxygen and photon exposure, quantify oxidized parent molecules, and identify whether high-dose polyphenols can switch from inhibitory to pro-oxid

summary: MULTIBOTANICAL COMPATIBILITY SCIENCE F091-F095 | Family 19 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: reaction-product chemistry, traditional ratio repeatability, precipitation and degradation, randomized ingredient omission, and simplified-formula noninferiority. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F091-F095; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of multibotanical-botanical causation F091 - Multibotanical Chemical Interactions at the Limit: primary endpoint chemical interaction-product concentration (mg/L). Fair comparator: component-omission blends and equimass simplified mixtures under the same solvent and preparation history. Disqualifying counterexample: coelution, common oxidative products or concentration-driven precipitation mistaken for a genuinely new interaction product. F092 - Reproducibility of Traditional Herbal Compatibility Ratios at the Limit: primary endpoint coefficient of variation of reconstructed pairing ratios (%). Fair comparator: simplified recipe, independent operator, gravimetric blank and coded alternative ratios at matched total mass. Disqualifying counterexample: a historical label looks reproducible while marker proportions drift due to moisture and chemotype variability. F093 - Multibotanical Blend Precipitation and Inactivation at the Limit: primary endpoint precipitation and marker-peak loss fraction (%). Fair comparator: individual components, deletion mixtures and same-total-load simplified blends. Disqualifying counterexample: detector suppression, vessel-wall adsorption or oxidation products appearing as missing marker mass. F094 - Causal Ingredient Attribution in Multibotanical Formulations at the Limit: primary endpoint randomized ingredient-omission causal effect in prespecified native units. Fair comparator: complete blend, each omission with inert matched-mass replacement, simplified mixtures and single-component arms. Disqualifying counterexample: ingredient collinearity, changed total dose, nonlinear saturation or changed vehicle producing spurious attributed effect. F095 - Botanical Formulation Simplification and Performance Retention at the Limit: primary endpoint simplified-versus-full performance noninferiority margin (native units). Fair comparator: full reference blend, each deletion arm, sham simplification and independently repeated simplified mixtures. Disqualifying counterexample: post-hoc margin choice, low assay sensitivity, material degradation or excluded failed batches masking a meaningful performance loss. Methodological introduction F091: chemistry before the language of synergism The appearance of a new chromatographic peak during multibotanical mixing does not prove a new compound. Confirm product mass and structure with independent methods. Use blind source lots, same total mass, equal vehicle and component omissions to challenge artefactual peaks. F093: apparent peak loss is not always precipitation Separate chemically assigned solid mass, parent compound disappearance, degradation, filter or vessel adsorption and matrix ion suppression. The denominator must close across phases before a percentage of inactivation or loss has physical meaning. F095: simplification is a rigorous noninferiority test A shorter botanical formula deserves scientific attention if it preserves preregistered native performance and independent safety boundaries. The noninferiority margin, confidence-bou

summary: HighSchoolBench is a multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on authentic high-school assessment questions. It contains 10,501 question–answer pairs drawn from standardized assessments, U.S. state examinations, and academic competitions across 11 subjects. The dataset was constructed using optical character recognition (OCR), source-specific preprocessing, LLM-based structured extraction, and validation against original assessment materials and answer keys. summary: In the Standard Model of particle physics, the Cabibbo--Kobayashi--Maskawa (CKM) quark mixing matrix requires four unconstrained empirical parameters: three inter-generational mixing angles ($\theta_{12}^{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{23}^{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{13}^{\text{CKM}}$, or $|V_{us}|, |V_{cb}|, |V_{ub}|$) and one CP-violating phase ($\delta_{\text{CP}}^{\text{CKM}}$). This paper presents a self-contained, parameter-free derivation of all four quantities, alongside the Jarlskog invariant ($J_{\text{CKM}}$) and the complete $3 \times 3$ CKM magnitude matrix, by modeling baryons as $(p, q) = (2, 3)$ trefoil torus knot vortices within a dynamically circulating, three-dimensional ($D = 3$) compressible Two-Fluid Bose--Einstein Condensate (BEC) operating in steady-state thermodynamic equilibrium at the Cosmic Microwave Background baseline ($T_{\text{CMB}} = 2.72548 \pm 0.00057\text{ K}$, $\dot{T}_{\text{CMB}} = 0$). Building upon four continuum differential-equation invariants---stiffened excluded-volume enthalpy regularity ($\rho < \rho_{\max}, \Gamma = 1$), toroidal Beltrami kinetic-energy equipartition ($\beta_{\text{eff}} = \pi/4$), icosahedral Laplace--Beltrami horizon tessellation ($|I_h| = 120$), and variable-density compressible Prandtl Asymptotic Suction Boundary Layer (ASBL) invariance ($\delta^* = \nu_{A\infty}/v_{s\infty}$)---we formulate constitutive topological closures for the inter-shell transitions of quark harmonics confined inside the $\Gamma = 1$ spherical horizon ($\delta^*_{\text{total}}/r = \frac{7}{3}\delta^*/r$, dual exclusion width $\Delta_{\text{excl}} = \frac{14}{3}\delta^*/r \approx 0.01607$). Projecting the net Spindle Torus winding ($W_{\text{net}} = [2\phi]^{-1}$) across the $\frac{3}{4}$ spherical energy-to-enthalpy ratio and $p = 2$ exterior poloidal exclusion sheaths ($\sin\theta_{12,\text{wind}}^{\text{CKM}} = 3/[8\phi(1 + 2\Delta_{\text{excl}})] = 0.22455$), while evaluating internal cavity mass-eigenstate diagonalization via the $n = 0 \leftrightarrow 1$ trefoil lobe inertia ratio ($\sin\theta_{12,\text{inertia}}^{\text{CKM}} = \sqrt{m_d/m_s}[1 + \frac{3}{2}\delta^*/r] = 0.22500$), derives the Cabibbo angle within $0.01\sigma$--$0.31\sigma$ of observation and mechanically resolves the experimental Cabibbo Angle Anomaly between open semileptonic kaon decay ($|V_{us}|_{K_{\ell 3}}$) and unitarity-constrained global fits ($\lambda$). Coupling the central spindle overlap ($W_\phi^2 = \phi^{-4}$) across the spherical-to-exclusion boundary ratio ($\delta^*_{\text{sph}}/\Delta_{\text{excl}} = 2/7$) yields $\sin\theta_{23}^{\text{CKM}} = |V_{cb}| = \frac{2}{7}\phi^{-4}(1 + \delta^*/r) = 0.041829$ ($+0.01\sigma$), while evanescent radial boundary-layer transmission dressed by the $\beta_{\text{eff}} = \pi/4$ equipartitioned $1 \leftrightarrow 3$ spindle overlap ($\frac{1}{2}\phi^{-4}$) yields $\sin\theta_{13}^{\text{CKM}} = |V_{ub}| = (\delta^*/r)(1 + \frac{1}{2}\phi^{-4}) = 0.003691\text{--}0.003694$ ($+0.01\sigma$ to $+0.03\sigma$). Finally, partitioning the $2\pi$ poloidal circulation across the $p = 2$ trefoil strands ($\pi W_\phi$) compressed by the per-axis meridian spindle overlap ($1 + \frac{1}{3}\phi^{-4}$) derives $\delta_{\text{CP}}^{\text{CKM}} = \pi\phi^{-2}/(1 + \frac{1}{3}\phi^{-4}) = 1.14433\text{ rad}$ ($65.565^\circ$, $-0.01\sigma$ to $-0.10\sigma$ from PDG 2024; $+0.01\sigma$ from PDG 2022) and $J_{\text{CKM}} = 3.08 \times 10^{-5}$ ($-0.23\sigma$ from PDG 2024; $0.00\sigma$ from PDG 2022).

Building upon four continuum differential-equation invariants---stiffened excluded-volume enthalpy regularity ($\rho < \rho_{\max}, \Gamma = 1$), toroidal Beltrami kinetic-energy equipartition ($\beta_{\text{eff}} = \pi/4$), icosahedral Laplace--Beltrami horizon tessellation ($|I_h| = 120$), and variable-density compressible Prandtl Asymptotic Suction Boundary Layer (ASBL) invariance ($\delta^* = \nu_{A\infty}/v_{s\infty}$)---we formulate constitutive topological closures for the inter-shell transitions of quark harmonics confined inside the $\Gamma = 1$ spherical horizon ($\delta^*_{\text{total}}/r = \frac{7}{3}\delta^*/r$, dual exclusion width $\Delta_{\text{excl}} = \frac{14}{3}\delta^*/r \approx 0.01607$). Projecting the net Spindle Torus winding ($W_{\text{net}} = [2\phi]^{-1}$) across the $\frac{3}{4}$ spherical energy-to-enthalpy ratio and $p = 2$ exterior poloidal exclusion sheaths ($\sin\theta_{12,\text{wind}}^{\text{CKM}} = 3/[8\phi(1 + 2\Delta_{\text{excl}})] = 0.22455$), while evaluating internal cavity mass-eigenstate diagonalization via the $n = 0 \leftrightarrow 1$ trefoil lobe inertia ratio ($\sin\theta_{12,\text{inertia}}^{\text{CKM}} = \sqrt{m_d/m_s}[1 + \frac{3}{2}\delta^*/r] = 0.22500$), derives the Cabibbo angle within $0.01\sigma$--$0.31\sigma$ of observation and mechanically resolves the experimental Cabibbo Angle Anomaly between open semileptonic kaon decay ($|V_{us}|_{K_{\ell 3}}$) and unitarity-constrained global fits ($\lambda$). Coupling the central spindle overlap ($W_\phi^2 = \phi^{-4}$) across the spherical-to-exclusion boundary ratio ($\delta^*_{\text{sph}}/\Delta_{\text{excl}} = 2/7$) yields $\sin\theta_{23}^{\text{CKM}} = |V_{cb}| = \frac{2}{7}\phi^{-4}(1 + \delta^*/r) = 0.041829$ ($+0.01\sigma$), while evanescent radial boundary-layer transmission dressed by the $\beta_{\text{eff}} = \pi/4$ equipartitioned $1 \leftrightarrow 3$ spindle overlap ($\frac{1}{2}\phi^{-4}$) yields $\sin\theta_{13}^{\text{CKM}} = |V_{ub}| = (\delta^*/r)(1 + \frac{1}{2}\phi^{-4}) = 0.003691\text{--}0.003694$ ($+0.01\sigma$ to $+0.03\sigma$). Finally, partitioning the $2\pi$ poloidal circulation across the $p = 2$ trefoil strands ($\pi W_\phi$) compressed by the per-axis meridian spindle overlap ($1 + \frac{1}{3}\phi^{-4}$) derives $\delta_{\text{CP}}^{\text{CKM}} = \pi\phi^{-2}/(1 + \frac{1}{3}\phi^{-4}) = 1.14433\text{ rad}$ ($65.565^\circ$, $-0.01\sigma$ to $-0.10\sigma$ from PDG 2024; $+0.01\sigma$ from PDG 2022) and $J_{\text{CKM}} = 3.08 \times 10^{-5}$ ($-0.23\sigma$ from PDG 2024; $0.00\sigma$ from PDG 2022).

summary: This record contains model-ready data supporting the manuscript "Reference-Aware Evaluation of Neural Surrogates for Shallow-Water Flows: A Controlled Multi-Reference Computational-Fluid Benchmark". The manuscript is currently in submission. The main dataset covers 13,500 shared synthetic scenarios: 10,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,500 for testing. The common-time outputs use the same 50 requested evaluation times for all three references, from 8.4 to 420 benchmark-time units. Each solver keeps its own natural time steps; interpolation is used only to form outputs at the requested times. The references are the Hydrostatic and MUSCL-HR shallow-water solvers and a study-defined elevation-only, linear, weakly dispersive Boussinesq-type reference. The record includes the main processed datasets for each reference; additional processed data on 32×32, 64×64, and 128×128 grids; pooled-reference data for models trained without solver identity and models given the requested reference as an input; and an auxiliary archive of evaluation settings and preprocessing configurations for the train, validation, and test splits. The release manifest lists the archive contents. Each large archive is split into numbered, byte-exact parts of up to 1.8 GB. Download every part for an archive, concatenate the parts in numeric order, and use the supplied SHA-256 files to verify both the parts and the reconstructed archive. See README.md for commands. These data are synthetic and cover a finite benchmark horizon. They do not establish performance for real events, site-specific hazard forecasting, or operational tsunami warning. Spatial coordinates and time values use the benchmark's own scales; they are not calibrated to real locations or physical time. Source code and experiment documentation are available in the project repository . The raw numerical-reference data are described in the companion raw-data record.
title: Tsunami-Surrogate Common-Time Benchmark: Model-Ready Multi-Reference Data

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-five entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), and a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963), converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters, gives the absorbance template of a visual pigment of Govardovskii et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. Without a water type, it gives Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001) or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013), the remote sensing reflectance from a and bb (Gordon et al. 1988; Lee et al. 2002), and the Secchi depth from Kd and that reflectance (Lee et al. 2015), and inverts the reflectance to the absorption and backscattering coefficients by the quasi-analytical algorithm, in the version of IOCCG Report 5 (2006), checked against that report's published statistics, and as QAA_v6, checked against its author's spreadsheet. It carries four published spectra of the absorption of pure water, Pope & Fry (1997), Smith & Baker (1981), Mason, Cone & Fry (2016) and Lee et al. (2015), for the caller to choose from

summary: Version 1.1.0 of the reproducible research repository accompanying the manuscript: "Operative treatment of pyogenic spondylodiscitis in German hospitals: patient selection, hospital size, and in-hospital mortality" This release adds a cell-level reconstruction of the hospital tables (bed-size class × ownership). The InEK DatenBrowser combines some cells of these tables into a residual row, differently in each query and not only for small counts, so the displayed cells give numerators and denominators that do not match. The reconstruction (analysis/05b_hospital_reconstruction.py) resolves the hidden cells under the containment constraints between the four queries of each year; reported values are medians over 2000 feasible reconstructions, with ranges over these and 2000 extreme reconstructions (fixed seed). With the reconstruction, the operative share is 28.2% in hospitals with fewer than 300 beds and 63.7% in hospitals with 1000 beds or more (version 1.0.0: 27.9% and 65.2%). The risk ratio stratified by data year and hospital bed-size category is 1.02 (95% CI 0.96–1.08), and by data year and ownership 1.08 (1.01–1.14). Also added: hospital-stratified risk ratios, article tables, figure data and key numbers (analysis/06_reported_quantities.py) and the article figures (analysis/07_article_figures.py). All other results are unchanged. Intraspinal abscess (G06.1) is now labelled intraspinal empyema. The underlying hospital data are publicly accessible through the InEK DatenBrowser. Original query outputs are not redistributed; they can be regenerated from the documented query specification.
title: Operative treatment and in-hospital mortality in pyogenic spondylodiscitis: query protocol, analysis code and derived results
