summary: Gravitational-wave observations have opened new opportunities to study massive object events like merging binary black holes. When combined with electromagnetic counterparts, accurate localization of gravitational-wave sources could allow us to identify their host galaxies and carry out follow-up studies, such as study the environment of merging black holes and determine the Hubble constant. One of the possible methods for precise localization is strong gravitational-wave lensing. Previous studies have considered strong gravitational-wave lensing with galaxy lenses. However, galaxy clusters have yet to be investigated due to the complexity of their mass structures. Here we take the list of known cluster lenses from the Hubble Frontier Fields, simulate lensing properties of gravitational waves from their reconstructions as they would be observed by the ground-based gravitational-wave detectors. When same model family is used in simulation and localization, we find that the correct lens is identified for around 90\% of the simulated events. We also show that the source positions within the cluster can be pinpointed at sub-arcsecond precision with an estimate on source redshift. When we marginalize over all possible lens models for the clusters, the lens identification and localizations remain valid as long as the correct lens model is contained in the available cluster lens models. However, most localization attempts fail at initialization if the correct cluster model is excluded. These tests establish a proof of concept of localization under idealized conditions, while more work is needed to understand the cluster lens modeling discrepancies and reconstruction bias to validate the approach further.

summary: This paper investigates the global geometry of loxodromes and loxodromic curves on surfaces of revolution in $\mathbb{R}^3$. A loxodrome is a regular curve avoiding the poles and making a constant directed angle with the meridians. To allow curves to reach or pass through poles, we introduce loxodromic curves, whose pole-free interior portions are loxodromes. The directed azimuths of these portions agree modulo $π$. We classify surfaces of revolution into four types based on the number of poles and whether the profile curve is closed: cylinder-like, torus-like, paraboloid-like, and sphere-like. For cylinder-like surfaces, every maximal loxodromic curve other than a parallel is non-self-intersecting. For torus-like surfaces, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves are closed or dense according to the rationality of their rotation numbers. For paraboloid-like and sphere-like surfaces, only maximal meridians can pass smoothly through poles, while nonmeridional, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves have poles as endpoints. We derive the differential equations for arc-length-parametrized loxodromes and introduce coordinates in which they are represented by straight lines. We solve the direct and inverse problems for loxodromic segments on all four surface types and give criteria for maximal loxodromic curves to be geodesics. We show that diffeomorphisms preserving maximal loxodromic curves preserve surface type and that their inverses preserve such curves. These maps preserve maximal meridians and parallels on surfaces with poles, but need not do so on pole-free surfaces. We characterize azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms and, for cylinder-like surfaces, establish criteria for conformality and isometry. In particular, azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms are conformal when both surfaces have poles.

For torus-like surfaces, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves are closed or dense according to the rationality of their rotation numbers. For paraboloid-like and sphere-like surfaces, only maximal meridians can pass smoothly through poles, while nonmeridional, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves have poles as endpoints. We solve the direct and inverse problems for loxodromic segments on all four surface types and give criteria for maximal loxodromic curves to be geodesics. We show that diffeomorphisms preserving maximal loxodromic curves preserve surface type and that their inverses preserve such curves. These maps preserve maximal meridians and parallels on surfaces with poles, but need not do so on pole-free surfaces. We characterize azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms and, for cylinder-like surfaces, establish criteria for conformality and isometry. summary: Machine learning coupled with device simulation is widely used to optimize thin-film solar cells, but almost exclusively in the forward direction, from device parameters to predicted performance. The inverse problem encountered after fabrication, namely identifying the mechanism that limits a given device, is still addressed by manual inspection of characterization data. In this work, both directions are examined for lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells using approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations. Replacing the Spiro-OMeTAD hole transport layer with CuI increases the simulated power conversion efficiency from 19.6\% to 21.6\%, almost entirely through the fill factor. Surrogate models trained and tested on a factorial parameter grid substantially overstate their predictive accuracy. An XGBoost regressor attains $R^2 = 0.9997$ on held-out grid points but only 0.58 on independently sampled devices, whereas training on a Latin hypercube design of comparable size restores $R^2 = 0.995$. For the inverse problem, a multi-label classifier identifies which of six degradation mechanisms are present from simulated temperature- and illumination-dependent open-circuit-voltage measurements. It achieves a macro $F_1$ score of 0.938, compared to 0.687 for a calibrated physics-rule baseline. The classifier does not, however, generalize to combinations of mechanisms absent from the training set.

summary: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10σ$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. (Abridged)

summary: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. summary: CREAM v1.1 provides an ensemble reconstruction of East Asian summer monsoon circulation for May–September 1855–1907, constrained by monthly wet-day counts from the historical Seoul Cheugugi rain-gauge record through offline ensemble data assimilation. The dataset contains frozen prior and posterior ensemble-mean anomaly fields for sea-level pressure (SLP), 850-hPa geopotential height (Z850), and zonal and meridional winds (U850 and V850) on a global T42 grid (64 latitudes × 128 longitudes), together with point-wise posterior ensemble standard deviations. Anomalies are referenced to the historical ensemble’s own 1855–1907 monthly climatology. A separate file, CREAM_v1.1_prior_members.nc , provides the ten GOGA prior ensemble members used in the reconstruction as full fields, together with this reference climatology. These allow users to examine the prior ensemble and recover model-referenced absolute prior and posterior mean fields on valid grid cells. The package also includes the western North Pacific subtropical high (WNPSH) western-edge index, per-year 5 × 5 monthly index covariance matrices, monthly Z850 reliability grades, historical and modern observation records, a provenance-based observation-error budget, assimilation feedback, and verification results. The assimilated historical wet-day counts incorporate eight adjudicated daily readings supplied with the observations. Python production, analysis, and figure-generation scripts, numerical figure inputs, four worked examples, and reproducibility documentation are provided. Posterior field-level ensemble members and full field covariance matrices are not included. CREAM v1.1 is a weakly constrained reconstruction intended primarily for WNPSH-index, seasonal, and epoch-scale analyses. In the development-exposed 2015–2024 modern holdout, near-Korea monthly Z850 root-mean-square error (RMSE), evaluated against NCEP/NCAR R1, improves by 1.6% relative to the SST-forced prior (95% confidence interval: +0.4 to +2.7%), although absolute monthly-field RMSE remains above climatology. The supplied reliability grades assess improvement over the prior for specified monthly Z850 composites within the East Asian evaluation domain; they do not certify absolute accuracy, other variables, or seasonal and epoch averages. May–June monthly fields are not recommended for use. WNPSH seasonal uncertainty derived from the supplied monthly covariance matrices represents conditional ensemble uncertainty and does not include stationarity or model-structure errors. Development exposure and recommended-use limitations are documented in the accompanying materials. The supplied numerical inputs support manuscript-figure rendering and selected verification and confidence-interval calculations without rerunning the full assimilation. The fourth worked example checks the released prior ensemble against the frozen product and reproduces a selected year’s assimilation update over the WNPSH Z850 index region. Full field-level production requires adapting the supplied scripts’ archive loaders and configuring paths. The original production script also retrains the observation operator using external NCEP/NCAR R1 fields; reusing the packaged operator-space observations and observation-error variances instead requires an additional code adaptation. Modern verification and other full-pipeline analyses require additional external AGCM and reanalysis inputs, as described in REPRODUCE.md . The ten historical prior members are included, but the broader raw AGCM archive and most external reanalysis source fields are not. The manuscript and rendered figure files are not distributed in this package. CREAM-authored data, code, and documentation are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) license. KMA-derived files retain the Korea Open Government License Type 1 and attribution to the Korea Meteorological Administration. The included NOAA

summary: CREAM v1.1 provides an ensemble reconstruction of East Asian summer monsoon circulation for May–September 1855–1907, constrained by monthly wet-day counts from the historical Seoul Cheugugi rain-gauge record through offline ensemble data assimilation. The dataset contains frozen prior and posterior ensemble-mean anomaly fields for sea-level pressure (SLP), 850-hPa geopotential height (Z850), and zonal and meridional winds (U850 and V850) on a global T42 grid (64 latitudes × 128 longitudes), together with point-wise posterior ensemble standard deviations. Anomalies are referenced to the historical ensemble’s own 1855–1907 monthly climatology. A separate file, CREAM_v1.1_prior_members.nc , provides the ten GOGA prior ensemble members used in the reconstruction as full fields, together with this reference climatology. These allow users to examine the prior ensemble and recover model-referenced absolute prior and posterior mean fields on valid grid cells. The package also includes the western North Pacific subtropical high (WNPSH) western-edge index, per-year 5 × 5 monthly index covariance matrices, monthly Z850 reliability grades, historical and modern observation records, a provenance-based observation-error budget, assimilation feedback, and verification results. The assimilated historical wet-day counts incorporate eight adjudicated daily readings supplied with the observations. Python production, analysis, and figure-generation scripts, numerical figure inputs, four worked examples, and reproducibility documentation are provided. Posterior field-level ensemble members and full field covariance matrices are not included. CREAM v1.1 is a weakly constrained reconstruction intended primarily for WNPSH-index, seasonal, and epoch-scale analyses. In the development-exposed 2015–2024 modern holdout, near-Korea monthly Z850 root-mean-square error (RMSE), evaluated against NCEP/NCAR R1, improves by 1.6% relative to the SST-forced prior (95% confidence interval: +0.4 to +2.7%), although absolute monthly-field RMSE remains above climatology. The supplied reliability grades assess improvement over the prior for specified monthly Z850 composites within the East Asian evaluation domain; they do not certify absolute accuracy, other variables, or seasonal and epoch averages. May–June monthly fields are not recommended for use. WNPSH seasonal uncertainty derived from the supplied monthly covariance matrices represents conditional ensemble uncertainty and does not include stationarity or model-structure errors. Development exposure and recommended-use limitations are documented in the accompanying materials. The supplied numerical inputs support manuscript-figure rendering and selected verification and confidence-interval calculations without rerunning the full assimilation. The fourth worked example checks the released prior ensemble against the frozen product and reproduces a selected year’s assimilation update over the WNPSH Z850 index region. Full field-level production requires adapting the supplied scripts’ archive loaders and configuring paths. The original production script also retrains the observation operator using external NCEP/NCAR R1 fields; reusing the packaged operator-space observations and observation-error variances instead requires an additional code adaptation. Modern verification and other full-pipeline analyses require additional external AGCM and reanalysis inputs, as described in REPRODUCE.md . The ten historical prior members are included, but the broader raw AGCM archive and most external reanalysis source fields are not. The manuscript and rendered figure files are not distributed in this package. CREAM-authored data, code, and documentation are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) license. summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.
title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization

summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.
title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

summary: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $Ω(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $Ω(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.
title: Regret Bounds for Quantum Linear Bandits

For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $Ω(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $Ω(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.

Fermented material should be compared using authenticated botanical lots, inoculum identity, predeclared sampling windows and matrix-spiked standard recovery. Named products require authentic standards or orthogonal structural evidence and metabolite annotations must carry confidence. Source-to-source variance must remain visible rather than pooled into a flattering heat map. In the strongest design an external laboratory receives a blinded source and a new culture batch. The fingerprint is meaningful only if competing explanations such as abiotic acid treatment, biomass-associated peaks and analytical drift cannot reproduce its claimed transformation. F037: Enzymes can reveal, transform, and destroy Fermentation can liberate an existing phenolic from a plant cell wall, hydrolyze a glycoside into an aglycone or convert a released compound into smaller downstream products. These are different processes with different mass ledgers. A purified beta-glucosidase may alter a named glycosidic bond, but a crude culture may also change pH, solvent exposure and degradation simultaneously. One should preserve absolute parent moles, identified intermediate moles, product moles and the unrecovered fraction. Reaction rates require independent enzyme activity and defensible substrate concentration; saturation models should not be trusted when particle diffusion or enzyme inactivation dominates. The scientific success is not the largest product peak. It is the ability to identify which molecular bond changed, where its atoms went and which comparator could recreate that pattern without the proposed enzyme. F038: Why molecular weight, structure and viscosity disagree A fermented polysaccharide cannot be characterized from one high viscosity number. A polymer chain may shorten through hydrolase cleavage, become compact through ionic screening, associate with a peptide, or be replaced by newly produced microbial exopolysaccharide. All can generate contradictory relationships between apparent molar mass, diffusivity and the feel of a gel. Size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, monomer composition, linkage analysis and calibrated wet-state rheology ask different questions. Even SEC-MALS requires attention to aggregates, optical parameters and sample recovery. A claim about botanical polymer remodeling should not be made when the measured high-mass fraction originates from microbial material. The pathway from polymer molecular structure to a future carrier must be preserved rather than simplified into a claim that all fermentation increases hydration. F039: A nanoscale carrier is not proof of delivered benefit Ferment extracts include many chemically distinct products; not every fraction is carried into a lipid or polymer nanostructure in the same way. DLS size and polydispersity describe a scattering-weighted population, not the chemical identity of material inside the droplet. Free cargo, micelle-bound cargo, vessel-wall loss, carrier-associated cargo and degraded cargo need separate inventories. Residual enzymes can weaken a shell while fermentation acids alter emulsifier charge, so a formulation that looks stable on preparation day can change after storage. Release tests must distinguish actual molecular diffusion from dialysis membrane retention. A useful crossover experiment tests the same chemically named cargo both with and without the carrier, matching total mass and vehicle conditions. The model asks whether a reproducible material state was formed, not whether a new cosmetic product has already been proven. F040: Safety is the constraint that cannot be paid away Fermentation can create attractive chemical diversity while introducing hazards that cannot be inferred from the name of the microbe or the absence of visible mold. Biogenic amines, solvent residues, unintended microbial metabolites, active residual enzymes, contamination and extraction impurities need explicit risk-based decisions. Microfiltration removes some physical particles, but dissolved hazards can pass through untouched. Adsorption may reduce a hazard while destroying the named botanical cargo; purification must therefore have an identifiable mass balance and a noncompensatory safety gate. Dark extracts can interfere with reconstructed epidermis assays and should be subjected to validated blanks. OECD TG 439 concerns a defined irritation hazard and is not human tolerance or product efficacy proof. The Ben Cao Gang Mu tradition invites care in preparation, provenance and proportion; scientific inheritance requires that care to be expressed as testable identities, transparent failures and safe stopping conditions.

summary: A companion paper argued that biological memory is a record that is rewritten by its own consultation, and wrote this as a readout-write channel that preserves the index of a record and revises its content. That treatment assumed the codes addressing different records do not overlap, which is the one assumption the distributed, superposed memories of the holographic lineage never make. We relax it. In a mushroom-body layer where odour codes overlap, every write has the same form, addressed by the code of the record being read, and one line of algebra gives an identity: the change a revision of record a produces in the readout of record b is the code overlap times the change it produces in a. Because training is a write of that form too, the fraction of a revision that transfers to b and the fraction of training that generalises to b are the same number, and it cancels. The prediction has no free parameter and no measurement of overlap: transfer of revision equals generalisation of training. Four consequences follow. Leakage splits into a term set by mean overlap and a term set by the fluctuation in overlap that does not fall with sparseness, so there is a floor at a coding level of 1/√N, about two per cent in the fly. Trading read noise against leakage gives an optimal coding level that falls as the revision load rises. Leakage inherits the window of the companion paper, so a record can be protected by timing alone. And in the quantum layer, index invariance turns out to be a conservation law, one charge per record, belonging to an abelian symmetry of the channel; overlap breaks that symmetry, and the index charge moves only at second order in the overlap while content moves at first, so the objectivity result degrades more slowly than the content does. We then show that the two classic results that look like confinement, synapse-specific reconsolidation and the protection of indirectly reactivated memories, are both compatible with leakage, because neither tests two records that share synapses. The fly is where that case can be tested, and we give the experiment, its controls and its power.   Spanish version included in this record: "Lo que toca una revisión: reescritura en la lectura en una memoria superpuesta". The English version is the reference text.
title: What a Revision Touches: Rewrite-on-Read in a Superposed Memory

summary: KenyaESG is a sentence-level dataset for three independent binary ESG classification tasks (Environmental, Social, Governance) built from the annual, integrated, and sustainability reports of firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), 2010–2024, combined with reference sentences from Schimanski et al. (2024). For each pillar, the dataset provides a fine-tuning set of 3,900 sentences and a disjoint held-out human evaluation set of 300 sentences. Each evaluation sentence carries the judgments of two independent annotators and an adjudicated reference label. Training and evaluation sentences share no sentence (exact match after normalisation), which prevents leakage. Version 2 (November 2026) changes: (1) the evaluation sets were extended from 100 to 300 sentences per pillar, the 200 new sentences being drawn at random from Kenyan reports outside the training pool and balanced across sectors; (2) all Kenya-sourced training labels were re-read against an explicit, meaning-based annotation guideline (45 E, 80 S and 124 G labels changed, all documented); (3) an adjudicated evaluation label was added, with agreement between the adjudicated label and annotators A/B of κ = 0.79/0.81 (E), 0.66/0.68 (S) and 0.70/0.72 (G); (4) the companion models were retrained, reaching F1 against the adjudicated label of 0.926 (E), 0.886 (S) and 0.918 (G); (5) precision, recall, confusion matrices, bootstrap confidence intervals and full training details are reported in the dataset card. Training labels for the Kenya-sourced sentences are keyword-derived and reviewed, not fully manually annotated, so the human-annotated evaluation sets are the appropriate benchmark for performance estimates. The dataset captures disclosure intensity rather than disclosure quality. The corpus is predominantly English but retains a small number of Swahili and OCR-degraded sentences, reflecting the original NSE reports. Company names and personal names have been masked in the text field ([COMPANY] and [PERSON]) in line with the anonymisation principles of the Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019) and Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR). Masking is semi-automatic and not guaranteed to be exhaustive. A small number of false-positive masks on common words (e.g. “equity”, “equality”, “Standard”) were subsequently restored, as documented in the correction log. The dataset must not be used to attempt re-identification of individuals or firms. Files: three training sets (KenyaESG_train_environmental_v2.xlsx, KenyaESG_train_social_v2.xlsx, KenyaESG_train_governance_v2.xlsx); three evaluation sets (KenyaESG_evaluation_environmental_final.xlsx, KenyaESG_evaluation_social_final.xlsx, KenyaESG_evaluation_governance_final.xlsx); the list of revised labels (KenyaESG_train_v2_changes.xlsx); the dataset card (KenyaESG_dataset_card.pdf); the correction log (KenyaESG_correction_log.txt). The dataset is also available on the Hugging Face Hub (DOI 10.57967/hf/11590). The companion fine-tuned classifiers (version 2) are KenyaESG-RoBERTa-env (DOI 10.57967/hf/11591), -soc (10.57967/hf/11592) and -gov (10.57967/hf/11593). Licensed under Apache-2.0. Companion working paper: Agossa, J. (2026). Pricing the Cost of Compliance: Equity Reactions to Mandatory ESG Disclosure in Kenya. SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6933338
title: KenyaESG: A Sentence-level ESG Disclosure Classification Dataset for Nairobi Securities Exchange Corporate Reports

summary: BOTANICAL NANOEMULSIONS: OIL-PHASE CHEMISTRY, NANODROPLET DISTRIBUTIONS, SURFACTANT EXPOSURE, THERMAL STABILITY AND SKIN COMPATIBILITY Integrated Scientific Technical Notebook | Botanical Family 10 | F046-F050 | November 2026 Author: White Rainbow Epoch / 33 x STARLI Five botanical nanoemulsion mechanisms, one traceable evidence chain F046 authenticates botanical oil identity and distinguishes oil composition from apparent emulsification performance. It exists through competition among free-energy cost, oil composition, interface coverage and imposed mixing work. F047: A mean radius is a poor description of a diverse droplet world An intensity-weighted DLS peak can be ruled by a small number of large scatterers. Number-weighted counts and volume-weighted oil fractions answer different questions. The same mean hydrodynamic diameter can belong to two populations with different rare large-droplet tails, different oil mass distribution and different stability trajectories. This is why the tenth family refuses a one-number specification. A richer experiment defines the droplet population at the moment of collection, after a controlled dilution, and after thermal aging. An unblinded analyst can always find the prettiest distribution. A credible research method should make a high-tail or poorly fitting distribution visible even when it defeats the preferred recipe. A lower cytokine concentration can arise from fewer living cells. A higher local skin-associated chemical signal may arise from barrier injury or unwashed surface material. summary: Coal Mine Overburden Waste (CMOW) material in the coal mining industry possesses serious environmental risk through the leaching of hazardous and toxic heavy metals along with geotechnical constraints because of the low strength. Hence, the primary objective of the present study is to examine the efficacy of Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) technique to immobilize the metal ions present in the CMOW and simultaneously to investigate the enhancement in the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS). Leaching tests along with highly advanced Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) have been performed to examine the immobilization potential of MICP treated CMOW samples. ICP-MS analysis indicated that MICP treatment resulted in more than 90% immobilisation of several investigated metal ions, based on comparison of their initial concentrations in untreated CMOW obtained by direct digestion with their concentrations detected in the leachate following MICP treatment. However, the extent of immobilization was more pronounced in metals due to changes in the pH, controlling precipitation of calcite and thereby ionic exchange.   Further, UCS test of CMOW has achieved significant improvement in the average strength i.e., 437.76 kPa, 324.46 kPa and 141.83 kPa due to corresponding average precipitation of calcite is 7.46%, 6.06%, and 4.15% and thereby enhancement in particles bonding using bacterial strains (SP79, SP77 and SP78), respectively. Further, PFC(2D) based discrete element modelling was performed by calibrating particle-scale stiffness, friction, and parallel-bond strength parameters to reproduce the experimental stress–strain response of the MICP-treated CMOW samples, with UCS deviations of less than 4% for all three bacterial strains. The calibrated models further captured the development of bond failure and localized fracture patterns, which are consistent with the strain localization and shear-band evolution observed using Digital Image Correlation (DIC). This pronounces that the process is switched to localized brittle failure as cementation increased. In addition, FESEM examination has confirmed the presence of calcite between the particles, validating the results of XRD analysis. Finally, MICP technique is established to be used for heavy metal ions immobilization and improvement in strength of CMOW materials.
title: Metal Ions Immobilization and Strength Behaviour of Coal Mine Overburden Waste Materials Treated with Microbial Induced Calcite Precipitate Technique – Experimental and DEM Analyses

summary: This dataset contains hydrological model inputs, simulation outputs, spatial data, analysis code and reproducibility materials for the Mandena coastal mineral-sand mining basin near Taolagnaro, southeastern Madagascar. The SWAT+ simulation period covers 1987–2022, including a warm-up period of 1987–1992. The principal analysis covers 1993–2022, with an additional analysis window ending in 2020. Auxiliary source datasets may extend beyond these periods. The archive includes basin, mining-area, reference-area and hydrological response unit geometries; elevation, land-cover and soil-class rasters; meteorological inputs and rainfall-processing materials; model configuration files; annual and monthly hydrological outputs; scenario definitions; numerical results; scientific figures; and documentation describing data structures, model formulations and analytical methods. Source materials for the independent evapotranspiration comparison include MODIS MOD16A2GF Collection 061 data and associated quality and spatial-support information. The experiment registry defines 35 simulation configurations. These include standard and coupled surface–soil water formulations, static composite parameter-perturbation scenarios, individual parameter-family experiments, rainfall-forcing alternatives, identity experiments and dated synthetic interventions. The parameter families are curve number, overland roughness, leaf area, biomass, residue cover and soil available water capacity. Perturbations target a documented selection of 158 hydrological response units. The dated synthetic intermediate intervention begins on 1 January 2008. Temporal analyses examine simulated mining–reference contrasts using BACI-style and interrupted time-series formulations. The baseline uses static land-cover and soil configurations; its temporal contrasts describe outputs from that configuration. Dated interventions are imposed numerical experiments rather than reconstructions of historical mining disturbance. The analytical materials include annual step, trend, segmented and ramp regressions; alternative breakpoint and pre-intervention placebo analyses; heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent inference; confidence intervals and Holm multiplicity adjustments; monthly and quarterly analyses; conditional detectability and minimum-detectable-effect calculations; block-bootstrap experiments; residual and influence diagnostics; and sensitivity to reference selection, spatial support, analysis period, forcing and parameter configuration. Spatial analyses document polygon coverage, HRU intersections, shared supports, the representativeness of selected HRUs, and differences in configured soil, vegetation and terrain characteristics. Water-balance diagnostics include annual export-based assessments and high-precision daily coupled-budget checks for the documented diagnostic period. Evapotranspiration comparisons report results under alternative quality and spatial-support filters. The archive provides model source code, Windows AMD64 executables, Python analysis scripts, offline dependency wheels for Python 3.12, experiment-specific inputs and outputs, file inventories, checksum manifests and execution instructions. The main entry point supports file-integrity verification, simulation execution and analysis regeneration. Reproducibility testing completed all 35 registered simulation configurations and confirmed numerical agreement for three designated summary tables using an absolute tolerance of 10⁻⁶ and a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁹. Author-created data and documentation are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. The MIT licence applies to the robust-statistics component identified in the archive. Third-party data, model components and software dependencies retain their respective licences, attribution requirements and copyright notices.
title: Mandena hydrological simulations, data and analysis

The record contains three archives frozen at the commits used for the experiments: EDMORE core (event layer, Triage/Planner/Judge coordination, workflow execution; Apache-2.0), the Nion Swift plugin with the MCP agents, the parameter calculator and the half-dataset FRC verification tool (GPL-3.0), and ptycho_sem for SEM/Timepix3 acquisition (Apache-2.0). title: EDMORE: code for "Workflow-Constrained LLM Agents for Automated 4D-STEM Ptychography in the SEM"

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask whether numerical histories shape generation, whether process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls, and whether learning from construction histories improves the next corpus and the learner trained on it. Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: This software and selected-data release accompanies the manuscript “ Symmetry defects and state-dependent order reduction in Fourier Laplace–rotation splitting ” by Fei Xue and Tianqi Zhang. Version 2.0.0 substantially extends the previous scalar MATLAB release (v1.1.0, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23151617) to provide a unified reproducibility package for scalar and spinor Bose–Einstein condensate dynamics. The package includes: MATLAB implementations of three-dimensional rotational BEC solvers, including explicit Laplace–rotation integrators, merged compact splitting, and full-step forward–method-adjoint (FB) constructions, together with scalar and spinor model components. Python verification tools for the seven-factor (EEI7) and five-operator (EEI5) symmetry-defect certificates, selected spinor subflows, and independent numerical reference calculations. Numerical benchmarks and selected data , including a small-grid matrix-exponential reference test, accuracy-versus-work comparisons, and arbitrary-axis rotation experiments examining the dependence of defect visibility on spatial resolution. Reproducibility documentation , including execution instructions, validation records, file provenance, version comparisons, and SHA-256 checksums. The associated manuscript establishes rigorous fixed-grid symmetry-defect results, analyzes their state-dependent visibility, and develops an adjoint-based implementation that restores the designed temporal order under the stated assumptions. The software provides numerical verification and reproducible examples supporting this analysis. Scope and limitations: The small-grid reference benchmark and selected verification tests have been rerun for this release. Historical large-grid MATLAB production experiments have not been rerun, and some historical terminal-state arrays are not redistributed. The documentation distinguishes independently verified results, archived computations, and derived data. The Python certificate tests are numerical cross-checks rather than substitutes for the mathematical proofs. This release supersedes the scalar-only software distribution while preserving the earlier version in the Zenodo version history.
title: MATLAB reproducibility package for "Symmetry defects and state-dependent order reduction in Fourier Laplace–rotation splitting"

summary: Replication package for the article "Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service with Language Model Implementations, Seeded Faults and Blind Test Suites" (I. Tiievskyi). The study compares three black-box testing techniques on an executable contract of a learning agreement revision service inspired by the Erasmus Without Paper (EWP) Outgoing Mobility Learning Agreements workflow: example scenarios (EX), random request sequences (RND) and contract-guided breadth-first exploration (SYS). The package contains everything needed to rerun the experiments and recompute the reported numbers. Contents - contract/: the executable contract (ten obligations), a description of which parts of the EWP workflow it covers, the reference implementation REF with ten dependent faults, the fourteen example scenarios (EX) and unit tests. - study/impl_I1, study/impl_I2, study/i3: five implementations in total – REF plus I1 (Python) and I2 (Node.js) written from the contract and interface only, and I3 and I4 written by two further language models from the same brief; implementers' notes on ambiguities and file hashes. - study/faults, study/mutants_ext: 40 seeded mutants (F01–F10, G01–G10, GM01–GM10, PM01–PM10) with their catalogue, exact edits, revealing sequences and seeding briefs. - study/human_faults: ten faults (H01–H10) written by a backend developer without AI tools, together with the task sheet stating the inclusion criteria. - study/blind: ten example suites written by six language models from the contract text alone, the writers' brief, the pre-registered evaluation harness with its hashes, the corrected harness and the results before and after the correction. - study/harness, study/controls, study/robustness: the test bench (EX, RND, SYS, differential oracle), the black-box contract observer, oracle and budget controls, the census of disagreements between implementations, observation-level, pruning, hash-seed and fault-mechanism analyses, and regression tests of the scenario comparator. - Raw results (JSON) for every reported table; README.md maps each table of the article to the script and result file that produce it. Requirements and use Python 3.11 or later and Node.js 18 or later, standard libraries only, no network access. Each script is run from its own folder; a run of 20,000 requests takes about 5 seconds. README.md gives quick checks, the exact commands for the full blind-suite run and the census reproduction, and the random seeds used (RND seeds 1–5, 1–10 for the dependent faults, census seed 1, PYTHONHASHSEED 0 for the robustness analyses). Version 1.1 The census of disagreements now draws the request selected from history from a local generator initialised with the census seed, so the census is fully reproducible. All ten pairwise census runs were repeated; the sets of disagreements and the first detection of each point reported in Table 5 are unchanged. The version 1.0 census results are kept in study/census_v1.0. The main mutant and blind-suite runs are not affected by this change. Provenance The contract, the reference implementation, the example scenarios, the dependent faults, the harness and the analysis scripts were prepared by the author with AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5). I1, I2 and F01–G10 were written by isolated Claude Opus 5.5 agents without access to the tests; I3, I4, GM01–GM10 and PM01–PM10 by GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon from the same briefs; the blind suites by Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.2, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. The archived briefs cover the blind suites, I3/I4, the GM/PM mutants and the developer task; full agent and chat transcripts are not included. The developer agreed to the publication of the faults. Integrity SHA256SUMS lists the SHA-256 checksum of every file in the package (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS in the package root).
title: Replication package: Example Scenarios, Random Sequences or Contract-Guided Exploration? Testing a Stateful Learning Agreement Service

summary: Contents This release provides the NN-FF-FD-RA numerical implementation, training and evaluation scripts, selected trained model artifacts, archived evaluation arrays, and reproducibility materials. Included materials comprise: Training dataset and baseline, V3, and original pointwise RA model checkpoints, normalization parameters, and training summaries. Archived evaluation artifacts for TEST28, TEST29, TEST37, and TEST38S. Error-distribution metrics used by the result-export workflow. REPRODUCIBILITY_MANIFEST.csv , including file sizes and SHA-256 checksums. The original pointwise RA lineage is preserved. The separate grouped-split RA candidate is not substituted in this release. summary: POLYPHENOL-LIPID COUPLING SCIENCE F096-F100 | Family 20 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: molecular interface binding, oil-peroxide kinetics, polyphenol redox depletion, genuine lipid nanocarrier co-loading, and nonclinical barrier/viability evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F096-F100; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of polyphenol-lipid-botanical causation F096 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Interfacial Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint apparent binding constant K_app (L/mol). Fair comparator: free polyphenol alone, free oil/lipid alone, missing-component mixtures and matched blank liposomes. Disqualifying counterexample: surface adsorption, self-quenching, polyphenol autoxidation, incomplete recovery or bilayer disruption masquerading as molecular binding. F097 - Botanical Polyphenol-Plant Oil Antioxidant Coupling at the Limit: primary endpoint plant-oil peroxide formation rate (meq peroxide/kg oil per h). Fair comparator: polyphenol-free oil, oil-free polyphenol, matched vehicle, dark isothermal control and tocopherol reference. Disqualifying counterexample: autooxidation, probe quenching, transient induction-period selection or peroxide breakdown without suppressed secondary oxidation. F098 - Lipid Oxidation and Botanical Polyphenol Activity at the Limit: primary endpoint slope of polyphenol depletion versus lipid oxidation (prespecified native units). Fair comparator: unprotected oil, polyphenol without oil, oxidized-polyphenol spike and matched light-oxygen factorial controls. Disqualifying counterexample: reverse causality, time-confounded oxidation, ion suppression or antioxidant depletion without protection of the lipid phase. F099 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Nano-Codelivery at the Limit: primary endpoint true co-loading fraction (%) of independently qualified polyphenol and lipid compartments. Fair comparator: free botanical in oil, empty carriers, equal-total-mass physically blended carriers and independent single-loaded formulations. Disqualifying counterexample: adsorption to particle surface, unseparated micelles, centrifugation loss or fluorescent overlap mistaken for shared nanocarrier loading. F100 - Barrier Evidence for Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Formulations at the Limit: primary endpoint joint qualified barrier-surrogate effect and RhE viability (%), reported separately. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched control, polyphenol-only, lipid-only, blank carrier and positive reference irritant. Disqualifying counterexample: optical-probe self-quenching, surface occlusion, damaged RhE tissue, dye interference or unmatched vehicle causing false barrier evidence. Methodological introduction F096: apparent interfacial association is not proof of binding Different redox states and lipids require independent molecular identity. A change in fluorescence or oil-water partition can arise from self-quenching, adsorption or photochemical loss. An apparent binding constant must survive reversible washout, recovery checks and a separately measured lipid interface area. F098: oxidative depletion and lipid preservation are different A statistical slope between polyphenol depletion and lipid oxidation is a descriptive estimate, not a causal mechanism. Independently perturb oxygen and photon exposure, quantify oxidized parent molecules, and identify whether high-dose polyphenols can switch from inhibitory to pro-oxid

summary: MULTIBOTANICAL COMPATIBILITY SCIENCE F091-F095 | Family 19 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: reaction-product chemistry, traditional ratio repeatability, precipitation and degradation, randomized ingredient omission, and simplified-formula noninferiority. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F091-F095; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of multibotanical-botanical causation F091 - Multibotanical Chemical Interactions at the Limit: primary endpoint chemical interaction-product concentration (mg/L). Fair comparator: component-omission blends and equimass simplified mixtures under the same solvent and preparation history. Disqualifying counterexample: coelution, common oxidative products or concentration-driven precipitation mistaken for a genuinely new interaction product. F092 - Reproducibility of Traditional Herbal Compatibility Ratios at the Limit: primary endpoint coefficient of variation of reconstructed pairing ratios (%). Fair comparator: simplified recipe, independent operator, gravimetric blank and coded alternative ratios at matched total mass. Disqualifying counterexample: a historical label looks reproducible while marker proportions drift due to moisture and chemotype variability. F093 - Multibotanical Blend Precipitation and Inactivation at the Limit: primary endpoint precipitation and marker-peak loss fraction (%). Fair comparator: individual components, deletion mixtures and same-total-load simplified blends. Disqualifying counterexample: detector suppression, vessel-wall adsorption or oxidation products appearing as missing marker mass. F094 - Causal Ingredient Attribution in Multibotanical Formulations at the Limit: primary endpoint randomized ingredient-omission causal effect in prespecified native units. Fair comparator: complete blend, each omission with inert matched-mass replacement, simplified mixtures and single-component arms. Disqualifying counterexample: ingredient collinearity, changed total dose, nonlinear saturation or changed vehicle producing spurious attributed effect. F095 - Botanical Formulation Simplification and Performance Retention at the Limit: primary endpoint simplified-versus-full performance noninferiority margin (native units). Fair comparator: full reference blend, each deletion arm, sham simplification and independently repeated simplified mixtures. Disqualifying counterexample: post-hoc margin choice, low assay sensitivity, material degradation or excluded failed batches masking a meaningful performance loss. Methodological introduction F091: chemistry before the language of synergism The appearance of a new chromatographic peak during multibotanical mixing does not prove a new compound. Confirm product mass and structure with independent methods. Use blind source lots, same total mass, equal vehicle and component omissions to challenge artefactual peaks. F093: apparent peak loss is not always precipitation Separate chemically assigned solid mass, parent compound disappearance, degradation, filter or vessel adsorption and matrix ion suppression. The denominator must close across phases before a percentage of inactivation or loss has physical meaning. F095: simplification is a rigorous noninferiority test A shorter botanical formula deserves scientific attention if it preserves preregistered native performance and independent safety boundaries. The noninferiority margin, confidence-bou

summary: HighSchoolBench is a multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on authentic high-school assessment questions. It contains 10,501 question–answer pairs drawn from standardized assessments, U.S. state examinations, and academic competitions across 11 subjects. The dataset was constructed using optical character recognition (OCR), source-specific preprocessing, LLM-based structured extraction, and validation against original assessment materials and answer keys. Dataset components The benchmark consists of two components: HighSchoolBench-MCQ: Contains 7,549 multiple-choice questions, including single-answer and multiple-answer questions. Answer options may be represented as text, images, or tables. The dataset is organized into 15 configurations based on the modalities of the question context and answer options. HighSchoolBench-OEQ: Contains 2,952 open-ended questions with free-text reference answers. These include worked solutions, explanations and descriptions, multi-part responses, and exact or short scientific answers. The dataset is organized into 18 configurations based on the supporting context and expected answer form. Questions may include supporting text, images, tables, or combinations of these modalities. Dataset structure The HighSchoolBench archive is organized into two components: multiple-choice questions (MCQ) and open-ended questions (OEQ). Both components are grouped by question configuration and dataset split. HighSchoolBench/ ├── HighSchoolBench-MCQ/ │ ├── README.md │ └── subsets/ │ ├── context_text_only__text_options/ │ │ ├── train/ │ │ │ ├── metadata.jsonl │ │ │ └── images/ │ │ ├── validation/ │ │ │ ├── metadata.jsonl │ │ │ └── images/ │ │ └── test/ │ │ ├── metadata.jsonl │ │ └── images/ │ ├── context_text_images__text_options/ │ ├── context_text_table__text_options/ │ └── ... (15 configurations in total) │ ├── HighSchoolBench-OEQ/ │ ├── README.md │ └── subsets/ │ ├── context_text_only__calculation_with_work_answer/ │ │ ├── train/ │ │ │ └── metadata.jsonl │ │ ├── validation/ │ │ │ └── metadata.jsonl │ │ └── test/ │ │ └── metadata.jsonl │ ├── context_text_images__explanation_answer/ │ ├── context_text_table__multi_part_answer/ │ └── ... (18 configurations in total) │ └── README.md Each configuration directory contains the available train , validation , and/or test splits. metadata.jsonl contains the questions, reference answers, and associated metadata. images/ contains the image files referenced by the corresponding JSONL records, where applicable. README.md provides dataset documentation, configuration descriptions, and usage instructions. The MCQ and OEQ components can be accessed independently. For benchmarking, researchers can select the relevant configurations based on the modalities supported by their models. Online access The datasets are also available through Hugging Face: HighSchoolBench-MCQ HighSchoolBench-OEQ This archive represents a versioned dataset release intended for reproducible research and benchmarking. The Hugging Face repositories provide direct access to the datasets for model evaluation. Citation If you use HighSchoolBench in your research, please cite this Zenodo dataset record.

summary: In the Standard Model of particle physics, the Cabibbo--Kobayashi--Maskawa (CKM) quark mixing matrix requires four unconstrained empirical parameters: three inter-generational mixing angles ($\theta_{12}^{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{23}^{\text{CKM}}, \theta_{13}^{\text{CKM}}$, or $|V_{us}|, |V_{cb}|, |V_{ub}|$) and one CP-violating phase ($\delta_{\text{CP}}^{\text{CKM}}$). This paper presents a self-contained, parameter-free derivation of all four quantities, alongside the Jarlskog invariant ($J_{\text{CKM}}$) and the complete $3 \times 3$ CKM magnitude matrix, by modeling baryons as $(p, q) = (2, 3)$ trefoil torus knot vortices within a dynamically circulating, three-dimensional ($D = 3$) compressible Two-Fluid Bose--Einstein Condensate (BEC) operating in steady-state thermodynamic equilibrium at the Cosmic Microwave Background baseline ($T_{\text{CMB}} = 2.72548 \pm 0.00057\text{ K}$, $\dot{T}_{\text{CMB}} = 0$). Building upon four continuum differential-equation invariants---stiffened excluded-volume enthalpy regularity ($\rho < \rho_{\max}, \Gamma = 1$), toroidal Beltrami kinetic-energy equipartition ($\beta_{\text{eff}} = \pi/4$), icosahedral Laplace--Beltrami horizon tessellation ($|I_h| = 120$), and variable-density compressible Prandtl Asymptotic Suction Boundary Layer (ASBL) invariance ($\delta^* = \nu_{A\infty}/v_{s\infty}$)---we formulate constitutive topological closures for the inter-shell transitions of quark harmonics confined inside the $\Gamma = 1$ spherical horizon ($\delta^*_{\text{total}}/r = \frac{7}{3}\delta^*/r$, dual exclusion width $\Delta_{\text{excl}} = \frac{14}{3}\delta^*/r \approx 0.01607$). Projecting the net Spindle Torus winding ($W_{\text{net}} = [2\phi]^{-1}$) across the $\frac{3}{4}$ spherical energy-to-enthalpy ratio and $p = 2$ exterior poloidal exclusion sheaths ($\sin\theta_{12,\text{wind}}^{\text{CKM}} = 3/[8\phi(1 + 2\Delta_{\text{excl}})] = 0.22455$), while evaluating internal cavity mass-eigenstate diagonalization via the $n = 0 \leftrightarrow 1$ trefoil lobe inertia ratio ($\sin\theta_{12,\text{inertia}}^{\text{CKM}} = \sqrt{m_d/m_s}[1 + \frac{3}{2}\delta^*/r] = 0.22500$), derives the Cabibbo angle within $0.01\sigma$--$0.31\sigma$ of observation and mechanically resolves the experimental Cabibbo Angle Anomaly between open semileptonic kaon decay ($|V_{us}|_{K_{\ell 3}}$) and unitarity-constrained global fits ($\lambda$). Coupling the central spindle overlap ($W_\phi^2 = \phi^{-4}$) across the spherical-to-exclusion boundary ratio ($\delta^*_{\text{sph}}/\Delta_{\text{excl}} = 2/7$) yields $\sin\theta_{23}^{\text{CKM}} = |V_{cb}| = \frac{2}{7}\phi^{-4}(1 + \delta^*/r) = 0.041829$ ($+0.01\sigma$), while evanescent radial boundary-layer transmission dressed by the $\beta_{\text{eff}} = \pi/4$ equipartitioned $1 \leftrightarrow 3$ spindle overlap ($\frac{1}{2}\phi^{-4}$) yields $\sin\theta_{13}^{\text{CKM}} = |V_{ub}| = (\delta^*/r)(1 + \frac{1}{2}\phi^{-4}) = 0.003691\text{--}0.003694$ ($+0.01\sigma$ to $+0.03\sigma$). Finally, partitioning the $2\pi$ poloidal circulation across the $p = 2$ trefoil strands ($\pi W_\phi$) compressed by the per-axis meridian spindle overlap ($1 + \frac{1}{3}\phi^{-4}$) derives $\delta_{\text{CP}}^{\text{CKM}} = \pi\phi^{-2}/(1 + \frac{1}{3}\phi^{-4}) = 1.14433\text{ rad}$ ($65.565^\circ$, $-0.01\sigma$ to $-0.10\sigma$ from PDG 2024; $+0.01\sigma$ from PDG 2022) and $J_{\text{CKM}} = 3.08 \times 10^{-5}$ ($-0.23\sigma$ from PDG 2024; $0.00\sigma$ from PDG 2022).
title: Derivation of the CKM Quark Mixing Matrix and CP-Violating Phase via $(2,3)$ Trefoil Vortex Topology in a Compressible Superfluid

summary: This record contains model-ready data supporting the manuscript "Reference-Aware Evaluation of Neural Surrogates for Shallow-Water Flows: A Controlled Multi-Reference Computational-Fluid Benchmark". The manuscript is currently in submission. The main dataset covers 13,500 shared synthetic scenarios: 10,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,500 for testing. The common-time outputs use the same 50 requested evaluation times for all three references, from 8.4 to 420 benchmark-time units. Each solver keeps its own natural time steps; interpolation is used only to form outputs at the requested times. The references are the Hydrostatic and MUSCL-HR shallow-water solvers and a study-defined elevation-only, linear, weakly dispersive Boussinesq-type reference. The record includes the main processed datasets for each reference; additional processed data on 32×32, 64×64, and 128×128 grids; pooled-reference data for models trained without solver identity and models given the requested reference as an input; and an auxiliary archive of evaluation settings and preprocessing configurations for the train, validation, and test splits. The release manifest lists the archive contents. Each large archive is split into numbered, byte-exact parts of up to 1.8 GB. Download every part for an archive, concatenate the parts in numeric order, and use the supplied SHA-256 files to verify both the parts and the reconstructed archive. See README.md for commands. These data are synthetic and cover a finite benchmark horizon. They do not establish performance for real events, site-specific hazard forecasting, or operational tsunami warning. Spatial coordinates and time values use the benchmark's own scales; they are not calibrated to real locations or physical time. Source code and experiment documentation are available in the project repository . The raw numerical-reference data are described in the companion raw-data record.
title: Tsunami-Surrogate Common-Time Benchmark: Model-Ready Multi-Reference Data

title: Tsunami-Surrogate Common-Time Benchmark: Raw Outputs from Hydrostatic, MUSCL-HR, and Boussinesq-Type References

summary: Version 1.1.0 of the reproducible research repository accompanying the manuscript: "Operative treatment of pyogenic spondylodiscitis in German hospitals: patient selection, hospital size, and in-hospital mortality" This release adds a cell-level reconstruction of the hospital tables (bed-size class × ownership). The InEK DatenBrowser combines some cells of these tables into a residual row, differently in each query and not only for small counts, so the displayed cells give numerators and denominators that do not match. The reconstruction (analysis/05b_hospital_reconstruction.py) resolves the hidden cells under the containment constraints between the four queries of each year; reported values are medians over 2000 feasible reconstructions, with ranges over these and 2000 extreme reconstructions (fixed seed). With the reconstruction, the operative share is 28.2% in hospitals with fewer than 300 beds and 63.7% in hospitals with 1000 beds or more (version 1.0.0: 27.9% and 65.2%). The risk ratio stratified by data year and hospital bed-size category is 1.02 (95% CI 0.96–1.08), and by data year and ownership 1.08 (1.01–1.14). Also added: hospital-stratified risk ratios, article tables, figure data and key numbers (analysis/06_reported_quantities.py) and the article figures (analysis/07_article_figures.py). All other results are unchanged. Intraspinal abscess (G06.1) is now labelled intraspinal empyema. The underlying hospital data are publicly accessible through the InEK DatenBrowser. Original query outputs are not redistributed; they can be regenerated from the documented query specification.
title: Operative treatment and in-hospital mortality in pyogenic spondylodiscitis: query protocol, analysis code and derived results

summary: Markov chains for a Bayesian inverse problem with a 100-parameter Karhunen-Loeve log permeability field and an elliptic PDE, following P. G. Constantine, C. Kent and T. Bui-Thanh, "Accelerating Markov chain Monte Carlo with active subspaces", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 38(5):A2779-A2805, 2016, doi:10.1137/15M1042127. pde_mcmc_chains.npz (load with numpy.load, no pickle) holds the synthetic data, the misfit gradients at 1000 prior samples and their active subspace, 20 random-walk Metropolis chains and 4 + 4 active-variable chains (reductions), and a grid of the misfit on the active variables. kl-short.npz is the Karhunen-Loeve basis the model uses. generate_data.py in the repository regenerates the chains from saved seeds. These files are deposited as the full-size archive of the data set uq_benchmarks/PDE_Inverse_Problem_MCMC in the as-data-sets repository ( https://github.com/paulcon/as-data-sets/tree/main/uq_benchmarks/PDE_Inverse_Problem_MCMC ), a collection of Jupyter notebooks that apply active subspaces (parameter-space dimension reduction) to science and engineering models. The notebook there analyzes these data; its DATA.md documents every file, column, unit and unknown. The repository keeps each file under 10 MB, so it ships the same arrays split into files under 10 MB. License: CC BY 4.0. Cite Constantine, Kent and Bui-Thanh (2016).
title: Markov chain Monte Carlo on the active variables of a PDE inverse problem: chains, subspace and grid

summary: BOTANICAL SHEET-MASK SCIENCE: FROM SERUM CHEMISTRY TO VERIFIED WET CONTACT F121-F125 | Family 25 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch | 33 x STARLI | Edition v1.0 / November 2026 Five integrated nonclinical research themes: storage marker integrity, lyocell sorption, three-dimensional wet contact, mass-based evaporation and qualified reconstructed-epidermis evidence. Scope and scientific authority This long-form technical notebook is a proposed investigation, not a laboratory or cosmetic product performance report. The primary source is the 817-page STARLI Botanical Master Blueprint v1.0, Family25 F121-F125; older Mothers F12 and F28 provide method and evidence constraints. The numerical charts are synthetic hypotheses. Chinese materia medica inspires provenance, processing and compound questions, not a biological proof. Claims about a commercial sheet mask, sensitive-skin suitability and humans would need independent ethically and legally appropriate evidence. Five different objects, five different vetoes F121 - Botanical Sheet-Mask Serum Active Stability at the Limit. Native measurement: stored mask-serum marker retention (%). Fair reference: equal-formula serum stored in an inert vessel, blank lyocell, matched nonwoven mask and light/dark paired packaging. Disqualifying rival: adsorption onto cellulose, packaging migration, altered extract recovery, optical co-elution or oxygen-driven degradation. F122 - Lyocell–Botanical Serum Adsorption at the Limit. Native measurement: identified botanical marker adsorbed on lyocell (mg/g). Fair reference: matched nonwoven material, no-sheet serum reservoir, same-area inert substrate and prewetted lyocell control. Disqualifying rival: surface liquid mistaken for bonded sorbate, unequal sheet density, incomplete desorption or retained marker counted as delivered. F123 - Botanical Mask Conformability and Liquid Distribution at the Limit. Native measurement: verified face-surface wet-contact area (cm2). Fair reference: shape-matched nonwoven mask, same-serum container exposure, equal-load flat phantom and reversed sheet orientation. Disqualifying rival: pressure shadows mistaken for contact, pixel threshold bias, droplet pooling in folds or high contact area with low local transfer. F124 - Botanical Mask Wear Time and Evaporation at the Limit. Native measurement: evaporation mass flux (g/m2/h). Fair reference: no-sheet serum film, humidity-matched nonwoven, impermeable occlusive reference and evaporation-free gravimetric blank. Disqualifying rival: short-term occlusion masquerades as barrier repair, variable wet area, edge leakage or ambient humidity drift. F125 - Botanical Nano-Sheet-Mask Sensitive-Skin Tolerability at the Limit. Native measurement: qualified reconstructed epidermis viability (%) and marker exposure (microg/cm2). Fair reference: same-contact-time matched serum alone, blank lyocell, nonwoven sheet with matched vehicle and qualified positive-irritant reference. Disqualifying rival: pigmented botanicals distort viability reagent, local occlusion hides evaporation, tissue necrosis mimics reduced flux or uncontrolled dose. Methodological sources and foundations Five independent scientific identities under one mask F121 tests marker retention through storage without confusing cellulose sorption with degradation. F122 resolves lyocell-bound and freely available serum markers. F123 measures the genuine 3D wet-contact area and spatial transfer rather than a photographic silhouette. F124 reconstructs evaporation by mass, time, true area and environmental gradients. F125 tests qualified RhE viability only with chemically verified exposure, matched vehicle and cell-free interference controls. None of the five outputs substitutes for another. F121: chemical stability versus package partition A marker lost from the liquid phase may reside inside lyocell, on packaging film, in a precipitate or as a true degradation product. The difference is decisive. I

summary: BOTANICAL PLANT PEPTIDE BLENDS AT THE LIMIT F111-F115 | Family 23 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: authenticated peptide HPLC retention, reversible polyphenol binding, carrier protease protection, degradation half-life and qualified reconstructed-tissue evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F111-F115; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of source-resolved peptide, carrier and nonclinical evidence F111 - Plant Peptide Extraction Stability at the Limit: primary endpoint sequence-resolved HPLC peptide retention (%). Fair comparator: authenticated free peptide, dark isothermal batch, deoxygenated vehicle and equal-solvent extraction control. Disqualifying counterexample: chromatographic coelution, peptide sequence substitution, oxygen/photo stress confounding and extraction-matrix suppression. F112 - Plant Peptide-Botanical Polyphenol Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint chemically verified peptide-polyphenol bound fraction (%). Fair comparator: free peptide, polyphenol alone, no-polyphenol equal-carrier control and fixed total-solute mixed vehicle. Disqualifying counterexample: irreversible aggregate precipitation, filtration surface loss, fluorescence self-quenching or polymer viscosity artifacts. F113 - Botanical Peptide Nanocarrier Protection at the Limit: primary endpoint parent peptide survival after external protease challenge (%). Fair comparator: free peptide, surface-spiked empty carrier, blank carrier with enzyme, and matched no-enzyme reference. Disqualifying counterexample: inhibited protease masquerading as protection, peptide surface adsorption, incomplete fractionation or analytical recovery loss. F114 - Plant Peptide Enzymatic Degradation Control at the Limit: primary endpoint peptide degradation half-life (h) under a qualified protease assay. Fair comparator: matched protease without carrier, heat-inactivated protease, intact free peptide and equal-matrix blank. Disqualifying counterexample: enzyme inactivation, substrate depletion, product detector saturation, adsorption loss or photochemical decay mistaken for proteolysis. F115 - Skin Compatibility Evidence for Botanical Peptide Blends at the Limit: primary endpoint qualified RhE tissue viability (%) and separately specified irritation surrogate. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched blank, peptide-free carrier, free peptide, polyphenol-free equal carrier and validated irritant reference. Disqualifying counterexample: colored peptide assay interference, tissue nonviability, contact occlusion, vehicle osmolality or cytokine nonspecificity. Methodological introduction F111: sequence-resolved chromatographic stability A single HPLC retention value can hide amino-acid sequence substitution, peak coelution or instrument suppression. The candidate experiment begins with parent-specific peptide LC-MS/MS fragments, assigned oxidation products, matched dark and isothermal comparisons, oxygen monitoring and complete extraction recovery. The critical falsifying world contains a stable-looking HPLC signal while the true peptide has already fragmented. Source and analytical identities must be separable before a stability claim is meaningful. F113: nanocarrier protection demands an active enzyme A peptide retained after protease exposure can appear protected because a shell excludes protease or because the carrier poisons the enzyme. The difference is decisive. External pr
