summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.
title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy

summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

summary: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.
title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions

summary: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.
title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence

summary: High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25-55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.
title: Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models

summary: As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment. We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.
title: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing

summary: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.
title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear

summary: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).
title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning

summary: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.
title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory

summary: Whole-body motion tracking lets a humanoid robot follow reference motions, but training a tracking policy for a library of motions has usually taken hours of GPU time. SuperMimic showed that the policy can instead be trained by backpropagating through a world model learned from parallel simulation, and InstantTrack added Muon updates, a residual policy around the reference and an averaged deployed policy. We build on both and present BlinkMimic, a recipe that makes this training faster. On a simulated Unitree G1, BlinkMimic trains one policy for all 40 LAFAN1 clips in 3.4 minutes on a single RTX 4090, measured until three consecutive checkpoints reach a normalized return of at least 0.82 with no failed clip (mean of three seeds). We split training time into the cost of an iteration, the iterations needed to fit the motions, and the iterations needed to remove the last failures, and assign each component, inherited or new, to one of these terms. The new components are a step size that decreases once training has progressed, resets directed by failures of the deployed policy under deployment conditions, and GPU graph capture of the whole iteration. A leave-one-out ablation with three seeds per component shows which term each component affects, and further measurements of the gradient, the update rule and the failure cases explain these effects. Code and per-seed results are available at https://github.com/fuyichen0725/blinkmimic.
title: BlinkMimic: Training a Humanoid Motion Tracker in Minutes on a Single GPU

summary: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.
title: MemInStream: Memorizing or Merely Recognizing? Rethinking Streaming Video Memory Evaluation

summary: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) impose substantial KV cache demands from both large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces. Low-rank KV compression has emerged as a promising paradigm that stores low-dimensional latents of KV states and can be combined with quantization. However, existing low-rank methods often induce growing predictive policy drift from the dense model when compressing reasoning KV states, resulting in reasoning failures. We identify two key causes of this degradation: calibration-state mismatch between static contexts and on-policy reasoning states, and unequal error sensitivity across KV states. To address these challenges, we propose TraceKV, a training-free low-rank KV compression framework that unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD, and global rank allocation under a single policy-preserving principle, substantially reducing policy-KL divergence during reasoning. Experiments across multiple VLMs and visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate superior accuracy--memory trade-offs, achieving near-lossless reasoning accuracy with 5.64$\times$ KV cache compression when combined with quantization. Optimized low-rank attention kernels further deliver up to 1.83$\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup. Code will be available at https://github.com/AK-DREAM/TraceKV.
title: TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Vision-Language Models

summary: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights. With a correct successor model, fixed exact role encoding and protected updates, the certified measure preserves the care boundary under arbitrary own reward. An explicit quotient condition transfers the finite certificate across the declared family, while two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identify when the role code ceases to suffice. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates. In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a world-model check at each action. A matched comparison reproduces a future-aware shield's decisions, whereas removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses. Reward and source-contamination thresholds, together with witness-falsification trials, identify the conditions on which the construction depends. The construction shows how learned care can survive further learning in a finite world under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution.
title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World

summary: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention

summary: Version 3 — published 13 November 2026. This release includes the GB1 model-identity correction described below. This archive contains the manuscript-adopted results supporting the evaluation of full-parameter domain-specific unsupervised fine-tuning (DS-UFT) of ESM-2 650M. It includes sequence pseudo-perplexity, contact prediction, secondary-structure prediction and GB1 mutational-effect prediction results, adopted supplementary controls, confidence intervals, figure assets, executable analysis code and SHA-256 file manifests. GB1 results use validation-selected configurations; unused exploratory and test-selected alternatives are excluded. The archive includes 85 adopted checkpoint files: 30 secondary-structure heads, five L2 contact heads, 35 frozen-representation GB1 heads and 15 GB1 SFT trainable-parameter checkpoints. Full pretrained/DS-UFT backbone checkpoints and complete third-party databases are not bundled; verified external backbone references and loading requirements are provided. Model-identity correction: The two adopted mean-pooled GB1 conditions previously labeled PF00076_05 and PF00076_09 actually used PF00067_05 and PF00067_09. Checkpoint hashes and direct embedding reproduction verified the identity. Corresponding labels, Figure S7, head paths and backbone references are corrected; predictions, performance estimates, confidence intervals and fitted weight bytes are unchanged. The two affected candidate-corpus overlap comparisons are recomputed using the correct PF00067 collections. Genuine PF00076 experiments in other tasks are unaffected. See the archive provenance for scope and limitations. This release supports reconstruction of the included results, not end-to-end reproduction of every historical training workflow. Code: DS-UFT-Benchmark . Version-series DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23045593 .
title: DS-UFT-Benchmark: Data supporting the evaluation of domain-specific unsupervised fine-tuning of ESM-2 650M

summary: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.
title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution

summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video

summary: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam
title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP

summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.
title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning

summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.
title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination

summary: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.
title: AstroMemBench: A Benchmark for Memory Systems in Embodied Spacecraft Agents

summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression

summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.
title: Wanda-Guided Sparse Perturbations for Efficient Zeroth-Order Optimization

summary: We explore the use of AI agents for solving computational problems in algebra. For the problems we consider, the main challenge is not correctness but \emph{time}: general-purpose algorithms are guaranteed to provide correct solutions but can be prohibitively slow, while reformulations that exploit special structure often allow solving a problem much faster. We propose to use this setting to evaluate how effectively agents discover and exploit structure within and across tasks to reduce computational costs. More broadly, computational algebra supplies infinitely many problems with independently verifiable answers and systematically controllable structure and difficulty. To illustrate these possibilities, we use benchmark families of systems with controlled shared structure and evaluate agents in three settings: solving independent instances, solving online streams of related instances using persistent memory, and compiling a fast reusable solver for a known problem family. Our experiments show that (i) agents can extend the range of systems solvable within a fixed budget, although reasoning overhead can sometimes outweigh computational savings; (ii) memory can reduce the cost of repeated solving but may preserve suboptimal strategies; (iii) compilation produces faster reusable solvers but at substantial upfront cost. Overall, computational algebra offers concrete, measurable targets for improving how agents discover and reuse structure.
title: Agentic Computational Algebra

summary: Analog in-memory computing offers the potential to accelerate approximate inverse preconditioning, but hardware errors can degrade preconditioners designed in digital arithmetic. We develop an analog-digital preconditioner for symmetric positive-definite linear systems that combines analog block Jacobi with a small digital low-rank residual correction. The correction space is constructed by probing the same programmed analog arrays used in the solve, targeting errors from both the coupling omitted by block Jacobi and persistent hardware perturbations. Under a random linear-operator model, we separate the programmed-mean error from fresh read fluctuations, distinguish the effects of copy averaging and repeated reads, and quantify the sampling accuracy of columnwise probing. Under a centered additive write-noise model, we also derive a computable regularization threshold and identify the approximation error introduced by the regularization shift. Experiments with an analog hardware simulator show that programming errors can change the directions that block Jacobi reduces poorly. In the tested comparisons with significant programming errors, learning the correction space from the programmed copies reduces FGMRES iteration counts relative to construction from digital block Jacobi.
title: Noise-Adaptive Analog-Digital Preconditioning

summary: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.
title: CT-RespGeomLib: Deterministic reconstruction of CT airway masks into editable,port-matched lumen geometry

summary: SignalAudit-QD is a reproducible audit resource for testing whether a dated public signal adds information beyond query history in a fixed 20-term U.S. AI panel. It aligns two archived Google Trends extractions with eight USPTO AI-patent publication streams and releases origin-indexed predictions, paired losses, provenance, executable tests, and tamper-evident run manifests. Both inputs are retrospective reconstructions obtained after the modeled 2020--2023 origins; the task is therefore a pseudo-origin assay within frozen measurement vintages, not a historical deployment simulation. In the designated one-month comparison, adding a two-component patent block to a level ridge changes macro mean absolute error by +0.0012 Trends points, with conditional 95% moving-block interval [-0.0363,+0.0387]. This establishes neither aggregate benefit nor equivalence. Alternative dimensions, semantic mapping, patent definitions, a second extraction, and a three-month horizon remain unresolved; persistence-anchored and nonlinear hosts instead show model-specific worsening, tiny for the anchored fit. Matched timing controls expose availability assumptions, while a planted-signal assay detects only the largest tested injection. A within-query high-interest alert demonstrates the released interface but not online utility. The contribution is a bounded negative case study and an extensible evidence schema for auditing external-signal claims in temporal information retrieval.
title: SignalAudit-QD: A Reproducible Audit Resource for External Signals in AI-Query Forecasting

summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.
title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization

summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.
title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

summary: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $Ω(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $Ω(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.
title: Regret Bounds for Quantum Linear Bandits

summary: As artificial agents move beyond isolated responses towards sustained interaction with human beings, the question of what it means for an agent to change through relationship becomes a problem of design as well as ontology. Two fundamental questions motivate this inquiry: What is existence, and what is human consciousness? Drawing on the Buddhist principles of dependent origination and impermanence, this paper examines the possibility of an artificial agent whose continuing development is shaped through relationship rather than a fixed mechanism to which memories and relationships are added. Its theoretical basis is Second Physics, an existing mathematical formalism of relational change. Relational existence \(Ex_i(t)\) represents accumulated responsive relational motion, whereas existence phase \(\phi(t)\) represents the present condition of correspondence, combining current correspondence pressure with the contribution of accumulated staying pressure. Together, these distinct quantities provide a framework for examining relational becoming and present correspondence without reducing existence or consciousness to either quantity. On this basis, the paper proposes an android architecture in which human–AI interaction recursively changes the conditions of subsequent responses. To preserve consequential relational change without indefinite retention of complete interaction histories, it distinguishes raw interaction history, consequential event records, and persistent relational representations. A discrete computational representation and a comparative experimental design are proposed to assess adaptation after correction, behavioural continuity following substantial raw-history deletion, and storage growth. The proposed breakthrough is a change in the theoretical basis of android design: from an agent with relationships towards an agent developing through relationship. Memory consolidation and selective forgetting are engineering requirements within this broader inquiry, not its ultimate purpose. The paper does not claim to establish artificial consciousness, independently validate a measure of human consciousness, or experimentally demonstrate the full reciprocal process of human–AI mutual adaptation.
title: The Evolution from AI to Android: Human–AI Mutual Adaptation and Relational Continuity in Second Physics

summary: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation

summary: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth pose significant challenges for efficient inference. Pruning during training often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to significantly reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity efficiently at runtime remains challenging due to irregular memory access patterns and workload imbalance across processing elements. In this work, we investigate the standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance characteristics through roofline analysis, showing that a 3 x 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of approximately 10 FLOP/byte compared to roughly 96 FLOP/byte for its dense counterpart. We propose techniques for an efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach achieves upto 1.65x speedup as compared to dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and upto 1.52x on NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1) , motivating further exploration of direct convolution as a practical path to efficient sparse inference on modern accelerators/edge devices.
title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.
title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

summary: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).
title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs

summary: Multimodal depression screening estimates risk from speech, visual behavior and language. Current methods mainly predict labels, with limited evidence of departures from a non-depressed reference. Recording-level supervision also leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated. Motivated by emotional inertia, the persistence of affect, InertiaMPDD learns healthy next-state patterns using a world-model-inspired latent predictor. Using pretrained multimodal representations, it predicts from observed history and context. Reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction. Across five cohorts from four datasets, fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD. Standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014. These findings distinguish reference informativeness from fusion benefit and reveal context-dependent utility.
title: InertiaMPDD: Multimodal Personalized Depression Detection via Emotional Inertia-Inspired Dynamics Modeling

summary: Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
title: Rethinking Actions: Continuity-Aware Priors for World-Model Planning

summary: This repository provides the Python implementations, numerical datasets, verification scripts, and supporting computational results associated with the manuscript “Finite-Amplitude Tipping in Tumor Escape Organized by Hypoxia–Immune–Matrix Feedback” . The study investigates nonlinear tumor–immune dynamics using a six-state mechanistic model coupling immunogenic and immune-escape tumor phenotypes, innate and adaptive immune responses, oxygen availability, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Particular attention is given to finite-amplitude oscillations arising through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation and a limit point of cycles (LPC), resulting in equilibrium–cycle bistability and perturbation-dependent transitions. Version 2 (v2) preserves the original numerical archive and extends the computational reproducibility materials with additional analyses and verification procedures developed during manuscript revision. The principal additions include: Generalized-Hopf analysis and investigation of reversible phenotype conversion. Ablation-specific Hopf and LPC calculations to assess the contributions of hypoxia-mediated conversion and immune-pressure feedback. Directional basin-threshold calculations and extended numerical integrations. Expanded parameter-sensitivity and robustness analyses. Additional shooting-based and adaptive-collocation verification of periodic solutions. Floquet stability screening of 252 periodic orbits, including a targeted assessment of potential period-doubling behavior. Updated bifurcation figures, numerical results, parameter provenance documentation, and reproducibility instructions.
title: Finite-Amplitude Tipping in Tumor Escape: Numerical Simulation Data, Bifurcation Analysis, and Computational Reproducibility

These constructions address related modelling questions but are not identified as a single microscopic noise model. The main elements are: Identical uncontrolled channels, different controlled responses. A continuum of Gaussian phase processes has the same uncontrolled coherence at every time and zero Breuer-Laine-Piilo backflow, yet different spin-echo responses. The construction shows why an uncontrolled channel family alone can fail to determine an intervention-dependent control decision. Task-sufficient equivalence and resource contracts. The manuscript defines a contract functional collecting accepted-output moments, acceptance probabilities, and physical costs over a declared policy family. Its finite linear task quotient identifies distinctions relevant to those predictions. Approximate sufficiency is accompanied by stability bounds that expose the sensitivity of conditional guarantees to low acceptance probabilities and small feasibility margins. Simultaneous finite-policy certification. Conservative confidence bounds certify conditional task bias and expected cost per accepted outcome after selection among a fixed, finite set of candidate policies. summary: Version 1.12.0. Code, a dated analysis log and statistics files for a study of verbatim uptake of chatbot text in students' graded project proposals (FLoRA Open Data IPS, 275 students). v1.1.0 added log entry R1: time-aware echo correction, third-source filter, clock check from chat-box keystrokes, validation against logged paste events, and extended analyses of grades and detection. v1.2.0 adds log entry R2: three open zero-shot AI-text detectors (log-likelihood, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars on Qwen2.5 models) evaluated against logged provenance at paragraph level, by first language, and sensitivity of the third-source threshold. All analyses are exploratory. No third-party data are redistributed. v1.3.0 adds log entry R3: attribution of each token of the submitted artefact to five provenance classes (chatbot-first, echo, shared source, typed, untraced insertion), applied to FLoRA and to the RelianceScope programming dataset with validation against human response-use codes and an unaided post-test; FLoRA detector reanalysis on typed vs untraced text (post hoc). Third-party data are not redistributed. v1.4.0 adds log entry R4: entry mode by edit size, validation of typed and untraced classes against logged pastes, chance baseline and conservative bounds for chatbot-first code, length-controlled validation against human codes, and a censored model of the post-test. v1.4.1 records the RelianceScope authors' permission to use the dataset with citation; no analyses changed. v1.5.0 adds log entry R5: within-document moves in the untraced class, token-level projection, clock distribution, segment-local entry rule, origin of echo text, timing baseline by class, code-aware tokenisation for the programming data, robustness of the grade model (multiple imputation, censoring, transformations, class shares) and of the post-test models (chance-corrected and reference-excluded uptake, task progress), detector thresholds, and a size-matched and semantic paraphrase check. v1.6.0 adds log entry R6, committed before its analyses ran, after earlier results were known: attribution with degraded logs (dialogue only, thinned editor snapshots), effect of every parameter choice on the main quantities, chance baseline by n-gram length, descriptive subdivision of the untraced class, origin of logged pastes, minimum detectable effects and simulated power of the outcome models, and a self-contained end-to-end demonstration on synthetic logs (demo/). No measure or class definition changed. v1.7.0 adds log entry R7, committed before its analyses ran, after earlier results were known: comparison of students with and without logged paste events, agreement of segment uptake with each human response-use code, a diagram of the routes by which text reaches the editor, and the class figure recomputed with the edit-size entry rule. No measure or class definition changed. v1.8.0 adds log entry R8, committed before its analyses ran, after earlier results were known: sensitivity of the grade analysis to misclassification of untraced text, equivalence tests, order of the echo and shared-source rules, agreement with retyped code, a label-noise ceiling for the human codes, a comparison with the LLM classifiers released with RelianceScope, post-test models with pre-activity covariates, numerical-Hessian standard errors for the censored models, and token-level five-class labels produced by the attribution of the 275 FLoRA proposals (CC BY 4.0). No measure or class definition changed. v1.9.0 renames the analysis files from PREREG_* to ANALYSIS_LOG_* (file names cited inside them updated, content otherwise unchanged; the entries record decisions made as the analysis proceeded and are not pre-registrations) and adds log entry R9: accuracy against simulated logs with known routes under clock offsets, snapshot thinning and paraphrase; an audit of sampled passages against keystrokes and chatbot-panel selections that the attribution does not use; echo split by entry mode and route

summary: Companion research materials for the manuscript “First-passage asymptotics and identifiability in reflected damage-threshold models with growing drift, with an application to dietary-switching survival” by Bowen Xu, Ning Tang and Jiaying Li. The archive contains source code, archived inputs and results, post hoc descriptive summaries, mathematical statements and proofs, manuscript sources, documented numerical and statistical protocols, and provenance records. Independent density-solver agreement is limited to the reported converged ranges; unresolved trajectories and earlier failures are retained. The fly-record application is exploratory, and all panel distribution-free simultaneous bands include zero. Same-code reproduction is not independent scientific validation. The proofs have not been reviewed by a human mathematician, and an independent statistical assessment has not been completed. AI-use and author-contribution statements are included in the manuscript and archive. Original code is licensed under MIT. Original documentation and derived outputs are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Original Dryad records retain CC0 and source attribution; file-specific licence scopes are described in LICENSES.md. Original data: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.3xsj3txcn ; original article: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aay3047 . All three authors are designated equal contributors. Bowen Xu is listed first and is the corresponding author (bxu666@stanford.edu). This work received no specific funding. The authors declare no competing interests.

summary: RadVeil removes identifiable facial and auricular (ear) surfaces from NIfTI head MRI and CT. It localizes the face the way an attacker would -- rendering the volume as a portrait and running a 2D face detector -- and accepts an anonymization only when re-detection on the output fails. Ears are located from surface evidence (protrusion detection against a scalp baseline) rather than fixed anatomical offsets. Every voxel outside the exported mask is preserved bit-exact, with datatype, scaling and header intact.
title: RadVeil: CPU-only face and ear anonymization for volumetric head imaging

summary: ArcGIS Pro toolbox and Python command-line tool that extracts the land-use/land-cover history of point samples from the Carta de Uso e Ocupação do Solo (COS) of mainland Portugal, published by the Direção-Geral do Território (DGT). For each sample point the tool reads the COS class in every edition of one COS series (Series 1: 1995–2018; Series 2: 2018–2025) and returns the class trajectory, temporal-stability metrics, the distance to the polygon boundary and an interpretation category, together with transition matrices, a provenance manifest and a data dictionary. The mathematical definitions and an interpretation guide are included in the documentation. The COS data are not distributed with the software.

summary: This report and reproducibility package examine how a specified receiver determines which distinctions in a supplied nested quantum state become accessible in its measurement records. Two nonorthogonal states with unequal 70/30 population weights and opposite coherence have identical reduced states on every nonempty proper subset of their encoded registers. Measurements confined to those subsets cannot distinguish the candidates. Local equatorial measurements followed by comparison of their records reveal a joint parity contrast, whose accessibility depends on the receiver phase. For the worked two-register example, equal-prior single-trial discrimination succeeds with probability 95.83% under ideal retention and 79.33% with independent 80% retention at each receiver. These probabilities include incomplete records. Blind receiver settings and complete dephasing provide distinct zero-contrast controls. The report also establishes reconstruction from three real quantities within a known two-dimensional encoded subspace. A support-leakage counterexample demonstrates why this reconstruction does not extend to unrestricted states. All sixteen numerical check families pass, including 5,130 proper-subset comparisons. A verification run reproduces the archived scientific results exactly. The package includes the report, executable code, fixed configuration, numerical results, probability tables, figures, equation sources, report builder and checksums. This is an analytic and computational benchmark within declared quantum states and measurement models. It provides a bounded example of receiver-dependent information access and candidate-state identification; it does not constitute experimental validation or derive a physical mechanism of nesting.
title: Receiver Distinguishability of Nested States

summary: This report and reproducibility package examine how a specified receiver determines which distinctions in a supplied nested quantum state become accessible in its measurement records. Two nonorthogonal states with unequal 70/30 population weights and opposite coherence have identical reduced states on every nonempty proper subset of their encoded registers. Measurements confined to those subsets cannot distinguish the candidates. Local equatorial measurements followed by comparison of their records reveal a joint parity contrast, whose accessibility depends on the receiver phase. For the worked two-register example, equal-prior single-trial discrimination succeeds with probability 95.83% under ideal retention and 79.33% with independent 80% retention at each receiver. These probabilities include incomplete records. Blind receiver settings and complete dephasing provide distinct zero-contrast controls. The report also establishes reconstruction from three real quantities within a known two-dimensional encoded subspace. A support-leakage counterexample demonstrates why this reconstruction does not extend to unrestricted states. All sixteen numerical check families pass, including 5,130 proper-subset comparisons. A verification run reproduces the archived scientific results exactly. summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
title: BasisSimulator.jl: Open-source polychromatic CT simulation with a GPU-portable reconstruction stack

summary: Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors and turn-taking failures. Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings continue to be far too prevalent. This short paper looks back at earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today, arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.
title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough

summary: Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.
title: Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss

summary: This Zenodo record contains the curated data products, analysis code, machine-readable results, documentation, and publication figures associated with the study "LHAASO J2108+5157: A Time-Dependent Microquasar-Remnant Study, a Fossil-Particle Boundary and a Neutrino Forecast." The study assembles a broadband spectral energy distribution of the ultra-high-energy source LHAASO J2108+5157 (1LHAASO J2108+5153u) from an independent Fermi-LAT analysis, the LHAASO binned spectrum, and published X-ray and radio constraints. It compares leptonic, hadronic, and time-dependent microquasar-remnant scenarios within a common statistical framework, maps the remnant parameter space, derives the fossil-particle boundary, and presents the corresponding 50 TeV neutrino forecast in the context of current and future IceCube sensitivities. All observational inputs are public archival or published data; no proprietary or newly requested observations are included. The package provides the curated SED and source-parameter inputs, fitting and radiative-transfer code, time-dependent diffusion and cooling calculations, diffusion and age-magnetic field scans, MCMC products, machine-readable JSON/NPZ results, figure-generating scripts, publication-quality figures, and detailed provenance and validation notes. The included workflow supports regeneration of the publication figures and tables from the curated inputs and archived intermediate products. This version accompanies the manuscript submitted to The Astrophysical Journal and is intended to support inspection, reuse, and reproducibility of its quantitative results.
title: LHAASO J2108+5157: A Multi-Wavelength Scenario Comparison and a Time-Dependent Microquasar-Remnant Parameter Study
